Little bitch.

situation: While on the rest time of the Army, I almost died from a heart attack during a 22-kilometer run with friends.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But I wasn't gonna stop. It was tough. We were out of water-- We're on fumes. At 22 miles, I had a heart attack and died. A textbook case... Straight outta med school... Enlargement of the left ventricle. In accordance with the family history on both sides, fatal. According to the EKG and according to statistics, I had a 97.3% chance of dying, or 2.7% chance of living. Anyway, dead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You actually died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: In the clinical sense. No pulse, no brain activity. Total clinical death. But here I am. And now i'm gonna disappoint you, doctor. Don't you wanna know why i'm gonna disappoint you? Let me help you out. The light, the tunnel, the whole life-flashing-before-my-eyes, That's what you're interested in, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I wasn't actually thinking of that at all. But I am interested. Please, tell me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I couldn't give a shit about it either. But that's all everyone wanted to know about. My father, my wife... Everyone. They just wanted to hear about the goddamn tunnel. Just-- Such bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel that maybe you... disappointed people by not having that experience? That maybe... in some way, you failed to deliver the goods?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody really knows

situation: In the haze of a coma caused by a heart attack from excessive running, I pondered my situation and thoughts.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody really knows what was going through my mind during those last few moments. Soon as there was no more tunnel, no one was interested.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what was going through your mind?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, I knew what was happening. You can tell. And you're afraid it's the end. In all that time until I lost consciousness... All that time... I don't know how long it was, Maybe seconds, maybe half a minute. All that time, I kept trying to figure out if I had a hard-on.

situation: I recalled the moment my grandmother described my grandfather's passing and his physical condition at that time, which filled me with fear that I might be in a similar state.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: See, I don't know how I remember this Something my grandmother told me when I was in high school. And she said, when grandpa died, she found him lying naked in the bathtub with a huge erection. Now he was 92 years old. She hadn't seen an erection like that in 20 years. She liked it. She said that was god's final gift to a man... A dead man's boner. They call it angel lust. Anyway, so i'm lying there and i'm thinking about that story. I know what's happening to me and I said to myself, God almighty, just... don't let me have an erection right now, not a hard-O.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because if you had an erection, it would mean that...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That would mean that I was dead.

dialogue.text: And your friend daniel was with you throughout this?

dialogue.text: Okay, with all due respect, I think we've come to this way too early. All this stuff about the father son relationship, I don't think it should come up so soon.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Toxic fumes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Toxic fumes, yes. His loneliness, his fears, his dependency on you. You said that he'd call you up in California and say how unhappy he was and how much he missed your mother, begging you to cut your vacation short and come back home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's this got to do with anything?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You took a liking to these people who were athletic, healthy, the exact opposite of your parents in every way. And you described David very vividly. And you said he was very kind to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, you know, he used to take me camping. We'd go surfing, used to just... talk about stuff, you know? Teenage bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were very attracted to him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was a hunk, yeah.

situation: As a child, I yearned to be taken in by David, developing a dependency on him. My therapist  observed that my current feelings echo that childhood dependency, reflecting a similar emotional attachment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He looked like Nick Nolte. They smoked a lot of grass. A lot of grass. I smoked with them. It was my first time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And... When that summer was over, they said it was a shame they couldn't adopt you. They said, We want a daughter just like you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I actually asked them to see if it was possible. If there was some legal way to... Aanyway, they just laughed at me. They didn't take me seriously. They said I was so cute. Actually, I wanted him to adopt me. She was great... Celia. But, you know, I was 15. I wanted him all to myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Makes a lot of sense when you think about it. You were 15 years old, your father was... grieving, completely dependent on you. David must have seemed like a life raft. just perhaps I am now... from Andrew. Perhaps I'm an alternative to everything that Andrew represents... Dependency, anxiety. But I am not a realistic option for you. This is a safe place where you can come, like David at the beach.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, but with one big difference.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want you to adopt me, I want you to fuck me.

situation: The therapist expressed pleasure that I was back from Baghdad, a trip he had previously been concerned about.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Come on in. Would you like some coffee? I've just made a pot.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, coffee's good.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you like it? I got... Skim, whole milk. Got some soy here...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Black. I like to taste the beans. I bet you need a lot of coffee to listen to the fuck-ups in here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't drink coffee. Just tea... I keep it... I keep it for my patients.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Blood plessure. Irregular heartbeat.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I've just... I've just never really liked the taste.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Ah, a subconscious irregular heartbeat. What, do you get checkups? EKG?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yep! Every year.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And? How's your heart?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's perfect. Look, Alex, I'm... I'm really glad that you came back. To tell you the truth, I was... I was a little worried after you left last week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 'Cause I wanted to go back to Baghdad? Well, I went.

situation: The therapist gave me a coffee that was hard to drink.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Man, Paul! Sorry, but the one thing I don't compromise on is coffee.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that your reaction whenever the coffee isn't perfect?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Isn't perfect? Paul, this is like attempted murder, your coffee. But let me hear your interpretation. It's obvious you have one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not really, I... I remember I used to have this patient, once, and... He would come here and before each session he would say, Stop. And then he would pop a pill. And... it was just... a ritual...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you trying to say?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I think in his particular case, what he wanted to show me was his distress and his... His pain. I don't know, maybe with the coffee, it's... Maybe you're just telling me that you're only gonna come to therapy under... your conditions, and anything that you don't like, you're gonna... spit out right away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't you think you're being a little dramatic? Come on, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe.

situation: I visited a post-war site and saw the impact of the war on the area, but I felt no emotional turmoil inside.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, Alex. Why did you come back?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I want your advice on another little matter. Besides, you deserve to know how my trip went. Being that you helped me decide to go. For all the wrong reasons, by the way, because my visit didn't do what it was supposed to...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what was it supposed to do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let's just cut to the chase, okay? Saturday morning, I'm standing near the bomb site. It's like London after the Blitz. Just rubble, you know? This area had been hit again and again by us, by them, by suicide bombers. We hooked up with a Red Cross unit. They take us to this makeshift hospital. This triage unit. There weren't enough doctors to treat everybody. It was chaos.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was just watching. You gotta understand, in my line of work, I'm 10, 15,000 feet up in the air. Missile locks in on a target, by radar on a screen. I don't see people. I just press a button. Just it was kind of crazy to be down there all of a sudden.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did that make you feel? Coming face to face with the victims?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How would it make you feel?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Scared? Guilty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: See that would be the normal reaction. I knew this should have been the trauma of my life, but I felt... nothing!

situation: I don't feel guilty about the deaths caused by the bombing; at that time, I just wanted to know if I had completed the task assigned by the army.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And then I realized... the system did a great job on me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, the system?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Listen, there's people down there. Arms and legs missing, faces blown off... It's carnage. And the parents are walking around, they're waiting to see if their children are gonna live or die all because of what I did. But what can I tell you? To me they look like... 200 people standing in line at a pharmacy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you feel any connection with them? Did you feel in any way... responsible for what they'd suffered?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: no, no, In that moment, all I cared about was whether they cheated me or not. I mean, the system. The people in the madrasa... it wasn't any different to seeing it on TV. The only thing on my mind in that moment was whether the system knew that the buildings near the target's bunker, the one that was supposed to get my one ton bomb... If they knew these buildings were full of children... Or not, as they claim. Nothing else mattered.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it was really important for you to know that you had done the right thing. Like you said last week, if you hit the target, you sleep well. And all those people whose... suffering you were responsible for... Could you not see them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I saw them. I felt nothing for them. And then I realized how ingenious that my body has a built-in separation mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What does that mean separation?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Compartmentalization. I'm standing there and all I cared about was whether I made a precise hit.

situation: I had no sense of the damage caused by the war, and the therapist's self-disclosure of his emotions when his friend died suggested that I was actually sad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The enemy is a formula... Size of building, amount of people, multiplied by the amount of explosive divided by 100 equals a number of estimated casualties. You understand? I'm standing there and I don't feel anything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I had this friend who died. Four months ago. Anyway, I... I went to the funeral, and... All throughout the service I kept saying to myself, Why don't I feel sad? I though to myself: Maybe I didn't love him, Maybe I didn't care. I tormented myself for about a week. Anyway, finally... I realized that actually I felt a great deal. Even the fact that I was so busy with my guilty feelings... Even that attests to how much I felt about him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but what are you saying? That I was feeling... But I didn't feel what I was felling?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think... that you have very, very... deep feeling about these people. But something strong inside you prevents you from acknowledging those feelings. Not just to me or to anybody else. But to yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't understand what you're saying. I don't get what you're telling me. Feelings are not a philosophy. You either feel or you don't. You can't bullshit about it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think I'm bullshitting?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Listen, I'm paying you 150 bucks for less than an hour and I don't see you making an effort.

situation: The therapist, analyzing his own emotions when a friend died, indicated that I care about the harm I caused.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 150 bucks for less than an hour and I don't see you making an effort. You're supposed to be smarter than me and I'm not feeling that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So we're competing? To see who's is the... Who's the smartest. You know, Alex, I think that here like everywhere else, like with the coffee for instance, you're concerned with what's the best. It must be... It must be difficult.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, give me a break.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It must be kind of frightening for you to feel... empathy with these people. So you create this kind of ultimate reality for yourself with those people where, Oh no, they were just waiting in line at the pharmacy. I'm just the accidental tourist. Not the pilot who bombed them. Who killed their family.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wish you were right. But it's much more fundamental.

situation: I think the army's system has eradicated my sense of guilt, but the therapist does not agree with my feelings upon returning to the post-war site.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you hold on to this organ... called guilt feelings... And I believe that's what it is. It's an organ. Like the spleen or liver. The system will cut it out of you completely. Understand? I have no way of feelling guilt anymore. I don't have the organ.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you really believe it's possible to... amputate such an organ? You went back to Iraq. Why was it so important for you to go back? To risk your life just to... Just to be there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you I wanted to check if anything was left. And... And I wanted to see what happens when I come down from that top view.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But nothing happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's right, nothing.

situation: I encountered an injured old man in the post-war area who kept staring at me, not letting me leave.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can we... Can we go back for a moment to the site of the bombing? Can you describe one moment when you said to yourself, I should be feeling something now, right now. And I don't.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There was a moment. I don't know if it's what you're looking for. But there was a moment when this old man came over to me... He had been burned. His arm was bandaged. He kept looking at me with a strange little smile. Which means I know you. I know you. I ignored him at first, but a few minutes later he was back. I know you, I know you, he kept saying. For a second I thought he recognized me, but I didn't really believe that. I doubt he'd ever seen the internet but... In some deep intuitive way... He knew. He knew I was the man who dropped the bomb that destroyed the whole street we were standing on.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: um...ha You could be... You could be describing a mystical experience, like a dream.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, it was like a dream, like a totally bizarre dream. He started looking like some old warlock out of a fairy tale or something. He wouldn't leave me alone. He kept pointing at me. I know you. And I looked in his eyes. And he was sort of amused, kind of friendly. Like my father looks at me when he thinks I've done something wrong. Like he knows my secrets. Like no matter what I do, I can't hide from it. And I was frozen there. And by that time people had gathered and they were watching us. Finally someone from the church group came and pulled me away, but that old man, he never took his eyes off me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You still think it's too early to talk about your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why, because he popped into my head for a second?

situation: I told that among the people around me, my father was the one who couldn’t feel guilt. He killed his own father when I was a child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You people. What is it with you people? I give you a little crumb and you lunge at it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just asking myself, alex, what was it about that old man that makes you think about your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let me tell you something: If there's someone who does not know the meaning of guilt, it's my father. You know why? Because if he could feel, he wouldn't have survived. You know, my father killed his father with his bare hands. Yeah. And that's a fact. Man, i'd love to see him on this couch. Man, doc, you'd have a field day with him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You want to talk about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, now I got your attention.

situation: When I was a child, my father killed my grandfather with his own hands.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think I can tell it as well as he does. But i'll try. Mid-'50s, right? Jim Crow Oklahoma. My old man had pissed off the local good ol'boys by trying to organize some black labor at this factory. They tried to threaten him but my dad didn't back down. He's a tough son of a bitch, i'll give him that. Anyway, the whole thing, it just escalated. And... this mob with hoods attacked his house. My uncle Ronnie was on the front porch with a rifle. They shot him down. Shot my aunt Jeannie too. And then they came inside. My father takes the rest of the family, they run downstairs to the boiler room, to the basement. Right near the boiler, they all crammed into this area, this hidden room. My grandfather, his father, was very sick. Dying of lung cancer. And he had this... Apparently he had this... This wheezing and this hacking cough. So my father puts his hand over his father's mouth and nose and he kept it there while they searched the basement, kept it clamped tight. Then when they finally cleared out, my grandfather was dead. He'd suffocated. There it is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's... That's a horrific story.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Tells it every year on my grandfather's birthday. It's a tradition.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you really believe he doesn't feel guilty about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm telling you, he always used to say, leave the guilt for the white man. We can't afford it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's possible that he's saying that... it's dangerous to feel guilty, that it's a kind of weakness. Maybe that's a message that... you've grown up with.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What can I say? That's just my father's way.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But is it your way?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Hey, it works for him.

situation: Seeing my wife sleeping, I feel that I don't understand her at all.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Doesn't necessarily make him an asshole. People love my father. My wife is crazy about him. You should see him at... At family dinners. He's got her off in a corner and... telling jokes and... I don't know. She appreciates him. Maybe that's why we lasted as long as we did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You say lasted as if it was past tense.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, actually, that's why I came to see you today. There's this issue with my wife. What happened was, when I came home from my trip, it was late, and the kids were already asleep. And I saw my wife.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, you saw your wife?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I looked at her. I really looked at her. She was sleeping in front of the television. For an hour, an hour and a half nonstop I sat there without taking my eyes off her. When was the last time you watched your wife sleep for an hour straight?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I usually fall asleep before she does.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, try it once, you'll be surprised.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What'll surprise me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What you'll discover... About her, about yourself.

situation: My wife grinds her teeth while asleep, which is also strange to me; she is a repressed person.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was looking at her, looking at every inch of her body. And I said to myself... Who the hell is this woman, sleeping on the sofa in front of the tv? What the hell does she know about me? What does she think she knows about me? And what the hell am I doing, living with her in the same living room, in the same house with the same kids for the past 15 years? Understand? And i'm sitting there opposite her, right? She doesn't imagine what's going through my head. And you know what happened? She starts grinding her teeth. Now it's the first time i ever saw her grind her teeth in her sleep. And I'm talking something sick, frightening. The sound that came out of her mouth... How do you... You could cut diamonds between her teeth, okay? It really fucked me up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sounds pretty upsetting.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shocking, I tell you. And suddenly I understood. For the past 15 years this woman's been so busy pretending that everything's okay flowing. She's a model mother, a model wife, an outstanding lecturer at a communications college. Very impressive in front of my fellow pilots. And it turns out she takes it all out on her teeth at night.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, that's pretty common, actually. They don't think it has anything to do with stress. It has to do with flaws in the structure of the jaw.

situation: My wife is a repressed person who does everything by the book.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You really believe that? No, it's connected to her stress.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In what way?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: In what... She is a totally repressed person. And all her repressions come out at night, in her sleep. So she grinds her teeth.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: em, You think Michaela may have trouble with her feelings too?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I don't feel? Wait till you meet her. Everything is just like clockwork. Clockwork, that's what... It's clockwork. The kids have been going to bed at the same hour since they were two days old. They got sick on a fixed date. We'd have sex on a fixed date In a fixed position. And Michaela even farts once a year on a fixed date. Once a year on the night after Easter Sunday she farts. She lets herself fart once, maybe twice, a little one, not that much. Then it's over. No farting for the rest of the year. Man, she's a programmed person. Every emotion is under control.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sounds like you're a little angry with her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, What... Why...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just the way you talk about her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. Takes a lot more than michaela's schedule to make me angry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I got the impression before when you were speaking that... Maybe you're a little angry with yourself, Alex. I mean, you went all the way to Iraq and you couldn't feel anything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe. Have you spoken to Michaela about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course. Over our morning coffee.

situation: My wife wants me to return to the army soon, but I am not in a hurry to go back.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She says, Yes, honey. I grind my teeth. You only noticed it now? You are such a sweetheart. That's what I call love. Then she said, Baby, please cut down on your coffee. Remember what the doctor said? Since my heart attack she lets me have one cup of coffee a day. And that battery acid you gave me, that's not coffee. That doesn't count.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. So you don't like Michaela worrying about you, treating you like you're sick?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's just... It's like she's on a mission. To get me back up in the air asap. She says i'm fit as a fiddle and I need to be knocking on the navy's door to get back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How long has it been since you've flown?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Two months since my heart attack.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It must be hard to be away from that world, Not to be part of what used to be the... The center of your life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: First of all, i'm still one of them. So you can relax on that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But meanwhile, sitting at home thinking about the possibility that you... That you might never fly again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course i'll fly again. People with worse injuries have bounced back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to go back, Alex?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When the time is right. But Michaela's dying for me to go back. And at night she grinds her teeth like some kind of...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Alex, it's not like she changed overnight.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think there are things about michael that really bother you. Because they reflect something inside you that you can't live with.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like her passion for you to fly again. I'm not 100% convinced that you actually want to go back. Maybe because... you're having trouble forgiving yourself.

situation: I no longer love my wife and have decided to leave home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, all of this just reinforces my decision to leave home.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I don't think... It's pointless to drag this out for years. When a person decides he's not in love with his spouse he shouldn't have to put off leaving home. Isn't that so? It's over. it's dead. I've had friends who've reached this conclusion. They go to 3 years of couples therapy and they end up separating. So what's the use? I say cut that shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Don't you think that's a little extreme? I mean, it is possible to overcome a crisis.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you know what I realized? That I was never in love with her. With Michaela. Do you know what that means? What a terrible realization that is? What do you expect me to do? Find a lover like my dad? Start coming home late at night? I don't even have a good excuse anymore. I won't do anything but sit on my ass and watch tv. So what? You look upset.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, i'm just... I'm just a little concerned.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, don't be. I feel a great relief.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, i'm sure. There must be tremendous relief in just... walking away. I'm not convinced it's the solution.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I suppose because i ask myself: Who are you really leaving? Maybe you're leaving her because she's such a frightening reflection of you. Maybe you're leaving yourself, not your wife.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's irrelevant. I have no reason to go back. We're finished. We're done.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you said anything to her about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not yet.

situation: I decided to leave my wife, which is related to the therapist's treatment of me, but the therapist thinks it's not like that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought i'd consult with you first.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is this really a consultation? Because you know something? Again, I feel like I'm a rubber stamp for decision that you've already made.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: On the contrary, this meeting clinched the matter, not before. You can take credit for it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why are you always giving me credit? You know, it's not that you give me credit. What you're really doing is you're asking me to accept responsibility for your big decisions. And you know what? It's not me making these decisions, it's you. You knew before you walked through that door that you were gonna go back to iraq. You knew before you ever brought up the subject of Michaela's teeth grinding that your marriage was deeply in trouble. These aren't conclusions that you've come to here on this couch in the last week with my permission. Aren't these things that have been boiling over inside you for a very very long time, alex?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got to go. Like you say, my time is up. Hey, don't worry. I'll keep you posted.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I didn't write the evaluation report because my father was too busy and I didn't want my mother to write it for me directly.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you write my evaluation? No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What the fuck?! Why didn't you? That's why i'm here. That's all i need from you, That stupid evaluation.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, i don't think i know you quite well enough Yet, Sophie. So why didn't you write yours?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, i tried With my dad, but, But he's too busy with his exhibition.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He's an artist?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A photographer. He hates the word artist. He always has his exhibitions at home Because he's against galleries. Anyway, he said it was totally unprofessional For me to write my own evaluation And that you sound like a quack. Are you a quack?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, i am not a quack. I promise.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And then i tried to write it with my mom. That didn't work-- Obviously.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you say obviously?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because she's a total tool and a retard.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A tool and a retard?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. We got in a fight. And i was like, i so do not need this right now. So i left.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I argued with my mother and ran away from home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I went to this apartment near the gym Where the foreign girls stay. I told them my parents were going out of town, so, they let me crash there. And then i tried to get Cy to help me write it, But he's too busy getting everyone ready to leave for training camp, so, So i didn't do it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So why did you and your mom get into a fight Trying to write the evaluation together?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She actually wanted to write it for me. And i was like, no, mom, i can do it myself. And she was like, we'll be here until the next olympics. And i was like, bite me. So i left.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you didn't want her to write it. You just wanted her to help you, What, phrase it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It doesn't matter. We got in a fight, for a change.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But this time, Sophie, You left home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you done that before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So something was different about this particular fight. What do you think it was that was different? Did you-- Did you come from home Or did you come from the gym today?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The gym.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Gym-- Is that far away?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's why i was late.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I was late because of a fight with my mother, and I was angry that the therapist accidentally overheard my phone call.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sophie, Before you arrived, i, uh-- I got a phone call, and, um, i heard you asking somebody To let you out of the car.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: well, i-- I tried to call you to tell you i was on my way, But, um, then i figured That we were like five minutes away, so... i thought i hung up before the call went through.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was that your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You could've hung up, you know? Or do you always eavesdrop on other people's conversations?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sophie, if you were my patient, i'd ask if you thought It was a coincidence that i overheard that conversation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But i'm not your patient. I wouldn't see a therapist Who i thought was an eavesdropper. I'd be out of here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So did your dad bring you in?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you, i had a fight with him!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought you said the fight was with your mom.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's really none of your business who i came here with.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I was late because of a fight with my mother, and I was angry that the therapist accidentally overheard my phone call.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Earlier on you said that you'd like Kate to go to the gym with you. What would you like Kate to, to tell the girls at the gym?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Your daughter's clothes are gross. Why is that funny?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, why are they gross?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're hideous.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm really not getting my evaluation today, am i? This is stupid. I should go. Are my clothes dry yet?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wouldn't think so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, can you check? And call Kate, because i need her to help me put them back on. You people are such tools. I can't believe you get paid for this. Why didn't you tell me before that you heard my conversation?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I was waiting for you to tell me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So now i'm a liar too?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I did't say you were a liar, Sophie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's what you're thinking.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you need Kate to go to the gym with you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need her to.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The girls in my gymnastics team diet because being overweight means they can't compete.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can i ask you something? How do you get along with the girls at the at the gym?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're assholes, okay? All of them. The whole place, it reeks of hypocrisy. Did you know, like, every girl there is a Mia or an Anna except me? They know it. They just don't do anything about it. They encourage it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These girls, Anna and Mia, Are they friends of yours?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't know these girls? They're fun girls, especially Anna. Rexic?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anorexic. Okay. And Mia, bulimia?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're sharp as a tack.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you. So the girls at the gym Are anorexic or bulimic except for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't keep your weight down otherwise.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The girls in my gymnastics team diet because being overweight means they can't compete.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't keep your weight down otherwise. And if you're not skinny you can't compete, so, So you have no choice, you have to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But who says you can't compete?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cy and Regina. Regina is our physical trainer. All the girls follow Cy around like little groupie sluts. Cy, was that okay? Cy, can you show me how to do that move? Cy, i'm about to fall. Quick, put your hands between my legs. But not Regina 'Cause she's russian. So her bullshit detector is like nuclear. And at the end of the day Cy and Regina decide everhing-- Who competes, who's gained weight and can't compete.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: After my car accident, the girls in my gymnastics team either didn’t visit me or just offered insincere greetings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After my accident, Karen Scott and Audrey England came to visit me. They had these pathetic looks on their faces, like, Like they felt my pain. But i knew they were happy. I would have been happy if something had happened to one of them Right before the olympic tryouts. Honestly, If it was me, I would have done what Shirley did. She didn't even come. Me and her, we're like the best ones there by far. It was like she was saying, drop dead for all i care. Just get out of my face. At least that's honest.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: em...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I wanted to return to the training camp, but was rejected by the gymnastics coach.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So they're leaving tomorrow For training camp in California And i have nowhere to go. They won't let me stay at the apartment by myself. They promised Cy i could go, Even though i can't train. And now he says they've changed their minds.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who's they?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The sponsors-- The money people. Anyway, I picked a fight with him. That's what you heard on the phone. It wasn't his fault.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why is it so important for you to go with them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To the camp? Everyone will be there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean, Karen, Audrey and Shirley? But-- But you said you can't stand them. You said you don't even like them. And you can't train anyway, so, i don't understand why it's so important to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not important. But i was looking forward to it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sounds like, um... you and Cy are, uh-- You're very close.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I have a good relationship with my gymnastics coach's family and have even taken care of their child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why? Can you tell that over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said he wanted to take you to camp Despite the fact that you had an injury, and, didn't he-- Didn't he drive you here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was on his way. He wants me to come to the camp to at least watch the training So i don't lose focus. But no. He couldn't make them pay for Darlene either.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Darlene?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cy's wife. She has to pay her own way and Dana's too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Dana is the little girl you used to babysit? Why did you stop?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Who told you i stopped? Did i tell you that last week? You have good memory for an old fart.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you. So why did you stop?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They didn't need me anymore.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I took care of the coach's kids for a long time, but now they don't need me to take care of the child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Dana used to have all these breathing problems, but, then she had this surgery and they got better, and, And darlene came back from Wisconsin Where she was like learning to process her own cheese or something, so, So they didn't need me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you work there for a long time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. Sort of.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And Dana must have become very fond of you. Did she become attached to you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. She's the cutest. She hasn't stopped talking about me since i left. She said she doesn't want to go to California If i'm not going to be there.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I had a good relationship with Coach cy's child, but stopped caring for her after her mother returned.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They told her that i wouldn't be able to babysit her anymore Cause i'd had this accident. But see, i'd already told her before That i couldn't keep living with them once her mom came home. I waed to prepare her, you know? But they didn't tell me what they were telling her, so, the whole lie became mixed up in her head. What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You look scared all of a sudden.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I look scared?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like you're looking at a psycho or something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I was just remembering that the last time you were here you put your-- Your casts together. Do you you remember? And you said, this is Cy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, the mermaid that he drew.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that when Darlene came home You knew you couldn't keep on living there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I never said i lived there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you told dana you wouldn't be able to go on living there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, because she's a child But, so it felt to her like i lived there. It was just, Cause she'd go to school and, come back and i'd be there, and, you know, she got used to me being around. So even when he was home she'd nt me to stay-- Cook them dinner, do her homework with her. Sometimes she'd wake up screaming Because she stopped breathing in her sleep. Cy told me that.

situation: I was classmates with the therapist’s daughter, who was considered odd at school. The therapist thinks my topic change indicates I'm hiding something.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What the hell is going on here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, what the hell is going on here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad was right. I'll go to therapy And i'll end up a psycho Just like your daughter. Everyone thinks she's a freak.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you trying to hurt me, Sophie?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. But you should know what people say about her. She had this thing with this guy And afterwards everyone says she'd turned out psycho Cause her dad is a shrink. Shrinks' kids are psycho. Everyone knows that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, maybe that's because-- Because some people are afraid of therapy. They're afraid of what they might find out. They're afraid that it might touch those wounds That are deep inside them. I think there are things that... perhaps... you feel deep inside, Sophie, that you'd like to talk about.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm fine. You wanna worry about a little girl? Worry about your own kid.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does it bother you that people talk about my daughter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why would it bother me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because maybe you know what it feels like.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe I don't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We were talking about your coach And then suddenly you brought up the story of my daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, because i thought you should know.

situation: The therapist thinks I'm afraid of being talked about behind my back, a question I prefer not to answer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are there people who say things about you, Sophie? At the gym maybe? You know, Sophie, sometimes when people are jealous They say things to hurt us Because they envy us. Do you think that some of the girls at the gym might be jealous of you, and, how close your relationship is with Cy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't talk to me like i'm a child, please.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Sophie, i get the feeling that you're afraid To tell me something that other people say about you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are my clothes dry yet? Can you go check? If i won't be getting an evaluation today I'd at least like dry clothes.

situation: I wanted to know the results of my psychological evaluation, and the therapist read them to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. Well, i have started to write it.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can i see what you've got?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm, uh-- I'm not quite finished yet.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll bet you haven't written a word.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sophie's evaluation: 16 years old, a gymnast. She is an olympic hopeful. She came in for evaluation After a near-fatal accident. During first session appears to be Very impressive, sensitive, Mature for her age, Very intelligent And a highly-Independent personality.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I tried to write it... with my mom but-- We didn't fight. I just said never mind. Do you really think those things you wrote?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Absolutely. They're just generalities at the moment. It's not enough for a real evaluation. You know, This morning i tried to brush my teeth like you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Em-huh, Like--

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How'd it go?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I couldn't do it.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I spoke again about being angry that my father doesn't support me attending the training camp.The therapist believes my lack of security stems from people around me crossing personal boundaries.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just stick it in there. Why do you try that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: 'Cause i wanted to know how it feels.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How did it feel?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I felt useless, Like demeaned or something.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm homeless. I have nowhere to go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What about your dad?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you, i had a fight with him. Not a real fight, but he pissed me off. He knows how much i wanted to go to that training camp with them And he didn't even offer to pay. I wouldn't have taken his money anyway. Obviously, the exhibitions are expensive, but--

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why is it so important for you to go to this camp, Sophie?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not important... anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you get along with Cy's wife?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine. I don't wanna talk about them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. When you're ready, we will. You know, when you walked in here I thought to myself Somebody in your life has broken the rules. And i felt that, That if i had helped you change your clothes, That i would have been doing the same thing. I felt like you were testing me. I felt like you wanted to make sure That this was a safe place, That the same things that happen out there Don't happen in here.

situation: I shared my feelings about being hit by a car and the reactions of the medical staff and people around me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right when the accident happened... i don't remember anything, but, But right afterwards I remember the whole world was silent. Not just silent, soundless. You know, like there had never been any noise ever, Not even that hum that you hear when you're in an empty room. Nothing. Even inside the ambulance, People were talking and it was like-- It was like i'd gone deaf. I felt relieved. I thought that i would never have to listen To anybody ever again. Sound came back though, At first from far away. The E.M.T., she kept saying, I have to hear your voice. I have to hear your voice, sweetheart. She wanted my parents' phone numbers. She wanted them to come meet me when i got to the hospital. There was no way. They can't even sit in the same section at my meets. I have to wave to two different spots after my routine. I look schizo. I tried to sit up. I told the emt that i wanted to see the outside.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, when you see an ambulance Tearing down the street, you turn and look.

situation: I recounted how I felt in the ambulance and how stupid I was to have both hands broken.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, i wanted to see what it was like Being on the inside looking out. You know, seeing people's faces on the sidewalk Wondering, who's in there? Is she going to be okay? I couldn't sit up. The E.M.T., She had this mirror that she tried to angle So that i could see out, But all i could see was myself. And i remember thinking, both arms, Sophie? Did it have to be both arms, you idiot? Our time is up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. We'll, um-- We'll take it up there When you come back next week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're not going to training camp with everyone else in the universe?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'll go get your clothes And call Kate.

situation: I talked about my wife's affair and recent issues about patients simultaneously, which were many and complicated, leaving the therapist confused.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's... It's true. Kate's been... She's been seeing... this guy. Supermarket manager, employment agency guy... I forget what he does, but anyway, he's divorced, got a kid. She made sure to tell me all the details.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did she say how long?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Everything's gone to hell... Patients, family. If I was... If I was into astrology, I'd say there was something cosmic going on, planets colliding somewhere. First, one of my patients... The pilot I was telling you about... He's leaving his wife. Just like that. She grinds her teeth in her sleep, so marriage over. And the 16-year-old, the gymnast? She's having an affair with this guy in his mid-40s, married guy... Her coach. At least I think that's what she's hinting at. And she also goes to the same school as my daughter so I had the pleasure of finding out that... Rosie was having a... A thing... with this boy at school. I don't even know what a thing is. I don't even know if it's true. I asked her. I got nowhere. She wouldn't tell me anything. And then finally...Kate... Is it me? Kate says it is. She says it's my fault. I don't see her, that's she's invisible. She says I don't see the kids either, they're invisible too. As far as I know, Rosie could be having sex with a drug addict. Everybody talks about her at school... at least that's what she said.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who said? Kate said that? I'm lost, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The girl, Sophie... the gymnast.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You talk about 10 things at once.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, she's in the same grade as Rosie.

situation: I found out about my wife's affair and don't know what to do. I despise this behavior of hers.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let's focus on Kate.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What am I supposed to do, Gina? I mean, what... what am I supposed to do... now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did she say what she thinks will happen now between the two of you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. She said it's... She said it's up to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you think that means?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You tell me. She's banging some insurance salesman and it's up to me? She gave me all the details. She blows him, she screws him... It's like a porno film.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She told you that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Absolutely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, my conception... maybe I should say my misconception of Kate is that everything... Everything about sex was always connected to intimacy for her. There was never anything weird or dirty about sex. It was always about intimacy. Now I feel if someone throws the word intimacy at me, I want to punch her in the mouth.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Punch her in the mouth?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said punch her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, all that bullshit that I thought meant intimacy to her... The candles, the backrubs, feeling safe. Meanwhile she's in her own porno film, fucking this... This guy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm trying to figure out why she would tell you graphic details.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because she wanted to hurt me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you ask for details?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just wanted to... I wanted to get a grasp of the situation, you know?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She made sure you wouldn't ignore what she was saying. I think you knew what was going on. Last week when we spoke, I think you knew. I'm sure Kate sensed that as well... your suspicion. Maybe I'm wrong.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew. I did know.

situation: I caught a cold and needed medication, so the therapist poured me some water.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You'd think that would make it easier, you know? Almost threw her out of the house. It was like, You hurt me, Okay, I'm gonna hurt you. Now just get the fuck out of here. I mean, there are a thousand ways that people can deal with these things. We could have gone to therapy, for example. I mean, not everybody has to fuck around.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Coldex Night. They're supposed to be stronger than Coldex Day. I've had two of them already. They kind of make you a bit stoned.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want some tea, Paul?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Water would be good, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

situation: While I was providing counseling to a patient, she suddenly had a miscarriage. The couple was supposed to reconcile.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had a session yesterday with that... Thanks. With that couple who called me a... Who called me a murderer. In the middle of the session, she runs to the bathroom and she starts to bleed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Miscarriage.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My God.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was pretty scary.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is she allright?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think she's fine. I just spoke to her at the hospital. They're running some tests, but she seems to be okay. At least I'm not a murderer. Though I wouldn't be surprised if the husband blamed me for everything. You know, stress as a result of therapy. It's possible.

situation: During a counseling with a patient, she suddenly had a miscarriage, and my wife also caused trouble, making it a very eventful week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Ironically, they'd both just kind of worked out their problem. They weren't arguing, which for them, is a major accomplishment. And he said to me: This is our last session. And then... Then it happened. Anyway, I was trying to get the blood out of the couch, 'cause when she got up, she left a stain, and Kate walks into the room. And she looks around and she says... What goes on in this office?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: haha

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Quite a week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Quite a week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Ultimatums from two women. Kate and Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Laura?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She tells you she's in love with you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's... What are we going back to that for? I was talking about something completely different.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't think it's relevant? You describe two women attacking you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Two women? What about three women?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does it feel like I'm attacking? Maybe that's why you're taking pills to protect yourself against me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have a cold, see?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Last week you called me a sleepy spider, in wait.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Were you... Were you insulted by that? I take it back. You're not sleepy.

situation: The therapist thinks the relationship with my wife acts like a wall, hindering emotional connections with my patients, but I don't believe I've fallen in love with a patient.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you agree that your relationship with Kate has been... a wall between you and your patients so that you're safe, you're not attracted to them?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Attraction's... It's not a problem.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Freud, Messer, Davies, all the big guys, they all talk about how attraction is inevitable, it's part of therapy. But if you brush it under the rug, the message you're giving to the patient is that their feelings are perverse, are dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Their feelings? I'm talking about your feelings. I'm not worried that Laura will try and break down the wall on her own. I'm worried that you want her to.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The wall? What is this metaphor? My wife is a wall?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't agree?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not hiding from my patients. That essay that Bolas wrote about...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Forget about Bolas. Every time we go deeper, you reach for some theory... These male therapists tormented by lust for their patients. Right? I mention Laura and that's who you start quoting.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But why are we even talking about Laura?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because I want you to hear what you're saying. That you're surrounded by women who demand that you respond and love and be angry and feel, that you face your feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did I mention that Laura is... Is getting married in June? So Laura's over. That's finished.

situation: There's a conflict between my wife and me, though we used to have a good relationship and would talk about my patients.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If anyone wants to pull down a wall, it's Kate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Secrecy. She... She hates it. She hates that I can't share it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean work?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She resents my office. It's like enemy territory to her. She's always trying to make it her space... a piece of it. Like Let's get a new sofa. Or new blinds or a rug or something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you let her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I don't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I agree with her. It's not her space. There was a time when I used to talk about my patients, when Ian was a kid. I would share... share details.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: With Kate. You don't mean Ian.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Both of them at the dinner table. I see that look of horror on your face. No, I was pretty discreet actually. I never mentioned any names. If someone mentioned rats, I'd say, I had a patient with a fear of rats, dreamed about rats every night. You know, stuff like that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't do that now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. But I remember when Ian was about 10, he asked me, Dad, what's an alcoholic? And I told him about this patient of mine who needed a drink actually to get out of bed in the morning. One day this man came up to the office and he was... kind of staggering and Ian said, Dad, is that the alcoholic?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were careless. This situation now, I think... There's more at stake. Do you agree?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because we're talking about a woman?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sexual attraction.

situation: While consulting a patientt, a patient named Luara asked to use my bathroom. I was scared and refused.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can I ask you a question? You're in the middle of a session and a patient needed to use the bathroom and your bathroom is blocked up. Would you let them use the bathroom in your house?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did that happen?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Laura said that she had to pee. And I told her, Well, the toilet's blocked up. So she headed for the door of the house and... I freaked out. I jumped up and I stopped her. I'm keeping your metaphor going here. I hope you appreciate that about the...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She tried to scale the wall.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's always a patient who wants to know about you... More about your private self. Anyway...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I jumped up. I panicked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What made you panic?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was doing it on purpose, I felt.

situation: My therapist asked me if I had ever had other patients refuse to use the toilet, I told her that I lent clothes to another patient, Sophie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was doing it on purpose, I felt. I thought, Why can't she hold it for another 10 minutes? Why did I panic? I don't know really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Has that ever happened with another patient?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sophie, the gymnast... She came in last week and... it had been raining and she was completely soaked. So I let her change into my daughter's clothes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That didn't make you uncomfortable?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's a lot more intimate than using the bathroom... Rosie's clothes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: well, She had casts on both her arms from the accident. And she held up her hands like this and she said, Undress me. So, I got Kate to come in and help her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How old did you say she was?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's the girl who's sleeping with her adult coach?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She might be sleeping with her coach.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's a loaded situation, her asking you to undress her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was messing with me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You had no problem handling that? You had Kate help her, undress her, give her your daughter's clothes. But when Laura needs to use the bathroom, you freak out. Why is that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Laura is a woman. Sophie's just a... she's just a child.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Shouldn't that make it easier?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: umm

situation: I clearly rejected the advances of my patient Luara and have no intention of being with her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, there was... There was a part of me that really wanted Laura to go through the door, to see where I live. Maybe to... to see Kate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wanted that? Was that what scared you? Did you discuss what Laura told you last week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said that the reason that she was going to marry this guy, this boyfriend Andrew, was because I told her I wasn't interested. I know what you're thinking, but I made it really clear. I said nothing is going to happen between us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Good.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm... I'm just... I'm not going to play along. This is not going to happen.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In your mind, is there any possibility that the affair could become a reality? No, in your mind.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, I have to admit sometimes, it's... It's flattering. I can't help but enjoy the feeling. But I told her no. I said, This cannot happen. You cannot go through that door. There are limits.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what upset you, that she was testing you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not that abstract.

situation: I turned down Luara's overt advances, which made me anxious.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's a beautiful woman. She says she wants to have sex with me. I know what's in her head, so I don't want her going through the door and maybe bumping into Kate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you said you did want that. Some part of you wanted that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The point I'm making is that I want Laura to understand that we can survive this, that any attraction that comes up between us I can handle. I am not going to let this derail the therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Her wanting to sleep with you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did she put it exactly?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That she knows that... I want her.

situation: I was flustered when Luara expressed love to me, and I was angry that the therapist recommended referring Luara to another therapist given the current situation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That she knows that... I want her. She said that she wants to... to fuck me and that she knows that I want to fuck her too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's a lot to stave off, that kind of intensity.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She can be very direct... Laura. Maybe that's why I panicked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Here's what I think, Paul, and you can accept this or tell me I'm interfering again, but given the situation with Kate, I think we... we might explore the option of transferring Laura to another therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just hear me out on this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because Laura thinks she wants to sleep with me? Last week you thought we were already having sex.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought you had an affair and you were trying to justify it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thanks, Gina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I was wrong. I'm sorry. I jumped to conclusions. You've reassured me. But now this situation with Kate... How emotional you are and the pressure you're under. Listen to yourself. You're injured. You're vulnerable. You're angry. This isn't me being stubborn, Paul. I think we should just discuss the possibility that Laura's better off with a different therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A female therapist, you mean.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, preferably.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You, for instance?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm retired, remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is so typical of you. You always begin by saying I hate to say this, but... But... And you lay some pronouncement on me that you've already been thinking about before you've come into the session. This isn't a debate club, you know? It's not like we take a position and we hunt for ways to support it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not what I'm doing. I'm listening. You have Kate on one side and you have Laura on the other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But they're two totally different situations, Gina.

situation: I refused the therapist's advice to refer patient Luara to another therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you saying that I pushed Kate into this situation? That I created this environment at home so that Kate could go fuck an insurance agent because really I'm in love with Laura? Isn't that your theory? Your notes somewhere?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look at how you're reacting.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How am I reacting? I am not sending Laura to another therapist. End of story. I can handle whatever comes up in the sessions. That's why I'm here... Because I want you to help me to handle it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We just need to discuss this, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want to pawn her off on somebody else.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But what's best for Laura?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Honestly, if it wasn't for Kate cheating... I wouldn't be here, Gina. And we haven't talked about your comment the last time. I was pretty pissed off about that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: About what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You made a crack about my father leaving my mother for a patient. What was that supposed to mean? That I can't treat Laura because of what my father did years ago? I'm not my father, for Christ's sake.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you're not your father. I'm suggesting a pattern that might be threatening to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you or are you not, Gina, saying that because of my father, that I'm in danger of having an affair?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My gut...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't answer it, can you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I can't.

situation: I recounted how the therapist had previously faced a patient's emotional transference and the therapist had avoided the situation due to fear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If I remember correctly, you were faced with the same scenario yourself. So maybe this really isn't about my father. Maybe it's about you, Gina. Don't forget I was the one who referred Charlie to you. I remember he called me after one of your sessions. And he confessed to me that... that he was in love with you. No, actually he went further. He said that you were in love with each other. Maybe he was wrong, I don't know. Either way, you needed to face that, and you didn't. You just ran off to England. You know what? I could not believe when that happened. That was a wake-up call for me, watching you behave like that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't run away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, a sabbatical with David? At that moment? By the way, is that what your novel is about? I figured. You failed the same test yourself, Gina, but you abandoned a patient. He tried to get hold of you over the years, didn't he?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A few letters. I didn't answer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You do know that he died a few months ago? Prostate cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was right after David and I couldn't go to another funeral. I just couldn't... I couldn't face it.

situation: The therapist had also experienced emotional transference before, and we discussed whether a therapist should refer a patient in such cases.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's funny, you know? I was talking about Charlie the other day to a patient of mine. I was saying that I... I'd been to his funeral and that I was... I couldn't feel sadness. And I was, you know, beating myself up about it. The truth is, I was... I was so disillusioned with you, Gina, for keeping you on as a supervisor. After what you pulled with Charlie, I should have just walked out then. You know that he never ever got over you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Since we're digging for the truth... May I ask how you really feel about Laura? I haven't heard a clear answer. Not what you're going to do about her, but how you feel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you mean, am I attracted to her?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, Gina. If I transferred every patient I was attracted to at some point, I wouldn't have any patients left. And it's not your place to say I should transfer a patient. It's like me telling that couple they should have an abortion. It's not what therapists do. We don't tell people how to run their lives.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm suggesting that we talk about stopping Laura's therapy and look at your reaction. Paul, do you really need another pill?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know. Tomorrow's Saturday. I can sleep all day Sunday. I don't really care if they knock me out or not, really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What you're going through with Kate is so complicated.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I arrived late and shared a traumatic experience involving a dog being hit by cars.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Really sorry. You wouldn't believe what just happened to me. I... I almost didn't make it here at all. God! I've got to calm down first. Can I get some water, please?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What, were you going to punish me for being late?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sorry. Ahem. I don't know how that got there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's yours?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought someone left it here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, what happened? Why are you 25 minutes late?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right. I took a cab here. We were flying down Madison, right, and about 200 feet away from me is this dog. She... he... it tries to cross the street, and you know it's impossible to cross that stretch of Madison. And of course he gets run over. Well, not run over, hit. The car in front of us hit him so he ran into the street and another car hit him. It was awful.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
