situation: I stopped the car because I saw the hit dog on the road and asked the therapist if he would get out and check.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cars were playing Ping-Pong with him. It was like, ping... ping. He didn't stand a chance. (Sighs) The cab I was in almost hit him, the driver stopped short but then the car on the left hit him really hard. I thought he was dead but he wasn't. I saw him limping across the street so I yelled at the driver to please stop, but he couldn't because the traffic there would have caused a massive pile-up. But I couldn't not stop, you know. I mean, if the dog was alive I had to get him to a vet. I mean, didn't I? You would have pulled over. Or maybe you wouldn't have given a damn.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think everybody would pull over.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you would have pulled over, Paul. I'm sure you would have. You wouldn't have pulled over?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wouldn't have pulled over.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I would have assumed the dog was dead and there wasn't anything I could do for him. Sure, I'd be sad just like you were but I wouldn't have pulled over.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't believe you.

situation: I explained that I was late because I saw a dog hit on the road, but the therapist thought I did it on purpose because I was never late.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, anyway, I couldn't not stop, OK? So I yelled at the driver to make a U-turn so I can get to the other side of the street, but, shit, there's no U-turns. This idiot cabbie is telling me that wounded animals prefer to die alone just because he can't make a fucking U-turn. So I yelled, Please, can you stop, I need to figure out what to do, and then I looked at his dashboard and it's five to, and it's another 25 minutes to your office. It was incredibly frustrating.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sounds like it was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Imagine, stop for a dog that may die anyway, and be very late.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You would have been late anyway.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were still very far away, and it was already five to. Dog or no dog, you would have been 25 minutes late. The fact is you're never late, Laura. I would have appreciated a call.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are you like that?

situation: I thought the therapist had a bad attitude, but the therapist explained that he was trying to understand me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are you like that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, er... Anti.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anti? Anti-what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Anti-me. I come feeling like shit for what I've witnessed and you're giving me a really negative vibe.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think I'm being negative, Laura. I'm just trying to understand you, that's all. It's possible that your being late today wasn't entirely coincidental. Maybe you're trying to tell me something.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh. (Laughs) What, I paid the dog to get run over in front of my face? I planted him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you were late already, Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: (Sighs) I don't know what you want from me, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You have a very tight schedule. You're a busy woman. You always call if there is a problem, an emergency at the hospital, or whatever. You always call me. You are never late. In fact, very often you're early.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And so?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what do you think your being late is trying to say to me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing, Paul. I... Nothing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe... (Clears throat) Maybe you think that, erm... That I'm not doing my job. Cos if that's the case then we should talk about that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: About what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Laura, I know you're upset about...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look at you, Paul. Listen to you. You're scheming.

situation: The therapist asked me if I was angry about his treatment and suggested discussing the effectiveness of therapy, and I questioned being kicked out of therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know you're up to something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What am I up to? It seems to me that the last few sessions have been difficult for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The last few months, Paul. Very, very difficult. And wonderful.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you angry with me? Because if you are, then that's something we really need to talk about. Maybe we need to talk about what good this therapy is doing you, or not doing. Maybe you've had enough of it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was late and you're kicking me out of therapy? Fucking hell! Use the belt, it's a more humane punishment.

situation: I was angry and felt misunderstood by the therapist. I accuse the therapist of provoking me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, I'm not angry, I have been, I... I even thought about not coming here at all... Just as, like, a small protest. When I left here last week, I phoned for a cab and the line was busy. And I was just walking around in circles, round the block, round the garden. And then I realised I was in shock, Paul. I felt like someone had punched me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's how you felt? Like I'd punched you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do I need to remind you what you said to me right here at the door? At the end of the last session? I have a feeling that if I hadn't mentioned it, you never would have brought it up. You would have hidden behind the rule that therapists don't initiate topics of conversation. You're supposed to let the patient lead, right? You'd have taken advantage of that rule so we'd never talk about what happened again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would you like to talk about today?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You act as if you don't know me, Paul. That's what pisses me off the most. You look at me, Remind me again what your name is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: On the contrary, I think I'm coming from somewhere that I think you know very well.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's why I'm dwelling on this point... What point?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your anger.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My anger over...

situation: I was angry with the therapist, thinking he misinterpreted me, and then the therapist explained why and I forgave him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're trying to make me angry. You're provoking me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm suggesting that you already were angry before you came in. You were so angry you were considering not coming here at all. And you expressed that anger by coming late.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fuck, I can't win here. You're...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was gonna tell you the conclusions I reached but you're not interested, are you? You'd prefer to bait me, to piss me off, to... But the truth is, I'm the opposite of angry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anti-angry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fuck you, Paul! When you said you didn't want me, my first instinct was to tell you, Who cares? I don't want this. I won't come. But then I realised that it's not your fault, it's my fault. You don't owe me anything. You don't have to love me in return.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right, I realise that I may have slammed the door too loudly in your face. Maybe I was a little...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cruel?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I don't think I was cruel. I was resolved.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You demanded an unequivocal answer and I gave you one. I don't apologise for giving you that answer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: (Sighs)

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I am sorry that I hurt you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: OK. So, a) I accept your apology... and b) I think your answer last time wasn't so unequivocal, and c) I think my excuse for coming late was perfect.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The excuse may have been perfect but the timing wasn't coincidental.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: (Laughs)

situation: I was unhappy with my therapist's attitude and thought he refused to listen to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now I see why they laugh at shrinks and all their bullshit. What do you really mean? What does that mean? It's bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Annoying bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wouldn't it annoy you if your therapist forced you to accept a ridiculous interpretation, and you couldn't defend yourself because you're the patient? Everything you say will be held against you. I should've stayed with that dog. I should've taken it to the vet instead of coming here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Here, where you're not being adequately treated maybe?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you want from me, Paul? I mean, you refuse to listen to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think you're listening to yourself. Maybe you're identifying with the dog.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That dog deserves more than being co-opted as some idiotic interpretation. You wanna explore some theory, well, then at least make up something original. Jesus, make an effort!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think I don't make an effort? Do you think I don't try hard enough in therapy? Is that what you think? That I sit here like a parasite who feeds off your stories, and your reality, and your pain? Maybe I'm not helping you at all.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wow.

situation: I suddenly remembered Andrew and expressed my disillusionment with the therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All of a sudden I miss Andrew. For the first time I'm sitting here facing you, and I miss him. So strange to miss Andrew. Andrew who loves me... who admits it, who shouts it out in public.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What if I did that? Have you ever imagined that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, no, Paul. Uh-uh. I've stopped fantasising. I've kicked the habit. It's hazardous to my health.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about my dream of getting married and my fiancé informed everyone to come to our wedding, but I didn’t even tell my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm getting married in a few months. I need to conserve every last drop of energy for my wedding.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're finding it requires energy that you don't have? I thought brides were supposed to be whirling dervishes of activity.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: (Both chuckle) Oh, my God! Just the word bride creeps me out. I told Andrew to pick a caterer and location without me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, well, what difference does it make if you get married at the Hilton or the Hyatt? It's all the same. You try hard to be different, you still end up looking like everybody else. Even worse. God, I wish I could just get married in Vegas. No caterers, no guests, just an alcoholic justice of the peace and a transvestite organ player.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: (Laughs)

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what he did? Andrew? He sent an email to everyone in his address book. I mean, everyone. His insurance agent, his mechanic. We had an exterminator over a couple of months ago, even he got an email. He's told everybody. I haven't even told my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I haven't had time... I mean, you know... Been busy and... I didn't want to tell him over the phone. Andrew suggested that we both go and tell him together but... something happened, and we didn't get around to it. Besides, I don't want us to both go in there hand in hand, all lovey-dovey, like the movies, Guess what, Daddy!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it's not exactly that it didn't work out, you've just... you've avoided telling him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He hasn't been feeling well lately.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I discuss my father's health issues and her hesitation to share her engagement news with him. The therapist suggests that sharing the news might be a welcome distraction for her father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's had all these tests done. Of course I take him. He doesn't know what questions to ask, and he thinks as I am a doctor, they'll be more straight up with me. And to be honest, it'd be much nicer to be in the dark, not know the truth. It could be positive, encouraging, optimistic. He has an MRI today.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe the news of you and Andrew would come as a welcome distraction to him. Make him happy. Yeah?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes. Well, that's the problem.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What is the problem?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, it'll give him something to look forward to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean, if you tell him, it'll be real.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I guess so. Oh, I don't know, maybe...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I was hesitant about getting married. I felt that it was not a happy marriage and that it was just a show.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know Andrew's been so happy these days. I feel like I'm cheating him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just by being sad. Not sad exactly but not happy either. Neutral, indifferent. Andrew made us do the rounds last week, see all our friends, tell them the good news. And I just feel like... Did you ever see the movie King Kong?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know how they capture him from the wild and bring him back to civilisation, and put him on display for the whole world to see.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But he wasn't indifferent. He was angry if I remember.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Whatever. It's a freak show. I feel like a freak show. Everyone's looking at me with these fake smiles plastered over their face. I just... It's like they're all waiting to see what I do next.

situation: The therapist said it was time and I got angry and thought he was pushing me away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mm. Laura, we don't really have, erm, we don't have that much time left.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, I just got here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were half an hour late.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We're back to that again. That bullshit about me being late.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know you don't think it's important. I do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I give up. It's pointless. You might as well just bind and gag me because whatever I say or do doesn't make a difference.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe that's what you'd like to do, shut me up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I would. Cos you keep saying the same thing. I hear you, Paul. You want to kick me out of therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I don't want to kick you out. Absolutely not. (Clears throat) I do think that we should allow the possibility into the room. The possibility of us winding down our therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Believe me, you let it in.

situation: I thought the therapist wanted to get rid of me and end the session, and the therapist said I had crossed a transfer line and he wanted to end the session.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How long have you been thinking about this? Have you been thinking about getting rid of me for a long time? It looks to me like you've been waiting for this to happen, hoping this would happen. My being late today is the perfect excuse to get rid of me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: First of all, I'm not getting rid of you, Laura. I'm just asking you to consider whether this therapy is really helping.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, so now you're trying to soften the blow. Thank you, don't bother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Secondly, I think that you tossed me out a long time ago. You don't want me to treat you as a psychologist. You want me to treat you as somebody who's in love with you. And in my opinion, that is ruining any chance of this therapy being truly productive. Let's face it. I have not been your therapist for a very long time, Laura. I'm the one who says no to you. I'm the one who humiliates you. I've been humiliating you for the last year by not responding to you. My honest opinion is that it is really difficult to continue therapy this way, from such an emotionally charged place. Therapy should not be a source of constant humiliation for you. You really deserve more.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What, you're not a good enough therapist all of a sudden? Am I the first patient to be in love with you, Paul? You've been a therapist for 20 years. Don't you know what to do in these cases? For Christ sakes, just deal with it. Maybe you can't treat me because you're in love with me too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I... I can't treat you, Laura, because the boundaries have been breached too often. You've breached them by telling me that you no longer want to be my patient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So fucking what? What, our time is up?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I'm afraid it is.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Couldn't you give me extra time? There was this little dog, remember?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm afraid I can't, Laura. It's, erm...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I have to be somewhere else, I'm sorry. It's... Erm, it's the end of the month. I, erm... I presume you will need a... a receipt. I've done out an invoice. I've billed you for the...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: (Door opens)

situation: I presented the therapist with a coffee machine and coffee, which I bought cheaply online.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Check this out. Your coffee... was horrifying. I don't want to hurt your feelings. I won't tell you the truth about your coffee and what it says about you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What does it say about me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I may tell you later. How do you like your coffee machine?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's, uh, really nice. But I, um... I can't accept it. I'm... I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What, are you a government employee? hey, I got this for an amazing price in an auction.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In a what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: An auction. On the internet... Ebay. I pick the times when the whole country's glued to the television. Prices drop 70%, 80%. Like... eight speakers and a receiver for only $1,000. Would've cost $4,500 retail.

situation: I gifted a coffee machine and coffee to the therapist, but he didn’t seem very pleased.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway, thursday... was the American Idol finale... And I thought of you. So I went online and grabbed this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could you turn that off, please?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just switch it off, please.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you afraid of? What's the big deal? It's a coffee machine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look, I think it's a really sweet gesture, and I... I thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't you want to upgrade the standard of living around here? And I know you only drink tea, but what about your poor patients?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Um, no offense, but... don't you feel there's something aggressive in what you're doing here? I mean, you haven't even asked me if it's something that I want, if it's okay with me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, fine. It's just a stupid machine. Jeez.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just trying to understand what you wanted to say with this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing. What do you think? That by me bringing this to you that I'm, what, trying to buy you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know. Why is it important for me to have a coffee machine?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe because the coffee that it makes is top quality. I come here once a week for the time being and I need coffee here more than anywhere else to open up and all that crap. So I brought the machine with me and... Six different kinds of beans from the... totally bitter gourmet Guatemala... To the kind that postal pilots drink... Jungle java, which is sickeningly sweet. You know what? I've got an idea: deduct it from what I owe you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sorry.

situation: I bumped into Luara by chance and worried that the therapist would be angry due to consultation rules.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Could you be mad at me for something else altogether?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I met a patient of yours.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You met a patient of mine?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yesterday. I got the days wrong and I accidentally met Laura. I gather it's a delicate situation when patients meet, yeah?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean a delicate situation?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I don't know. I thought you therapists had some kind of... ethical code. Like I tell you intimate details about her... Things she may not want her therapist to know about her. I leave, she walks in and tells you the same kind of information about me. Could that be considered a breach in your ethical code?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think there's any ethical problems, no. Of course I'm not allowed to discuss other patients, but you are free to talk about what's happening in your life and... What's happening between you and Laura like... Like anything else.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, but... what's happening between me and Laura wouldn't have happened if we weren't patients of yours. I met her right out front here. That probably wouldn't have happened anywhere else on the planet.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you believe there's kind of a unique significance to... the fact that you met a patient of mine? What do you think it is?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm asking you.

situation: The therapist and I agreed to keep the coffee machine at his place for the time being.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think we've started therapy, Alex.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You brought me a coffee machine because you intend to come here more often and you want to feel at home. Through Laura, you're trying to relate that message to me. She's your patient and I am too. So we are... officially in therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: About the coffee machine, let's do this... Let's just say it's here on loan. As long as I keep coming here, it's here. When it's over, I'll take it with me. Deal?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. I guess, um... I... I would like some... Some time to think it over, though, but it's okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Think positive.

situation: I've told my wife about my decision to leave home, and she was surprisingly calm.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If I remember correctly, your wife doesn't allow you to drink coffee at home.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's correct.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel that this is a place where you can say and do things that you might not be allowed to do at home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, that issue's solved. Thanks to you. I left home. You really helped me with that in our last session, Showed me that leaving home was my own personal decision. Hey, doc, I'm serious. You really did help me. I left here much more determined than when I arrived... to carry out this disengagement. I went straight home and told Michaela I wanted to leave home. And I said it in the same way I'd tell her I was going to take the car to the garage.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And is that what you really felt, that it was so trivial?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's what I felt. Absolutely. And here's how it happened. Michaela was making salmon... It's always salmon on tuesdays... And I told her I wanted to leave home. Let me tell you, she didn't even turn her head away from the stove. She just said that... I could've guessed this would happen. And you never surprise me, Alex. Not even now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you feel about that? Were you... Were you... hurt by that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She wasn't trying to hurt me. It's just the way she is and...

situation: My wife is an intelligent woman and remained calm when I told her I decided to leave.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I may have done her wrong last week, the way I presented her. But you've gotta understand, she's a superintelligent woman. When she was 22, she was already working on her PHD at Georgetown, so if she says she was expecting it, then I've gotta believe... she saw me going through something since the bombing and the heart attack and the suspension from the force. She saw much more than I was willing to show. And realized that it could result in us separating.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know what's interesting is that you're talking today about your wife like... You know, she was some mythical superwoman that's able to anticipate everything 10 steps in advance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: As far as intelligence goes, absolutely. Really, no matter what else you say about her, she's got the brains of a rocket scientist on the Manhattan project.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Still, wasn't there something in her reaction that disappointed you? I mean, you come home, you drop this bombshell and... she's indifferent to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but that isn't the case here. We're not one of those couples that creates drama all the time. On the contrary, we could've dragged this on for years just for the sake of the kids, as they say.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you told the kids yet?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, not yet. Now Roy, my eldest, he's been locked up in his room for days doing some kind of chess championship on the internet. And Noelle, my daughter, she's on some kind of school trip.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you will have to tell them at some time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I haven't told my children about my decision to leave home yet, but I think my son will understand. My son is a unique individual who prefers solitude, which worries and saddens me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Someday they'll have to accept the fact that their father left home to look for a new life. They can't understand that at their age.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you think they'll feel about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Roy will understand me. For sure. He's a very special boy. he has... inner truth. You know... Roy's 11 years old. And he hardly ever leaves the house. He just sits at home and he sits by the computer and plays chess and... I mean, he just... No girlfriends, no buddies, no basketball. And at first it drove me crazy, 'cause he just seemed so miserable, so lonely, unpopular. I tried everything. I... I organized tours at the air force museum for all the kids. They could come and sit in the cockpit of a real F-16, play with the simulators and... It was no use. I mean, those tours, he'd walk around all alone. The only one near him was like some... I don't know, some ugly leper kid all the kids were afraid to get next to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's kind of hard to see that, isn't it? Sometimes it's harder for us as parents to see our kid lonely than it is for the kid himself.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I've come to accept my son's introverted nature, acknowledging his strengths in other areas.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It took me a long time to realize that. Then I realized that... he was happy. That I had the problem. That I... I couldn't accept the fact that he wasn't popular. That he's an outsider, and that's okay. It's just his personality. I used to give him and michaela such a hard time. I'd call the counselor, I'd call the teachers, and everybody said, There's no problem. The boy feels good about himself. It's just the way it is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was it hard for you to accept?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but, you know, today...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I've come to accept my son's introverted nature, acknowledging his strengths in other areas.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm jealous of him, Cause he doesn't need anybody. He's got his own world. He's got his movies and books and computer games and chess. And the kid was born without a competitive bone in his body. Even the chess stuff, it's not about winning. He doesn't care if he wins. He just likes the thinking it requires. A few years ago I tried to organize this ping-pong tournament for his... for his class in the backyard. He turns to me and he says, Dad, don't you feel sorry for these kids? Only one will win, and it's probably Robert. And the rest will look pathetic in front of the girls.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: haha..

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't you feel sorry for them? I swear, I don't know where he got those genes. Certainly not from me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think he's too good to be connected to your genes?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you making fun of me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I want you to listen to what you're saying about yourself. This boy is your own flesh and blood. You... you love him. Dearly. You're very proud of his beautiful qualities and yet you think, Well, he's the exact opposite of me. He couldn't possibly be connected to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Please, let's not get into that again. No. This is completely a genetic issue. Look, he got the female genes from Michaela and my mother.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: Both my mother and wife are people of good character, in stark contrast to my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She saved his life. By that I mean at... At the march on Washington... In '63. Right before King's big speech, Mahalia Mackson sang that song I been 'buked and I been scorned. And they caught eyes in the crowd, and... They both had tears flowing down their faces. And they felt connected. My father was this lonely angry man, and she... Well, she melted him. She was the only person he ever trusted. He was at war with the rest of the world. And the war ain't over, believe me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And still he... He cheated on her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Constantly. The guy just wanted more and more. All the time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But he didn't leave her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, what are you crazy? Why would he leave her? He loved her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're sure about that? Are you sure that... it wasn't just that he held her in very high esteem and that... he was really grateful for everything that she'd done for him throughout his life?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: to justify him? He could've left her. Why make her life miserable?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, And you, unlike him, you're trying to do the right thing? You're leaving home just like that. You're not dragging out things like he did.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay. All right, all right.

situation: My father was a jerk, but my mother was wonderful, and I miss her dearly.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I see you believe in the whole theory that children try to rectify what their parents did wrong. All right. Okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Perhaps you might not have loved Michaela because you admired her so much for being so perfect.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wait. Why are we still talking about Michaela? That story is over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because I'm not sure that your leaving her is really the solution to how you feel about yourself.

situation: My father was always unfaithful to my mother, yet he never left her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I see you believe in the whole theory that children try to rectify what their parents did wrong. All right. Okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know that it's about rectification. I think it's more what we call a pattern. We unconsciously repeat patterns that... we have witnessed in childhood.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you said I was trying to rectify what my father did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you're presenting it that way, but on a deeper level... I think there may be more similarity between you and your father's view of marriage.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know what you mean.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really? You can't see any way in which you and your father may have married the same kind of woman? It seems to me that you both married women whom you admire, but... But you don't necessarily love.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's some bullshit. You actually buy this shit? That I'm repeating my father's mistakes? Let me tell you something: what's going on in my marriage has got nothing to do with my father, so stop comparing us.

situation: The therapist thinks the marital issues of my parents have influenced my own marriage, and I'm trying to correct the unhappiness I witnessed in their relationship.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wanna go back to Laura for a minute.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why is it so important to go back to Laura? Is it because she's my patient and you think it might bother me that you met?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't get this. Why can't I talk about her? What is the big deal about meeting her? You won't believe how much this cost. $450. I mean... That's crazy, right? Too bad they don't sell property on the online auctions. I mean, now that Michaela has the house, during the Indy 500 or something, I could go on get a place in the same neighborhood for almost half a million bucks. You got the deal of your life here, doc. Someone who doesn't know about the whole tv factor would've paid $1,500 for it, minimum. so if I'm here for a year, then that means you're renting it for... $8 a week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could we get back to our therapy session, Alex?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay. Well, Laura couldn't get over it. I showed her the machine and she just... she couldn't believe it.

situation: I refused to discuss my wife and shifted the conversation to talk about Luara. I talked about getting a good deal on a coffee machine through a TV shopping channel.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you like to... Would you like to tell me how you two met?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sure. I lost track of time. I moved in with my gay friend Daniel and his little boyfriend. I told you about them. And they are real happy I left home. They bring their friends over to meet me and they've turned me into the talk of the gay community. So I've been going along with it. you know, I go to dinners, drinks. I even went to this gay club with them on sunday. They told me there'd be some hot ladies there, somebody I could pick up that aren't even lesbians. And it didn't do anything for me. What it did was make me lose track of time. I was up all night long, so I could've sworn yesterday was tuesday, so I came here. but when I got here I saw Laura leaving. I walked up to her and I asked her if everything was okay. She said everything wasn't okay, that she ran over a dog, or almost ran over this dog yesterday morning. The way she described it, it sounded like this... the airedale terrier pedigree. The airedale terrier is the only dog in history to be knighted by the king of England for bravery in battle. Did you know that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't know that, no.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah well, it did. It's an amazing story. I mean, this dog... Okay, well, maybe next time.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I went to a gay bar with my friends and came early and happened to meet Luara.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I asked her if she had been leaving a session with you. And she was a bit taken aback like I had caught her in something shameful. Hell, I thought only Navy pilots felt that way about seeing a shrink. Anyway, I admitted to her that I was seeing you also. And I realized that I was here a day early. She thought that was just hilarious. That someone could get the days mixed up. And she's got this... I don't know, she's got this way of looking at you. It's like this girl, she's got... There's something fierce about her. Right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.text: I found something for you. I thought you should have it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, in the front pocket. It's for your collection.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's a catboat. It's beautiful. Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a going-away present. This is our last session, right? You said three.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I said at least three.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you're totally sick of listening to other people's insipid lives, Then maybe you can look at it And it will make you feel like you're somewhere else.

dialogue.text: Insipid-- That's a good word.

dialogue.text: I read thesauruses for fun. I'm not a freak, okay? I just like words. I thought you could use it. It must really suck having to listen To other people's problems all day. So does that chair, like, enhance your brain function?

dialogue.text: i don't think so.

dialogue.text: Can you read minds?

dialogue.text: Unfortunately, no.

dialogue.text: It would.

dialogue.text: Can I try the chair?

dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.text: Please.

dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.text: I'm okay.

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: Maybe.

situation: The therapist interpreted my act of giving gifts as a sign that I wanted to leave something behind.

dialogue.text: I've noticed that, uh, Cy's drawing is-- Is gone. Did you erase it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe a little scared Because this could be our final session?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: You said you liked the boat.

dialogue.text: I do.

dialogue.text: If you don't want it, i'll take it back.

dialogue.text: Do you want to take it back?

dialogue.text: So... if someone my age wants to start therapy, How would it work?

dialogue.text: if someone my age wants to start therapy, How would it work?

dialogue.text: Well, we'd take it at that person's own pace, Not like these last few sessions-- The evaluation, the three-Session deadline-- Nothing like that. See, the person who's in therapy controls the gas, So to speak, And the wheel for that matter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So it's like driving a car? Yeah,

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's a bit like driving a car.

situation: As a child,  I went on a family vacation with my parents and bought a sailboat as a gift.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So... pretend i'm in therapy now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said pretend. So, what do I do?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why don't you tell me a little bit more about the boat?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got it years ago from a homeless woman in New York when I was just a kid.

dialogue.text: What were you doing in New York?

dialogue.text: We were on a family vacation.

dialogue.text: Why do you say that, family vacation?

situation: As a child, I went on a summer vacation with my parents and bought a sailboat as a gift, but after we returned, my parents got divorced.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad took me to central park. There was this old woman right at the park's entrance Selling these little wooden toys. She looked so miserable. And I remember thinking, it's worse for her. I had just enough money left from my allowance To buy the boat. By the time we came home, it was over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was over?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Their marriage. Actually, I think it was over during the vacation but they were, like, pretending or something. I went to school, i went to practice And I came home and they were waiting for me in the kitchen, Smiling like those movie stars.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like movie stars?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, those smiles that movie stars do? Those big smiles but their eyes are all glazed over. Like-- And then my mother starts to cry. Then my father says to her in this voice... Olivia, leave it to me. And then he starts to cry. And i'm just standing there stuck in the kitchen Hungry as fuck with these two babies.

situation: My father and mother divorced and then left us; the therapist thinks I am very sad about the way my parents separated.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't remember the day he actually left. I just remember that day in the kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where did he go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Back to New York With his new wife. And I stayed here with my mother Who's totally depressed. Cy and Darlene-- They lived close by, So, they helped me get to practice and back. They didn't want me to give it up. Why are you looking at me like that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's just the way you talk about it, Like you're not so upset about the breakup As the way they did it. Maybe that's what's making you sad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not sad. Is that what people are supposed to do in therapy? Sit around and whine over all their problems? It's never going to happen. That's what she would do. I am nothing like her--

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your mom?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where was your dad while all this was going on? I told you, in New York with Natasha.

dialogue.text: Did you ever consider living with them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. We once thought maybe, but... It didn't work out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They needed their space. They didn't last anyway. He wanted me to live with them. He was really pissed that she said no, so, it really soured their relationship.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you blame yourself? Whatever way the cookie crumbles, you're still to blame?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How old are you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, how old am i?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: People really don't talk like that anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really? Your logic has has some flaws, Sophie. You aren't responsible for what your parents did. You couldn't be.

situation: My gymnastics teacher and his family had been very kind to me. When my parents had just divorced and I was in poor health, they took care of me all the time. But I ended up ruining their family.

dialogue.text: Were you a gymnast before-- Before you met Cy?

I was dancing around on a log in the backyard To entertain Dana. You know, doing spins and things. He put me on a beam the next day. Their house was like my house. I had a key. Before my father left, When he and my mom were fighting all the time, I slept over. I had these really bad attacks back then. My stomach would start to shake And then my whole body would start to shake. Sometimes i'd start throwing up And I couldn't make it stop. They took me to the emergency room one night. We never told my parents.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I ruined their family. I did, I really did.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I betrayed Darlene's trust and developed inappropriate feelings for the gymnastics coach, but I did not cross any boundaries.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Darlene was so good to me. I was-- She really was good to me. She told me before she left for Wisconsin That she was only going because she knew I would be there To take care of Dana. She said she didn't trust Cy, but she trusted me. She trusted me and I ruined it. You're thinking he used me. You're wrong. He kept trying to stop me. He kept saying, Sophie, you don't know what you're doing. We'll get to a place and there'll be no turning back. He's a really good person, Cy is. He's a gentleman. He kept saying, you don't know what you're doing. But the thing is, I did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what were you doing, Sophie?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: At first, I thought it was my imagination. And then he stopped talking to me while Darlene was home. You know, like he was embarrassed, Like he was hiding something. And sometimes i'd catch him holding his breath While he was looking at me. He loves me, I know he does. So I knew even before Darlene went away, I knew that he loved me. And then she left for six months But Cy wouldn't have sex with me Even though everyone assumed we were doing it, That we'd been doing it for months. Cy said it was a line that we absolutely Positively would not cross.

dialogue.text: Like nothing? Not good? Not bad?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Kind of like-- Kind of like I was watching it happen... on a really small black and white television. Like i was checking my e-mail At the same time. Like I wasn't really there. I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The next day we pretended like it hadn't happened. Then at practice that afternoon We had this big fight in front of everyone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because of what happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I fell off the beam. I'd been going for this back bend And for some reason I thought the beam Was longer than it really was So, i bent right off of it. I fell flat on my back. dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That night I slept on the couch. Then in the middle of the night Cy came in And i thought that-- But he wanted me to put Dana back to bed. He said it would ruin both of our careers if this got out. He said we had to stop. That's it. We almost had sex again that night, but he didn't want to. That's it. A few weeks later Darlene said she wanted to talk to me. She said that Dana had become too attached to me While she was in Wisconsin And I probably shouldn't come over for awhile. But it was pathetic Because I know her, you know? She was lying to me. I couldn't look at her. I just said i'm sorry. She said, don't be silly. Kids forget quickly. Grownups don't but kids do. Dana will forget you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Dana will never forget you, Sophie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't think so? No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sure of it. Darlene is terribly wrong. Grownups can forget. Children can't.

dialogue.text: When I left, darlene gave me a present That she got for me in Wisconsin.

dialogue.text: An apron... with cows on it. She knows I like to cook and I collect things with cows on them, so, it was sort of... Perfect.

dialogue.text: The accident... it happened that night?

dialogue.text: I woke up in the ambulance.

dialogue.text: Do you remember how you got there?

dialogue.text: I don't even remember walking away from the house. I remember her giving me the apron. I didn't want it. I tried to give it back... but she said, Take it so you don't get dirty. dialogue.text: What did you see?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing. I saw thhouse from the outside, That's all. I'll huff and i'll puff And i'll blow your house down.

dialogue.text: I don't wanna fuck everything up here too.

dialogue.text: No, don't worry about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you had to write the evaluation now--

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I don't have to write the evaluation now, Sophie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If someone held a gun to your head--

dialogue.text: No one's holding a gun to my head. Are you holding the gun?

dialogue.text: I wanna know what you think !

dialogue.text: What do you think ? Do you think that you did this to yourself ?

dialogue.text: I don't remember! How many times do I have to tell you?!

dialogue.text: What does your instinct tell you?

dialogue.text: What does your heart tell you?

dialogue.text: I don't have a heart.

dialogue.text: You know from what you've told me already, I think that you're having quite a difficult time Taking care of yourself recently.

dialogue.text: So?

dialogue.text: So it doesn't mean that you deliberately ran into that car.

dialogue.text: So what would you write?

dialogue.text: i don't know, something along the lines of... as a result of the anxiety She felt preceding the incident, The subject may have been distracted, Acted irresponsibly but we cannot conclude That the accident was a premeditated, willful act--

dialogue.text: That sounds really vague.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't be any more specific than that. I'm not a magician. I don't know anything more than what you've told me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I fucking hate you! You never say what you really mean. You know, you're just like all the rest of them. Why can't anyone ever tell anyone else the truth? dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's a difference Between not being careful Because you feel vulnerable And wanting to commit suicide.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't see the difference?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No !

situation: The therapist thinks that my mental state is not good, psychological problems still exist, and there might be another incident.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's just like the picture frame. I didn't mean to break it. I didn't even see it, But it's broken. I broke it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In terms of the evaluation, There's a really big difference. That's what i'm trying to get you to understand.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sophie, the problems that you had Before the accident-- They're still there. Even when they take off the neckbrace and take off the casts, Those problems are still going to be there When you go back to your normal everyday routine. You're gonna have to face them again. 'Cause if we're not careful, something like this could happen again. That's what you're really asking me, isn't it? dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You make me sound like a time bomb. I ruined everything。

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you don't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I do. You said I wanted to go home because there's nothing more For me to ruin there. It's obvious.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, let's look at it another way. You could really build something at home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: With my mother? Are you on crack? I have to go soon.

dialogue.text: Can I ask you something before you go? Where do you feel... safe?

dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.text: Where are you happy? Where do you feel-- Where do you feel safe?

dialogue.text: I was happy with Cy and Dana. I ruined it.

dialogue.text: You erased the drawing from your cast.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 'Cause I was angry.

dialogue.text: Is there anywhere else that you're happy?

dialogue.text: On the beam. I can spend hours walking back and forth-- Dive, dive and swish.

dialogue.text: Dive, dive and swish? What does that mean?

dialogue.text: It's a song I sing to myself when i'm up there. It reminds me of a pelican diving down to catch a fish in its beak.

dialogue.text: Could I hear the song?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have a wish, to sing and fish, Down by the sea, just you and me, ♪♪♪ Dive, dive and swish. And on the dive i've drop my foot off the beam and, And on the swish I swing it back up.

dialogue.text: You feel safe up there?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know you can't live up there forever. You have to come down, eventually. Goodbye, Sophie.

dialogue.text: Yeah. It's getting better. But, it's still a terrible sensation. You go to the bathroom, you're staying there, you... will it to happen, nothing. Not a drop.

dialogue.text: So uncomfortable. This and the stress you're under. What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Jesus. You think it's psychosomatic?

dialogue.text: No, not at all.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A symbolic urinary infection.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Symbolic how?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My head's telling me one thing, my body's telling me another, my precise issue manifesting itself, as a physical malfunction of the...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said it was on the right? Excuse me for a moment. There's no soap in there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really? I thought I saw soap.

situation: I am angry about the consequences of accepting the therapist's advice and suggesting to the patient, Luara, to end the treatment.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you angry? It feels you are very angry tonight.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let's say that's a fairly accurate assessment.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wanna tell me why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Actually... I'm angry at myself. For taking your advice. Even though... I knew better.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My advice?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Taking your advice like a novice, like a naive intern. Ignoring every cell in my body, and listening to you, instead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I met with Laura, and we talked about ending our sessions. A total disaster. Did the opposite of what you predicted. It was just... destructive. It sabotaged a year of therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because it undermined her faith in me and in the work that we've done together. She asked me if I was ending our sessions because... I'm in love with her. That... Well, that what she heard me say. What she heard was: I'm in love with you so... I can't see you anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you put it exactly?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you suggesting that I handled it badly?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. I just want to hear what you said.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I said we should discuss the options of... Of ending therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't just drop it on her out of the blue?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course, I didn't. I built up to it.

situation: My patient, Luara, was late for her appointment, and then I suggested ending the treatment following the therapist's advice.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She came in late. I thought that was important. Like it was her way of telling me something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not following.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said I thought that her being late was her way of saying that she was angry at me. That she was... ambivalent about her therapy. Of course, she threw it back and she asked if... She does have a point, she asked if she wasn't the first person ever to fall in love for her therapist. And then, she told me to deal with it. Meaning, you know, this is my job. She's right. She said, You are an experienced therapist, just deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you surprised to the reaction? You put it on her and she threw it back.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How was I supposed... You hammered me about this last week. You went on and on about what I... I knew it was a bad idea. And now, I'm coming to you with this mess... And all you...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're not an intern. Far from it. Don't play the intern. If you think something is a bad idea, you don't do it because I suggested it. I said we should talk about it. You were furious. Like I was trying to take Laura away from you. Two days later, you abruptly tried to stop her treatment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said that ending the therapy was the best good solution.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I said it might be necessary for her sake. When you say good solution, I think you mean a solution to your problems.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is that what I mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm assuming you acted hastily because you thought it was necessary. That it had to be dealt with quickly.

situation: After I rejected the patient, Luara, I experienced problems with my urinary system. I have had fantasies about Luara and discussed with the therapist the differences between the relationship of a patient with a psychotherapist and that with a gynecologist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you want, Gina? Do you want to... What do you want to hear? Do you want me to talk about Laura? Do you want us to have a Laura session? What do you want me to say, that I sit opposite her and say: Oh, what if? Well, I do. You think I'm in denial about it? I'm not. Laura is... She's attractive. Anybody who is a therapist knows that... Look, I know all the ways in with her, all the doors I could open if I wanted to...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you imagine opening them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes I do. I fantasize about Laura. Look, it's like a gynecologist. It's easier for women to believe that their male gynecologist doesn't have any sexual desire for them. Of course, they want him to find their bodies attractive as well. Don't they?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, Don't even try to break down a relationship between a woman and her gynecologist. That's a deep end.

situation: I know how to excite the patient, Luara, how to manipulate her, and I discussed with the therapist the issue of boundaries between a therapist and a patient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway, last week, I... I got this... sharp... kind of pain... So I went to the urologist and, on Monday, and I thought: This is... This is really scary. And then this random thought comes into my head because it's so cold in the room, and I think: My dick is shrinking, and I don't want the doctor to think that, you know, that's the real size. Never mind... It was just...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, You know, there is no connection between a gynecologist office and... the intimacy between therapist and patient. I'm curious about What do you think the connection is?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What I'm saying is that... As a male therapist, sitting across from a beautiful patient, I... I know exactly... How to engage her. I know exactly what it would take to... To turn her on.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know what turns her on?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Any number of things. But I could manipulate her to do anything I wanted. I know that. And I doubt if it's only male therapist who have those thoughts. Do you know what I'm talking about? For example, if a male doctor performs an examination on a female patient, there'd be a nurse present, right? I mean, that's for a reason.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Am I the nurse? I keep you from crossing the line. Is that why you came to me? Let me tell you what worries me. You have boundaries too, and just like you, this woman knows how to cross them.

situation: I encountered emotional temptations while diagnosing the patient, Luara, and the therapist thinks I am fragile.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All I'm saying is that the temptation is there for any therapist. I know what I'm doing. I mean, if I were a gynecologist, and I were performing an examination, I wouldn't accidentally start to...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Listen to yourself. You know, you say you have no problem discussing Laura. And then, I bring her up, and suddenly, it's... It's all about genitals. Gynecologist, and urologist, and... You know, it seems to me that you're taking all of this to an extremely intimate realm. And you're saying to me... I'm extremely vulnerable, here. Help me here... Where it hurts.

situation: I am angry that the therapist's earlier suggestion to have the patient, Luara, change therapist failed to yield results, and the therapist thinks I am avoiding the issue.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what? What gets to me is that... I lay it out for you. All I want is for you to give me... the Gina treatment,, to get in there with your cold, analytical scalpel, and get some perspective. Say: Try this, Paul, try that! What I didn't expect was that... That you give up on me, telling me to find her a new therapist.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Give up on you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You suggest a course of action. When that fails, you say to me: Hey, you did it, don't come blaming me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you really believe I convinced you to do something destructive? Let's talk about that. It seems like a distraction from talking about your feelings about her, but okay, let's start by looking at how you're conducting her therapy, which seems to me impulsive, unorganized, and if I'm honest, very problematic.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Really, is it now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Whenever I try to talk about this, you unleash all this aggression to show me this area is off limits. Touch this, I'll burn it down.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All right, we'll deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right... Right.

dialogue.text: You remember I was talking about Alex, the fighter pilot?

dialogue.text: Paul, God, listen to yourself!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You say Let's talk about Laura, and then you bring up Alex, or anything you can think of, so long as it's no Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is about Laura. Alex, the fighter pilot... met Laura.

situation: I told the story of my patient, Luara, who accidentally met another patient of mine, Alex, and the two were dating. The therapist was surprised by this and I was disgust about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is about Laura. Alex, the fighter pilot... met Laura.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After a session we had this talk about stopping therapy. The session ended and she wouldn't leave. She wanted extra time, I told her I couldn't, I had an appointment with... urologist.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't tell her that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. I said I had an appointment. Anyway, she stormed out, and lo and behold, who does she meet?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He was there and you had a conflicting appointment?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was a day early by mistake, which is weird, because this guy is such a military perfectionist. A machine. He can probably tell the time by triangulating the stars or something. Anyway, he forgot what day it was. So he comes back the next afternoon, tells me that they met, and now... They're dating. You think it's funny? Because I don't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, It's not funny. It's curious, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's so... What's curiously funny about it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know. Just give me a minute and let me figure out what I'm thinking.... It made me smile, I don't know why.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're dating.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Dating?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She went out with him to get back at me. I pushed her into it. You don't see that? I reject her unequivocally. And the next minute, she's hitting on the nearest guy. I mean, a guy literally on my own doorstep. That's not a reaction to me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would it be?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because she knew Alex would tell me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, first of all, isn't that a reaction against her boyfriend, the man she's going to marry? Why are you the betrayed man, here? Which would be the worse situation? If you realized that you were the center of Laura's life and that she was dating another man to get at you, or... If... the transference simply faded, and she was back to viewing you as a therapist. She thought about you during sessions, that's it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think I'm an egomaniac?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm asking which would be the worse situation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't get off on being worshipped by my patients,

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't get off on being worshipped by my patients, if that's what you mean. It's not like I'm in some kind of... Some kind of a cult.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If her feelings were to change, you wouldn't have a sense of loss?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Pretty clear, how you want me to answer this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you not get that I'm concerned about the right and the wrong of this, as it affects all my patients?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're very concerned, I can tell that. But you know, sometimes, helping a patient view the world differently it's a powerful experience. It's a little addictive.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a powerful experience because it contributes to somebody's well being. It's not about an inflated sense of... Power. Do you think I'm addicted to power?

situation: The therapist asked me to describe how I appear in patient Luara's eyes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How... How does Laura see you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When she looks at you, what does she see?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Bear with me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What does she see? She sees... a man, obviously. A lot older than she is. An authoritative strong man. She thinks if she could get close to him, that she could maybe take on some of his strength. At the same time, she's waiting for him to disappoint her, because, somewhere down the line, inevitably, that's her story with men.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What else?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She thinks I won't be interested in her unless she offers herself sexually. She associates concern for her as a woman with sex. For her, sex is... a currency that she uses to pay for... emotional protection from men.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Don't analyze. Just describe.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where is this going?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, just stay with it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She thinks I'm a coward, which is a bit of a turn off.

dialogue.text: She believes that I'm totally in love with her, that... I think all the rest of my patients are a drag and... that I can't wait for her session. I assume she... I assume she finds me attractive. Otherwise, why would she... Isn't this enough?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Now, you describe her, how you see her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I would say... An hysterical disorder...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Don't analyze. Describe.

dialogue.text: Did you mean what does she look like? If one had to pick her out of a crowd, I'd say...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, if you had to pick her out of a crowd.

dialogue.text: God, you're such a stickler. Okay, She's thirty. She's... beautiful. Great smile... Inquisitive look in her eyes. Really sharp... Very smart... She's got this great laugh that just... situation: I talked about the time when patient Luara's mother passed away during her childhood, and the therapist asked about the things that are related between me and Luara.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She told me about a summer after her mother died. She was 15. And she went to live with this couple in San Diego, friends of her father. dialogue.text: Like you did after your mother's breakdown.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing worse than a kid... playing parents... to a father or mother... It's unnatural. It reverses of the order of things, it's like... kind of death, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For you, it was after your father ran off with his patient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You keep coming back to that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I try to find the roots of your connection to Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's got nothing to do with my father. Laura's the one re-enacting, not me. Laura's re-enacting this... escape. Because that's what I am to her.

dialogue.text: Escape from what? Her boyfriend, her wedding?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've tried to explain it to her that... She's really making me into... another David. Not your David but... The older guy from that couple, that took her in. She wants me to be that guy... again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're sure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, God forbid... I should say anything you agree with, no matter how clearly I lay it out. Her attraction to me, her wanting to run away with me, there's something bigger that's... that's driving that impulse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe you wanna run away?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Escape from Kate, from your work.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God, you're so fixated on your pet theories. Everything has to...

situation: My wife cheated on me, so I slept in separate rooms with her and told the therapist about the child’s reaction to it. I felt like the child knew everything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did I tell you that... That Kate is going to Rome next week with her insurance-agent boyfriend? She's the one that's running, not me. I told her: Fine, just get the hell out. I don't wanna, I... I don't want to look at you. We don't live together, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I sleep in the office. During the day, we act like everything is fine, but at night, I'm... I'm on the couch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Since when?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Last four nights. I brought in my blankets and my clothes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How are the kids taking this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Rosie didn't come home on Tuesday. Said she'd be back late, but... In the morning, she wasn't there. She said she slept over at some friend's. Ian had a week off from college. There's no food in the kitchen. I went to the fridge, I look in... Nothing. Not even an egg. Max and I ordered pizzas, then I put him to bed. I was gonna sleep in the office, then I thought: What if something happens? You know? He's upstairs by himself, he's all alone. I... couldn't bring myself to sleep in that bedroom. Not even for his sake. I find that bedroom kind of... repulsive. I was asleep for while. I don't know what time it was, and... I wake up and I hear this voice saying, Daddy. And Max is there, you know, just standing at the door. He asked me if I could sleep with him and... I said, Sure. He hasn't done that since he was 5 years old. My guess, that's the answer to your question: is the kids know everything. Anyway, she's leaving in 3 days, and... Probably for the best, really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How is it for the best?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not for the best. It's a nightmare.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's painful. But in a way, you're free... to go through... whatever it is with Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wanted my wife to leave me for a salesman?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe not, but it's convenient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Convenient? She's flying to Rome to fuck an insurance salesman, for Christ's sake!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that really what he is?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. He's a... runs an employment agency or something. What am I supposed to do? Chain her to the bed? Track every move she makes, like that guy I have in therapy, Jake? Or Alex who, you know, whose wife grinds her teeth in her sleep and... wakes up the next day and says, The marriage is over, I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You keep bringing patients into this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My wife is running off but... apparently, it's not my wife, really it's me. According to you. Since I'm my father, it must be me.
