dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've been trying to understand since our first session why you came to me. Me, specifically. I remember, on our first visit, you said that you felt like you were cutting corners. You have no patience for your patients that's what you said. And that, if they knew what you really... thought about them, they'd stop coming. I'm wondering if maybe, that's what you want, for them to stop coming.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why would I want that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not literally, on an unconscious level.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Unconscious...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe you want to transfer your patients to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where did that come from?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's not a real option. It's a wish. You could dump your patients on me... your problems. When I suggested that we find another therapist for Laura, you immediately assumed that I would treat her. And then, you went down the list. You described each patient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But isn't that what the sessions are for?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. It felt like you were preparing me metaphorically... for the day when you hand them over, when you say Here, their problems are not my problems. I have to leave.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm gonna run off to the Caribbean and... I'm gonna be sipping cocktails with Laura, and scuba diving. I mean, what on earth are you on about? I just took on 3 more new patients.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said you did that to prove to yourself that everything's OK. That couple, you said you don't care if they ever come back. You don't like the navy pilot. And sometimes, it seems you're not that upset about Kate.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not always. Sometimes. Maybe all these things that... should be bad are really okay. And then, there's me. You're using me as your accomplice. Not in a practical way. But emotionally, to help you move on from them. That way you're free to be with Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I don't even want to say to that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you'll explain him if he finds out. Can you make sense of it for him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what exactly do you want me to tell him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That I'm fucked up! That I can't help myself. That it's bigger than me. Tell him that I'm fucked up!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So even if he forgives you, do you think that you can forgive yourself?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I always forgive myself. That's my problem. I... I just close my eyes before I go to sleep at night and I ask God for forgiveness and I forgive myself for everything. Even the unforgivable things. I never get punished.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think that sex with Reeves will go unpunished?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Who's gonna punish me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe you've already started to punish yourself. Do you really think that sleeping with Reeves is gonna bring back the good old reliable angry, controlling Jake? The one who fights you and threatens you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And now that he's expressing his love through tenderness, do you feel that you deserve his love?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not love! It's neediness. It's weakness. It's unbearable.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it's only love if he chases you, stalks you, tapes you, is jealous of you, is that it? I think you need to look at this a little more carefully, Amy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's like it's happened already.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But it hasn't. You still have a choice. Nothing happens without you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have to go to the bathroom.

situation: My superior officer asked me to return to the military base to train new pilots.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sorry the gravy train is ending here, doc.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's okay. So why are you leaving?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got you curious, huh? Remember I told you my squadron commander called me? Well, last week they finally brought me in. Now I thought they wanted to ease me back in, but no. They need me to train the next wave of pilots for their deployment, Get them ready to fly asap. Always playing catch-up in this war.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what did you say to them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said, Fuck you! I'm 39 years old, in the prime of my life and one of the most decorated fighter pilots in the Navy. No, you're not gonna put me out to pasture, not in the middle of a war. Get yourself another boy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's what you said to them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, not really, but I thought it. Actually what I said was, Yes, sir. However I can be of service to you, sir. And... I reported for duty the next day. You think I'm crazy? I can only get away with that bullshit with you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, at least we know why you come here. So what's it like being back at base?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When they look in my eyes, they know i've been places they couldn't conjure up in their worst nightmares. Makes them think twice before fucking with me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, training young pilots... Is that something you can see yourself doing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, maybe in another context. But this is set up to fail.

situation: While training young pilots, I led them in cross-country running, underwater training, and swimming for survival.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's no way these kids are gonna be ready for combat missions in a month. I mean, it's crazy. I'm taking them through tactical situations. Some of them are doing better than others, but when you're up in the air, it's read and react. Read, react, like a machine. No thinking. It's like split-second decisions that can cost thousands of lives, including their own. Most of these kids, they look at me on the simulators and they're like, whoa! Well, they're blown away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must feel really great.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I overheard a couple of these kids talking shit about me, Saying that I might be good on the simulators but they'd kick my ass on the obstacle course. Called me old man, all that bullshit. Well, hey...

situation: While training young pilots, I led them in cross-country running, underwater training, and swimming for survival.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I called their bluff. Check this out: now the drill is called the gauntlet. It's a five-mile run through dense woods and sand traps, and rope-and-barrier hurdles, balance beams and a maze. Now after all that, there's the helo-dunker. Nothe helo-Dunker is like this giant... It looks like a beer can. It's basically a crash simulator. We hit the water hard, upside down, strapped in tight. And we have to get out with almost no oxygen. We're in full gear: helmet, spacesuit, G-suit, gloves, the whole nine yards. Now there are four immersions. The last two, the water's dark. It's like a night landing. A lot of these kids, they get disoriented and start flipping the fuck out. So we have to rescue them. It's tough. It separates the men from the boys, let me tell you. So, doc... how do you think I did?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do I really have to guess, Alex?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Touche. I never panic. I'm at home down there in the dark, swimming for my life. And not only did I beat all their asses, I came within two seconds of a base record. Not bad for a broken-down old pilot, huh? Come on, Paul.

situation: A high-ranking military officer asked if I could return to duty and wanted to call my therapist to inquire about my psychological state.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, so my squadron commander calls me back up to his office. This time all the brass were there and they want to know if i'm interested in going back to active duty. If I am, I have to go through a modified basic training at Pensacola, a battery of tests... Physical, psychological... Just to make sure I've recovered. So I said, bring it on, baby! I'm ready for anything! Are you surprised?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, a little, I guess. I shouldn't be, but I suppose it was always a possibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you think it's too fast, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think it's too fast?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Doc, you have no idea how good it feels to be useful again. To tell you the truth, I think that's been the real problem. I've been sitting around feeling sorry for myself. I'm a doer, not a talker, so all of this... That's over. Those days are over. So here's what I need from you: You're gonna get a call from one of your compatriots. He's a Navy doctor named Connell. He's gonna be checking up on me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You told the Navy you were seeing me? I thought that was professional suicide.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, they caught wind that I had left the house. They wanted to know if it had anything to do wit the bombing and the aftermath. So I told them i'd been doing some counseling with you... You know, my marriage... And that I was fit as a fiddle.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel fit as a fiddle?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Paul, don't fuck with me on this. You're talking about my career now. Just tell him all good things. Plus, the Navy needs me. You think they can afford to have someone like me just pissing around? Just tell him i'm ready.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let's just talk about whether you are ready or not.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hey, cut the crap! I need this.

situation: The therapist thinks it's too early for me to return to duty now, as it's not appropriate and my mental state is not yet adjusted.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hey, cut the crap! I need this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're putting me in a very difficult position, Alex. We talked about a lot more than michaela. You don't expect me to lie, do you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, physically i'm fine. I had the heart attack almost four months ago. All the cardiologists say that... They're amazed by my recovery. I can handle it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But what about emotionally, Alex? Can you imagine yourself back in an airplane flying a mission after what happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're talking about the madrasa thing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The madrasa thing is the crisis that brought you here in the first place. Are you sure that you're ready to put yourself in that kind of situation again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, listen. Terrorists hide among civilians. It's a common tactic. It's their fault if there's collateral damage, not ours. They're the ones putting their women and children at risk.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let's put aside the question of who's at fault or who isn't. Could you live with yourself if you were responsible for more civilian casualties?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Alex, you gave yourself a heart attack a few months ago. Can you honestly tell me that you're not worried, that you're not scared that your guilt will lead to...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Guilt is not an issue for a pilot in a time of war. We're not trained to think that way.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not asking what you think. I'm asking you to tell me what you feel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And i'm telling you it doesn't matter. Let me just see who this is. Sorry.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I received a call from my wife, who really hopes I return to the navy and fly again, and so does my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It went fine. Yeah, they did ask me. No, I can't talk about that right now. Can I call you back? Michaela, let me go, all right? I'm with somebody right now. Yeah, I will. Yeah, bye. Sorry. She wanted to know how the meeting with the brass went. You know, she's totally obsessed with me flying again. You know that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think she's so anxious for you to fly again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, my little sabbatical upset her sense of order. If it was a couple of weeks, it would be all right. I was taking a break, whatever. I told you we were having dinner to discuss me coming back home. Yeah, well, the heat is on. I don't think I can fight it any longer. Plus it's what everybody wants.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Everyone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Everybody... My father included. Well, he and michaela, they're united in everything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why is you father so anxious for you to fly again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, there's nothing deep behind it, Paul.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist asked why I think everyone wants me to return to the military, and I talked about a family event for my son's birthday.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He thinks I need to get back to my job. It's what a man does. And he's right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you tell me how you got to that conclusion?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you sure you have time for that? Cause I...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We've got plenty of time. I think this is something important we need to talk about especially if you are trying to push me for an assessment.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's hot as hell in here. We had a party for my son, A birthday party... And everything became clear. I told you my son roy is a special kid. Have I told you that? He doesn't seem to need friends. So, when we asked him what kind of party he wanted, he said only family. I supported that. I didn't want to force him to be anything he isn't. So all the uncles and aunts came and the cousins, and everybody was in a good mood. My dad, he got there early. He's establishing and setting up everything and acting like he owns the place, ordering my wife around.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recount the details of my time with my father and family on my son’s birthday.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I could tell he had been there a lot since I left. And the bitch he married, she was there too, in the kitchen cooking as if my mother never existed. It made me feel like shit, Like a... A stranger in my own home. My father sees me and he gives me one of those cold smiles. Alex, nice of you to make it. I could tell he had a wild hair up his ass about something. But I didn't ask. 'Cause when he wants to share, he shares. And then he's all over me, And i'm in no rush to get there. But he is great with roy, though. They connect. Somehow it's easy for them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you feel like you weren't connecting with roy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There were a lot of people there. We didn't have much time alone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you seen a lot of him since you left home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Once, twice. I don't know what you consider a lot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did he ever ask why you weren't living at home anymore?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. I told him his dad was on a special mission.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist asked about my relationship with my son, and I mentioned how happy I was at my son's birthday party.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, i'm gone half the time. He's used to it. To tell you the truth, i think it's been a relief for him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would it be a relief for his dad to be away?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well... Well... He was loose as hell at the party. He's running around, he's playing with his cousins, he's talking to everybody. You should have seen him. He was a different person. He was open, he was outgoing. It's like he bloomed in my absence. Well, not bloomed. Jeez, he's not a fucking flower. It's like he spread his wings. Yeah, that's what it was like.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe he was happy because you were there, Maybe because he was just glad to see you. It's interesting when you talk about flying, Alex, because you make no bones whatsoever about the fact. that the Navy really needs you, that they can't do it without you. Yet when it comes to talking about your son...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Paul, Paul, slow the fuck down.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist thinks my attitude towards my son is influenced by my father. I talked about playing chess with my son.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The boy was having a great day before I ever got there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is it possible that you're projecting your own feelings about your father onto your son?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, that you might be doing better yourself|| spreading your wings too if he wasn't there, If he wasn't... in your way, so to speak.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, doc, my being there didn't make the kid happy that day. Just the opposite in fact.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How? What happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you roy was obsessed with chess, right?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about playing chess with my son on his birthday. My son stopped playing because he feared that I would lose.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got him this magnificent set. It was all ivory, imported from Nairobi, Just a real work of art. And he just looked at the pieces, mesmerized. But the board, that was only half of the gift. The other half... was that I had been working on my own chess game And I was gonna play my boy. So we sat down at the chessboard. Everybody's watching. I thought i'd open with something simple... The king's indian, which is where you establish your pawns in the center of the board. Then he moved, and I countered. And he moved again. I countered again. And we're moving along at this real nice clip and I think I'm holding my own. And then... I'll never forget it. He looked up suddenly and it was like a shadow fell over his face. And he stood up from the table and he said, I'm not feeling well. I don't want to play. He goes up to his bedroom. I follow him up the stairs. I knock on the door. He doesn't answer. I crack the door open and I see him. He's sitting at his desk. He's got his back to me. I don't know if he heard me. I was about to say something, but I didn't. I just stood there and I stared at the back of his head. Something about him... I don't know what it was... It broke my heart. Then I heard these footsteps coming up behind me, I turn around and it's my father. And he says, you know why he quit, don't you? I shook my head. And he gives me that look, that look that sees right through you. He says, He knew in three moves, Alex, You were gonna lose. He didn't want to beat his father in front of the whole family. He felt sorry for you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think he was right?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I know he was right. That's my son to a tee.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: After my son's birthday, my father scolded me upon learning that I was seeing a therapist, which my wife had told him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then my father, he pulls me into a room and he just ripped into me. He says, You are pathetic. One thing goes wrong in your little cushy life and you turn soft as butter. He didn't understand why I wasn't eager to fly again or why I was away from home doing god knows what With god knows who like a fucking teenager. He says, You disappoint me, boy. I raised you to be stronger than that. I raised you to be a man. And he wanted to know who put all these ideas in my head. Who turned me into a... What did he... Who turned me into a selfish, whining little bitch. Was it the fags I was hanging around with? Or was it... And this one he really seized on... Was it the shrink?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How would he know you were seeing a shrink?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Michaela told him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You told her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I had to. You know i've been paying you cash, cause I was trying to avoid a paper trail. But that means i've been withdrawing from atms all the time. Michaela looks at the bank statements and she saw there wasn't money there, she wanted to know where it was going. Anyway, look, I told her I've been consulting with someone about my thoughts... And that was the word, thoughts... My thoughts about me and her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you get into that, your thoughts about the two of you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, she shut down. So anyway, listen. My father... Yeah, my father... He gives me this whole earful. He goes downstairs, and, man... I felt like I had been hit by a freight train. I locked myself in the bathroom and I sat there so I could just catch my breath.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I saw my father and son playing chess together, but nobody noticed me, so I quietly slipped away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And when I finally got my shit together I went back downstairs, and... And everybody was around the chessboard again watching another match, including Michaela. And... You know what it was? It was my father and my son and they are locked in this epic battle, Matching each other move for move. Totally out of my league. And everyone's oohing and ahhing Aand they didn't even notice that I was there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it about Roy that broke your heart when you were watching him in his room?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He seemed so... Vulnerable, somehow.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Vulnerable to what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, really. Everything... Forces, expectations, Stuff coming at him that he can't control, I can't control. So I slipped out of the house without anyone knowing. It was for the better.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For whom?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For my boy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you really think that your son is better off without his father on his birthday?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I do.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I drove to a gay bar to drown my sorrows, feeling the urge to hit someone at that moment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After that I got in my car and I drove, And drove and drove, fast. And when I finally ran out of gas it was after dark. I wound up at this bar that Sean and Daniel had taken me to. And I started to drink hard, looking at all the faggots prancing around. I felt like knocking somebody's teeth down their fucking throat. But nobody came near me. They didn't even look at me. It was kind of like they knew like I had this invisible force field around me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said before that when you started telling me about the party, that everything became clear that day. What was it that became clear?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That I needed to go. I needed to get back to the Navy... Discipline, order, Yes, sir, no, sir. Knowing when to go to sleep, when to wake up, what to wear, what to eat, what to do. To get out of my own head. This is not for everyone, you know, this self-Examination. Some of us... we just need to live our lives, man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think you went to that particular bar?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. I wanted anyone to so much as breathe so I could beat the living hell out of them, that's why.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But nobody did.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

situation: The therapist thinks that I haven't fully understood my relationship with my father, my career and that my psyche is not well-adjusted.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could it be, Alex, that you were there for exactly the opposite reason? Cause no one would question you or ask you to be anything other than yourself? You see, these issues with your father, with your own identity, with what you really want for yourself, these things, they have to be looked at. Don't you think it would be better to deal with them here on the ground than have them follow you 20,000 feet into the air?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wait, are you actually expressing an opinion here? Are you telling me not to fly?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't answer that. It makes me feel like you're asking me to share responsibility for another major decision in your life. You know, go back to baghdad, leave michaela. I think we're way past that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not asking you to decide, Paul. I can decide. I have decided. No, i'm asking you, man to man... Tell me, what would you do if you were me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Alex, if I was you, I would stay in therapy. I would continue to deal with the complex, difficult issues that we've been talking about, not sweep them under the carpet like you've been doing in your life. I can tell you one thing: They will creep up on you again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you won't tell me not to fly.

situation: I asked the therapist not to say anything in front of the navy's therapist, but the therapist is very worried about me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, you're wrong. I don't make mistakes. When i'm up in the sky, that's when i'm in control. You don't get it yet. I am the best. Now, Paul, listen to me. Don't fuck me up with this Navy shrink. Please. Don't take my world away from me. Well... I think we're done. What is it, doc?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Here's my cell phone. I want you to call me any time, day or night, if you need to talk about anything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just had a thought. Soon i'm going to be flying over the armpit of the fucking world, and i'll be thinking about you in your... In your chair.

situation: I dreamt that my father was in danger, and it turned out to be true. I believe I have a psychic connection with my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hold up, Paul. I just got to finish this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Take your time. I'll just google myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's my dad, he's in Boston. I might go visit him next week. Oh my god, the most amazing thing happened last night, You wouldn't believe me, but I don't care.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why wouldn't believe you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because you think me and my dad being connected is bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I never said it was bullshit, I said I might be surprised...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Free your mind, Paul, the rest will follow. Oh my god, that was incredible. I had this dream that my father was in danger. I woke up feeling a little freaked, so I called him. He's staying in a hotel with his girlfriend. Turns out, last night... Someone broke into his room and stole his favorite camera.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: em...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So, I guess you must be feeling pretty silly now, huh? Because you have all this doubts about my father and I telepathy. You basically hate the man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I hate your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Last week, you were insinuating... Forget it, the point is we're connected. It's been prove once and for all, you can't take that away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that you might go to Boston. Don't you have the olympic trials coming up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Those are after I get back.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I am excited about the upcoming meeting with my father and talked about seeing him before six months.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Those are after I get back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it's okay to miss training this close to the competition, is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh I'm sorry, Cy, I was looking for my shrink. Look, it's not a big deal. It's just more important to me to spend quality time with him. It's been too long.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe he can come here. That way you can see him and you can still continue to train.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you care? Did you bet on me to win a medal or something?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When was the last time you saw your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: About... six month ago... He was in town for a week-end.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was that fun?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was fine. We went to this fancy restaurant. His girlfriend came with us. My dad started flirting with the waitress. His girlfriend started to cry. So we had to leave which kinda sucked, but it doesn't matter, it was fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was it the same girl from Boston?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think so. Who can keep up?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you get on with her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine. She's peachy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's her name again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Darren, Tarren, Karen, something like that. Clea. I think it's still Clea. I'm like the little sister she never had.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father used to take me on trips, and once I vomited because of the strong smell of perfume.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He should leave her in Boston. We haven't taking a trip together, just my dad and me since my thirteen birthday.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where did you go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We went to Paris. He took me to everything. From the Eiffel Tower to Monet's garden, the works. At this sidewalk cafe, I had this cup of chocolate you had to eat with the spoon. Two words: Awe-some! We stayed in this huge apartment, it was like a loft. Belonged to some woman, I met for like... five seconds, just as I was leaving to fly back home. She was going into the apartment as I was going out. The elevator reeked of her perfum, made me wanna throw up. I did, literally, right on the street, in front of the cab. Nobody saw it. That's not true, the cabby saw it, but my dad didn't, he stayed upstairs.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you took the cab to airport by yourself?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, yeah, I was thirteen, Paul.

situation: I feel a psychic connection with my father and asked the therapist about dreams. The therapist then talked about her own childhood dreams.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you want to tell me more about that dream that you had?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really, it doesn't matter, it's just a stupid dream. But I felt he was in danger, that's the important part. I can feel him, we're linked, radar love. It was a terrible dream. Or like a nightmare. Do you get those?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What happens in yours?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's one I've... I've had... consistently since I was a kid. I'm sitting in this rocking chair, and I'm rocking back and forward. Everytime I go to get off, I can't. The chair keeps rocking back and forward. And my... My mother is calling me... from upstairs. I'm trying to get out of the chair, but I... I just can't let go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you think it means?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think it means that... maybe that I... scared to disappoint my mother, that I'm not gonna be there for her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you disappoint her, in real life?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I... I don't think so. Anyway, back to your dream.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay. So... I was waiting for my father in a hotel room, when a man knocked on the door.

situation: I continue to narrate my dream, dreaming of a serial killer wanting to kill my father in a hotel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was waiting for my father in a hotel room, when a man knocked on the door. I let him in. He asked me where my father was, I told him he was on his way. But just as I said it, I was so stupid, I realize that this guy was a serial killer. So he sat down to wait with me, and I knew that the moment my father walked into that room, this guy was going to kill him. And I didn't know how to stop it. It was awful.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did the man look like?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't remember.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Had you been in this hotel room before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it like? Can you describe it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was dark... Dark wood, dark furniture. Sort of like a cave or a tunnel. Yeah, like a tunnel, but it wasn't scary. You could see light at both ends, like where the tunnel started and where it ended. I remember looking back and forth, trying to figure out which way was the entrance and which was the exit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anything else you remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The man was wearing shoes like yours.

situation: I continue to recall the dream and find that the killer's shoes are the same as the therapist's. I believe that the dream reflects that the therapist does not like my father, but my father is very important to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The man was wearing shoes like yours. Not those shoes. The black ones that you usually wear.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like my other ones?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not like your other shoes, they were your shoes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So this serial killer was wearing my shoes?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was you... In the hotel room. You were waiting to kill my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did I tell you why I was gonna kill him? Did your father ever show up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: no. We just sat there. We made small talk. And the whole time I was trying to figure out how to get out of there... To call somebody or something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember what this small talk was about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't... I'm not sure. Something about... It makes perfect sense, doesn't it? You're always insinuating shit about him. That he's the mystery man, that there's some big secret, that he's the person who really fucked me up. But the joke's on you, because there's nothing there. My father didn't cross the line or break any rules or any of that crap you love to throw around. You're so wrong it's ridiculous. My father has always been there for me. His work and me are the only important things in his life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you feel about his photographs?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're beautiful... If you look at them with an open mind, which of course you can't.

situation: The therapist asked me what I think about the works of the models photographed by my father, and what I think of my father's job.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He loves the human form. He believes the body can be the perfect... expression... of every human emotion and experience.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that how he speaks about his work?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you saying, Paul? That I can't form an opinion of my own father's work? You think I'm quoting him? You know, he says a lot of shrinks are failed artists or writers. Maybe you're jealous of him. He travels around the world, he works with models. Meanwhile, you're trapped in your cell with fuck-ups like me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, I'd take a fuck-up like you any day over one of those supermodels.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you wouldn't. Shut up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I would. It's true.

situation: The therapist inquired how I feel about the fact that the women my father works with during his job are nude.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, how was that for you, your father being constantly surrounded by beautiful women when you were a kid?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's an artist. It was his job. Besides, nudity was totally normal in my house. I got used to it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Nudity?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nude models. The female form. It's like drawing class 101, Paul. An artist must work from the purest inspiration. His studio was at home, so there were a lot of models walking around naked. It wasn't a big deal. We were cool.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So this was normal for you, to be exposed to adults being naked, yeah?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Exposed. Ooh, nudity. How scary. Breasts... Terrifying!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So were you ever naked around the house?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course not. Look at your face. You think that's my big secret? I saw my father naked and now I'm scarred for life? Isn't that kind of a cliche?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So your father was naked and your mother as well? Why are you laughing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother always wore her clothes,

situation: My mother didn't know about the models being nude at home during the day.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother always wore her clothes, even in the shower.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But she was perfectly comfortable with... the models?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was clueless about the whole thing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sorry, I'm having a difficult time following this. I thought you said that people were naked all the time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, not all the time. A lot of the time. During the day, while my mother was at work.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So would you say that your father was... hiding it from her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd say she was a fucking idiot who couldn't see what was right in front of her. They were having sex.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who was having sex, Sophie?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad... With the model du jour.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you know?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I saw them.

situation: I saw my father having sexual relations with a model during the day, but I did not tell my mother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I came home from school early one day. The mom who drove carpool that day had to pick us up early. I walked into my parents' bedroom and my father was there with a model.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does your father know that you saw?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah. He got up. He came over to me and just looked at me. I said something like, I thought the models only came at fixed times.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did he say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't remember. Something like, you're supposed to be at school. And then he shut the door... And locked it. I remember the sound of the latch sliding.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How old were you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Seven and a half? Why are you being so dramatic? It was no big deal. My father is an artist. They don't live like other people do. They have to be in touch with... They have to crap on conventional things in order to create.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you say it to your mother?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did your father tell you not to?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: no.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you walked away from the door knowing... you weren't supposed to say anything, that you had a secret. Maybe that's when the idea of telepathy between you and your dad began? This idea that you can understand each other without words.

situation: I think the therapist implied that I was sexually assaulted, and the therapist believes that I am hiding something.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's your big theory? After all your insinuations? Pretty lame.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You keep accusing me...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You keep suggesting that somebody crossed the line with me, that I don't have the ability to say no. You're saying that...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That I've been sexually abused.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think that's the secret I'm looking for?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm not.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think something happened to you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you listening to me? I told you nothing happened. You're the one who keeps implying...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think you were sexually abused, Sophie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Good. Now we can finally stop talking about that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why didn't you ever tell your mother what you saw?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't be an idiot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So this secret has been there between you and she all these years?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So what? I barely speak to the woman anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't think there's any connection between those two things?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't speak to her because she's pathetic.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist asks me why I didn't tell my mother about my father's affair. I believe it is not my responsibility, and my mother should find out on her own.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't speak to her because she's pathetic. She's a moron. She couldn't see what was right in front of her face. Sometimes I think she's still waiting for him, like Santa Claus or something. She would never admit it, but it's so obvious, it's pathetic.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But if you told her, she might not be waiting for him any longer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not my job to make her face reality! I'm the child. She's supposed to be smarter than me. You know, she sits there, day after day, waiting for him to come to his senses. I want to scream at her, He doesn't give a fuck about you! You're stupid. You're useless. Just get the fuck up of your clueless ass and get a life!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why didn't you tell her about his affairs?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not my fucking job!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe you didn't tell her because you were afraid. Maybe you were afraid they'd separate and it would be your fault, just like you thought that you'd ruined Cy and Darlene's marriage? Why didn't you tell your mother after they divorced?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was I supposed to do? Rub her face in it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're angry she couldn't see that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes! Fuck yes!

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist believes that deep down, I still hope for my parents to reconcile, which is why I dared not tell my mother about my father's affair. Carrying this secret has created a rift between my mother and me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sophie, you know in all the weeks that we've been in therapy, you've never once allowed yourself to be angry at your father. It's never even been a possibility for you. Why do you think that is? See, I think that your father made you his accomplice. He burdened you with this secret way too heavy for any child to carry, and he drove this wedge between you and your mother with this secret. Maybe you're afraid to get angry at him because if you did, you'd lose him for good. Maybe you never told your mother because part of you still hopes that they're gonna get back together again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know that's never going to happen. I'm not an idiot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Wouldn't have to be to believe that. I know plenty of grownups whose parents have separated 20, 30 years, who have even died... They still hope in their heart of hearts that their mother and father still share a bed in heaven.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He wouldn't be a good husband if he came back. He'd just leave her again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He left you too, didn't he?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. He just moved out. He's still my dad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course he's still your dad, but he did literally leave you, didn't he? He moved away. He's not around, he doesn't even know whether you're dead or alive.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was working.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why can't you let yourself be angry at him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why should I be angry at him?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist analyzed that my mother is a great person, and I shouldn't be angry with her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's the one who... Who pisses me off.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because she's pathetic and annoying and...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And she's always around. I can understand why you might be angry at her too, though. Cause you feel she didn't protect you from what was going on at home. But she's also a rock. She's incredibly patient. She's persistent. She's not going anywhere. She's really something when you think about it. Isn't she?

situation: I informed the therapist that I was no longer interested in gymnastics and asked for the reason. The therapist believes it's due to my childhood environment, a lack of a sense of security, and gymnastics provided me a safe haven.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's something I haven't told you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not really that interested in gymnastics anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Used to be everything to me, and now it's not.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And why do you think that is?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you tell me, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, I think that when you were growing up, there weren't enough boundaries at home. Boundaries to protect a child from... What we you, six, seven? From... things that could impact your... Your view of sex, your body, your attitudes toward men. It was also an environment where you were expected to be complicit in the lies of grownups. I think you wanted to escape, so sports became the perfect outlet for you. A place with rules and order, where discipline protected you and guided you. Gymnastics was always a place that you were able to run away to, to be in control. Maybe... Maybe you don't need to run away to that world anymore.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shit.

situation: I don't think my current attitude is good enough for gymnastics to compete for the Olympics, my therapist encouraged me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: i'll never make the olympic team now, not with that attitude.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I don't think that's necessarily true.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm gonna suck at it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you ever failed before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Never, but...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ... the times, they are a-changin'. It's from a Bob Dylan song. My gift to you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're welcome. He's an old geezer... Like you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thanks.

situation: I came to inquire about things related to my son Alex's life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Hello, excuse me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry. I didn't know which one of these doors was the right one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's okay. It's a terrible day.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Didn't want to knock on your residence.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No problem. This door is usually for people who come in. That's usually the exit door. But it doesn't... It doesn't really matter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You have an entry door and an exit door?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's for people's privacy. Some people don't like to... They don't like to run into each other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are they ashamed?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. It's just... It's protocol really. Would you like some coffee?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I'm a tea man. But no, nothing, thank you. I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Please, sit down.

situation: The therapist mentioned that there was a privacy agreement with patient Alex, but I wanted to know what happened to my son.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got a lot of questions.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sure you have. And I hope that I can answer some of them. One thing I do have to stress from the outset is that anything that is said between myself and a patient in this room... is private.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Even then the patient has died.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, even then.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I am sure we have something to talk about, Something to help me understand what happened to my son. You weren't very forthcoming about who you were when we met at the services. A friend, you said? That's hardly the case.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I didn't want to betray Alex's confidence.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel didn't hesitate in explaining exactly what your relationship to Alex was. He's very direct... Daniel. I like that about him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were you surprised to hear that Alex was in therapy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That he didn't tell me surprised me. I mean, what's the big deal?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think he didn't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We'll never know the answer to that, will we? Or I won't. Maybe that's something you discussed here.

situation: I think it's ridiculous for therapist to keep secrets, and that sharing private matters should be with one's own family, not with a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, it always puzzled me, the whole process here, you know? I mean, that... That a person is in therapy at all often is never discussed... Who the doctor is, what he's there for, how much it cost. Funny thing is that it's secrecy or misunderstandings, things never spoken that... usually land people in therapy in the first place. Isn't at ironic?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think it's about secrecy. I think it's about creating an environment where people can come and feel safe to talk about anything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Safer than with their loved ones?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sometimes it's easier to talk to somebody who's totally uninvolved in your life... Somebody objective. Somebody who has no stake in it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean like a prostitute, hmm? Someone who's paid for their intimacy and their discretion. A man should have someone to talk to who cares about him, Not someone who charges by the hour.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I really did care for Alex. And if I hadn't, I'd actually be a pretty poor therapist.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: The therapist asked how I would describe my son Alex. I think he is very creative, like his grandfather.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think Alex spoke about things in this room that he never... spoke to anyone else about?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That is usually the case with patients.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you probably know as much about him as anyone did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel that you knew your son well?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew Alex when he was... a little boy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what was he like then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, he was... quiet. Introspective. Daydreamer. Inventor. Did he ever mention that to you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He never did, no.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He invented this thing for his mother... A pan that made flipping an omelet over very easy. He worked very hard on that thing. It was really good.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So where did he get that from? Were you an inventor?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, no. No, man. I was a knucklehead. My father was an inventor. He invented this knife-sharpening machine. It didn't make very much money. He was proud of it. Alex reminded me of him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In what way?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You trying to shrink me, doctor?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just curious.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Or perhaps you can't help yourself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's probably true too.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father and Alex... had the same mannerisms, the same sense of humor.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I mentioned how my son Alex resembles his grandfather and asked the therapist about his own relationship with his father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was unsettling. When Alex was a little boy and my father had been dead almost 20 years... There he was... Sitting across the dinner table looking at me... Through me with those eyes of his on Alex's face. Is your father still living, Mr. Weston?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes. Yes, his body is in good health, But his... His mind is gone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Were you close?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We had our differences, of course. But we were close. We are close, I mean.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How often do you see him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: About once a month.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does he know you're there?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. I don't think so. But the visit is more for my sake.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you get out of it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Connection, a sense of... belonging.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you ever have conversations with him in your head? Both sides of the conversation?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes. When I was younger everything he said went in one ear, out the other. Now I hear his voice in my head Loud and clear every day.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's the sense of connection that you mentioned. That's... That's what I feel slipping away with each passing day since Alex's death.

situation: The voice of my deceased son Alex echoed in my ears, and my therapist thought I was still in pain.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That sense of... I'm trying to find his voice, you know, but... He won't talk to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If you don't mind me saying so, Mr. Prince, I think that it's still too soon. You're probably still in a state of shock. But his voice... will come back to you.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: I asked the therapist for his evaluation of my son Alex, and how he sees Alex.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I apologize for comparing what you do to, uh, prostitution. I don't believe they're the same at all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Apology accepted.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How would you describe my son Alex? I'm not asking you for a diagnosis. You don't have to tell me what he thought, just what you thought of him personally.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought that Alex was... an extremely... capable man. Strong sense of mission. A very strong sense of what was expected of him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Uh, mission or purpose?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
