situation: The therapist suggested that I forgive myself and not have to pay for my parents' actions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you really think the rash and spasms are coming from my head?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm, but that doesn't mean they're not real. But I don't think that it's-- That it's a disease.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So what do I do about it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you need to start to forgive yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Forgive myself for what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For not telling your mother about your father's affair. You know, what you have to understand is that they were gonna break up anyway no matter what you did. You are not responsible for your parents' actions. The only actions that we can control are our own. And the only power we have is how we treat other people and how we treat ourselves.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you want me to forgive myself?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: how?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Slowly. It's gonna take a while. It's taken you a few years to fall into this and it's probably gonna take you a while to get out of it. But you have to start trying now. 'cause you know something? You deserve to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Que lástima.

situation: I decided to the therapist's advice and forgive myself, and sang a Spanish song to the therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Que lástima.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: hmm?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's from a Spanish song. It means what a shame.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Ah. Que-- que lástima.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A ciertas luces pareces una estrella de cine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Wow -- my Spanish is dreadful. What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It means, In a certain light, you look like a movie star.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh. Oh. Well, gracias.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The competition is on Friday. Should I go?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think so. I think that you really want to and... I agree that you should go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have to go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mom's waiting for me in the car. She wants to take me shopping.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, shopping. Wow, that sounds rough. Listen, if you decide to compete and you start to feel anxious, I want you to call me, okay? You know, don't be shy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm never shy. Sometimes, I'm circumspect or wary, but not shy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I stand corrected. And listen, if you're up on the beam and your legs start to shake, try saying this to yourself: im making this happen. It is coming from inside me and because I am making it happen, I can make it stop.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does that really work?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mmm, I think it can, yeah. I used it on myself a few years ago and it did work.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, I'll try it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My son tells jokes to lighten the mood between my spouse and me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what's been up with you, Jake?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's been a pretty weird week since we saw you last, Paul. Very quiet around the house. Awkward. He's such a funny kid. Man, I wish you could meet him. He was telling us this joke the other day about these... These two cannibals that eat a clown. And one cannibal turns to the other and says: Does this taste funny to you? Anyway, Amy and I are laughing despite ourselves. It was very surreal.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Kids tend to do that when they sense tension. They try to get the parents to come together.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're probably right, but he shouldn't have to do it. It's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're right. It's not fair.

situation: My wife tries to reconcile with me after her affair, but I find it hard to forgive her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Amy's been trying to reach out to me this week... You know, make it all OK, the whole Ben thing, but how can you make up for something like that? To tell you the truth, it's pretty sad watching her try. When Lenny fell asleep the other night, she ran around the house, pretending to be busy with house shit, which she never does. Not saying anything, just trying to run into me. And at one point we were pretty close together in the kitchen, she tried to kiss me... And I just...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just couldn't do it. I wasn't into it. My heart wasn't there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It can be hard to relate to somebody... After something like an affair.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're telling me. Bizarre. Late that night, she had... fallen asleep watching TV and I just... I just stood there looking at her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you feel?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She sleeps with her both hands tucked under her cheek like in those kid books. You know, the way they draw the angels sleeping. She didn't look like a woman who had just fucked some other guy. She looked really beautiful. And I was thinking how easy it would be to just... go lay down next to her and put my arms around her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I couldn't.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I find it hard to forgive my wife, so I drove to my parents' house in the middle of the night. The therapist asked about the relationship between my parents and my son Lenny.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just remembered how easily she could chip away at me and lure me back in. So I jumped in my car and I got the fuck out of there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In the middle of the night?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where'd you go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: First, at Elliot's, but then I remembered he had a date. I didn't want to walk in on anything. It's been about 6 years since the guy got laid, so I just kept driving and I ended up at my parents' house. The kicker is they live about four hours away in Virginia. And it was too early when I arrived to ring the doorbell, so I just sat out front in my car and fell asleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How often do you see them, your parents?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Mom comes into town to see Lenny pretty frequently every couple of months. Maybe we go out there for the holidays a couple of times a year, not much more.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And is your father close to Lenny?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is my father close to Lenny? That's a good question. I think so. They spend time together, Lenny likes him. But it always feels finite. I can't help but get the feeling that he leaves him hanging, like he's just spent a few minutes with the neighbor's grandchild and now it's time to move on. Of course, my dad, being the narcissist that he is, is oblivious to it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Has Lenny said anything to you about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. He seems fine with it, so who knows? Maybe I'm just seeing things.

situation: My father is very capable, and my mother is also a highly educated intellectual, but I am not like my parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was asleep in the car outside their house, and all of a sudden there's this knock on the window and its wake me up. And it's a cop. And who's the cop? Mike Garnett. Went to school with me, wanted to be a cop since the 1st grade and now that's what he is. It's really funny. He fulfilled his childhood dream. I don't think I know anyone who became what they wanted to be when they were a kid. When I was growing up, in the wintertime, there was this guy and he would come over with his chainsaw, swing from tree to tree cutting branches before they froze and fell off like a fucking monkey. It was unbelievable. And he was the only guy I knew who my father didn't tell how to do his job. That's who I wanted to be.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: emm

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The old man, he's such a know-it-all. The funny part is though, he does know it all. He can tell you the exchange rate for a Guyanese dollar, how to cook a freshwater salmon in a clay oven, or the history of the silk worm.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does he write encyclopedias?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You'd think, right? No, he's a college professor.

situation: My parents are both highly educated intellectuals, but I am not. I have stopped studying since graduating from high school.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mom too. Intellectuals. Big readers, unlike me. I don't read. I don't think I've read a book since I left high school.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does that mean you don't or you won't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I haven't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really? I remember once I misquoted Roland Barthes and you corrected me. Where did that come from?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I grew up in a house where everyone was reading at dinner. That shit was everywhere. Any parrot could pick it up and spit it back verbatim. That's what happens when your dad is an emeritus professor of Renaissance studies and your mother teaches classics... Greek and Hebrew. But I don't read. I mean not literally. Obviously I read. I read music, manuals, headlines, but I just... I don't know. I'm not like them.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: I'm very good at crossword puzzles. When I was younger and not reading, I would play the guitar by myself, smoke marijuana, and talk to myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I do kick ass at crossword puzzles though. You do those?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not very good. Sunday New York Times crossword does me in every week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a tough one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know to do crossword puzzles, you need to have an extensive vocabulary, no? It's kinda hard to reconcile the idea of somebody who doesn't read with somebody who's really good at crossword puzzles.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's nothing to reconcile. I'm good at it and reading makes me restless and bored.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So did you acquire your love of crossword puzzles from your parents?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really. My mom's all right at them. My dad sucks.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you do as a kid when everybody else was doing all this... reading?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Play guitar, collect baseball cards, smoke pot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did that get you into trouble?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really. Nobody noticed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Nobody noticed that you got high? So who were you getting high with?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Myself mostly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So would you say that you had a lonely childhood?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nah. Why? It was okay. I talked to myself a lot.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I really enjoy communicating with my son, but I rarely communicate with my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what one of my favorite things in the world is? Talking to Lenny. And we talk about anything but mainly, we talk about sports. And he can just go off. Aluminum bats versus wood... Fuck, anything. That kid has a brain like a computer. He's not even 10 and he can list off all of Boog Powell's stats from the 1970 world series. That's just amazing to me. I never get tired of hearing that little fucker talk. You get like that with your kids?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not so much anymore because they're older, but with my youngest, yeah, I still do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And how old is he?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He's nine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just like Lenny.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you have that kind of relationship with your father as a kid?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I avoided talking to my father when I was a kid. It just wasn't worth it. He was the kind of guy who would wince if you said sure instead of surely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you find it easier to talk to your mom?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She wasn't as bad, but what was frustrating was... she would always defer to him on everything. It's like she saw him as this hotshot professor at another level from everyone. He got tenure at 33 and it just wouldn't occur to her that she could have an opinion different from his... than his. If you were him, you would have just corrected me on my grammar. If you were he. Hey, they didn't beat me, right? It could've been a lot worse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's true. It doesn't... It doesn't mean it wasn't difficult.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My brother is a writer, but I am not. The therapist thinks I like to belittle my own knowledge and intelligence.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So when did you start to write?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't write. My brother Nathan is the writer. He's a novelist. He was just shortlisted for some prize last year, some big national award. I can't even remember the name. I'm sure my parents remember it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you're a writer too. Or don't you consider songwriting to be writing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, sure, I do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Some of my favorite writers are actually songwriters, people like Dylan, Cohen, John Lennon.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hey, I agree with you, Paul. I would put Dylan on par with Walt Whitman, Ezra Pound, Langston Hughes. Just try telling that to my family.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, for somebody who is not a great reader, you seem to be pretty familiar with great poets.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody's really familiar with Pound. They just fake it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I get the feeling you like to play down your knowledge, your intelligence.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. It's just my folks' world. I guess some of it has rubbed off on me. But it's just not me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your parents ever expressed an interest in what you might do for a living?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad probably wanted me to be some kind of academic. It's the family business after all.

situation: As a child, I gave up on school because I couldn't meet my father's expectations, but my mother would secretly help me prepare for exams, although she was afraid of my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad probably wanted me to be some kind of academic. It's the family business after all. But what did he expect? I don't know. I think he gave up the dream on me pretty early after I flunked out of high school.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Which do you think came 1st, your father's low expectations or your low grades?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What you meaning?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Often with expectations, there's a self-fulfilling prophecy. Maybe you decided earlier on you couldn't match up to his expectations and so you gave up trying.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Could be. My mom was always trying to get me interested. She'd help me study for tests on the sly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: On the sly?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, it pissed my dad off. He thought she was spoon-feeding me things I should've known or figured out by myself. And she was terrified he'd find out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was she... generally intimidated by him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're so right, Abe. I never looked at it that way, Abe. Yeah, it made me want to scream.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: The therapist asked what my parents think of my wife Amy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: One thing you can say about me, is I sure as hell didn't marry my mother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean you didn't marry a woman who was intimidated by you. So how do your parents feel about Amy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's a successful businesswoman, she's got an MBA, they fucking love that she went to grad school. Their high-school dropout of a son married a hotshot businesswoman.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's interesting you use the same word to describe your father, hot shot. Do you think that they're alike in other ways?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're not. They're total opposites. He's all rumpled corduroy, stains on his shirt, and she's, well... Hell, you know what Amy is... Meticulous, put together, very materialistic. She loves her stuff. You know, when we met, I was crashing in this crappy apartment over a garage. I think it turned her on. And the woman had never fucked on a bed without a box spring, and... she liked it. Coming down from her pedestal, hang with the riffraff.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you feel like your father was also on a pedestal?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, let's get off this, alright? This is not why I'm here.

situation: I am afraid that divorce will result in losing custody of my son; my wife Amy is very unstable, and suddenly the power went out.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't have that many people to talk too right now. And I'm scared shitless of losing Lenny in some custody battle. Amy is... unstable. This is the second time she's getting a divorce after having an affair, and I think she's gonna fuck him up. You said yourself she needs losers around. I think she's gonna teach him to be a loser. She's damaged, Paul. She's fucked up. I haven't gotten much right in my life except that kid, and that kid is... What the fuck? You don't pay your electric bill or something?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Looks like it's out on the entire street. You want to go on?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can see you fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're sure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For the first time... It really feels like we're splitting up.

situation: I told the therapist that I felt this time was different from the past, and that my wife and I were getting divorced. I need help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No matter how many times we've talked about it, or... brought it up, it's never felt so... Real.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think it feels different this time? The last time you were here, you implied that you'd fallen out of love with Amy. Would you still say that's true?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. How would I know? What does it feel like? I've only been in love with one girl... her. I've never fallen out of love. Tell me what it feels like and I'll tell you if I'm feeling it. Have you ever felt it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's a huge sadness there. Cause you know what's been lost. And you begin to lose the desire to... connect. Maybe you should ask your father. He's the guy who knows everything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did I tell you what he said when I told him my marriage was over? This isn't entirely unexpected, is it? He expects me to fail. Every time. At everything.

situation: The therapist asked why I suddenly drove back home; it's because I wanted to talk to my mother about the divorce.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why did you go home, Jake?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. It's an extend. I just started driving, that's where I ended up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This is therapy. We don't believe in accidents here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Alright, fine. I'm about to be a single dad. Maybe I... Maybe I just felt like I want to talk to my mum.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or your dad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Have you been listening to a word I say? I can't fucking stand my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's interesting that you use the same words to describe Amy and your father. Hot shot. But you keep insisting that they're nothing like each other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're not. Where're you going with this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look. You married an intelligent overachieving woman who seems absolutely certain of her... authority in the world. The criticism and disappointment that you got from your father do me feel that that's what you get from Amy. Your relationship with Amy's falling apart, so you get in a car and you drive for 4 h to Virginia and you find yourself... by accident... outside your father's house?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I was going back to the source? Jesus, that's sick.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's not sick. The more we open ourselves to the... The therapeutic process, the more we can examine these...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: More therapy. What're you talking about? I need that like I need a hole in the head.

situation: I don’t want to mess up my marriage; I need help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what? Who cares why I went home that night. What is it matter how my parents talk at the fucking dinner table, alright? I've learned from my father's mistakes and I'm a much better father than he is. I don't want to fuck it up. I don't want to fuck my kid up. I need... I need the help. I need your help. I need help. All the help I can get. Or some road map, you know? I feel scared.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wish I could say it was that simple. That I could just give you a road map, a book of instructions, but... unfortunately, life isn't like that. But you know, that old saying that... a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Or in my case... two steps up and one step back. You know, if this was a movie... the lights would come on, right now. If this were a movie. Were a movie.

situation: I feel helpless and futile about Alex's passing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you think our sessions with Kate went?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd say they were chaotic. I was a little annoyed with you over that but I suppose I'm partly at fault too. And I also think that she felt sandwiched between two therapists. I do have to say though that you did manage to make connections that resonated with both of us, especially with Kate. Whether anything is gonna come off that I don't... I don't really know. You know who I envy? Writers. let them live or die, or let them be happy or unhappy, let them be failures or successes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wanna write everybody's story for them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I really think I'd be a shitty writer. I'd want to give everybody a happy ending.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Pual, I'm very sorry about your patient.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Alex, Yeah... Thanks. Not the ending I would have written for him. The funeral, Jesus Christ. I'd forgotten how awful funerals are. That dreadful sense that... That in the end, there's only silence... You think as therapists, we'd have better tools to walk through it. Well, I don't. I feel the same sense of... futility and hopelessness as the next guy. You know what's also interesting is seeing the relatives of patients you've treated. Their participance in the stories that you've heard a dozen of times, the father, the son, the brother, whoever. We think we know them. But we don't really know them at all. We know reactions of them, the versions of them idealized or vilified.... I was really struggling to reconcile this image that I had of Alex's wife with the woman that I saw there. He always described her as a demanding, exacting a constant source of pressure in his life. But I looked over and I just saw this... broken woman. She seems so soft and gentle. 'Cause I'll never really know her now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does that bother you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It does bother me. I ask myself all the time if I actually know what I think I know about my patients' lives.

situation: I don't really understand the lives of my patients, nor do I understand them very well.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That couple, for example. The one who were trying to have the baby. Amy. I don't think she can ever really be known. I mean, there are certain patterns that identified themselves from her past. But I cannot... shrink her. She's too complicated. And then I say to myself: Do I really know any of these people? Or are they all just one big fiction that I've constructed in my head, you know? Sometimes I dream about the family members of patients that I'm treating. People I've never met.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's curious. Apart from your.... intense connection with your patients, you're also now talking about I don't know, longing for your patients' family and friends.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean by that, a longing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe that's not the right word.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you mean curiosity about the lives of other people? Isn't that an aspect of what we do? It's just... It's curiosity. We're supposed to be fascinated by how people behave. At least... At least I think so.

situation: The death of my patient Alex had a great impact on me, and I thought about whether therapy could help the patient's life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Alex's death left me with this very strong feeling that I was like... a repository, really. A trustee. The things that he never told anybody else, his private thoughts. They've stayed with me, they're inside me. A big part of his life is is in vault I have inside me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. A part of his life, maybe, but not necessarily a big part. You were his therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Only his therapist. I know you've always been of two minds in relation to this that therapy is more than a discipline, that it's actually a religion, but you also say we're therapists, so we can't really... run our patients lives for them. As soon as they walk out the door, they're on their own, yeah?

situation: I think that patient Alex feels very guilty for following military orders and killing children, which led to his accident.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How would you describe Alex's state of mind when you last saw him?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd say he was pretty fragile, if I remember well, yeah. The ironic thing is that we'd really made some good progress, and he just... seemed to regress. It was like... He felt that he was so close to a breakthrough that it scared him. It was too much, and he just... He turned away from it really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you feeling in any way responsible for his death?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I'm friendly with a psychiatrist that consults for the Navy, Alfonso Casilles. You remember him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I asked him if he could find out anything. He said vertigo. It means that there's nothing wrong with the equipment.

situation: I think that patient Alex feels very guilty for following military orders and killing children, which led to his accident.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They were doing some kind of combat exercise. The plane he was chasing descended, Alex went into what they call vertigo and lost control. That's their... official conclusion. I think he killed himself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How can you be sure of that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, his life was a tragedy from the second he was born. His childhood, his relationship with his father, up to when he pushed the button and killed a room full of kids. How do you live with that? Even with the gadgets that they have now, they reduce people to dots on a video screen. All the spin from the Navy, none of it made any difference to him. It didn't work on him. He felt every single one of those deaths, I know he did. So many expectations... The best and the brightest. He was. He was... so strong physically, handsome, intelligent. Under all that... kind of posturing and male posing that he did, he was really... He was a good guy. Charming.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: I think the patient Alex committed suicide and the therapist asks why.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was endearing, you know. He looked and he sounded like what they call a winner. Suddenly, he becomes a murderer. How do you reconcile that? I think that's what really killed him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Endearing? I have never heard you talk about him like that. Quite the opposite.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Actually, he was kind of a funny guy. He was... I don't know. Am I already beginning to... idealizing? Yeah, maybe.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, it's not uncommon, after such a shock.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He gave me the chance to stop him from flying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Literally? Did he really offer that or are you projecting?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He asked me directly, Should I fly?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told him I was very concerned about his... About his state of mind.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that clearly?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But he wanted me to say it unequivocally. Do not fly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's not your place, Paul. A patient can't ask you to take his life into your hands. It's not your place to say; Don't fly. Anymore than it's your place to say to that couple, Have an abortion. Or to Laura, Marry or don't marry your fiancé.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I should have sent the Navy an evaluation. Guilt-ridden. Wants to punish himself. Shouldn't fly.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: Alex's father came to me, thinking that I shouldn't help Alex to confront and analyze his issues.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Alex's dad came into the office to... To talk. So I had this poor guy yelling at me, saying that his son's repression was what had kept him alive all the time and that therapy, the stuff that he was doing with me, was... The therapy was what had killed him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh God, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Up in the air at Mach 5, he's not supposed to have emotions. He's not supposed to think. That's actually why he crashed.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: As a therapist, I was confused about helping the patient Alex face his problems. I didn't know how to treat patients and let them face their problems.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was very different from what I imagined also. He was riddled, you know, with his own guilt. Actually, he did make a couple of good points. He said things were in the unconscious for a reason because the mind can not live or breathe or take a single step if everything that lies dormant in it were... out there in daylight, fully lay out. That a fully conscious human being would be paralyzed, would be like a cripple. Alex didn't need to be conscious, but just merely efficient.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you really accept that? That life is better lived unexamined. And when... anxiety and fear and pain bubble up from below, how can that be dealt with, except by looking at it? Except by analyzing it? We don't run the show, Paul. I sometimes think that therapists can start to imagine they're like writers, you know, that they can control the outcome. We don't live their lives for them, we don't even live them with them.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know that you want to believe that we really do have an influence that's always positive.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We help people to understand.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Understand what they're feeling and after that, if they make a wrong turn, then it's not our fault, it's human error. But... Anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who're you really angry at?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Myself, obviously. You. Every therapist from Freud to Mitchell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because we force patients to look at themselves and pat ourselves on the back for it.

situation: I have doubts about whether I, as a therapist, can truly help patients.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because we force patients to look at themselves and pat ourselves on the back for it. Then we say to them, Here's what's wrong with you, now off you go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you feel this way before Alex died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: More or less, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Has it been on your mind recently in any other context?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm asking. Have... other patients, other than Alex made you think like this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're insinuating.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm just trying to get a sense, a history... of these feelings about psychotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean, if I've been wondering for a while if our... profession is actually helpful to people? Yes, I have. I think about it every day.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you feel you're not able to help your patients?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The gymnast, for example, Sophie? Honestly, I feel like she made a lot of progress. We connected, there was a bound between us. But I think it was the personal relationship that helped her, not the therapeutic process. You know, maybe Yallom is right. Maybe it is the relationship that actually heals. But that other couple, Jake and Amy, I can not tell you, honestly, if they're better off together or apart. I don't know if I helped them at all. Anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you okay, Paul?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think I'm tired, Gina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Put your feet up.

situation: I discussed my understanding of psychology and my views on it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know Alex said... He was talking about... vertigo and he said that when it happens, they're supposed to trust their instruments and not their senses.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How do you know that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I once had a boyfriend who was a commercial pilot. This is before David. He taught me that. Among other things. Yes, Paul. I have been more than a sleepy spider.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So it seems. Anyway, I think it's the opposite for a psychologist. I think we'd be far more effective if we relied less on instruments and theories and books and more on our own instincts.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So all your training, all your knowledge can lead you astray?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think so.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel this generally or about certain patients in particular?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean? What is it, Gina?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You've got that look of yours.

situation: I was disgusted with my therapist's performance and critical of conventional psychology.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You've got that look of yours.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What look is that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You have the look that says I have a theory.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Regarding what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, Gina, cut the crap. Just tell me what you think.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just sitting here, listening to you. I'm listening to your newfound theories about the uselessness of psychotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Certain patients in particular? Come on. We're back to Laura, again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are we?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think everything is a reaction to Laura.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's a reaction?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Me criticizing psychology, dismissing theories. You think I'm making an excuse. Even Alex getting killed, that's an excuse, right? Psychology is collapsing so I might as well sleep with Laura. I think that's kind of the way you're...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what I'm thinking?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Am I wrong?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you guess what I'm thinking it's always about Laura. Like I assume that everything you say is connected to her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're the one who brought her up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not talking about Laura.

situation: I was angry and thought the therapist was out of touch with reality.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm talking about the fact that... I am having trouble lately believing in this... religion of yours.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of mine?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think traditional psychology answers anything anymore. You have two extremes, right? You have pop psychology, you've got these celebrity therapists writing best-sellers, getting on talk shows, making some miserable couple wipe on television. It's kind of a pornography. And then, on the other hand, you've got the experts. Psychologists like you, orthodox. Authority figures. Everything under control and supervised, examined under a bright light, examined to death. Completely and utterly divorced from real life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Am I divorced from real life?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Gina, you've never lived outside this room! The Institute, the graduate program, David's world and after David... died, you locked yourself up in here. I mean, it's a beautiful room. Look at it. Beautifully appointed, everything is in its place. But you sit in here, and what do you do? You write fiction! About how life could have been, should have been.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what I'm writing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just ask yourself, as a therapist, can you really help anybody, if you live in a bubble?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So now, I'm a sleepy spider in a bubble?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, I don't want to upset you Gina, I...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You won't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I forgot, of course... You don't get upset. You never lose it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've lost it here with you, several times in the past few weeks. Why are you trying to provoke me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I am not trying to provoke you. I just don't want to end up like this. Is this it? Is this how therapists live out their lives?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You are perverse.

problem_type: Self-Assessment or Assessment of Others or evaluation of others
situation: I hurt the therapist because of my assessment of  her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, something real and powerful came into your life, and you never gave it a chance. Not for Charlie's sake or for yours. I know you said it was because he was a patient. But you know what I think? I think it was bullshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, be careful.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You were terrified. Charlie told me that you were the biggest loss in his life. That his whole life could have been different.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You have no idea what you're talking about. And after all these years, Paul, you don't know me. You wanna know what I struggle with? It's not that I'm too reserved, too detached, it's that I'm too emotional. I'm impulsive and emotional. And I give myself over right away. And passionately. I pour myself out. Can't you see that I'm protecting myself? Because I'm afraid I get carried away, I won't be able to think, I won't be able to analyze, I won't be able to work. You've created this cold version of me that's limiting and castrating. Because, when you're arguing with me, you want to see yourself as battling the forces of repression. And if the truth is that I am an emotional person who has to rein herself in, it doesn't fit with what you need now, does it? Of course, I wanted Charlie. He was the most alive person I ever met. I wanted to sleep with him, I wanted to eat him up. But I didn't. And not because of ethics. I may have told him that it was because he was a patient. But the real reason was David. Even though David cheated on me for... however many years. I knew that all along. He was really shitty at hiding it. I didn't sleep with Charlie because... that's not who I wanted to be. I loved David, and I loved the life we had. And who I was with him. I loved myself with David. David's Gina. And you know what? When I was standing over... his grave at funeral, I felt... if I was magically reborn, I would choose him all over again. For all his faults, he allowed me to be who I wanted to be. I'm surprised you didn't see it. How crazy I was about him. He was everything.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I never heard you say it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh shit! Everything has to be said? Then now, I have to sit here and listen to your crappy, nearsighted, self-involved theories about my life. Oh, God. Listen to us. You know, I slap you, and you punch me. Sometimes I tell myself it's constructive but, you know, I'm not so sure anymore, maybe we should stop. You've been fighting me for two months. Saying Laura, Laura, Laura. And you've been waiting for this imaginary Gina of yours to jump in and stop you? I'm not what's stopping you. You're fighting yourself. It's up to you, it's like Alex. You carefully looked at his life, you opened doors for him. You gave him insight. But his life was his. And he decided to fly. Now, you decide. Perhaps, you're right. Maybe love can bloom in a therapist office. Ethics and rules, love is bigger than any rules. And what do I know? Maybe she's your David. Maybe you can only be the Paul you want to be... with her. So, go to her. Find out. But please, stop comparing your life to mine. Stop using Charlie against me. I'm sorry he was hurt by what happened. But I never loved him. Not for a day. I loved David. So, never talk to me about Charlie again, am I clear?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.text: I really like your office.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: D.I.Y.?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you do it yourself or did you use an interior decorator?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, no, I...

dialogue.text: So this is all you? I'm impressed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you. So, April... Well, maybe you can tell me a little bit about yourself.

My parents are both alive and still married to each other. I have a brother... Daniel. He's a year and a half younger. We're pretty close. I'm single... recently. Very recently. We were together since the first week at Pratt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So is... Is that what you've come to talk about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My breakup? I wish. No, my breakup was... really fine, totally amicable. Kyle was really incredibly civil about the whole thing. We're still good friends. And his new girlfriend's just... delightful. And her father owns five buildings on Park Avenue, so... that's nice. I'm sorry, I'm really bad at talking about myself. You're gonna have to ask me questions or something. Are you that kind of shrink?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can be.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I found your name online...

situation: The therapist told me I didn't need to constantly self-censor for his feelings or apologize frequently.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Pratt listserv. I wanted somebody close to school who actually takes my health plan. Nobody had commented on your page. There's a space where patients can recommend or not recommend. Yours was empty.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's probably 'cause I've just recently moved to the area.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I assumed it was a new practice. I thought you'd be younger.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you prefer a younger therapist?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, actually. You seem great. How's business? Hard? Why'd you move? I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I just can't help but notice that this is the third time that you have... That you've apologized to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not really sorry. I was just being polite.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: OK, I just want you to know that you don't have to apologize for anything in here... Anything that you say. You can't... You can't offend me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, of course you can, but... I can take it. What I mean is you don't have to censor yourself to spare my feelings. So is this your first time meeting with a psychologist?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I saw somebody at school.

situation: I talked about my therapy experience with Jenny.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They give you 9 weeks for free over the course of the school year, so...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Nine weeks, that's... that's not long.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It would've been plenty if she hadn't been such a fucking idiot. First of all, Jennifer... was barely older than me. One of those girls who... You could just tell she became a therapist because she didn't know what else to do with her life, like she woke up one morning and thought, I look like I'm a good listener and I have nothing really to say. I know! I'll be a therapist. No offense.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's fine. That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was just waiting for some... rich doctor in a bad marriage to crawl into her office and fall in love with her so she could give up the whole charade. I could just tell wen I was sitting there in front of her she was thinking, This girl is a complete waste of time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what told you that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. It was just this feeling I had, this... polite glaze in her eye. Also, she told me the same story twice, which was pretty disheartening.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In the same session?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, two different sessions.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you went to see her again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I figured I owed it to her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you mean that you owed it to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was a nice person.

dialogue.text: She was a nice person. She was trying.

dialogue.text: So what was the story, the one that she told you twice?

dialogue.text: It's not significant. I mean, It's not even a story. It's more of a joke. You probably know it.

dialogue.text: Maybe not. Try me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's the one about the hick who comes to New York... and... Everyone's moving really fast. Nobody gives him the time of day. Taxis cut him off. People try to pick his pocket. dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've heard it, yeah. It's a... It's a classic.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, she told it to me twice, and it wasn't funny the first time.

dialogue.text: When I didn't go back, she called me like... 87 times. I was like, Take a hint, lady.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How many phone calls does a person need to ignore before you realize they don't want to talk to you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you never spoke to her again after you decided not to continue therapy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't have anything to say to her. I just didn't want to come back to therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I just wonder why you felt that you couldn't just... just tell her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't want to hurt her feelings. The... Okay. First of all, the woman was borderline stalking me. I've had friends who've gone to therapy at school and... And if you quit, they're supposed to call you once, send you a letter and that's it.

situation: The therapist said he wanted to try to understand what I was saying, but I said I wasn't trying to tell the therapist anything in particular.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Jennifer was way over the line. Second of all, she was an idiot. And third of all, do you know her or something?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I don't think so. Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because you seem really invested in my relationship with her and the whole reason I came to you was because I didn't think that you knew anybody that I know.

dialogue.text: Dude, back up. I wasn't trying to tell you anything. You're the one Who brought her up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can I ask you if... If anything else happened in those sessions that might have disturbed you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh my god. I just told you the woman had oatmeal between her ears. She barely noticed me. dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think we've been wasting our time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course you don't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.text: How many people come to you with like

dialogue.text: In the army. He's supposed to be retired, but... Now he's working With the V.A., and they're so understaffed, it's impossible to get him on the phone. Anyway, where am I?

dialogue.text: Right. So I couldn't reach my dad and then... I started having these awful night sweats, so I went back to the center and guess what they did.

dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who would become hysterical if you told them? Your mother? Your father? And your brother?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel doesn't get hysterical.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel doesn't get hysterical. Violent, but not hysterical.

dialogue.text: Violent against whom?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? No, nobody. Himself. Don't worry about it...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You seem to me to be really... independent. And I can imagine that the idea of... accepting treatment... putting yourself in somebody else's hands... I can imagine that that would be kind of scary.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just told you I want to explore my options... Meditation, yoga...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These are good Stress-Relievers, but they're not gonna stop the progress of this disease.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not according to Western medicine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.text: What? Socially, a bit. This isn't lung cancer.

dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.text: I just don't like her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could that possibly be because she was telling you that you do have cancer?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just told you I want to look into alternative medicine, maybe a homeopath.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just told you I want to look into alternative medicine, maybe a homeopath.

dialogue.text: Do you see any pattern between going to different therapists and going to different doctors? Did you tell the other therapist about your disease? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: And how could you tell that?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, I've been thinking about that story. The man who needs assistance... dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was just a joke.

dialogue.text: But I'm just wondering if she told it twice for a reason, April. Is it possible, do you think, that she really was listening to you? She was a moron. That might be true, but she may have been trying to tell you that it's okay to rely on other people, that it's okay to ask for help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Everybody at some point in their lives needs help, and I think that you need help now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You haven't heard a word I've said.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you need to have a conversation that takes place outside your own head. I think that you need to talk to your oncologist. dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just stop it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're at stage three.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Stop it. Stop it. Stop it.

dialogue.text: How dare you tell me what to do? You do not know me. What, did you formulate your little theory as soon as I walked in? Young girl, cancer... This is an easy one. You have no idea what I am capable of.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're right, I don't. Would you like to tell me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I... I have to go... Our time's up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let me think about it.

dialogue.text: How is friday... Friday afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I actually... I don't have my schedule this week. I'll call you when I get back to the dorm.

dialogue.text: So I hear.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... What about the session?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll call you, okay?

dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.text: What I already know?

dialogue.text: No, that's not what I meant. You're in a different line of work. So, tabula rasa? Really?

dialogue.text: Is there something you would have liked me to know about you?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, sit. It's okay. I trust you. You should feel honored. I have people working for me who've spent years trying to earn my trust.

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I just know that you run a company, and... which leads me to believe that you're in charge of a lot of people who I'm sure need all kinds of things from you.

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: First off, it wasn't my idea to come here.

dialogue.text: It wasn't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It does?

dialogue.text: You've already mentioned her twice, both times referring to how she takes care of you. You seem to... You seem to appreciate her a great deal.

dialogue.text: Who was your psychopharmacologist?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you kidding? That's all I need now.

dialogue.text: The headline, Embattled C.E.O. under psychiatric care. I went to my internist, had him put the prescriptions in my wife's name. That way They couldn't be traced to me.

dialogue.text: I thought you said that coming here was your wife's idea.

dialogue.text: Only an hour?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's how I got where I am.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It wasn't because I was smarter than the other guys. It's because I could work twice as hard twice as long. Connie used to call me Superman. But now I'm just lying in bed. I'm not sleeping. I'm not working.

dialogue.text: When did your insomnia begin?

dialogue.text: What difference does that make?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It just might give me a clearer picture of any underlying problem there might be.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure. I know the book. But I think you should know that the kind of therapy that I practice, It's not a quick fix. It's a process. And eventually change happens, but it does take time.

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I think I do. I think what you're saying is, this isn't a casual matter for you. That the stakes are pretty high, and that before you invest your time in this, you want to be sure that I really can help you. All right?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So, blink test.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So, blink test. Help me. What's going on?

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.text: And when did your insomnia begin?

dialogue.text: You sure you're not just trying to get me in here for more sessions?

dialogue.text: Would you care to share it?

dialogue.text: With you? That's kind of what happens in here. I'm supposed to tell you everything that pops into my head? I just thought, I'll sleep when I'm dead.

dialogue.text: Please.

dialogue.text: I could use your expert opinion.

dialogue.text: Hi, dad. Rwanda is hard. I've never worked so hard in my life and understood so little. We've set up a rape clinic in the village of... I'm not even going to try to pronounce that. dialogue.text: She sounds like an extraordinary woman.

situation: I wanted to go to Africa to rescue my daughter, but the therapist thought I should trust my daughter to take care of herself.

dialogue.text: I should go get her out, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, get her out?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She is in some kind of trouble. This is obviously a cry for help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you telling me that if... you received an email like that from your daughter from some rape clinic in Rwanda, you wouldn't be on the first plane to Africa? There's a fine line between bravery and stupidity. I can't sit here and wait for her to be kidnapped and dismembered.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where did you say she was staying?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't. She's living in Kigali. And the clinic's somewhere in the countryside. Kigali...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's the capital, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? You think that makes it safe? Have you ever been to Africa? Well, I have, and let me tell you, what we consider stable here and what they consider secure are two very different things, my friend.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: They're two very different things here as well.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come again?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Stability and security. They are two very different concepts.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: OK, fellow.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, your daughter sounds... very stable. From a psychological perspective, given the... situation that she's in, she sounds remarkably healthy. She obviously feels very deeply and she has a very lucid way of expressing herself. And it leads me to believe that you should just... trust her. And trust her to take care of herself. As for her security.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Unless you've been there, you have no idea what it's like.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I became furiously upset over my daughter's situation and left.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you have a daughter?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If you're asking me if I'd be worried, if I had a daughter in Kigali, I have to say that I would be.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And you wouldn't go and get her out?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't say what I would or what I wouldn't do in your position.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you can imagine it, can't you? Come on, just give me an honest answer. I'm paying for your opinion, aren't I?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In a sense. But we are different people with different experiences. I'm wondering why, Walter, it's important... for you that I back you up on this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need your goddamn permission. I asked you for something very simple. I have insomnia. It's a real problem, a concrete problem that prevents me from functioning. I came here and I said, tell me what to do. Mental exercises, breathing techniques? Now you've got me... reading my daughter' private emails to you. I don't even know you. How much do I owe you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you okay? Answer me, please. Are you on medication? Do you have a doctor I can call?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just... give me some air. You're okay, Walt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's okay. Breathe. That's it. Are you sure you're okay to get up? OK, let me help you. You feel okay? You can stay for as long as you like.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you, I'm fine now. Listen, I'm sorry if I gave you a scare back there. It's not a problem. I knew it would go away. They always do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Has this happened before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They go away.

situation: The therapist persuaded me that Alex's death had nothing to do with me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You've done a nice job on the place.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I tried to warm it up a bit. Sit down.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Listen, thanks for taking the time out to see me. I know you're really... I know you're really busy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd always see you. So I've been worried about you. I haven't heard from you for a while.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I know. I'm not so great at keeping in touch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I know you had your reasons.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A lot's happened, you know? Did my lawyer call you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, he did. I'm so sorry, Paul. To have a patient die is terrible. But then to have the family sue you is...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did he say that he wants you to testify?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He did. I'm going to be deposed. Although I'm not sure how much help I can be.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what they want me to kind of suss out from you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't really talk much about Alex until after he died.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told them you weren't in the room. You couldn't possibly know whether or not I gave him the proper care.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't keep any notes, did you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need notes. You don't need notes. Was it my not taking notes that killed him? I haven't taken notes in 15 years, Gina. Should we put all the rest of my patients on suicide watch?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you call it a suicide?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Isn't that what everybody thinks?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, Paul, he died. That's all anybody can know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He either killed himself or I killed him. Take your pick.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Whatever happened between you and Alex in treatment, you didn't kill him. You were trying to help him. He left therapy. His plane crashed. He died. Those things occurred in a sequence, but they are not causally related.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know you know that do. I'm just saying it so you can hear it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what? I knew that too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When someone dies, you want an explanation. But it doesn't mean there is one. I don't know who that could be. Sorry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry, Gina. I left my glasses.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I met an old friend, and I was happy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry, Gina. I left my glasses.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, come in. I didn't see them, but take a look.

dialogue.text: Paul. Tammy. How are you? Good. And you? I barge right in. That's me. I'm sorry.

dialogue.text: I left my glasses, or at least I hope I left them here. There they are. Here you go. Thanks. Imagine, after all these years. Yes, it's been a long time. You look great. You too. I'm sorry. I should've called. Bye. Bye.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: See you next week. It's nice to see you smile.

dialogue.text: I keep forgetting how small this town is. That's Tammy Kent, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I am.

situation: I said I had never been alone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought you were a writer now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just the one book. But people seemed to like it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I saw the reviews. They more than liked it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't get a chance to read it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To tell you the truth, Gina, I don't think I'm ready to read it yet. You know what I mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I do. I enjoyed writing, but I feel like I've had enough time alone for now. Have you ever lived by yourself?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is the first time in for... forever that I've lived alone. Can you believe it? I'm 53 years of age and I've never lived by myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It takes some getting used to. But there are good things about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Gina, about this lawsuit...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What I'm going to tell them is that you did everything you could to help this patient in treatment, and that if you had felt he was in any danger, you would've tried anything to keep him from flying again. You think that'll help?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think it matters what you say.

situation: I and the therapist discussed the case, hypothesizing the outcome.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're gonna have their experts. And they won't know what they're talking about either.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What? They won't know what they're talking about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The whole case is gonna be decided by people who have no idea what went on in the room. Then the ethics board are gonna take away my license because it's the cheapest way to settle the thing. I don't have the money to fight it. If the jury awards them any more than the $3 million the insurance will cover, I'm gonna have o declare bankruptcy. I'll lose the apartment in Brooklyn and anything I have left after child support and alimony.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Brooklyn? You moved to Brooklyn? And Kate and the kids are still here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what? The way I look at it is, they can have my license. They can have my practice. I'm an educated man. I can do something respectable, or not. I just don't care. I don't care anymore. The truth is, I'm just fucking sick of sitting in a chair day after day after day listening to people's problems.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, boy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sorry. Amtrak dads. I see the kids on weekends.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must be hard.

situation: I explored why I went into psychotherapy, discussing my children and my love life, as well as my desire to be alone.

dialogue.text: I need some clarity in my life, Gina. I need you to explain how I let this... whatever you call it... love for Laura, blind me to the needs of my patient. Alex used Laura to get me. dialogue.text: Your love.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All right, my love for Laura, which, by the way, I never got to express physically or... My love for this...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Beautiful.

dialogue.text: I'm sorry. When you called, you asked if we could talk. This is how friends talk.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God. Would you stop?

dialogue.text: About all what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Everything. Everything in my life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't know how you feel?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know how I feel.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And that's why you're here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I need your help, Gina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So when you stopped Alex's therapy...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, he stopped it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, he stopped it. He showed up at my door in a uniform. He'd already made a decision.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, when he stopped therapy, did you feel that the therapy had failed?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Good.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He came to me because he was afraid to fly. And he stopped therapy because he felt that he was ready go back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you met his goals for the treatment. And did you have different goals for his treatment?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what were your goals?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I hoped that... I hoped that he'd be able to forgive himself for...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For what he did. He dropped a bomb on a school.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right. And Was he able to forgive himself?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Do people ever forgive themselves really? I know we talk about it all the time, but do people ever really do it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes, yeah. How long does it take?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you... talking about something you're not able to forgive yourself for?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What, like breaking up my marriage, destroying my kids' lives, wrecking my career, not being able to save my mother and not paying attention to my father?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That would about cover it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you laughing at me? Why not? We should both laugh. But I can't. So you go ahead, laugh at my mess of a life.

dialogue.text: Was she?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And even before that, she was the only one who knew...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who knew?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Her family lived down the hallway from us. And the night my mother was... She went to the hospital... Anyway.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let's not talk about Tammy Kent. Besides, she is... She's your patient.

dialogue.text: So, can we go back to the lawsuit? After Alex's funeral, nothing more happened between you and Laura?

dialogue.text: No, I couldn't even... I couldn't even think about Laura without blaming myself for his death. If I hadn't been in love with her, if I hadn't been jealous of him, if I hadn't been competing with him for her love...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: you might have saved him. Is that what you think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I guess so.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You guess so?

dialogue.text: Isn't that what we all want to do, save our patients?

dialogue.text: Is that what you want?

dialogue.text: This is beginning to seem like therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We're friends talking about work.

dialogue.text: Then let's... Let's talk about... the work.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have a new patient. Her name is April. She's just learned that she's got lymphoma. She's terrified and she's in denial. She hasn't told anybody. Not her family, not her friends, nobody except me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She says she doesn't want to have the chemo. I think she probably has an unconscious fantasy that if she doesn't have the treatment, she doesn't have the cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You haven't said that to her yet?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's not I don't think she's ready to hear it yet. And I don't have the time to get her there. Look, if it was my daughter, I would just take her by the arm and I would drag her to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course you would. That's what you do for your family.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But not for your patients? This is the question.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What does the good therapist do when the patient needs more than just... talk? Do you just sit there and listen until she dies on the couch?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You can only be responsible for what happens in treatment. You know that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So are you saying that you wouldn't take her to chemo?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd do everything I could to get her to go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And if she still refused? I'm just afraid that this girl is going to die. And I can't get involved because I'm afraid of another lawsuit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, Then stop being her therapist and become her nurse.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not that simple. Don't simplify it. I mean, are you saying that you wouldn't help her? I thought that's what we were on the earth for, to help each other and step up to the plate when somebody needs us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How long have you been treating her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You've seen her only once and she's made you feel this...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm just afraid that she's going to die and I'm angry that she won't let me help her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Isn't this the same anger that you felt towards Alex because he wouldn't let you save him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This isn't about Alex. This is about April.

dialogue.text: I don't think this is about your patients at all.

dialogue.text: I know you don't.

dialogue.text: You had this anger before these patients walked into your office.

dialogue.text: You're not gonna drag me down that path again.

dialogue.text: I'm not dragging you down any path.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think this is about my mother.

dialogue.text: Yes, I think this is about your mother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want to go into therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you leave things with her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I made her promise to call me.

dialogue.text: And I called her a couple of times twice yesterday. I called her three and 3 times today. She still hasn't called back. I just... You know, I have to help this girl.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, we're not gods. We can't save anybody. You really care about your patients. But I have to say you're no good to anybody as long as you are living with all this fear and anger.

dialogue.text: Fear that I can't save them, fear that they're all gonna die?

dialogue.text: They won't all die.

dialogue.text: In spite of everything you could do, your mother died. And if your mother could die, the one who promised you she'd always be there...

dialogue.text: Look...
