situation: The therapist asked me why I was angry, and I told him it was because Kyle told his current girlfriend about my condition.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This... This happens when I get angry. Tremors run in our family. It's genetic.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You must be really angry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess so. I actually like when this happens. It's this weird out-of-body experience. You know what'd help, I bet?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Using your phone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you like to tell me what's going on? Why your hand is shaking? Why you're so angry?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why don't you tell me why I can't just make a call?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you can, but I just don't think that it's the best use of our time together. You're sure it can't wait till the end of the session?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fuck her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Fuck who?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sienna Newhouse, Kyle's new girlfriend. Do you know she has a publicist?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not quite sure who she is.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I guess you don't really follow that world. I don't really follow that world either, except now apparently I'm stuck in it, mired in its peripheral muck. Thank you for that, Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I remember last week that you mentioned she was wealthy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's filthy fucking rich. I told Kyle I had cancer and you know what she does? She offers to pay for my treatment. We're at a school, you stupid cunt. We have insurance. If you ever actually went to class, you might know that.

situation: Kyle told his current girlfriend about my illness; I felt offended.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, I told Kyle not to tell anyone and he told herdeliberately so that he wouldn't have to deal with me. I hate them both.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't get this. How does telling Sienna ensure that Kyle doesn't have anything to do with you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told him not to tell her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So he... betrayed your trust.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, it's more than that. Look, Kyle knows me, he knows what I can and can't tolerate. He knows that if he tells his girlfriend I have cancer and if she calls me, I will hang up on her and never speak to either of them again, which is what he did, and what she did, and what I did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So that's who you were talking to when you arrived? And did you hang up on her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, the phone died, which is why I have to call her back so I can hang up on her. Could I just use your phone? Please, it'll take two minutes. I can't concentrate at all. She can't get the last word, Paul. I can't die and she gets to go on and live the perfect life with the only person I've ever loved.

situation: I talk about Kyle's current girlfriend.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thank you. Could I have a moment?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... What did you say to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. I told her my life was none of her fucking business.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That made you feel better? Did... Did you talk to Kyle as well?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I'll call him later.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that he was the only person that you had ever loved. Can I ask you how it feels to see him with somebody else?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've never actually seen them together.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't even know she existed until recently. I mean, I knew she existed... everyone knows she exists. Her father donated the money for the new library. She wears all these ridiculous scarves in these absurd configurations. You shouldn't wear scarves like that unless you're French.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. I just think they look stupid on American girls.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Including Sienna?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, not including Sienna.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said you told Kyle about your cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did.

situation: I discuss my experience of telling Kyle that I was diagnosed with cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was... pretty funny the way it all went down.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I could use a laugh. You want to tell me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We hadn't spoken since we broke up, because we're, like... radioactive together. But a few months had gone by, I thought maybe we were ready. I knew he was seeing someone else. I thought maybe we could have dinner, catch up. He always makes me feel... I don't know. He's older. He knows how to... take care of things, how to keep everything under control. I sent him an email. I said I was having trouble with one of my models... which I was. He came right over. He could see immediately that I was tired. He made me risotto and he brought wine. And I remember thinking, This is nice. We can be friends. We are friends. As he was leaving, he kissed me. And I remember feeling confused, but... It was like it took a little while for my brain to catch up with what my body was doing, where my hands were going. And I heard this sound, like a moan, and I thought, Who made that sound? And then I realized it was me. While it was happening, I started to cry, and then he started to cry. I'd never seen him cry before.

situation: The therapist speculates that one of the reasons I called Simone was to convey my anger towards Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When it was over I said, I have something to tell you. He said, I have something to tell you. And I said, You go first, and... So he said, I'm engaged. And then I said, I have cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's so painful.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's him. It's Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm going to ignore this, okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's fine. I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He must've gotten your number from the ice queen's phone. She must've told him what happened.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you feel about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I expected her to tell him and... I'm glad that he called.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think that might be part of the reason that you were so anxious to call her? Because you wanted her to convey your anger to him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need to go through her to get to him, clearly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you seen Kyle since that night?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I kicked him out and told him I never wanted to see him again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because... Because he told you he was engaged?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because he was mean to me.

situation: I recount how Kyle was anxious and believed I hadn't taken good care of myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After I told him I had cancer, he got really anxious, and asked me what my plan was. I told him I didn't have a plan and he got angry and accused me of not taking care of myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He got angry?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: His dad... was physically abusive to his mom, and she wouldn't defend herself, so... So when kyle sees women not taking care of themselves, he goes apeshit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, do you think...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I know what you're gonna say next.

situation: I admit that I let something slip when talking to Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Gee, April, do you think you tried to provoke Kyle with your apathy in order to get a reaction and see how much he cares about you and the answer is no, I really didn't expect to tell him. It just... It slipped out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you know what I'm going to say next?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, I think it's great that you see things from my point of view.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Really?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's really helpful.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you find it hard to let yourself be taken care of? It feels to me like you not only want to do your own work here, but you want to do mine as well. That way you believe you can get through this without... without me. You know, when... when you mentioned Kyle here first, I was a little worried about him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You sound like my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I guess I do react in that way. You said that he was older, that he had a rich wealthy girlfriend yet he slept with you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't blame him for that. I'm telling you, we have this thing...

situation: The therapist thinks I am unwilling to accept help and he understands Kyle's behavior.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't blame him for that. I'm telling you, we have this thing...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not blaming him. Actually, over the session, I think I'm beginning to understand his behavior.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because I think I know how he feels. You described the way he responded to your revelation... to your cancer, as being mean, but... it seems to me that he was behaving appropriately anxiously. You know, In the last session that we had you told me that you had cancer, and as soon as you did that you started to push me away. And I knew that the more times I called you this week, the less likely I was to see you again. You called me like 10 times this week. You must've never wanted to see me again. In the meantime, you told kyle and then you started to push him away. You vilified his behavior. But he can't help me anymore.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He doesn't belong to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He isn't mine. So because he's not your partner, he can't help you anymore?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's all or nothing with me. It's just the way I'm built. He didn't hurt me.

situation: I discuss the reasons for our breakup.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He didn't hurt me. I hurt him. It wasn't his fault we broke up. It was mine. I couldn't take it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, what couldn't you take?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How much he loved me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. It was just too much.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that you couldn't rely on Kyle because... he doesn't belong to you. Is there anyone in your life

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: who does?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about my brother, who has autism.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right now? Daniel.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you and your brother have a deep bond. Did you tell him about the cancer?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel has enough to worry about.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like negotiating the world, Paul. Have you ever known anyone with autism?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's that been like for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No one understands. It's... every second of every day it is like he is in a foreign country where he doesn't speak the language and where everyone hates him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He's lucky to have someone who understands him as well as you do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, well... he didn't deserve what he got.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do any of us deserve what we get?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When Kyle and I were together... it's hard to explain, but it's like I would... just... check out sometimes, but I wouldn't go far.

situation: I discuss my feelings about being with Kyle; the therapist says I am scared.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I would be watching myself, watching Kyle... brushing our teeth, making coffee. And I remember thinking, This is what it feels like to be Daniel.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How often would this happen?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A lot... Especially when we were in bed. Sometimes, we'd be having sex and then suddenly.... I'd be floating above us, looking down and thinking, Oh, they're in love. That's nice. It didn't happen this last time. I tried to make it happen, but I couldn't. I think that's when I started to cry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It sounds like you were what we call dissociating. It's a defense mechanism. It feels like you are outside your body, but we do it sometimes to get away from something that we feel is frightening.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was I afraid of?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's a very important question.

situation: I can't stop thinking about Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I slept with his best friend... Kyle's. I don't know why I did it. The whole time there was this voice in my head saying, Don't do this. April, please. You're gonna screw everything up. He won't forgive you. I did it anyway and... Then I told him. And I was right... He couldn't forgive me. Everything was really sort of perfect. I was this perfect girl to him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did that feel scary?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now I'm... that girl, the one who's still hung up on her ex. I hate girls like this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't like to see yourself as... flawed, do you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Kyle offered to take me to the hospital to see my oncologist, schedule my treatments, and I almost... I almost let him do it, because I... I wanted to see him again so badly. Isn't that horrible?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's so horrible about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I stopped myself.

situation: The therapist urges me to accept treatment, saying psychotherapy won't make the disease disappear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's been calling every day since we saw each other, like five times a day. I'm not picking up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You are gonna need somebody to take you to chemotherapy. And... From what I understand, you feel very tired afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've been feeling much better lately. I give you credit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, would you rather die than be weak? It is very rare for this disease to go away of its own accord. Basically, that's unheard of.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I have been feeling better since coming here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you ever have a... when you were a child, did you ever have a worry doll?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A worry doll. You tell it your troubles and it takes your troubles away. Maybe... Maybe that's what you think you have in me. You've told me you have cancer and now I'm worried about it. Now since somebody else is worrying, you don't need to. And since you don't need to worry, you mustn't have cancer. I have to tell you: talking about this to a psychologist is not gonna make it go away. You know, I... I spoke with this friend of mine who's an oncologist.

situation: I am angry at the therapist for consulting with others about my cancer; the therapist says it's his responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You did what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Basically, April, he thinks that your delaying chemotherapy is a sentence of death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You talked to someone else about me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't mention your name.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You had no right to do that. I came to you in confidence.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It would have been professionally negligent of me to do anything else. I need to find out whether your behavior might be suicidal.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Suicidal?!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would you tell me to do, April? You've been telling me what to do and say throughout this session. I cannot let you... It is my duty, my professional duty, to protect you, April, from self-harm.

situation: I and the therapist promise each other to keep information confidential and not to disappear without reason.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I want you to promise me that won't happen again, that no matter what I decide to do, you won't talk to anybody else about me outside this room.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I promise. But you have to promise me something in return.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That if you decide to stop therapy, you have to call me. You cannot sever ties unilaterally. I don't want you to disappear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I promise. Thank you.

situation: I talk about the company's troubles and the potential existence of a traitor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So I'm sure this week you read up on me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean about your company?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I won't hold it against you. We've got a target on our backs. Moved off that business section you never read into the front section, any day now there's going to be a feeding frenzy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually I did read a few articles, but mostly about the industry. Not specifically about you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Finefellow, fine. Connie thinks this reporter at The Times has it in for me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think she's right?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, like you said, the whole industry is reeling from this, but for some reason Brenda Starr over there has decided to make me the poster child for the scandal. It got so bad this week that connie asked me if I'd ever laid off the girl's father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you agree with her that this reporter is out to get you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Those articles... they're not based on facts. She's just listening to somebody. I don't know who, some malcontent who has just enough information to sound knowledgeable and do serious damage.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So if I follow you then, this may not be a reporter's vendetta, but it could actually be the work of somebody from inside the company.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I didn't want to think that, but the Donaldsons, that's the family with the majority stake, they're convinced of it. Old man Donaldson said, Walter, we have a Judas in our midst.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must be pretty disturbing,

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: not knowing who to trust in the midst of a crisis. Well, that's business. But what's really disturbing is for her to imply that I would endanger the health of children just to turn a profit. I mean, that's completely irresponsible.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I express my worries about my daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a father, for Christ's sake. Got a daughter who's probably reading about this online.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you worried about how she might react?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She knows who her old man is. But I am worried that these articles might be putting Natalie in jeopardy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not sure that I follow.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, God forbid they find out she's my daughter. For all I know they probably already have. Maybe she's already disappeared. Maybe they're stalling for time while he decides how much ransom he thinks he can ask for.

situation: I talk about my self-confidence in my work.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think I sound crazy?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think your anxiety might be influencing your judgment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I'm not the only one. Connie's allergies are acting up. She's losing weight.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or maybe she's worried for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Me? About what? My job? No, that reporter from The Times who's trying to get me fired, she's the one who should be worried. Or do I sound crazy?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually I think you sound quite confident for a man in the midst of a... what did you call it? A feeding frenzy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, there's a reason for that... the Donaldsons. I've worked for them for over 35 years. I'm like a son to them.

situation: I recall James, who has died.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can I ask you what you're thinking about now?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's right. You're the fellow who wants me to say whatever pops into my head. I was just thinking... they had a son. James. We were in the war together... army corps of engineers. We tried to build bridges over there, helping people who were taking shots at us. When we got back to the States, I got my degree and he brought me into the company. If I'd looked out for him as much over here as we did for each other over there, he might still be around.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened to him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He drove too fast. You see a family through a loss like that and they're not gonna... this crisis'll blow over. They always do.

situation: I believe I didn't have a panic attack and that it's not important.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think I've talked enough. Would you mind telling me what you're thinking?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, just now I was struck by the way you said that the... the crisis would blow over. It reminded me of what you said last week as... as you were leaving.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What did I say?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I asked you if you should call your doctor, and you said it'll go away. It always goes away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, last week. Look, I think I also said I was sorry if I gave you a scare. But... these things, they look worse than they are.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what are they exactly?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, whatever they are, they're not going to kill me. They're inconvenient, sure, but they go away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And have you ever mentioned them to anyone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have a gold-plated executive health plan. I don't really need it, but the company insists on it. If there's anything wrong a problem, they would have found out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you told your doctor that you were having trouble sleeping, but you didn't say anything about the panic attacks.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're not panic attacks.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What makes you so sure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They don't happen under stressful situations. They happen at dinner sometimes, or a movie. Or, evidently, during a therapy session.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you had one since then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Actually I had one this week in the elevator, of all places.

situation: I recount the process of my panic attacks.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Actually I had one this week in the elevator, of all places.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you care to tell me about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you want me to do, describe the elevator for you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, did anything unusual happen that morning? Why don't you just describe then... the details of that morning as you remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is like the game my wife used to play with our kids at the dinner table. We'd ask them how school was, they'd say, fine. Ask them what happened... nothing. Finally my wife made them walk through the day step by step. Is that really what you're looking for?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Humor me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, got out of the town car, went into the building, met the new security guard, showed him my passport, went through the gates, got on the elevator, my heart started racing, my throat closed up, elevator doors opened, went into my office. This is about the time that Natalie would usually say, can I be excused now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you saying that Do you find this exercise pointless?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't mean to be a doubting Thomas,

situation: I talk about the death of my security guard Bob, and the therapist connects it to my panic attacks.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't mean to be a doubting Thomas, but I don't see anything that would have caused a panic attack, do you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said there was a new security guard.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, a kid. What about him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anything unusual about... that? Did it upset you? Maybe, that you had to show him your I.D.?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't know me at all. I knew Bob for over 30 years and I always made a point of showing him my I.D.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what happened to Bob?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He died, according to the kid. Dropped dead of heart failure. Disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were you and Bob close?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd nod to him in the morning. He'd say, Hey, Mr. B, how about those Knicks? I'd say, They're breaking my heart, Bob. And just same conversation for 30 years.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It sounds like you two had a morning ritual. Do you think that you miss him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't miss Bob. I enjoyed our banter and I feel sorry for his family, but... He meant nothing to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I just wonder if there might be some connection between Bob's death and... your attack in the elevator, that's all.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think you're grasping for straws there, fella.

situation: I mention I once had a brother who was excellent, and he has passed away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where did you go to school?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Here. In the city. Are you worried I'm not qualified to treat you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was just a question. Anyway, it doesn't matter. Like I said, I've had these since I was a kid. I'm used to them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: From when you were a kid? Really?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Off and on.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember how old you were when you experienced your first one?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Four or five, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Four or five, that seems very young. Right...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Six. I had to be six. I was already sleeping in my brother's room.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were you close... with your brother?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He died when I was a boy. He drowned.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did it happen?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, this was in rural Pennsylvania. It was an old limestone quarry lake. A swimming hole really. 40 foot cliffs. It was a hot summer night.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what age was he?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 16. Getting ready to go to college in the fall... Yale. He seemed kinda young for that, but... he skipped a few grades.

situation: I talk about how my parents and I felt after my brother's death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All the brightest kids did back then. But of all of them, Tommy was the brightest. You have no idea. A real golden boy... valedictorian, full scholarship. Tommy walked on water.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How was it for you when... when he died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine. I don't even know if I really knew that was going on, I was so young.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And your parents... How did they... How did they grieve?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They didn't. Of course they did. They had to, but... they shielded me from that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you knew something was going on?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All I know is that one day Tommy just wasn't there. I think I stayed with the neighbors for a few nights. And then... I went home. My dad was sitting on the porch, drinking his lager, waiting for me. He walked me up to my brother's room. All his stuff was still there. Nothing changed. My father said, This is yours now. I just told your mother now I know why we had you. Then he turns around and leaves me there. Or at least that's how I remember it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's a very... That's a very powerful memory.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, like I said, I was young. I might have it wrong.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And when you tell it now to me, what emotions does it bring up for you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just feel sorry for the old man.

situation: The therapist thinks I am having panic attacks and tries to explain.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just feel sorry for the old man. Tommy was everything to him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And your mother? How did she react?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Her hair turned white. She had this gorgeous auburn hair. And then overnight... she changed into an old woman. I thought she was a changeling for a while. That my real mother was... trapped somewhere far away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, what... What you're talking about... describing, it's... it's significant. It must have been... hard for you... to cope with the loss of your brother and your parents' grief.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Kids are resilient. They survive.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you began to have these attacks after you were sleeping in Tommy's room.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did. So what? Like I said, they only occurred while I was sleeping.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And... what were they like back then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd wake up sweating and shaking.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you ever tell your parents?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, they had enough on their minds.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And these panic attacks, just like now, they would go away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There you go again with this panic. Haven't you been listening? How could they be panic attacks? They happened when I was asleep. How stressed out could I have been?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: As a child whose brother had just vanished, and whose parents offered no explanation, I think, you could have been very stressed out even in your dreams. Especially in your dreams. You know, it sounds to me like your parents placed a heavy burden on you after Tommy died. Did you ever feel that they wanted you to fulfill his potential?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody could ever fulfill Tommy's potential. But I tried.

situation: The therapist believes the events concerning my brother, Natalie, and Bob have stressed me; I deny it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did try. You are a very successful man. I'm ROTC from Penn state. Tommy had an Ivy League scholarship. Tommy would have cured cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think about Tommy a lot?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But actually, I've... been thinking about what it must have been like for my folks when I was in Vietnam. They'd already lost one and their only spare was halfway around the world. I must have put them through hell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did they ever say anything to you about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, like I said, they... They didn't talk a lot about their feelings.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you told your daughter how worried you are for her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where's that coming from?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, Natalie is now also halfway around the world. Do you recall the word you used when you were describing Tommy's death?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But I'm sure you do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said he disappeared. It's the same word you used to talk about what you fear may have happened to Natalie. And also what happened... to Bob.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't read too far into this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's a strange thing to say to a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on. I'm joking.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were you? Really? It seems to me, this whole session, any time I've tried to... read into things, or suggest another way of looking at a problem, you've shut me down.

situation: The therapist believes I fear that people who leave will not come back, that my panic is a response to the imbalance of stress.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not that. It's just that if you're wrong, you're wrong. Am I supposed I have to worry about your feelings?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course not. But I'm supposed to pay attention to yours and you've given me the strong sense, I have to say, that if I tell you something you don't want to hear you might very well just walk out of the room.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean fire you. Well, you're wrong about that too. Look, if you think I need to hear something just come on out and say it. I'm a big boy. You think Bob the security guard is my rosebud, tell me how.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually I think this precedes Bob and Natalie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Go on.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think that you trust that... people who leave you will ever come back. Your brother never returned. Your mother looking like a different person. Your father was never the same. And nobody made sense of it all for you... as a kid. Perhaps you still fear that if someone... disappears... even momentarily, whether they're... overseas or just out of touch for a few days. That something horrible must have happened to them. Perhaps in certain situations, you experience a disproportionately stressful response.

situation: I want to take medication; the therapist wants to continue treatment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So if I'm understanding you, all this started when my daughter left for Rwanda. It's an overreaction, like my wife's allergies.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does that make sense to you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you have some sort of psychological antihistamine?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you mean a prescription? I thought you said you didn't want to take pills.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe that was because my doctor didn't have your diagnosis.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There is medication for panic attacks. But I think... it's really important that we continue the work that we're beginning to do here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Call my doctor. Tell him what you think.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'll do that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Good. Thanks, I appreciate it. Our time's up, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. You can pay me at the end of the month, if you...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you don't mind, one thing I learned from my father, pay as you go. It's cleaner that way. Maybe the medication will help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thank you.

situation: I don't want to talk to Gina like a psychological consultation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Tammy looked like she had a good session today.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We can't talk about another patient. You said that last week.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said a lot of things last week and the truth is I don't know what I was thinking. Look. I can't be in therapy with you. I mean, It's nothing personal. If I were to go to therapy, obviously I would come to you, of course. But it's just not a good time for me to... to make myself more miserable.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what we were going to do, make you more miserable?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't want to just phone, you know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure about this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Absolutely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry to hear this. But I respect your decision, so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You respect my decision? Yes, of course I do. Do you want me to leave?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You stay here and wait for the kids. It's fine. But since I've got some free time, I need to do some shopping.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're going shopping?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you need anything from the market?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What would I need from the market, Gina?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, right. I don't know. Did you want me to argue with you? Do you want me to persuade you to come to therapy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you want me to just, like, leave you a message?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, This is very polite. I'm gonna...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We can't have an hour of conversation?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's what we did last week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll pay you for an hour of conversation.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't sell my conversations.

situation: I want to talk to Gina for a while and apologize to her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe we should charge them. If anyone learns anything it'd be all the better.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, are you gonna stay here while I'm gone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I get what you're doing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What am I doing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Women, they're all the same, every last one of them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Excuse me? Maybe it's not a good idea for you to stay here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just want you to stay and talk.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 10 minutes, please. You don't know what kind of a week I've had, Gina. I've got this CEO guy, he pays me by the insight. When I give him the insight he doesn't want... I really loathe people who think they can just buy whatever they want. Then I've got this former patient who I haven't seen for 20 years who thinks that everything that's happened in the meantime is my fault. I just want to rest for a few minutes, that's all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just a few minutes though. You can't get any rest on the train?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: On the train I talk to you, but you don't talk back. Not just you, I talk to all the people I don't see all week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like Kate and the boys.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And Rosie. And this week I talked to Tammy Kent. Why am I thinking about Tammy Kent all the time?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was so happy at her house when I was 17. Was that the last time I was happy, I wonder.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think so, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was it about being at her home that made me so happy?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know. Maybe that's something you could work on in therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I could also work on why I say such stupid things about women. That women are all the same, what a stupid thing to say. Please, forgive me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: People say stupid things when they're angry. Anger is also a good thing you could work on in therapy.

situation: I talk about seeing my lawyer, who went to get a testimony from Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I called my lawyer from the train. It turns out that Mr. Prince's lawyers are... They're deposing Laura today. She had a relationship with Alex.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know she had a relationship with Alex, while she was in love with you. That's a dangerous triangle. Are you worried that she'll use this as a way to get back at you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know what she'll say. Maybe she really thinks that it is my fault that Alex is dead. That's another good thing to work out here. Fine. I'm like my patients, you know. I don't want to be in therapy, because I don't want to talk about my parents. My past is fine. It's the present that causes the problems.

situation: I say I keep thinking about Tammy because of my mother's issues.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm like my patients, you know. I don't want to be in therapy, because I don't want to talk about my parents. My past is fine. It's the present that causes the problems.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sure it's occurred to you, Paul, that... That why you're thinking about Tammy so much...
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing has occurred to me. Why do you think I'm here? I'm sorry. Please... Tell me what's occurred to you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It occurred to me that you're interested in Tammy Kent because there's something incomplete in your understanding of your father's abandonment and your mother's breakdown.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And how does Tammy fit into this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can't you guess?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's an idea. Guess therapy. You tell me a problem you have, and I'll try to guess what caused it and if I guess right, I win!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The only problem is I'd have to know what caused my problem in order to say whether you were right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right, true.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes... It had occurred to me too that my response to Tammy Kent was tied up with my mother's death somehow. That seeing Tammy opened a kind of a window onto that time. Suddenly with Tammy there, I felt I had to look in, you know, I think, to see myself... Before the fall maybe. And Tammy and I were lovers... And I'd want to talk about that too. But I can't talk about Tammy because she's your patient. So...

situation: The therapist says that if I understand what happened before, I won't be in pain like I am now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, maybe I'll just take Tammy out for a coffee sometime, but I won't go looking in the... In the mother window. I'll just... Let it all stay dead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The problem is it's not dead.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's the... Undead. Like in a horror movie. You kill it, you bury it, but then it comes right back, right out of the grave. Mother!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Those are the monsters... The things that won't stay dead.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And one night when you're too tired to kill the thing again, you let it kill you, just... Just so that it will at least be over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what you think happened to your Alex up there in his plane? That instead of fighting his guilt one more time, he just gave into it, so it would be over?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's hard to know how much fight a person has in him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: True.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You, for instance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't have to worry about me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm glad. But I wonder why you think you don't have the strength left aren't strong enough to fight your mother one more time. I mean, maybe this time you'd win.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you suggesting?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm suggesting that maybe you could finally lay them to rest.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: One of them... my dad... is still alive.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course I know that. But still, if you had clarity about what happened back then, maybe that could all rest in peace. And so could you. How does that sound?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: As a goal for therapy?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: As a goal, therapy or not.

situation: I don't know why I resist psychological counseling.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think I can do it without therapy. I know it. I won't do the work. I won't think about it. I'll just go on blaming myself, taking it out on everybody else. I'll start smoking again, drinking too much.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't know that drinking was a problem for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's... As long as I don't drink alone, it isn't. Why am I so resistant to you? Why do I come all the way down here, only to tell you that I don't want to be in therapy? Clearly I have to be in therapy. I have to figure out how this next part of my life goes. I have to know if I'm doing the right job. I have to know if I'm helping people. And if I'm not, I have to know what I'm going to do next.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you really worry that I couldn't hear about Tammy because she was my patient?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course I did. I do!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So I thought about whether I could treat you both, especially if anything were to happen between the two of you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think something is likely to could happen between the two of us?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not necessarily. But I have to aknowledge that something could happen.

situation: The therapist wants to provide psychological counseling for me and Tammy together.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I don't want anything like that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Absolutely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: As sure as you were that you didn't want to see me for therapy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Who doesn't want to be back in bed with his high-school sweetheart, the girl who looks at him in the way he used to be? I mean, don't you think about stuff like that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let's try and stay on the topic, Paul.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sure, sorry. I thought I was beginning to enjoy myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If I'm going to treat both you and Tammy, there's going to have to be some rules.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well... If you were the therapist and you had two patients who had a history, what rules would you want?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, well, I would make it clear that I couldn't tell either of them anything that I had learned in session about the other.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay? And... They couldn't expect me to analyze the other one and they couldn't use me to... send messages back... back and forth.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My seeing them would have to be a kind of open secret. We'd all know about it, of course, but we'd... all put it away and just not use it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All? Even you? You think you could do that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think so, yeah.

situation: The therapist gets me to make some promises through the matter of Alex and Laura.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think so, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When Alex and Laura slept together, you kept your response to that out of their therapy?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: As I remember it, I threw the affair in her face and a cup of coffee in his, but that, that... that was different.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How was that different?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Their affair was about me. Laura slept with Alex because I wouldn't sleep with her. And he slept with her because I wouldn't give... And he slept with her because she was gorgeous and he felt like...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What were you gonna say, before you corrected yourself? He slept with her because you wouldn't...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I wouldn't tell him not to fly again. Because I wouldn't try to control his recklessness. And he wanted to show me what kind of damage he could do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you didn't see that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I didn't. I guess I was too involved so I didn't get the message. He counted on me to control his self-destructive influences. Instead I lashed out at him, he lashed out at himself and... And down he went.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... You can see why I need to remain neutral if something were to happen?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I need you to promise me that nothing's going to happen.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sure.

situation: I talk about how Tammy comforted me when I was a child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing will happen with Tammy Kent until or unless we are no longer your patients.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I want you to know, that... What you've said about Alex today stays with me. I'm not going to mention any of that in the deposition.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay then. Okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to proceed?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Good, I'm glad. So, let's begin. Last week you mentioned your high-school sweetheart.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, Tammy Kent.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Last week you called her Tammy Kent, also by her full name.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what everybody called her. There was another Tammy in the neighborhood so we called this one Tammy Kent.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And she lived down the hall?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They moved in when I was about 14.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And that was about the time your father moved out?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, he moved out a little bit after that. You know, it should've been the worst time of my life with my father gone and my mother beginning her... You know, to suffer her bouts of... Depression, but... I wasn't sad, you know? I was... I was excited.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it that excited you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Tammy. She'd show up out of thin air when I was having the worst day and, you know, we'd just start talking. And everything bad about my house, it felt like a movie. It felt like a movie that I was watching but that I wasn't in. And even if my mother was crying all day, I'd tell Tammy Kent and she'd say, Yeah, it's going to be okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would be okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, she just made me feel that I could get through it and that...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about how Tammy was like my girlfriend when I was a child, making me feel not so bad, and how Tammy's family was also very sunny.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: if I let my mother cry that that was okay too. And I... had the hope that when I went back down the hall, things'd be all right. Or if they weren't, at least, you know, I could... deal with them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So she helped you take care of your parents. She was so young to be a grief counselor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, she felt more like my... My girlfriend. And the way I felt about it was if I had a girlfriend, then I was, you know, I was okay. I wasn't the poor kid with the absent father and the pitiful mother... I mean, I was that kid, yes, I was, but I wasn't a complete failure. At least, I had a... I had a girlfriend.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you have a physical relationship with her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Back then no. We were... 14. Different times, not like kids now. No, it was another three years before we had sex. After all that stuff had happened and, you know, I was over... Over everything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it that happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, after my father left.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: After your father... Left... You and your mother for one of his patients?

dialogue.speaker: client
