situation: I think my architectural assignment is terrible, but the therapist thinks it's great.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thanks for seeing me. I was on my way to school to turn this in and... I don't know why I did it, but I came here instead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This is... The big project you mentioned? Would you mind if I had a look at it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, go ahead if you're interested in shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's really cool.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's supposed to be a World Trade Center memorial... Of course.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean of course?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because god forbid any architecture student in the country gets another assignment ever again. I'm sorry. I'm an asshole. Don't listen to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I think it's just... I think it's beautiful. It's really... Exquisitely done. Very beautiful.

situation: I am tired and can't sleep at night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm so tired.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You haven't been sleeping this week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, not at all. Between my anxiety and my lymphoma there's just never a good time. That was supposed to be a joke. Was it funny?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Neither do i. Can I just... Do you mind? I tried so hard to sleep last night. It was 2:00 a.m., I was out of ideas and my hands were shaking so badly, I was afraid I'd wreck the whole thing if I tried to keep working on it, so I put it in the box. I changed my sheets, I... lit candles, put on music. It sounds like I was trying to seduce myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So did you eventually fall asleep?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I couldn't. My heart was racing and it felt like... I don't know. It felt like it wasn't blood running through my veins, it was something else... Fire, poison. I just... I wanted to... open myself up and get it all out somehow. Slit my wrists or take off my own head. I would never. Don't worry. I'm just trying to describe how it felt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It sounds like a terrible night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't have another one like that. I will lose my mind.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you said that the poison was running through your veins, Can I tell you what I thought of immediately?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Chemo.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Same thing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it isn't. You can choose not to have chemo.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Touché.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I say I want to go home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had this thought last night... I just kept thinking it over and over. It used to happen to me a lot when I was a kid. The summer before I went to high school, I got this song stuck in my head and I couldn't get it out. I really thought I was going insane.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you think it would feel like to go insane?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like falling... Into nothing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can we not talk about losing my mind? Would you like to tell me about the thought that you had last night, the one that you couldn't get out of your head?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wanted to go home. I really wished I could go home. And then I thought, You can't go home. Your home is so long ago and so far away. And then I just kept thinking, Your home is so long ago and so far away. Your home is so long ago and so far away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And this home that you're... that you're thinking about, where is it? Or was it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can I tell you in a moment?

situation: I drop the architectural model.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean... Can I just... I just need to close my eyes for a second. I'm so tired. What time is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Really? Already?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's... 7:59 actually.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Perfect. Could you... Could you wake me at 8:00, would you mind?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure. April, wake up. Wake up, April. Wake up

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What time is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Good. It's over. This project was due yesterday but my professor said we had until 8:00 in the morning to turn it in. It was hideous. It looks better now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you say that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It didn't work at all. The dimensions were all off. I relied too much on negative space. It was just sitting there. I couldn't make it soar.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I have to tell you, it's... it's very hard to see you destroy your own work.

situation: I dream of falling from the model, and the therapist says I am releasing pressure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did I did fall asleep last night. I just rembered a dream I had. I was on top of the model, but it was life-size, and I fell. Do you ever get those? Falling dreams?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I get those all the time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how do you feel when you wake up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. My heart is pounding, and I feel like... I don't even know how to describe it. It's a kind of joy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, different from falling into nothing? So falling is something that you're afraid of and yet you're attracted to it at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you're awake, you work so hard to keep everybody and everything under your control, so in your dreams, it makes sense that you find yourself finally falling, releasing everything, letting everything go, because it's a kind of fantasy for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are you telling me that? Is that supposed to help me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It'll only help you if it rings true. If it doesn't...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But it's in my head now. You put it in my head. Now I have to think about it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like that thought you had last night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You started thinking about something, you can't stop. Your thoughts become obsessive.

situation: I say I'm not paranoid, but the therapist says I'm ignoring my own feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't say that. You... You have no idea what you're talking about. Have you ever been on a subway car that breaks dow and there's some guy... some shy-looking kid who starts repeating something to himself over and over, like, 7:15, 59th and Lex. 7:15, 59th and Lex, over and over, louder and louder until just saying the words isn't enough and he starts hitting himself and thrashing around and finally has to be subdued and tranquilized? That is what it means to have obsessive thoughts. I just like thinking things through.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're talking about your brother. I've noticed that you're constantly trying to feel what he feels.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, he can't describe how he feels, so... he needs someone to interpret it for him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your empathy is... It's admirable, April. But it can be really draining trying to feel everyone else's feelings as well as your own. Maybe... instead of your own.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't... I'm sorry for losing my temper.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't have to apologize to me.

situation: I say I've fallen from a high place before.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did fall out of a building once.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We were on vacation in Miami. I was only 10. My mother is obsessed with Cuba... Cuban music, Cuban food, Cuban culture. Anyway, we were down there without my brother. We left him... For the first time ever, I think... with my grandparents, just me and my folks. I remember this one night there was a band playing Cuban music down below and my parents started to dance right there in the hotel room. I went over to the window so that I could watch them dance and feel the... The breeze from the ocean on my back at the same time. Somehow... I don't even know how it happened... I fell out the window. I must've just leaned back and fallen. I landed on the... What's the word? The awning one floor below. I mean, I was fine. I just laid there for a second, I looked up at the window and then I slid off and landed on the sidewalk.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember feeling frightened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I remember as soon as my feet hit the sidewalk I started to bawl. Then I walked back into the hotel and I rode the elevator up. I looked in the mirror and I made myself stop crying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you could stop crying, just like that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just looked at myself and I said, April you have to stop, and I did. I can still do that.

situation: I want to go back to Miami, back to the time without my brother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When I walked back into the room, my mother... Had her head on my dad's shoulder. They were still dancing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: They hadn't noticed you were gone?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why did you have to stop crying?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I mean, You were 10 years of age, you had fallen out the window. Why couldn't you cry to your mother?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was so happy. The way she held my father in that room, the way they swayed, my mother closed her eyes as they swayed. My mother never closes her eyes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She can't take them off Daniel. I'm not an empathetic person. I'm really not. You asked me where home was for me. It was there, in Miami. That's the place I want to go back to... that room with my parents.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Without Daniel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right.

situation: I say we had to end our trip to take care of our brother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you ever read that book On the beach? It's about the nuclear holocaust and these people are waiting for the radiation to reach Australia, but they're happy. They fall in love. They buy benches for their gardens. They don't think about the future. I was reading that while we were down there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were reading that book at age 10?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I used to be precocious. And that's what I had hoped would happen... a nuclear war would destroy everything else in the world, and we could just stay on the beach. We couldn't stay. We had to get back. Daniel had stopped eating, gone back to hitting himself. My grandparents called in a panic. My mother went to the airport and got the next flight home. My dad and I drove back that night. Daniel wouldn't even look at us. He couldn't speak. It was like we had set him back three years. My mother never forgave herself for that trip.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You are an empathic person... the way you talk about your brother, the compassion you feel for him. But you can be an empathic person and still feel contradictory emotions, still feel anger, still feel... jealousy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why would I be jealous of Daniel?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe because your mother never closes her eyes to him. Daniel was allowed to show your parents how he was feeling. When he got upset, hurt or scared, they knew it, whereas you had to be perfect. You fell out a window and your mother had no idea.

situation: The therapist says I can also be without empathy, and I say my mother is not wrong.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't blame her for that. Jesus, don't talk about her like that. How am I talking about her? As if she was a bad mother. She's a great mother. She gave me my confidence, told me how smart I was. She made me feel like I could do anything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But Maybe as a child, you took that to mean that you shouldn't depend on her, that you should take care of it all on your own.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not going to do this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What are you not going to do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Slam my mother. She may not have been perfect, but she did her best. She could have been a professional ballerina. She trained at Juilliard, but she gave all of that up so that Daniel could have some semblance of a normal life...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ... that he could not feel like such a freak. So don't sit there and tell me she made all these mistakes. She didn't have a choice.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not attacking your mother. I'm just trying to understand why you can't tell her that you're sick.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, how much more can she take? It's not your fault that she had to deal with Daniel. Lately Daniel has been doing so much better.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I do not want to bother my mother, but the therapist says my mother will regret it if she doesn't tell her about my cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She finally has some time on her hands. He's living in this group situation, he's got a job at the library stacking books, and she has started to teach a dance class for little kids. I went to meet her there. She is having such a great time. I am not gonna take that away from her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think being sick will do that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She would stop teaching the class. She'd think she has to drop everything to take care of me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe that's okay if she does. She should stop teaching for a while to help take care of you for a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She is finally getting the chance to live a little.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I respect your wanting to protect your mother, but I think at a deeper level you're also trying to protect yourself from seeing your mother's fear for you, from feeling how much danger you're in. You say that you want to protect her, but surely you know that if you were to die, if you were to die, she would never... and I know this. I can tell you this as a father... if that happened to me, I would never ever recover. Listen to me. You have to begin chemo immediately. The reason you haven't is because you're scared to go through it alone. Is there anyone you can imagine yourself telling? Anyone who you would want to be there with you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You can.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's too horrible.

situation: The therapist urges me to undergo chemotherapy and let my mother know about my cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What am I supposed to say? How am I supposed to tell her that her daughter...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean you. You.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That I have cancer? No, I can't. It's too horrible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Horrible as it is, not telling her is more horrible.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When you say it, it makes sense... just pick up the phone and tell her. But I know that once I leave here, I won't be able to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Call her from here then.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Go ahead.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I borrow a phone to call my mother, but my mother does not answer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She'll just be leaving for work. Can I use your phone again?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course. I presume you want the room again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How'd it go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was in the car. She wanted to call me back... It's illegal to talk and drive at the same time. With my dad in the army, she follows the law.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You can stay here for 10 minutes and call her back.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I'm so tired. I'm gonna take a nap and call her when I get up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Will you call me after you've spoken to her?

situation: I briefly talk about Jesse wanting to replace me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you need a moment, Walter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not gone three days and all hell breaks loose.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, if it's an emergency, we can...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We can reschedule. We've already rescheduled. I was supposed to be here at 6:00. It's 8:00. No, it's after 8:00. I'm really sorry. And I appreciate you're seeing me later. I know you must have a life outside of here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it's fine. I had an hour free.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you understood... if you really understood how loath I am to be late. I'm really sorry. This isn't me at all. Really, it's fine. Here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's for your time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're paying for the session in cash?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, it's not for the session. I'll write a check for that. This is... This is just something extra for you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's really not necessary, Walter. Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Someone... Unimpeachable, huh? I like that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wasn't trying to bribe you. I mean, I'm... That's not the way I operate. Although, I tell you, sometimes it might be easier for me if I did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand. You were just trying to make up for lost hours. I understand.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Exactly. I know you value your time and I've wasted some of it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was generous of you to offer. Thank you, Walter. But I...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, that's good. You're a straight shooter. That's a rare thing these days, someone who's dependable. I had to come to a walk-up in Brooklyn to find it, but... Marie, I said no calls, for Christ's sake! Can't... Are you sure? That son of a bitch. No, don't let him know that you've reached me. Just let him think I'm walking into it. I'll call you from the car. Just give me a half hour of peace. Can you do that? Unbelievable. This little pisser... Jace! He's not even half my age and somehow he thinks he's gonna use this to bring me down. He's so self-deluded he actually thinks they're gonna give him my job.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, you seem...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's my own fault.

situation: My company faces a crisis, and I squeeze in time for diagnosis and treatment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: In a way. I mean, he was very bright, eager, good schools. I brought him into the company. But he's green. He's in over his head. It's...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, can you listen to me for a moment? You seems like... you seem like you're in the midst of a breaking crisis here.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, Paul, it's not breaking. It's already broke. We cull ingredients from all over the world: China, Brazil, Indonesia. Somehow something got into the pipeline.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, whatever is going on...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: it could be contaminated milk powder or bacteria from one of the factories. It could be a cheap lubricant leeching into the machinery...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't seem like you're able to get away from this right now. I think that it would be a very good idea for us to reschedule.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Reschedule?! When? It's not gonna get any better tomorrow or the day after. Paul, I'm going into combat in an hour. And if I... if I don't talk to you now, it might be another month before I get a chance. It's off, okay? Both of them.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I believe my daughter is in trouble and go to pick her up and bring her home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can I get a glass of water?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hate this stuff. Connie's always telling me I should drink more of it. So does my doctor, but I don't have time for it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't have time to drink water?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes no, I don't. And this week, it's a good thing anyway, where I was.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You've been traveling?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I spent the last 44 out of 72 hours in an airplane. And the hours waiting for the six flights were no barrel of laughs either.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So the trip was in response to the... To the crisis.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you were just saying how you have suppliers all over the world, and I assumed that you were trying to track down the source of the problem.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wasn't flying for the company.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You weren't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I flew to Rwanda to get Natalie.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did something happen to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, she didn't say so. But I knew that she was in trouble.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So she didn't ask you to come?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She didn't have to. Look, Paul, she's... she's my daughter.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I explain my suspicions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She didn't have to. Look, Paul, she's... she's my daughter. And until she went to Rwanda, I had spoken with her every day of her life. Wherever I was in the world, I'd call her at bedtime and tell her I loved her. Before she could talk, I made these little clicking noises. Then after she went to Rwanda, we emailed every day. Suddenly, Suddenly a week ago, she writes her mother but not me. Connie doesn't do email so I had to print the letters out for her. And she was asking Connie if I was all right, if the company was really complicit in this baby formula mess. It was crazy talk.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mightn't she have just been concerned for your welfare?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, Paul, don't you think I know my own daughter?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not what I'm saying, Walter. I'm just trying to understand why, with your company in crisis, you would chose to visit your daughter in Rwanda.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The emails, her voice wasn't her voice. She would never doubt her father.

situation: I talk about my daughter's changes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now I'm not saying she's being brainwashed, but I knew she was hiding something and once I got there I found out I was right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was she hiding?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To start with, she cut all her hair off. She'd always had this long auburn hair, like my mother's when she was that age. Well, that's gone now. Don't you think that's disturbing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can see why you might find it so, yes. But cutting hair, dyeing it weird colors, lopping it off even, I mean, that's what what daughters do. What else was different about her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was the same about her? I didn't know who I was talking to. She had no shoes. She had given them away, it turns out. She was so thin. She had this child in her arms... a little girl hanging in her arms like a sack of potatoes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you okay, Walter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is where she's living, Paul.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I describe my daughter's reaction upon seeing me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is where my daughter has chosen to live... some hellhole near Goma.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When she saw you, how did she react?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think I spoke right away. I just stood there looking at her. Finally she got scared. She said, What is it? Mom? Is mom all right? And I said, Your mother's fine. She said, What are you doing here? And I said, I've come to take you home. Get your stuff.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And that didn't go down well?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. At first she was... distant. Dad, I can't leave right now. I have to finish a procedure. As if she'd got some medical degree in the last month. She said she'd meet me for dinner in a few hours in the big tent. Then she pointed in the direction of some little shacks in case I wanted to lie down. She was living in one of those shacks. They looked like outhouses and she was sleeping there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can see how upsetting that... that might have been for you. I mean, you spent your life... providing a good home for her and... this is how she chooses to live. So what happened at the dinner?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I didn't wait for dinner.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about wanting to bring my daughter's things back home, but her emotional outburst hurts me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I went back into the shack and I took all her stuff and... I put it in the jeep. I just... I just wanted to take it back with me to Kigali and at least have her clothes cleaned. I wanted to go back to the hotel that night and... take her to dinner and maybe talk some sense into her. The next thing I know, she's... tearing across this field, screaming at me insane stuff... How I'm trying to control her, how I don't respect her, how she's worked so hard to build up trust with these people and now... they're gonna think that she's some neocolonialist like me. And there was something about Connie I'm not even going to repeat. I swear to god, Paul, it took everything I had not to slap her. Instead I just said, Don't you ever speak about your mother like that. Then... she broke down and started to cry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you do then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I put my arms around her. I said, Natalie, we're going home. And then... she told me to go fuck myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She'd never said anything like that to you before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She broke my heart, Paul.

situation: I discuss my daughter's opinion of me and explain why I went to find her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She broke my heart.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think she was so angry with you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She made that pretty clear. I got an email from her when I got back to the hotel. It turns out that I'm domineering, obsessive, that I'm the cause of all her anxieties, that it's impossible to thrive or grow around me, and... that's why she had to go away and now I'm... ruining her only chance to free herself from me. Now you see why I went over there? I sensed this was coming from earlier emails. You know, hearing that email makes me...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can we talk about the way you... came in here today? Completely in charge on both phones, handing me your bag... Not quite like I was a bellhop, but... something like that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry if I offended you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you didn't offend me. But... it did catch my attention. Walter, we both know that... you are... an excellent... manager. World class.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But in other roles where... you're not entirely in control, like say being a patient here, or... maybe when you went to see Natalie. That's much less comfortable for you.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says I am afraid of my daughter slipping out of control.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But what are you saying? I never try to control Natalie. I gave her whatever she wanted.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course. You've given her everything. And that's... That's something that's hard for other parents to do but... not for you. Do you think it's possible that... what's hard for you is... just... letting her be? Letting her go? Did you think that... you felt her pulling away from you in those emails? And then when you saw her at the camp did you... did you get frightened? Scared... of losing her so that you felt you had to tell her to pack up her things and come home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can't a father worry about his own daughter?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course he can. But just look at... how you responded for a moment. In the midst of a major work crisis, you read an email that she wrote to Connie and without stopping to think, you get on a plane and you fly halfway around the world.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's all right. These work pretty quick. Xanax, it's...

situation: I say I dreamt of Tommy in a hotel in Africa and that I must leave.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Dr. Wells gave me the prescription. Thank God he did. Otherwise I'd never have been able to... get out of that place.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you take a pill... after you saw Natalie?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Later. I woke up in the middle of the night in a cold sweat. I had a nightmare... that Natalie was gone. Then I looked around me and with the... jetlag and the fatigue, I had no idea where I was for a minute. I thought I was... back in my parents' house, in Tommy's room, with all his sports trophies and awards. I just couldn't stay in that room another second. I had to get out of there. I was having trouble breathing. And then I remembered the pills.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think it's strange that you were... that you were thinking about... Tommy over there... in Africa?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's been on my mind lately.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you know when that started? Has it been since Natalie left?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said that you woke up and you felt that you had to get out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Hotels can be disorienting. But losing Tommy was... very painful for you, wasn't it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My folks had the pain.

situation: The therapist says I feel my daughter has abandoned me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My folks had the pain. With all due respect, when parents lose a child it kills them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's really admirable that you remained so close to your parents after that happened. Like with the Donaldsons, as you've said. After their son James died, you became like a son to them. The good son, the one everybody can depend on. And then you had this dream. And... you feel that you're suffocating in... in Tommy's room.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What does this have to do with Natalie?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe Natalie is trying to do something that you've never allowed yourself to do: to separate from her parents. For you to stay connected means to never... stray. Now Natalie is trying to do something in between, but you feel that she's abandoning you the way Tommy did.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He died, Paul. Jesus.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know. But maybe that night in the hotel, Natalie's separation from you... felt, in some way, it felt like a death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God forbid.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about how I felt receiving an email from my daughter, and the therapist explains why she did it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God forbid. There's no comparison. There's a big difference. When a child dies, he's gone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Isn't that exactly the nightmare that woke you up, that Natalie was gone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It wasn't the same. I was trying to find her. I knew that no matter how bad I felt, I had to put myself aside and think only of Natalie. I took the pills. And somehow it passed. And... I dragged myself back to the hotel lobby and I went online in the business center. That's when I read her emails and I realized... I realized...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You realized what, Walter? It's okay to have the... thought here. You can say whatever you like.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I realized that she didn't need me at all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or maybe that's just what she needs to feel right now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's done with her old man. I'm a booster rocket.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's launched, like your boys, isn't that what you said at our first session?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did I? I'm sure I also said that Natalie was different. I'd have to agree with you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You did raise her with the freedom to think for herself, to question authority figures, to confront the world of adults. You gave her an incredible gift. Now she wants to use it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: By telling me to go fuck myself?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's what you heard. But before that, she wanted you to talk things over with her. She invited you to dinner, no? She was just shining me on. Possibly. Or possibly she really wanted to talk to you. But you felt like she was disrespecting you and you reacted to that. You know, I think that... for her whole life she's been very aware of you and how you feel and what you think and what she can do to make you happy. Maybe part of the reason she's so angry is because maybe for the first time in her life she knows that... what she wants... is not what you want. And she's having a very hard time reconciling herself to that fact.

situation: I mention I haven't yet reacted to my daughter's behavior when another crisis hits the company.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's having a hard time? What about me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how did you leave things with her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't. I woke up the next morning to a barrage of incoming faxes, phone calls, emails, outbreaks of diarrhea, children in hospitals possibly from formula contaminated at one of our plants. I'd gotten out in front of this! I leave for a few days and... it's like they were just waiting for me to turn my back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry, Walter. With the late session, I forgot to shut the...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hello, this is Mr. Barnett's assistant, Marie. It's urgent that he speaks with Burt. If he calls me, I can patch him through. Back to battle stations. I'd better be going. Thank you. 26 messages.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Will you be all right?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll be fine. They can't get rid of me, Paul. Après moi, le déluge.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: After you, the flood?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's a lot of pressure. The glue, Paul, the glue. Just look what happened when I left. I guess... my daughter can survive without me but... the Donaldsons can't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Will I see you next week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, and thanks again. You're welcome.

situation: I talk about my father being diagnosed with Parkinson's.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, come in. It's good to see you. Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's just what Tammy asked me. Do I seem...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You seem nervous, yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not. My father's sick. Okay, that's not true. He's past sick. He's got late-stage Parkinson's.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's so easy to say, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It may be easy to say, it's very hard to hear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Forget it. Thank you. I'm sorry I snapped.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When was the last time you saw him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does it matter when I saw him? I try to talk to him, but he's... He's not there. Or maybe he is and he's just choosing to... To hide. Remind me again where he lives. He's been in the same nursing home for the last 2 years. It's called Valley Haven, but it's not in a valley and it's not a haven. It's filled with dead men walking and pissed off nurses.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is he in pain?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's in pain, I'm in pain, the whole fucking world's in pain. Lucky for him I'm there to pay the bill.

situation: I say my father is incompetent.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's in pain, I'm in pain, the whole fucking world's in pain. Lucky for him I'm there to pay the bill. Long as I do, he gets to take his nap twice a day. How did we get on to this? Jesus.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you surprised to find yourself talking about what a burden he is?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what I think? I think he mishandled his finances deliberately so that I'd have to take care of him. He threw himself at my mercy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He's been sick for a long time. Why is he at the front of your mind today?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. I talked to my brother Patrick. He said my father seemed a little bit... off somehow. Like Patrick would know what that was.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your brother's visited him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He goes over there and he eats his dinner, according to the nurses.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can't you tell them not to let him in at mealtimes?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't really care who eats his dinner. I just...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What were you going to say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was going to say I'm just waiting for the man to die. You asked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's very hard to have someone sick and dependent on you. It drains all your reservoirs. It makes you very very tired.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, it's not like he was this great father who got Parkinson's and disappeared. He was never present in my life. Somebody could always eat his dinner for all he cared. He ate at the hospital, he said. My mother stopped setting a place for him at the table when I was six years old.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did she stop doing other things for him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sure there were, but the man wasn't there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You keep calling him the man. Does that have any meaning for you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What, like... Like he was supposed to be the man of the house only I had to do that job for him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what it means?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I asked Tammy about him. You know what she said?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You spoke to Tammy about your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said that the first time that she saw him, she thought he looked just like the man was supposed to look.

situation: I mention I have met with Tan Mei and discussed the past.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So the man came from Tammy? Her father died that year. I don't know, maybe she was fantasizing about my father. Actually, I'm sure she was. She wanted to live in my apartment and I wanted to live in hers. Anyway, Tammy and I, we... We went out for coffee and I did what we talked about last week. I asked her what she remembered about that Christmas Eve, the night that my mother tried to... Tried to kill herself. Anyway, it turns out that Tammy remembers, but in a really crazy way. A lot of it was what I remembered, that my mother was at home, she was asleep, I was at Tammy's, we ate the cookies, we were singing. And then Tammy and I went... to her room to talk, but after a few minutes I jumped off the bed and ran down the hall to check on my mother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That was where your memory went blank. What about hers?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She says that I came right back and that I was really upset. That my mother was sick and my father was with her, waiting for an ambulance. By the time Tammy and I went back, my father had already gone to the hospital with my mother, so Tammy's mother brought us to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, that night it turns out your father was actually with her. That night he actually was the man.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't believe Tammy's version?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I believe it. Why would Tammy lie? It just doesn't add up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right, because if your father had already left home, how could he know that your mother was going to commit suicide?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But...

situation: I recount what happened on Christmas Eve.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: that was also kinda strange. Tammy said that he was always calling her mother to check on us. Well, of course he was. It must have been a fucking lot easier than coming over and seeing for himself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, but he did come over that night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So, yeah, he called the ambulance, so what? He happened to drop in one night when...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe he came over to see his boys and his wife because it was Christmas eve.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What difference does it make if he was there one fucking night? What about all the other nights? The nights when he was off with his girlfriend, when I was at home, guarding my mother?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All those other nights, where was your brother? He's older than you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, he played... He played sports. What kind of sports? Baseball.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you ever see him play?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I didn't. Can you see me trying to drag this lonely, crying woman out to a ballpark?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So your father was at work, your brother was at sports and you were on duty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After my father left, Patrick didn't even... sleep at home very much.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where did he go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Friends, I supposed.

situation: The therapist says memories are unreliable and believes something different happened on Christmas Eve than I remember.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Friends, I supposed

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember any of their names?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where are you going with this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm wondering if your brother was actually home. Could you have air-brushed him out too?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think that they were both there under the tree wrapping gifts?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Our memories can be very unreliable. We like to think of them as indelible records of our past, but every time we pull out a scene, we fiddle with it a little bit before we put it back in. If we hate our husband now, we re-remember the wedding as less joyous, or we say, He was never the right one for me anyway. We're constantly altering our memories so the past won't conflict with the present.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My memory is fucked. So what was my childhood really like, Gina?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, please, I'm not questioning your feelings about your childhood. They're absolutely accurate. I'm just wondering on this, you know, particular night that maybe some of the facts aren't what you think they are.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Gina, I'm familiar with the whole notion of a screen memory, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, of course you are. So then, you know your Christmas eve memory tells us about that whole period of your childhood, not just one night. You were overwhelmed. You felt that you were the only one who knew how much trouble she was in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father knew, he just didn't give a shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If he cared, he would have put her in an institution.

situation: I blame my father for not sending my mother to a sanatorium earlier, and Gina tries to console me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He'd have gotten her help, which he finally had to do but not before I spent every day of high school having no idea of what I was going to face when I came home. Would all the knives be sticking out of the wall, the bathtub be overflowing? Would she have an electrical cord around her neck? Or would she suddenly decide to take it upon herself to clean and paint the hall closets?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think he didn't institutionalize her sooner?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know, maybe he needed somebody to take care of the kids. Or maybe he didn't want to take your mom away from you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or you away from her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How about he and my brother ignored her, until she finally had to try to kill herself to get them to come home?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, Paul, one of the... confusing things about emotional injury in families is that it can feel so unfair, it can feel so random. It's like an automobile accident: everybody's in the car, but you're the only one who went through the windshield.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, actually it was my mother who went through the windshield.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you tried to grab her, but, Paul... Could you look at me? You were in the backseat. All you could do was watch.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And my brother walks away without a scratch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know what he suffered.

situation: I say I won't be like my father, who was always flirting with women.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father was in the driver's seat, struggling to keep our little family from crashing. Is that what you're saying?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I suppose that's what he thought he was doing. Is that what you're trying to do now with your family? You know, coming down to see the kids every weekend, calling them every day?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was nothing like me and I am nothing like him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, you're working very hard to keep from taking in any good information about him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Tell me why the hell I would do that? I mean, if he was half-decent, I would like to know it. He never did one fucking thing to help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But Tammy just told you a good thing he did: checking up on you from down the hall.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What does Tammy know? He was probably flirting with her anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your dad was flirting with Tammy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's a fucking doctor. They're all flirts. The whole time I was growing up, he was always...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He was always what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know... Well, it's just a memory of mine, excuse me, so it can't be trusted.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you afraid to say it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was always... With other women.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you know this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, I'll tell you how I know. I was 10 years old. My mother was yelling at him because he was... screwing this nurse and she wanted him to look at the effect that it was having on me so she pushed me at him, hard, and I hit a table and I split my forehead wide open: he sewed me up.

situation: I believe my father's infidelity made my mother ill, but then realize it might be my mother's illness that led my father to stray.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you're right. He wasn't completely useless. Are you happy now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These fights about other women, they went on for a long time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, early and often.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought that the fights began after your father left her. It seems that they were having trouble before he left her, before she got sick.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe his fucking around made her sick.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: His fucking around made her sick?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what I said. Christ! You know what? No wonder my patients complain about this. Would you stop repeating what I'm saying? Just say something else.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know it's irritating, but I just want to make sure that I understand. Fine. So you believe that your father's infidelity caused...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: drove my mother crazy, yes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When your mother was finally admitted, wasn't she diagnosed with bipolar disorder? In your experience, can bipolar disorder be caused by the infidelity of a spouse?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, Gina, bipolar disorder is not caused by events in a patient's life. Events can make you feel bipolar. No, I know that much. That's how I felt last year when Kate was... with her lover. But no, infidelity can't make you bipolar. You either are bipolar or you're not. But... if your wife... was bipolar, it... could make you want to have an affair.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, it could. Especially if you were a doctor and your wife's mental illness made you feel inadequate, helpless, incapable of helping the person that you were closest to. And since he couldn't heal her, he left her for another woman. And he left her with me.

situation: The therapist thinks me becoming a psychotherapist is a form of transference.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think I'm a therapist today because I feel guilty about my inability to heal my mother? No, I don't. Good.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you felt your mother's illness deeply. And I think even as a child, you had an empathic response to suffering. But you were too young and so you went to school. You worked, you studied, you thought. And now when people come to you, you can help them. But you're not a therapist because you think you failed your mother. You were a boy, Paul. You were in the backseat. You tried to grab her, but she was already gone.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about my feelings towards my patients.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So I have this patient Oliver. He's a kid who's trying to survive his parents' divorce. And it's taking everything I have not to invite him to come live with me. I know what he needs and I want to give it to him. It's the same with April and her cancer. I just want to stop them all going through the windshield.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does Oliver remind you of you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, neither of us... Neither of us knows how to be around our fathers. I mean, I have an idea, but it's the same idea I've had since I was Oliver's age. I think of my father and he's still screwing his girlfriend and I'm still scared to death that my mother's going to die. Only she's already dead. And he's almost dead. And I'm about to become the orphan I've always felt I was for 40 years.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know you're going to do well by Oliver.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's always hope.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe the boy that you really wanna be good to is yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Take me out to a ballgame.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Something like that.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist points out I want to be kind to myself, and I say I want to visit my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe what I ought to do first is... Be a good son to my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would that entail?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I Don't know, just go see the man. See how off he really is, maybe. Read him the sports page.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why haven't you been to see him this time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I'm busy... I'm seeing the kids and I've got patients. Actually the truth is I don't want to go. He stinks and he looks like hell.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about my relationship with my children and believe I need to communicate with them and my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll probably look... Look bad too when I'm about to die. I wonder if my kids will come and see me when I'm where he is. What if they feel about me the way I feel about him?

dialogue.text: Yeah, I was trying to fuck that man out of me forever. Oh shit! Jesus! Spilled milk, that's perfect, right?

dialogue.text: I think we need to talk about what's going on today.

situation: I told about my mother's response to the phone call. My mother was very stressed.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There was this girl behind the desk. She was like my age. She smiled at me and... she was like, Can I help you? And I know that's just something you say to people, but... I sort of took her at face value in the moment and... I was like, Can she help me? No, probably not. I mean, she doesn't know how to cure cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But still, she deals with it every day. The minute she looked at you, she must have known. Are you telling me that she didn't...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, My mom, just she called back and I had to leave to get reception. She was like, Where are you? You sound funny. And I was like, Well, mom, I'm... I'm actually a little sick. So she started to lecture me on how I don't take care of myself. I don't wash my hands when I get off of the subway and I need to stop biting my nails because I'm a grownup. She was really stressed out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why was she stressed out?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel tried to kill himself...

situation: My brother commits suicide again, and I meet the teacher for autistic children again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Daniel tried to kill himself... Again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Last week you said he was doing better.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I should've realized that that was a warning sign.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He tried to jump off the roof. Anyway he's meeting now with one of his old teachers, this... this miracle worker... Mr. Heath. He's the Anne Sullivan to Daniel's Helen Keller. He teaches at this special school for autistic boys. My parts sent Daniel there when he was 10. They took out a second mortgage to pay for it, because things had gotten so bad. Daniel had these two bald spots on either side of his head from hitting himself. The hair just stopped growing in.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what was it that this Mr. Heath did for Daniel?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He got Daniel to wear a helmet for a while. And daniel thought the... helmet gave him special powers. He thought it made him...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What? It made him what, April? Just stay with the thought. It made him what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He thought it made him smart.

situation: The therapist says the world is strange to both my brother and me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway... He's supposed to... He's supposed to call me after the meeting's over, so I might have to go pick him up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, can't your mother do that? She's busy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, she... She can't deal with him... Not when he's this bad. Not when he wants to die.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did he actually say that? I want to die?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, he says he wants to turn into a cloud and float away, but he knows what would happen to him if he stepped off a building. He's not stupid. He just... He gets so tired of everything feeling so strange.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, right now the world must seem pretty strange to you as well. And you're going it alone, without any Mr. Heath to save you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Isn't that supposed to be your job?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. But if you don't let me in, I can't help you. And that scares me, because I'm afraid that if you don't, we'll waste the little time that we have left.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Jesus. Kind of blunt today, aren't you?

situation: I think I have depression, and the therapist advises me to call him when it happens.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think I'm depressed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. Tell me why.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Probably because I have cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right. But can you tell me what you're feeling?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not feeling anything. I'm just sort of sick and tired and just... I don't know, just kind of disgusted with everything. I'll be brushing my teeth and I'll look at myself in the mirror and suddenly I'll look so ugly, just awful. And... And before I know it I'm on the bathroom floor, just starting at the lint in the bath mat, and I... I have no idea how I'm going to get back up again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That sounds like depression. It also might be what happens when you feel that things are slipping out of your control.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's horrible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you're feeling like that, I want you to call me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Listen to me. I don't care what time of the day or night it is, you call me. Do you understand? That's what I'm here for.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You want to talk to me when I'm on the bathroom floor?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Any time.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I say I saw my mom, who wants to leave my dad, and the therapist says I want to leave my brother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I saw my mom last week for the first time in a while. She took me to brunch. And what did you talk about? My brother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did she notice how... How tired you look?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I put on some makeup... A lot of makeup, actually.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you didn't want her to not see you at your best.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I always try to look good when I see her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It makes her feel better. But this last time I could've lost an arm and she wouldn't have noticed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because of Daniel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sort of. Also... she wants to leave my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did she tell you that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, It's not a big deal. She's been saying that for as long as I can remember. Life would be so much easier without your father. Never marry a workaholic. Blah blah blah. The fucked up thing is she doesn't actually want to leave him. She's crazy about him. She is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But she said she wanted to leave. Do you think it's possible that what she wants to leave is Daniel? You know, I think your mother passes a lot of her anxiety on to you. But I don't think the relationship is balanced, because you don't pass your problems back to her.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about my dad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry I brought her up. It's...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't talk about your dad a lot in here.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know. I don't have that much to say about him. He's never around. He's always at the hospital. For a while when we were young... Daniel kept forgetting who he was. He'd call him mister, like, Hey, mister. But Daniel kept getting worse as he got older and my dad couldn't handle it and he just checked out. On both of you? He and I have our own relationship. I used to wait up for him until he came home. I'd sit with him while he ate his dinner. He'd talk abouhis day, his patients.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So he treated you like an adult.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was nice.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It sounds like he understands you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But he didn't raise me. He just got to sweep in at the end of the day and talk to the healthy child for 15 minutes. She was with Daniel day in and day out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think part of the reason that you treasured those moments was because your dad was talking about something other than Daniel?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She needs to talk to someone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course. I understand that, but why couldn't she tell a friend?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It wasn't anybody else's business. It's okay, paul. I could handle it. I wanted to handle it. She gets overwhelmed. She needs to vent. So after she vents and she puts the stress, the disappointment and the worry of her own life on your shoulders,

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: who do you turn to? Or do you just carry it with you, your burden and hers?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are we out of time?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, we don't have to worry about the time. You know, I've been... I've been reading up on autism and it seems like there's some pretty promising research coming out.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's never gonna be a cure.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You seem pretty certain about that.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says the mom is trapped by Daniel, but I have other options.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not a disease. If it's not a disease, there can't be a cure.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, some scientists seem to be reconsidering that assumption.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, that's because they're being funded by rich, desperate people. Autistic children don't get better, they just get older. I'm sorry if that sounds cynical.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it doesn't. But you're right. Those children eventually become adults and their... Their parents die. And when that happens it falls on somebody else to take care of them. In Daniel's case, that would be you, April, for the rest of your life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a horrible person.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would you say that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I don't want to do it. He ruined their lives. He ruined their marriage. You can't... You can't give Daniel what he needs and have any space for anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, your mother couldn't, but you're not your mother. You can make different choices.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She didn't make any choices. She gotstuck.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She did, April. But every life is... It's a constellation of choices. Nobody escapes making them. You mother made choices that kept her locked into Daniel. You can choose differently.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's my brother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not suggesting that you abandon him, but you don't know what the future holds for either of you. You don't know what sort of innovations are gonna come along in the treatment of autism. You're not psychic, april. You can't predict the future. You can't control it. The only thing you can do in relation to the future now is to decide whether or not you want to be in it.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I make a call, and I have to go pick up Daniel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I look like such shit right now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, that's enough. We have to start talking now about chemo.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hi, Daniel. How was your meeting? You didn't see Mr. Heath? Where are you? I'm going to call you back in just one minute. Will you pick up the phone? Promise? Okay, bye. Mr. Heath. Hi, it's April. Yeah, I know. I just spoke to him. No, he's fine. He's in Central Park. He's at the sailboat pond. He likes it there. But if I go and get him right now could I still bring him to see you today? Do you still have time? I'm in Brooklyn now, so it'll take me a few hours. Thank you so much. Damn it, pick up. Come on, pick up. I'm gonna come and meet you in about an hour, but I want you to stay right where you are. Okay, will you do that? Will you stay? All right, I'm gonna see you soon.

situation: The therapist says I can't take care of everyone, I think the therapist is panicking, and I want to change doctors.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You fainted!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? No way.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes way. You are sick and you're not taking care of yourself. Sit down! You need to eat. You need sugar in your system.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't have to do that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're not calling the shots now, I am! Now you stay there and you don't move!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just stood up too quickly. I have really low blood sugar. I'm used to it. I'm fine. Really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you see what you're doing? You're treating me just the way you treat your parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can we talk about it next week?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you so afraid that I won't be able to help you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I have to go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: 2 minutes ago you were passed out on the couch, now you're off to save the world.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not going to save the world. I'm going to save my brother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Call your mother. Tell her to go get him. Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I can do it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There has to be another option. You can't take care of everything and everybody all the time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Listen. It's okay if you can't handle this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I saw how you panicked there. I get it. It's scary what I have, what I'm going through. I don't have to come back here if you can't handle it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what you think I was doing? You think I was panicking?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, you freaked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, let's say I freaked. What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That means I can't come back here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because you can't handle me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's possible to live in a world where people panic, where people let each other down, where they disappoint each other but still help each other.

situation: The therapist urges me to undergo chemotherapy, and I say it's poison.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I will get sicker and sicker. I'm gonna keep passing out on your couch. I'll probably vomit on your couch. And then eventually I'm gonna die on your couch. Is that really what you want?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No! I want you to go to chemotherapy!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you even know what chemo is?! It is poison that they administer directly to your heart! They put this big pump right to your heart. And do you know why? Because if they just gave you a shot and some of it got under your skin, it would melt your fucking flesh!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That is not gonna happen to you!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't know that. You don't know anything. You can't stop what's gonna happen to me. The nausea and the pain, my hair. You'll tell me that life is beautiful and I have to be brave and I'll say, yes yes yes, blah blah blah. But I'll be lying and you know that I'll be lying. And one morning you're gonna wake up and... say to yourself, I just wish that fucking girl... I just wish that fucking girl would leave me alone so I can be happy again. You won't be able to handle it. You won't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So to help someone is... is torture. It's unbelievably painful. It's hell. Yeah? If you let me help you, I will hate you for it. Yeah? And I'll probably fail you anyway. Yeah?

situation: The therapist says I don't have time and need to go to chemotherapy, I can't do it, but the therapist is willing to accompany me to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Our time is up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you wait a minute? Just sit down for a minute.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't you have another patient?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I want to say something to you. Sit down. Listen. If we had more time, we could find a way to tell your mother and see if she could handle it. But you don't have time. Do you understand that? And, April, I'm not going to sit here week after week and watch you just slip away. We have to begin treatment today, now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I tried. I told you I went there. I couldn't do it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Last week you said that the things we discuss in this room make sense while you're here, and then when you leave everything changes. What is it about this room that makes things seem... Different?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. The isolation, the detachment. You.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What if I come with you to the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Would you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes. Right now.

situation: I say I was fired and lost my reputation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You should be happy about one thing: they took away my phone and my blackberry. I hated those things. In my day an exec never typed a note. Never took one. Never carried anything. I guess that makes me a dinosaur.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm glad you came.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hope you don't feel any pressure today. I finally have the time to talk to you, but it's too late for you to help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How are you handling it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm wonderful, Paul. Aces.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know you said that you're past the point where... where talking could be of help. But long as you're here, why don't we... why don't we try?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, what is there to say? I've lost my job, my name. I can't leave the house. There's a pack of reporters on the street waiting for me to come out so they can stick microphones and cameras in my face.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So coming here today meant you had to run a... run a gauntlet.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can handle that. I tell them the truth. I did everything I was supposed to, that I took the pages straight from the playbook.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What playbook is that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Johnson & Johnson, the tylenol scandal. Seven dead from product tampering and the companywasn't concerned, but they pulled every bottle nationwide.

situation: I read a newspaper article and share my feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's still the gold standard for crisis management. At the first sign of trouble, you do everything you can to inform and protect the public and protect your name long term.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what do you think went wrong?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Here, Connie let me read this one article... in the journal. They came flat out and said I did everything right. Played by the rules. The only thing is the world's changed a lot since 1982. It's more predatory. The minute we assumed responsibility the bloggers, the press, the class-action lawyers came after us. Then the short-sellers hammered the stock down and that's when the parasites in my own company saw this as some fucking opportunity for themselves. And then the Donaldsons capitulated. A perfect storm they called it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you read an article like this, how does it make you feel?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like an old man who stayed too long in the ring.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You feel like a... like a boxer taken a beating.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I dropped my guard, Paul. I deserve everything I've gotten.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you eating?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I eat when I have to.

situation: The therapist is concerned about my physical and mental health.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shredded wheat, chicken soup... that's what I had today, okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How about sleep, are you getting any?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you a therapist or a pediatrician? Yeah, I sleep. The pills help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
