dialogue.text: Has your doctor written any other prescriptions for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, under Natalie's name, yeah. Any day now there'll be a headline in The Post: Baby-killer C.E.O. binges out on pills.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Baby killer? Is that how you feel that you're being depicted?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I don't know actually. My wife isn't even letting me watch TV except for old movies. I'm in a bunker with a remote control and pills by my bedside.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What pills do you take?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's called... Kloni... klopi... something like that. Whatever it is, it helps me sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how many are you taking?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, it depends. Maybe three or four. A day?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that the dosage that Dr. Wells has prescribed?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what I need to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you have to let him know how many you're taking. I mean, you're not somebody who's had a lot of exposure to pills, so you may not have the tolerance that other people do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's gonna happen, Paul? I fall asleep and I don't wake up?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what you want? Take a pill, fall asleep, not wake up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No no, I want to wake up. I want to find that the last two months were just a nightmare, that the pipeline didn't get contaminated, that the press didn't vilify me, that the people underneath me didn't lie to me. That's what I'd like.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can understand that you might feel that way, but since you know that that's not the case, have you found yourself thinking that not waking up might be a solution?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do... Come on, Paul! I don't quit. You know me better than that. And I would never leave a mess like that for my wife to clean up. As it is, she can't even look at me without bursting into tears.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must be something that neither of you are used to.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I do not want my wife to pity me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, the tears, I've seen plenty of those. Usually right before I cave in and give her the second baby or the third baby or whatever else she's ever wanted. But what is new is this look of pity. It's just god-awful. I told her never to look at me like that again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You sure it's pity? I mean, she's your wife. You've been married for 44 years. She loves you. When she spoke to me on the phone...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's another thing! I told her never to do that again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She felt that these were extraordinary circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? I got fired. What's the big deal? The whole country's getting fried... fired... fired! But all of a sudden I get an orchestrated show of compassion, teams of people dropping in. It's like an episode of This is your life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it hasn't been a comfort for you to know how much you've touched these people?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's been embarrassing. I told her yesterday, that's it. I don't want to see anyone else. Tell them I'm sick. I had to promise her I'd see you before she'd go along with me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So basically you used me as a bargaining chip. I don't mind. Long as it got you here.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist thinks I am going through a trial, and I share my friend's experiences.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And now what? What are you gonna tell me, Paul? That life is beautiful? That nothing happened? That it could all be a blessing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think nothing happened. On the contrary, I imagine it might feel like you're going through some kind of crucible.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: People give me all these nostrums, this self-help garbage.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not what you need to hear right now, I'm sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: An old friend of mine, Dean Larue, came by the apartment all the way from Rochester. I don't know what Connie told him to get him there. But he's my age. We were R.O.T.C. buddies. Two years ago they fired him from a company that he had built from the ground up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So he's somebody up here who's gone through what you're going through.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He tells me he's found a hobby. He's started taking pictures... landscapes, old factories and fishing boats. He prints them up and makes them into books and gives them to his friends. He gave me one... a photographic essay of Centralia, Pennsylvania.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that the coal town with the underground fire? I'm sure you wondered why he gave you that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No... well, what do I care?

situation: I say I dislike self-deception.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't care about that. The point is, does he realize how stupid he looks?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you don't buy it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If there's one thing I can't stand it's people who fool themselves, lead fake lives, become fake human beings.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not always a choice, Walter, so much as the way the twig was bent.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I want to shake Dean and say, Don't you know everybody is laughing at you, you old fool? I threw the book out as soon as he left. What the hell am I gonna do with a picture of some smoldering meadow where a town used to be? What if he was really proud of the book?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think it might have given him a different sense of accomplishment, of achievement? Or brought out a side of him that maybe he...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're smart. You know better than that.

situation: I talk about how I see myself in the doctor's eyes, and the therapist expresses anger at my betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If that company called him back right now and said, We made a mistake, Dean, we'd like to have you back, he'd go running in a heartbeat. No, the truth is that... he's outlived his usefulness. I've got a couple of years left to take photos and lick stamps, but... let's face it... death is just the... official acknowledgment. The show's over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you don't want your family to show concern. You don't want friends or a therapist to offer you support or... nostrums. Your life's over, like Dean's. Is that what you really think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why don't you tell me? Better yet, why don't you tell me what you think of me? The first time I walked in here, what did you think I was? I'll tell you what you thought. You thought I was a piece of shit who didn't care if his products were killing infants. You thought I was greedy, insensitive, a son of a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You feel that I've judged you from the beginning?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you I can't stand fake fucking human beings. Don't patronize me, and don't lie to me. I've had enough of that this week. Just tell me the truth.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The truth is I'm angry. I'm surprised at that reaction, but I am. I'm angry at what they did to you and I'm angry at the way they did it. I think you're a man of integrity. I'm not going through what you're going through, obviously. But I can understand your sense of anger, your sense of... betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I teach... or taught... classes in business schools... on corporate responsibility.

situation: I believe my reputation was taken from me, and the Donaldson family did not step in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess those days are over. They'd bring me in as a guest lecturer and... I'd look at all those kids who'd all gone to biz school for all the wrong reasons, and I knew I had... an hour to maybe reach one or two of them. To try to get them to understand that a company's name, a product's reputation is all that you have. That... if you lose your name, you've lost everything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel that you've lost that now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't lose it. It was taken from me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean by the Donaldsons? You haven't mentioned their part in all this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What can you say? Mr. Donaldson's old world, like me. He got scared. I don't blame him. But isn't loyalty... part of being... old world? It's not just the old man now. He still has his wits about him, but... the daughters are involved and the grandkids and the fucking lawyers and punks like Jace. You know, they put him in charge.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you said that the family, I think, has a majority interest in the company.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, it wasn't just the press or the parasites who forced you out. The Donaldsons had to go along with it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They had... credit market's drying up. The stock was in the tank, well, everybody's stock is in the tank now, but this was... carnage. The minute they gave me up, the stock gained it all back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you spoken to them lately?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The old man, he could barely look at me at the meeting.

situation: The therapist thinks the situation with my daughter has affected my judgment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I went over to him after... afterwards and... I thanked him for the opportunities he'd given me and... He said, Good luck, Walter. That was it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How long have you worked for this man?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 35 years. You know, when I came in, his son James was... He was reckless. The old man asked me to keep an eye on him. James was his only son. And a few years later, James went West to... look for some new markets. And one night, he drove his car into a tree. Right away the sharks started circling the company. The old man was barely hanging on. But I told him not to give in. I promised him that we would build something special, and we did. We did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you saying you turned him into one of the wealthiest men in the country?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did okay too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And after 35 years all he has to say is good luck?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He said one other thing... before he wished me good luck. He said, They tell me Natalie's in Rwanda. What the hell is she doing over there?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you think he meant by that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think that was his way of saying... that I'd dug my own grave.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said yourself last week: in the middle of a crisis I ignored my responsibility to the Donaldsons and to the company.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I also remember saying that there were two crises, one with your daughter and one here. And we talked about the way you experienced your daughter's distance, how that anxiety might have colored your judgment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you're agreeing with me. I misread both situations. My judgment was bad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Perhaps your going away did contribute to this situation exploding. We know on some level that your body had been trying to tell you something was very wrong... your insomnia to the panic attacks. By going to Natalie when you did, you were trying to bring this crisis to a head.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was already past that point. Jace was a cancer I should have cut out long ago.

situation: I trusted the wrong person and the product went wrong and poisoned the child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I trusted the wrong people, the wrong labs. Under my watch... this poison got into the pipeline and onto the shelves.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you issued a recall the minute you found out.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The papers... the ones my wife won't let me read... they're all saying kids died, and it was my fault.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what you think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Natalie thinks so too. When she emailed Connie you could tell she thought I was some sort of... corporate criminal.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said I think you're guilty, the papers too. Now you're saying Natalie...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not paranoia, if that's where you're going.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Part of you believes you did everything that you could properly, and part of you is punishing yourself for not doing more.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm okay during the day, most days. But at night I wake up in a cold sweat, wondering... how I missed it, what I could have done, what I should have done, how much hurt I've caused... to families, to the company.

situation: I believe it's my fault that children drank poisoned milk, but the therapist says it's not entirely my fault.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But at night I wake up in a cold sweat, wondering... how I missed it, what I could have done, what I should have done, how much hurt I've caused... to families, to the company. God, if you could see the old man's face. He looked stricken.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must have made you feel terrible, to disappoint the old man. You seem to talk about him as if he's... a father that you've let down.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's my fault, Paul, not his.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I see you struggling to understand what happened and why it happened. But as hard as you're working to deal with this guilt, this sense of betrayal, it seems to me that you're working just as hard to avoid looking at him and his role in this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why do you keep harping on him? He did the best he could.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that when his son James died, old Donaldson was ready to just... give it all up. But you wouldn't let him. You took on the family business for 35 years.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Their son was dead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you feel guilty about that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd promised to keep an eye on him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And so for what, some penance you took on this enormous responsibility? The same way that you took responsibility for your parents' lives after your brother Tommy died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had no choice.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, you were just a boy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had no choice.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were six years old. You shouldn't have been taking care of your parents. They should have been taking care of you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was my fault!

situation: I think James's death and my brother's death are my fault.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's why I had no choice, it was my fault.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was your fault?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A hot summer night, before air conditioning, the air was dead still. Tommy was just going to sneak out to the quarry lake to cool off. He came to my room... and said... tonight was the night he was going to jump off the highest cliff. He was asking me, really, more than telling me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did you tell him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said, Tommy, you can do it. You can do it, Tommy. And I told him in the morning I'd... brag about him to everyone. Then he kissed me good night. And he never made it back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you felt responsible for your brother's death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was. I am.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, your brother jumped. You didn't push him off the edge. He chose to jump.

situation: I and the therapist schedule another appointment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And in a flash a family was destroyed. That's it. It happens. There are lots of them... destroyed families.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you okay, Walter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have to go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know this week your sense of guilt about all this, it must feel like an avalanche. I know you must... feel overwhelmed, but it's urgent that we talk about this feeling in here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My wife's waiting for me outside.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can we arrange something for tomorrow morning?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes if I'm up all night, I need the mornings to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What about Monday afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm fine, fella.
dialogue.fine_label: 回避-最小的回应(C1)  来访者

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you mind if I call your doctor and... talk about those prescriptions?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'll see you next week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My wife's waiting for me outside.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I couldn't get close to my daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sorry I'm late. Rosie kept me waiting for half an hour. She wanted to talk to me. Turns out all she wanted was the keys to the car.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you give her the keys?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was she happy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think so. I guess I wanted to feel close to her, wanted to hear about school and whether she has a boyfriend or not, how she's doing with Kate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you were all living together, did she tell you those things?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She wouldn't have had to tell me because I would have seen them. I could overhear them or Kate would tell me. So you didn't have conversations then either?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you talk on the phone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We try. But, you know, I can always tell she's IMing her friends on the computer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what can you do to feel close to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. I don't know...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember a time when you were living at home and you felt close to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There was one time... I took her. She broke her arm and Kate was out of town so...

situation: I talk about accompanying Apil to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got to take Rosie to the hospital. A lot of sitting... Emergency room, treatment room... and we were waiting for the cast on her arm to dry. And it was just... Just me and Rosie. All afternoon, just me and her. I read to her. I told her stories. Played 20 questions and I spy. That was a happy day. Yeah, pretty sad, huh? I missed so much.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing. I was just... I took... I took April to the hospital this week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's your patient who has cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. Well, she wasn't... She still wasn't telling anybody, her friends or her family. She was... She wasn't getting treatment. So after our session, I just... got up, I took my coat and I just brought her to the hospital. I know it was wrong. But you see, the oncologist had already made a treatment schedule so all she had to do was get there. So I took her there. I waited with her till she was finished and then I took her home.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you tell her stories?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, we were... just quiet.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were you reminded of the day you spent with Rosie in the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. You know, I'd give the last 10 years of my life to... To be back in the hospital with Rosie that afternoon waiting for her cast to dry.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I say my life is terrible, but Gina says I still have a lot.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hate my life. It's broken. Every day, it hurts. I'm not getting anything from my family, so I try to get it from my patients. I know it's wrong, but who else do I have?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Who else do you have to get what you need from?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody. But, okay, I have you. But you can't give me what I need. It's not your job.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let's talk about what you need.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you have any water? You're supposed to have water for your patients.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're so convinced I won't have any water for you, you don't see it. It's sitting right there. So, can you tell me what you need?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need anything special. Just what... What everybody needs.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you have food. You have clothing, you have shelter. Well, sort of.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have a den with no other bears. Is that shelter?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You need some other bears?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I miss them. You know what I'm talking about. I know you do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I do.

situation: I describe my life after meals and people's behavior in bars.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I miss dinner, you know? I miss the after-dinner.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you do in Brooklyn between dinner and bedtime?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes I go to... the local bar. They've got the soccer from England on. That's good, so... Then I have... Have a drink.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, do you ever meet any women at the bar?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I see them. I don't know if they see me. I'm like that... That lonely guy in the Edward Hopper painting, sitting at the bar.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Tell me about the women.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Some of them are pretty, you know? They wear bracelets that jingle.

situation: I mention patient Mia, which excites me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They go outside to smoke. Like my patient Mia.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think you've mentioned Mia.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was a patient 20 years ago. She came back this year. She's... Well, it's complicated. She's a lawyer that works for the firm that's handling the deposition. The lawsuit. We had a conversation about the case then she came back as a patient.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean, complicated?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Complicated emotionally. But... she's really smart. And she's... She's funny.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Challenging?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think you could throw that one in there, yeah. She's also the kind of woman that, if she managed to work through her issues, she could conceivably... be right for me. I'm not in love with her. But... Could see myself with somebody like her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You've cheered up just talking about her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I am drawn to her, yeah. But after last year and Laura, I don't think I'm going to fall in love with another patient for a while.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that a relief!

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But is she in love with you? Is that why you mentioned her? No I mentioned her because...

situation: I talk about my needs, beyond sex, to be close to someone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: we're talking about things that I need. I need a woman.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For sex?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is that what women think that men... really think that they want them just for sex?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I was just asking you if you wanted sex.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course I want sex. I'm not dead. Okay, well... Then good.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's something you need. That's our subject... What you need. So you need sex.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I need fun. I need release. I need contact with another human.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How are things going with Tammy?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you been seeing her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know I have.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I don't know. Actually, I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well,

situation: I talk about my recent encounter with Tan Mei; we slept together.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: she and I had coffee. Then we had drinks. Then... We had a night at my apartment. She was supposed to be traveling away on business. A furtive afternoon, then it was over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You had sex?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, mother. Like bad children. We had sex.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Gee, I...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You knew it would happen. You made me promise not to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I sound like a really tough and jealous mother. I won't let you have sex. I make you ask me for water.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You dared me to see her. You wanted to see f I could control myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know how hard it is to resist an old lover. Too bad I didn't have more of them. I'd like to come back to Tammy in a little while, if that's okay. I'd like to talk some more about the bears. Have you seen your father?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I... I don't know how he is. Jesus, I...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you go to see him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I didn't go to see him. I meant to, and...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not? Is he better?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. He may have taken a turn for the worse.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I discuss my father, whose condition worsened, and I didn't visit him; Gina says I care about my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He fell a few times in the hospital so they moved him into another room. He might have a fever. I'm getting all this... from Patrick. I was busy preparing this week for the deposition. That was a treat, let me tell you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you didn't go see your father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I didn't. And if you don't stop nagging me, I won't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not nagging you, Paul. I'm reminding you that bears do not live forever. And this bear, with whom you have very many unresolved issues, he's dying.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My brother says he's dying. That doesn't really mean that he is dying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you rather just get a call that he's dead?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let them call my fucking brother!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You may think that you don't care about this, but you do. If you didn't care, why would you have reacted this way when I brought him up? Paul, please sit down. You say you're not getting what you need from anyone, but it's worse than that. It's as though you're a baby. You woke up from a nap and you started crying, but nobody is coming in to see what you need. And so you cry louder and you shake the bars of the crib. And still nobody comes. The only problem is your father is there. He's in the room with you, but your anger at him is so profound that you can't see him.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says I am ignoring the help my father needs, and she urges me to heal my wounds.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father can't help me now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, he probably can't. But until you acknowledge his presence in your life, you're not going to understand anything about him. And you'll continue to shake the crib.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? I'm a grown man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course you are. But what you haven't been is a grown son to your father. And until you do that, part of you is always gonna stay a baby. Or at best, a teenager waiting for your mother to die.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother's already dead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's right. What you're afraid of, it's already happened. Neither you nor your dad could stop it. And the only thing you can do now is hope to heal this wound so then you can move on. We both know what it's like not to be there at the end. It's something you don't get over. Ever.

situation: I comforted the therapist and asked him if he was okay after his father's death.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Hello, Mia.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Paul, are you all right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm... I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm so sorry about your father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Uh, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I found out from Ellis at work. How are you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm... I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You can't really be fine. I know that I'm not supposed to talk to your lawyer, but you never canceled on me before. Some things are bigger than protocol, aren't they? I mean, life and death, and losing a father. Paul?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sorry. It's ironic that we were talking about your father last session.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've thought about that. You know, the strange thing is I haven't spoken to him since then. But I can't imagine what I would do if... I'm sorry. This is not about me today.

situation: I was very worried about the therapist's condition and asked him if he was okay after his father's death, and noticed that he is lonely.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you get my card? I stood in that store forever trying to pick it out, you know? What kind of picture? What kind of message? What did you think?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I haven't read it yet.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I sent it? You were away all last week and you haven't opened your mail? That's not a good sign.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sounds like you're worried about me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You do look tired and you're not wearing a jacket. Are you sleeping? Are you eating?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said that before. I know that you have to be the neutral shrink, but, you know, this is a relationship of a sort, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. I appreciate your sympathy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Granted, I am not the first person you would reach out to. Our last couple of sessions, I have been... A challenge to put it mildly. But I was concerned. I wondered who do you have? I don't know if you're close to your ex. I assume your kids are with her. You haven't been in New York that long and it's hard to find friends.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, are you worried I'm lonely?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No offense, but I can see it in your face.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is it possible that you're afraid I'm not ready to give you my full attention today?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, that's not it. I mean, this is me being caring. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, of course it is. It's not what you... Look, you don't have to worry about my feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does anybody? Would you rather I yell at you for canceling?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you saying you felt like yelling when I canceled?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No other reaction?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I got over it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Before or after you had seen Ellis?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, true, I went to Ellis. Also true I was a little upset... more than a little. And then I felt like a jerk when I found out why you had canceled.

situation: I am pregnant, and my situation at work becomes more merciful on the other side.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But that was last week, and now everything's changed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why is that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I'm pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, that's... ... that's really... big news.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No kidding. Are you surprised? Me too, especially with my F.S.H. levels. It's strange timing with us... life and death. Do you wanna have the session out in the snow? I mean...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sorry. You were telling me about your... F.S.H. levels.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, we were past that. I was talking about our timing. 20 years ago you were having your first child and I was losing mine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So have you been thinking about that time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's different this time. I know everybody says you get pregnant and everything changes, but it's really true. My body feels totally different. I've stopped smoking. There's this preschool on my block that I always avoid because it's... moms with their humvee strollers blocking everyone, like they're privileged because they procreated. Now I just walk through smiling.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you went from jealousy to feeling like part of the club.

situation: I say the pregnancy is a result of indulgence and don't want the child to be affected by patriarchal issues.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: At work, Bennett... who's leaving friday, finally... he had asked me to take over this big case, assuming that I would just crush the other side as usual. But I took one look at the poor family and I cut a deal. He was pissed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're sure you're not trying to punish Bennett?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He's marrying stefanie. That'll be punishment enough. I feel bad for their kid, you know? I mean, he's a double adulterer and she's a bimbo. Why are we talking about Bennett?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you brought him up. And he is somebody that you did want to have a child with.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's... it's not his. I did the math.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Still, it's interesting that you found out that Bennett was having a baby and a couple of weeks later you're pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you saying that I'm competing with Bennett?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's what you think I think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: that's what you think I think? Paul, I'm having a baby because I went on a sex spree that weekend without using protection. Maybe that wasn't the smartest thing but maybe it was.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So maybe you weren't just being reckless. Maybe you maybe you're trying to get pregnant...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I figure it was guitar boy and not the middle-aged cop, which is good, because there won't be any paternity issues if I decide not to tell. Guitar boy doesn't even have my number or my last name.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you don't want him involved?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know the baby needs a father, but not one like that. Does this silence mean you're appalled?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I hope for the doctor's blessing and discuss some issues; I say my mother hates me and won't help me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hey, I'm pregnant. I thought that you would be happy, that we'd celebrate. This is really bad timing. I know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would you like me to say, Mia?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wow, Mia! That's amazing! You came saying you wanted a family, a child, and then you got it. Congratulations.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In other words, you had a problem and now you have a solution?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, can't that happen ever?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course. It sounds ideal. What else would you like to hear from me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This game again? How about don't worry. You're going to be a good mom and I'll be there for you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could you tell me what that means, i'll be there for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have major decisions to make.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like do I need a doula? Should I have genetic testing? Will my apartment be big enough?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you want me to help you with this those decisions?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How much time should I take off? Or should I just quit and move to the country?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These are all big questions. Your sisters have children. Have you spoken to them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're busy with their own kids. And my mother? Forget it. And my dad, he loves his grandchildren, but he doesn't do anything. He just lets them admire him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You sound sure that your mother wouldn't want to help you, but she did with your sisters.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's different... they're younger, they're married... And she actually likes them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And she doesn't like you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For me she was less of a mom and more of a vase... beautiful, but hard to the touch. That's a very powerful image. She was beautiful until I ruined her figure.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh yes... her mantra. Has that been on your mind this week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've always kept in shape. I think men like that and now that'll all go.

situation: I ask the therapist if a child affects a man's desire for a woman.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hear your feet get bigger. I hate big feet. Not to mention what birth does to sex. I mean, you've been there. It stretches, right? The size of a baby's head compared to the size of a penis? That can't be good. And the man thing is over, isn't it? Guys my age, they have grown kids. They don't want to change diapers again. I mean, would you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What... what are you asking me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on, Paul, just answer my question.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If someone like me would be attracted to a woman like you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We've already done that. I get it... we're not a couple. I'm saying hypothetically if I got fat, emotional... more emotional... if I had to cater to an infant...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think that rules out all men.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So I could still get the drooling guy on the back of the 6 train? I mean, look, having a child can ruin even a good relationship. Is that what happened to you? Your wife did all the child-rearing while you sat in that chair listening to people's problems? She actually dealt with people's problems? It must've pissed her off.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Obviously, something did. But I'd rather talk about your anger than my ex-wife's.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fair enough.

situation: I misunderstand the therapist wanting me to leave; the therapist hears his father's watch.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Who... whose are those? Yours or your kids? And why are they in here? Are you this responsive with your kids or are you different as a dad? Okay, great. You're bored? You're annoyed? You can't wait till I get out of here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And we're back to your default... that I want to kick you out.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You did just look at your watch. You have never done that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've never worn a watch before.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That is not the point. I am right. You should not be working this week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm fine, Mia.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If I said i'm fine four times, you would be all over me. You're not even in the room, emotionally. Admit it. Why did you look at your watch?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's my father's watch. I'm sorry. I must have glanced without meaning to when you mentioned the word dad. It's not even ticking.

situation: The therapist thinks my feelings about the child and men are intertwined.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Time stops when I'm here. If I wasn't pregnant, we could call it a day and goo a bar. That would be better for both of us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is this the bar in soho where you hoped we'd run into each other?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, although this time we could act like we'd just met.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: As in hello, is this seat taken?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right. And I'd say, No, hi, I just found out I'm pregnant after a binge weekend of anonymous sex. And you would say my father just died. Then we'd get plastered and fly to vegas and get married.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And then what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know me, I'd fuck it up. But it was fun, wasn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can see how we both could think it would solve our problems.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't go overboard.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mia, I think there's two issues here: one, your feelings about the pregnancy; two, your feelings about not having a partner. And it could be that they're... Intertwined. I mean, you've said a few times that it feels like I'm not in the room today. You mentioned you're worried that having a baby is gonna make you feel less physically attractive. Is it that you're afraid that no one will be there for you if you have a child?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I will be a single mom. That's... harder.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes. It can be.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And okay, I admit it isn't my first choice but I can't have my first choice.

situation: I describe a perfect situation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is what I have. It's not picture perfect.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what's picture perfect?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Me, a baby and a man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what kind of man?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No idea?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's not the point. Why aren't you encouraging me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're in the mood to celebrate and you feel that I'm not joining in that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I think that you think that I'm too fucked up, and a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know that's not what I said.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Never mind. I will call guitar boy. I'm sure he'll take full responsibility. Or... or I'll just do it all on my own. I'll quit my job, I'll gain 100 lbs and I'm sure I'll still be as good as my mom except that this baby won't have a dad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why don't you just take a breath?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God, I need to smoke. Oh. You won't let me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought you had quit because you're pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: One cigarette isn't going to do any harm.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd rather you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm in withdrawal, okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you're agitated.

situation: I wonder why people have children and think children shouldn't be born.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why do people have children anyhow? They want little versions of themselves to gaze up and say i love you? They want to relive their own childhoods? That... that is the last thing I want to do. The truth is I like visiting my nieces, but I cannot wait to get home.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't give me that sense.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was I thinking, sleeping around like that? If I had wanted a child, I would've had one by now. Maybe I should give it up for adoption.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't want to have the baby?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm just...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Go on, Mia. Just talk through it. Tell me what you're feeling. It's okay. These feelings.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shut up. It's not okay. This isn't just my feelings. This is it, right? This is my last chance... And I'm... I'm too scared?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This sounds very similar to what you were saying 20 years ago.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're right. This is just how it felt back then, isn't it? I didn't want to have a baby. I wanted to have an abortion.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And is that what you want to do now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. I don't know. I mean, come on, Paul.

situation: The therapist believes I am capable; he says he will help me as a psychotherapist. I fantasize about starting a family with the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We both know I'm... I shouldn't go through with this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mia, look, I understand that you may be feeling just... overwhelmed right now...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, you think?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you are in a very different place than you were back then. Some of your concerns are... they're practical. You can handle them now. You know how to hire a nanny, how to buy a bigger apartment, how to make a living. But maybe the real question is do you want to raise a child if you have to do it on your own?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Will you help me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I... I can help you as your therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I know, but I've never been a mother - and you're the father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm the father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: N... no, I misspoke. You're not the father. You're a father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Nevertheless, you did want us to celebrate, you asked if I would stick with you if you were pregnant and then you imagined how we might run away and get married. So if you're creating a new family, Mia, it's possible that you'd like me to be there... in the picture or in the room.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And here we are.

situation: I admit my fear of being unable to cope and want the therapist involved.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And now I just want you to tell me that having a baby means I won't be alone for the rest of my life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, I can tell you that in my experience at times it feels like when you have a child, you'll never be alone again, or even have a moment to yourself. Who... who else have you told about the pregnancy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This time? No one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Even after you took the test?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think you're right, Paul. I do want to pull you in. Of course, you know I... I'm scared. I'm worried about doing it on my own. But I heard what you said. I'm not the same person I was 20 years ago. There's just this new life. I can feel it. And this time I want it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You really do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I'll try my best to be a good mother... Even if I'm afraid and even if it's just me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think maybe this is a good place to stop.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wow, that went fast. It's okay. I'd better get going. The subways are going to be all screwed up. But you... you should take the rest of the day off... a snow day. Go for a walk in the park. Eat something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And, Paul... Please be happy for me.

situation: I recall the treatment process and express gratitude to the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nice cap. Those stairs were so hard for me. This keeps happening, you're gonna have to start giving me therapy at chemo.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Two birds with one stone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what I like best about you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What? My morbid sense of humor?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Your eyes. I remember the first time I came here and as I was leaving I looked at you, and you looked at me and I lost my breath for a moment. It's a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't worry. I'm not gonna jump you. I'm in chemo... I can barely keep my food down.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, they have drugs they can give you that can counteract the nausea.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're not even my type. But your eyes are... Bottomless. I'm just saying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just... I forget I can't do that anymore because of the thing I have there now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does the port hurt all the time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Only if I move a certain way. I can't remember them cutting me open. I didn't faint or anything, did I? No. Do you remember them putting it in? Did you watch it happen?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not... not all of it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 'Cause you didn't want to see my breasts? Trust me, there's nothing really to see. But thank you for not looking. And thank you for taking me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're welcome.

situation: I describe how the therapist talks to me in my mind, encouraging me to live.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, It's funny... I've had so many conversations with you in my head over these last two weeks. I mean, literally every day we've talked for, like, hours at a time. We've had whole arguments in my head and then we've made up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what... What have we argued about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Whether life is just bullshit or there's something deeper behind it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what do I say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, You don't say much even in my head, which I find frustrating. But when I asked you if it was all worth it, you said, Of course it is, April, if you make yourself and others happy. What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm such an optimist in your head.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You wouldn't have said that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What you're essentially doing is giving yourself advice in the form of my voice.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And very sound advice it is. You're taking very good care of yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Once I asked you not to give up on me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did I say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said, Never. I just want to haze you for a while. What do you think I meant by that? You're testing me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how do you pass?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I live.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you get extra points for telling your parents?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Isn't it amazing how many people have cancer?

situation: I apologize for my previous behavior at the doctor's and thank him again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And just, like, having conversations, doing sudoku. Did you see those two girls in the corner on the computer? They were shopping online... For underwear. We have catheters coming out of our fucking hearts and they're buying new bras.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, sometimes a little denial is not a bad thing... but don't tell anybody I said that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry I've been such an asshole in here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I told you... no apologies.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, I didn't answer your calls. I made you let me talk to Sienna during a session. I smashed my freaking model in your office and I left it for you to clean up. I must be the worst patient you've ever had.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh no, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thank you for taking me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And thank you for going.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, really. Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I heard that.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: Last week I was so sick after chemo that I called my best friend.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had a bad night last week... Just a few days after the chemo. I wanted to call you, but...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why didn't you call me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You canceled our session. I thought you needed a break.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, That was nothing to do with you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It doesn't matter. I called my best friend Leah instead.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Leah. I haven't heard you mention her name before. What did you say to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I... I had woken up from this dream where I was already dead or... No, not exactly. It was more like I knew that I was about to die, like something was coming to kill me. It was horrible. But... I also kind of wanted it to happen, just to get it over with.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's another way of looking at that dream. Maybe it's just the part of you that refuses help...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want to talk about what the dream means. I was just, you know, setting the stage.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Understood.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My best friend called an ambulance for me, found out about my chemotherapy, and comforted me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway, I woke up with this really high fever, like so high I was shaking... I couldn't even hold a glass of water. And I totally freaked. I mean, I really thought it was all about to end. That's why I called Leah. She came right over. And she took one look at me and called 911. On the way there the ambulance guys were asking me if I was on any medication that they should know about. And I said, Well, chemo.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So was Leah in the ambulance with you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And her mouth just... sort of hit the floor. And... I was so out of it I just started apologizing. You know, I'm sorry. I wouldn't have called, but... I'm dying, and... She took my hand and... she said, April, you don't die this quickly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She sounds like a true friend.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She really is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yet you hadn't told her about the cancer till then.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recall how Leah helped me when we were younger; we help each other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I haven't seen her for a while. She's in law school, so she's been really busy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you known each other for long?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We shared a bus stop with a bunch of other kids. When I was 10, Daniel came to school with me for the first time. He was trying kindergarten. I was so afraid that everybody was gonna make fun of him. And that first day, I turned around for just a second and when I turned back around, daniel was standing there singing and holding his penis. And I wanted to die right there. I mean, everybody was staring at him. Nobody said anything until... Until Leah said, Daniel, you can sing or you can hold your penis, but you cannot sing and hold your penis. Everybody started laughing. Then all the guys started singing and holding their own dicks. It was amazing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So she's always looked out for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We've looked out for each other.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says I demand high loyalty from people around me but don't seek help from friends.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We've looked out for each other. Her mom died when we were in high school, so she came to live with us for a while. She's really more like a sister than a friend.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, her reaction when... When you called her reminded me of how Kyle reacted when you called him, when you were having trouble with the model, remember? You said that he also came right over.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, so?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So it seems like the people in your life are very committed to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have good taste in people.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think it's more than that. I think that you demand incredible loyalty. So the only people you allow to get close to you are the people you feel that can measure up, people you feel that can really go the distance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm incredibly loyal to them as well.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I know that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So why are you making it sound like it's a bad thing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I guess I just wonder why you work so hard to make friends who are... so fiercely devoted to you and then, when you need help, you seem reluctant to rely upon them.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I called leah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's true, but you waited until you thought that you were dying.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I think friendship can be exhausting; I believe Leah doesn't want to help me every time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's like a bank. You keep taking money out, then eventually there'll be nothing left.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you think that there's only a limited amount of support that one person can offer another and when that support is used up, it's gone forever? If Leah had cancer, would you get tired of helping her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But not everyone is like me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what do you mean everybody is not like you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: In the emergency room, the doctor told me I should expect more fevers just like this one. As he said it, I saw Leah's face. She just looked terrified.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For herself or for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Enough. I get it. I mean, I get what you're trying to say. I just don't agree with you. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not everyone is like me, Paul. I mean, I know you think I'm crazy, but I'm right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think you're crazy, April.

situation: The therapist says he will always help me; I fantasize about my middle age.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You canceled our session last week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I'm... I'm sorry about that. How did you feel when you got the message?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, considering we've determined that I have a tough time elying on people, it was a pretty ballsy move on your part. What happened?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I had a family emergency.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So what happened? You don't want to tell me? Come on. I told you I have cancer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just know that if I could've been there for you... I would have been.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know that. Hey, how old are you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A bit... a bit passed 50.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 'Cause I was thinking this week, when... When Leah's mom died she was 35... We were 15 and she was 35... And I remember her being so old, like middle-aged, and... now she seems so young to me. And I was wondering, you know, if I make it to 35, will I look back on the time in here and think, When I was 23 and Paul was 50, he seemed middle-aged. And now he seems so young.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You'll have to let me know when you get there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So we'll keep in touch?

situation: I ask the therapist to tell my mother about my illness.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My hair started falling out. They say I'll... wake up one day next week and the rest of it will just be there on the pillow. It's gonna be hard to keep it from my parents after that happens. I guess you and I should start strategizing. Or maybe you could just tell them. I bet you and my dad would actually get along. You're both sort of intense in the same way.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you should be part of that conversation. We could ask them to come with you to therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That might work.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We could schedule something before your next chemotherapy session.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, we can't. It's tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... Who's gonna take you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what about Leah?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What about her?

situation: I want the therapist to take me to chemotherapy; the therapist says he can't take care of me, but I have many relatives and friends willing to help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What about her?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Wouldn't you prefer if she took you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you not want to take me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's not a question of whether I want to take you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay, are you refusing to take me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You still haven't told your parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you've got a whole system of support in place that you're not using.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want my mother to take me to chemo.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I want you to take me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think we should talk about why you still can't tell this to your parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is this some kind of a joke?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it's not. I am your therapist and you need one a therapist, but you also need a caregiver and I cannot be both people.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean you won't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It isn't appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but you've already taken me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I... I had to do that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nobody forced you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was the right thing to do. April, you are very sick, but I crossed a line.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What line?! There's no line!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There needs to be a line if I'm to continue being your therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You just drew the damn line!
dialogue.fine_label: 否认-最小化(B4)  来访者: You

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, listen to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew you couldn't take it.

situation: The therapist says his father died; I care for him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew as soon as you saw that... them put that port into my heart, you said, Fuck this shit. This isn't my daughter. This isn't my problem.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's going on? Tell me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, you can.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't do this. I'm gonna fail your fucking test.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you won't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: People die of this shit every day.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But not everyone is as strong as you, remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought you were gonna take care of me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm trying.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you're dropping me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, I'm not dropping you. I'm here for you, April, as your therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Until you're not. I was so scared last week. I dreamt I was dead. I need you then. I know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I had a family emergency.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What happened? Did your dog die?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's okay. He... He'd been sick for a while.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Your father died? How could you let me go on blathering like this when your... your father just died?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I appreciate your concern...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Were you close?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, not really.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He left the family when... When I was young.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So was your mom at the funeral?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, my mom has been gone for a while.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A long time ago.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Jesus. So you've had it pretty rough, haven't you? I'm... I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We all have our fights to fight. Well, look at you. You deal with Daniel every day.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God, why do you have to do that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Turn everything around so that it's about me and my experience. Can't I just feel bad for you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure. Go ahead. So are you... Feeling bad for me now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes.

situation: I fantasize about mourning for the doctor; the therapist praises my emotional intelligence. I refuse to have others accompany me to chemotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We're having a whole conversation in my head. I have expressed my sympathies about your father, and you have gratefully and graciously accepted my condolences.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Good. You know, having a fantasy life as powerful as that... The ability to play out whole scenarios in your head... that's... That's the mark of a highly intelligent person.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Really?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes. Yes, according to some studies.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And what do the other studies consider it a sign of?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Utter insanity. Can we go back to talking about your chemo session tomorrow? Who can take you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand you don't want to talk to your mother... And I appreciate Leah can't take the stress...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. She's got midterms.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you must have other friends who would like to be there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess so.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What about Kyle? When you figure out who's gonna take you, will you let me know?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I want to know that you've found somebody.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry about your dad, Paul.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist asked me the reason for my visit, and I said I was bullied and that the teacher did not provide proper feedback.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you mad at me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not at all. But I am concerned about you. Do you want to tell me why you ran away from school?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Bad day.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can't I just sit here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I just thought... you came here so early, you must have something that you want to talk about.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you... my mom's still away and my dad's at work.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you've got keys to both their apartments, and you came here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you have any more ham?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You want me to make you another sandwich?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure. I can do that. But I hope by now you understand that if there's something bothering you, you can talk to me about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Somebody put dog shit in my locker.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's terrible. When was this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I came down from the roof at recess to get my gloves out of my locker.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about how I skipped classes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When I opened it there was dog dog shit everywhere, all over my backpack and all my stuff. And all my stuff. I went back to the roof to tell my teacher.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did she say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She got a janitor to clean it up. But recess was over, so everybody knew what happened.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you have any idea who was responsible?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But nobody saw him, so nothing's gonna happen to him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, well, I remember what he did to your shoes, so I guess this would be his next logical step.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All through math everybody laughed about it. The teacher got upset 'cause no one was paying attention. That was my fault too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Listen, somebody did something awful to you. That is not your fault, okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I asked my teacher if I could go to the bathroom. But I went to the lobby instead. While the guard was talking to someone else, I snuck out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You weren't kidding. You had a hell of a day. But I'm glad you came here so that we can talk about it.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recounted how my father yelled at me every day, blaming everything on me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My dad's gonna be so mad. And he's already really mad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's he mad about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Everything. I've been staying with him for two weeks since mom went away. And he yells at me all the time, no matter what I do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So What do you do when he yells at you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let him yell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you ever discuss the things you fight about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He doesn't talk to me unless he's yelling. I think he broke up with Nina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did he tell you that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, but she doesn't come over anymore. That's my fault too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That can't be your fault.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nina told my dad to make better rules for me. And then they had this big fight. Now she doesn't come over. And when I see her at school she doesn't smile at me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you miss her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really. But I think my dad does. He did a really bad thing the day after the fight.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did he do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I shouldn't tell you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's up to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He bought a six-pack of beer and drank all of it and he fell asleep on the couch. And what happened? He didn't get up in time for work. He yelled at me for that too. Why didn't you wake me up? But I didn't know I was supposed to do that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There was no way you could've known what you were supposed to do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mom was supposed to be back by now. But she had to stay on her vacation an extra week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you told her about the fights you've been having with your dad?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, she'll just get sad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If I were in your shoes, I'd be really upset about all that.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father came to find me, blaming me, and the therapist mediated between us.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, oliver, I keep thinking you've sunk as low as you can go, but it turns out there's no bottom.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why don't we just sit down? We can talk about what happened to oliver today.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I get out of my meeting... I have seven messages from your school. What the hell were you thinking to just disappear like that? Eric dumped dog shit all in my locker. He did what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
