dialogue.text: Apparently during recess today some kid vandalized oliver's locker. Oliver's locker. Nobody saw who did it. But all the kids knew that it had happened.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hate that fucking place and I'm not going back. Nobody told me that. Why didn't you ask me before you started yelling? Because you still shouldn't just run off from school. It's dangerous and you know better.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think that what your dad is trying to say is that he understands that you've had a bad day. And he's just concerned that you left school and you didn't tell anybody where you were going.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want to talk about this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand. Why don't you just go outside and I'll talk to your dad, okay?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where were you last week?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry I couldn't be here.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father talked to the therapist about my situation, and the therapist said I wanted to break free from control.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: First bess vanishes on this apparently permanent vacation, and then you go awol. It's like rats deserting a sinking ship.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was an emergency, luke.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's an emergency over here too. Every day he comes up with a new way to drive me up the fucking wall.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you've had a tough couple of weeks?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Bess calls every day. And we lie and tell her everything's fine. And she sa she needs a little more time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That must be pretty stressful on you and oliver.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: First he suddenly decides he won't do his homework. He says he's taking a stand on principle... the principle that school is stupid.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you talked to him about it or were you hoping I would say something?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I took away his tv privileges and his computer privileges, but he still won't do his homework. You know, He just sits there and stares at the wall.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He certainly knows how to push your buttons, doesn't he?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Next he decides to stop bathing. What the hell am I supposed to do? Climb into the shower with him and soap him down?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think Oliver feels powerless, so he's refusing to follow the rules because that's the only way that... he can get some control.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yesterday, after he left for school, I went into his room and looked under his bed. Past the mountain of dirty clothes, there was all this food hidden in there. I mean, half-empty packages of oreos and doritos and cheetos. I mean, there was...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you tell Oliver what you'd found?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, and he got furious, ran into his room and slammed the door. I should've gone in and talked to him, but I was so exhausted.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand that you'd be alarmed by all this. But you know what? I've worked with a lot of kids in situations similar to Oliver's and... overeating is a pretty common response.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, this...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father talked about how I was often bullied at school because of my obesity, and he did not want me to be friendless.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This thing that happened at school today, it isn't the first time. Oliver gets bullied a lot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you done anything about it? Now that the school knows there's a problem, they're obligated to help you find a solution.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, now... How are they gonna stop kids from picking on Oliver? I mean, you see why it happens, right? I mean, he's fat, he's shy, he doesn't have any friends and he smells bad. If I were his age, I'd probably bully him too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, the way he's been... behaving lately, I can see how that would make you angry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes I just wanna shake him, and say, if you keep acting like this, no one's ever gonna be your friend. Is that what you want? That's unforgiveable, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you wanna try and spare Oliver from the pain that he's going through right now. But you love him so much and that makes you frustrated and angry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but what good is loving him if I can't help him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But isn't loving him helping him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know anything about anything this week.

situation: My father, due to educational disagreements with Nina about me, became single again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know anything about anything this week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what else has been going on, Luke?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Looks like I'm single again. Nina and I had a huge fight about Oliver. And the reason I asked her out in the first place is because she liked him. I thought she'd be good with him. But it turned out she just isn't on my side.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And whose side do you think she's on?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Last week Oliver dropped a carton of ice cream on the carpet. Of course I got pissed off. Then Nina came over and... for some stupid reason, I expected her to back me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you wanted her to help you discipline Oliver.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But instead, she started screaming at me. She said I wasn't spending enough time with Oliver him, I wasn't setting clear boundaries for him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how did you respond to that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told her if I wanted somebody yelling at me all the time, I would've stayed married to Bess. That went over real well.

situation: The therapist said my father drove women crazy, refusing to take responsibility for me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, at first, Nina was a lot of fun. I could come home at the end of the day and just relax with her. Then, all of a sudden, she started scrutinizing my every move, marshalling evidence against me. I don't know, Paul. Why do I keep choosing these crazy women?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not so sure, Luke, that it's the women who are crazy. I think it's the position that you're putting them in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you're saying it's all my fault?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: From what I've seen, you enjoy having fun with Oliver. But when it comes to making the rules, creating a structure for him, for a long time, you let Bess do that job. And then you hoped that Nina would take her place. So when he misbehaves, you blame them. You refuse to take responsibility for Oliver yourself. So can you see how that might... how that might upset everybody?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Boy, now I could really use a drink.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you been drinking lately?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What did Oliver tell you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would you ask me that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because the night I broke up with Nina, I went out and got a six-pack,

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said I made efforts but did not improve the situation, so he wanted my father to feel bad too.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because the night I broke up with Nina, I went out and got a six-pack, drank the whole thing right in front of the kid. I thought, let him tell Nina, or Bess, or you. Why not?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you wanted Oliver to tell us?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't care. I never really had a drinking problem. That was Bess being paranoid. But the other night, I'd just broken up with my girlfriend, my kid was acting up, my ex-wife skipped town, you'd skipped town. Shit, who wouldn't need a drink after all that, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you saying you needed a drink?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, the week before Bess went on vacation, Oliver was on his best behavior. But the second she left town, he's turned into this monster. Is he trying to get some kind of reaction out of me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think that's part of it. But I also think that he was behaving so well because he was trying to get some kind of reaction from you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, look at it from Oliver's point of view. His family is breaking apart, so he puts a lot of pressure on himself, trying to behave perfectly, hoping that that would solve the problem.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you're saying he was faking it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In a way, yeah. I mean, He even tried to stop eating so that you wouldn't be concerned about his weight.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He told you that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But it didn't work. He did everything right, but it didn't solve any of the problems. So now, maybe he's behaving badly to try and make you feel as badly as he feels.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I tell you, I liked him a hell of a lot better when he was pretending to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, Oliver couldn't keep up that behavior forever.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The adults and I talked about adoption issues, with my father wondering if I loved myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He had me fooled. Bess and I We talked to him about the adoption, and that seemed to make him feel better. I honestly believed he was doing well.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Which is what I think he wanted you to believe. I've talked to him about the adoption too, and... The way he sees it, Bess and you were fighting... too much, and you gave his brother away. And things are so difficult for him right now that... I think that sometimes he wishes you'd give him away too.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does he even love me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would you say that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't love my dad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not even when you were Oliver's age?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sure. I did love him back then, but it was unrequited love.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You'll have to explain that to me, Luke.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father reminisced about his childhood, saying he never felt his father's love.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father was the dean of students and basketball coach at my middle school. He was in charge of every breath my brother and I took. When we did well, that's just what he expected of us. And when we screwed up, well, let's just say he was a man of limited sympathy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's quite a lot to live up to.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You'd think that. The year I was in the seventh grade, he started taking long drives on the weekends by himself. My brother and I got on our bikes and we rode around the neighborhood, looking for his car. And we found it in the driveway of this little house. My brother made me ring the buzzer. The door opened, and there was my father's secretary, this nice lady who'd give us candy. Then my dad came out of her bathroom and started screaming at us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you guys do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What could we do? We got on our bikes and we rode home. And then I was lying awake that night in the bed and I realized my father's secretary's living room looked exactly like our living room. Every piece of furniture was exactly the same as ours. He must've bought it all for her. My brother told my mother and shit hit the fan. She packed us up and we left town. We only ever heard from him when he sent his check every month. He was good about the money, I'll give him that. But we didn't wanna see him. I mean, he sure didn't wanna see us. He never met Bess or Oliver. And when he died, it was like a formality.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father said he was following in his father's footsteps, but the therapist said he had other choices.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But lately... It's like he's laughing at me. I did everything right. I proposed to Bess when I got her pregnant. I worked like a dog to make a good home. I never raised a hand to Oliver. And now I feel like I'm standing right where my father stood.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, just because you're getting a divorce, that doesn't... that doesn't mean you're turning into your father. And it doesn't mean that you're gonna lose your son.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But that's exactly what it feels like I'm doing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's inevitable that sometimes you'll remind yourself of your father. You see how you wound your own children so... so badly without even trying. Suddenly, you almost understand how he... he could hurt you the way he did. But you don't have to become like him. You're not doomed to live your father's life. You have a choice. I think our session is almost over. Would you like to say anything to Oliver before you go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, if we still have time.

situation: I believed I was fine and wanted to be discharged.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not hungry. I don't need any pills. Leave me alone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For Christ's sake. What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You missed your session. I called your home. Connie told me that you'd... You'd been admitted last night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And she asked you to check in on me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd have come anyway. I was worried about having to cancel my session last week, so...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, you can tell Connie you saw me and I sent you home. They're gonna be discharging me tomorrow. We'll have a session next week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not so sure they're gonna discharge you, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You... You may not be ready to go home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course I am. I had a little food poisoning. I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Food poisoning? I'm glad to hear it. Well, since you're fine, and I'm here, maybe we can... maybe we can talk.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Will it help get me out of here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It could.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, then tell me what you want to know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: First off, are they treating you well here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's... It's a little showy for a hospital, but the staff's good. They're in and out all the time, but no, I have no complaints.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So I'll bet you'll be glad to get home.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I really miss my privacy, knowing where my things are.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, I spoke with Connie. She told me that Natalie was leaving to fly back to Rwanda. You had an early dinner with both of them, she told me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, we ate in. I don't go out. People gawk.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And they both ate the same meal as you did?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right. Chinese.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But they didn't get food poisoning.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So maybe I got a bug.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I also talked to your attending physician. He said that you were lucky.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Lucky?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That Natalie's flight was canceled.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about recent events, including my children visiting me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't follow you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She got a call from the airline while your wife was driving her. They turned around before they even got to the airport.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So that's what happened.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Another half hour, you wouldn't have made it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess it wasn't my time. Not now, please.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to tell me what really happened?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's to tell? I kissed Natalie goodbye. I caught a chill after she left so I got back into bed. When I woke up, I was here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Had you been spending a lot of time in bed?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't have anywhere else to be, do I?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And your daughter Natalie, how long has she been in New York?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A week, 10 days. I told you Connie overreacted to my... My forced retirement, sent out an S.O.S. sent out an S.O.S. The boys came in first from California.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how was that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Awkward as hell. I didn't know how to talk to them, they didn't know how to talk to me. We watched basketball, reruns. My older one ate my food. The younger one was upset that there was no booze in the house, so he went out and got a bottle of single malt. After that I never saw him with an empty glass. Then Natalie came. And the second she got in, they beat it the hell out of there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And she came all the way from Rwanda.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Paul, I know where she was living. Yes, but it's just that you'd said before that you felt that she was... done with you. Yeah, well, Connie must have really laid a guilt trip on her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how was it seeing her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Uncomfortable.

situation: The therapist was worried about my condition, and I said I had checked on the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She wanted to talk about what happened over there, what happened here. I told her I wasn't in the mood for small talk, she made me get out of bed and shower, shave, get dressed. Made me go out on walks in the park. She even took me to the zoo. She used to love going there when she was a little girl.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So your mood improved when she was here. Did you find it upsetting when she had to leave?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, of course I was upset, but I wanted her to go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So whether or not you really were feeling better, you made sure that they both thought you were.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you, I was better.
dialogue.fine_label: 答案: A1 争辩-挑战(A1)

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you had your last meal with Natalie, you kissed her goodbye, they left and you finally had... Your privacy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What I had was the chills.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did you take for the chills?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Aspirin. Antacid. What difference does it make?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: They pumped your stomach, Walter. You were pretty far gone. And it wasn't from antacids.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So what? Probably what happened was I drifted off, woke up, reached out for the wrong pills in my sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't believe you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What the fuck would you know?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because it's my job to know. And I am obligated to express my concern to Dr. Wells and the rest of the team here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't have to be concerned, Paul. My family isn't going to sue you. They're not like that pilot's family.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's all you're worried about, isn't it? I should have vetted you sooner. But someone on your school... I'm on the board, by the way, or was... recommended you and, like I say, I've been dropping my guard lately.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you can still pack a pretty mean punch if you want to.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You seem like a smart fellow. And I know you wouldn't know anyone who could hurt me. But still, when the leaks started to really hit the papers, I told Marie to have HR run a background check on you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you think about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean aside from wondering if you were in over your head with me?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I wanted to be alone, not wanting to be watched by my family.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had other things going. I didn't even look at it until last week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Last week... after I had to cancel.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Probably around there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you feel I let you down by canceling?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, actually I was relieved. I didn't want to come in and go through the motions.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what coming feels like?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what everything feels like. I wasn't upset. But I was surprised. You convinced me that you were angry about what had happened to me and that you were on my side. And when I missed a session? Boy, you really have a high opinion of yourself, don't you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't help but notice that's when you decided to read the background check.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had time on my hands. And blood. Just like you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that also what you thought when you read about the lawsuit?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What difference does it make?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You keep saying what difference does it make, but I think it does.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: With all due respect, Paul, don't flatter yourself. If you'd been there or not it wouldn't have mattered one bit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you're saying your mind was made up, you would have done it anyway one way or the other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Done what? I went to sleep. I went to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it, a handful of pills? A couple of shots of your son's scotch? It must have been everything you could do...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: To hold on until Natalie was gone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What was she supposed to do, take care of me for the rest of my life? Both of them, opening the blinds, fluffing the fucking pillows, making sure I'm dressed. They were worrying themselves sick about me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you didn't want that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So I...

situation: I talked about my planned way to die.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I forced myself to start eating again. I stopped taking the pills. I squirreled those away. I pretended to sleep through the night just so they'd... finally leave me alone for a few hours.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A few hours, that's all you needed then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told Connie she couldn't let Natalie take a car service to the airport.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You figured she wouldn't just drop her off. She'd wait at the airport for a while. So you would have enough time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wanted Natalie up in the air, as far away from this as possible. Connie was just supposed to come home and find me asleep. A millionaire's death. You know what that means?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think I heard my father use that expression.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, mine too. You go to bed one night and you don't wake up. Just close your eyes. I took the pills, chased them down, took a few more. I don't even remember the girls coming back. I must have vomited all over the bed. I just wanted it to be over, that's all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's okay, Walter. It's okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't even do that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just leave it on the table. Thank you.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I believed my family would be better off without me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Does everyone in the hospital know?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You have a very good team of doctors. They assessed the situation the night that... you came in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is it in the papers? For how long? I didn't leave a note. I left the TV on, left the lights on. Nobody was supposed to know. Just an old man... asleep under the covers. The doorman would have helped. Short term, Connie would have mourned, but... she has a support system. Long term, she'd be a helluva lot better off as my widow than my wife.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sure she would not agree with that, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She didn't sign on for this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To have a disgraced basket case as a husband. Do you know what it's like for her?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's been a C.E.O's wife and now she has to sneak out through the service entrance of the building next door like... Like you do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not the same. It's different for me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And why is that? Because she didn't do anything wrong. And you did? Everything that's happened to you, you feel that you've deserved it? Is that the way you think?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: People died...

situation: The therapist said my daughter would blame herself for a lifetime.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: People died... on my watch, Paul. Let's not pretend otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And anyone who's worried about you would be better off if you... weren't around?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's just... the objective truth. You met my daughter? She's got her whole life ahead of her. Now what? She's supposed to just put it on hold and... and worry about whether her old man got out of bed that morning or took a shave?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've met Natalie. And she's in a terrifying place right now. But as hard as it is for her to worry about you, I'm absolutely certain that if you'd managed to kill yourself, she would never have forgiven herself. The same way... that you've never forgiven yourself.

situation: The therapist said I was always punishing myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not the same.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Isn't it? You blamed yourself for Tommy's death even though he was the one who jumped. You blamed yourself for James even though he was hell-bent on destruction. And you blamed yourself for this crisis even though you did everything possible to avert it. It wasn't enough, Paul. Of course it wasn't. I mean, how could it be? You've had... blood on your hands, as you say, your whole life. And it's shaped everything. That's why this time when kids died, it wasn't punishment enough to sacrifice your life to your parents, as you did. This time you had to impose the death penalty on yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I see what you're doing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what am I doing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is this how you deal with your guilt? You tell yourself that what you feel isn't real? That... you did the best you could?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's always there. I always wonder what else I should have done, what the limits truly are of responsibility to another person.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And you can live with that? It doesn't affect you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course it does. All I can really do is try to... understand what happened and... why I made the choices I made. To... learn from the loss and to...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, it's different for you. You're a young man. You can recover from your mistake, move to another state, start over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you don't feel that you can?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's too late for me. We both know that.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My daughter was outside waiting for me, and I wanted her to leave.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look at you... One eye on the door, wondering when you can get out of here and cut your losses.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not what I was doing. Natalie is outside.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What is she still doing here? I told her to go home to her mother. She doesn't listen to me anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's on watch, Walter. She doesn't trust that somebody is going to look in on you every 15 minutes or so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Every 15 minutes? Is that what that is?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're at risk.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you tell her that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She told me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So? Tell her I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Tell her I'm fine. You're safe to fly.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Whatever.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't really do that, Walter. I think you're gonna have to stay here for a little longer.

situation: I wanted to sue the doctor, asking the therapist to leave.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But I'm fine. I'm eating. I'm sleeping. I just got a little dehydrated. Just tell them you're my therapist and that there's nothing wrong with me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can't do that. In my opinion... you need to be kept under observation. And you've made it clear that you don't want your family standing guard duty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you trying to have me committed?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What I'm saying is that I think it would be a very good idea for you to stay here for a few days. This hospital is one of the best.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll call my lawyer. He'll bounce you on your ass so fast you won't know what hit you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You want to sue me, Walter, get in line. But it's not gonna get you out of here any sooner.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How long?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Until it's safe for you to leave. And if the doctors haven't released you within two weeks, then you have the right to make your case before a judge.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A judge? Are you kidding me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wish I were. I don't want anything to happen to you, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Too late.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Walter, it's not too late. There's a lot...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Get out of here, will you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just get out of here.

situation: I talked about my father's funeral.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How are you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm okay, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you like some tea or some water?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Water'll be fine. Thanks. Thanks for the orchid that you sent. It was beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm glad you liked it. I've been thinking about you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a pity you weren't there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't think it was my place to be there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, well, it was a nice service... Except for the priest's cell phone going off. My kids spoke. They each had... a memory to tell. And some people from the nursing home came. They talked about his card playing and his singing. Did he sing when you were a boy? Not that I remember. But one of the surgical nurses said that, you know, he used to sing in the operating room. A fine Irish tenor, she said he was. Of course, there was a lot of women at the funeral.

situation: I tried to mourn my father, and the therapist said family and work were two different experiences.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Women really liked my dad, as you know. Then too, women live longer than men so when you get to a certain age, there are always going to be more women at funerals. You know what I've decided? Women are really good at loss. Men don't really... They haven't got a fucking clue.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you get to speak to your father before he died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, for men loss is... It's a defeat. In a game or a fight, losing makes you mad. You want to get even with the guy. Like this man who's suing me, Alex's father. This guy is so angry that all he can think of is coming after me. Like that's gonna help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you trying to understand how to grieve for your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Among other things.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What other things?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: One of the things I'm trying to understand is how I can help my patients with death and dying when I myself have been so stupid and so wrong about it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, Paul, it hasn't even been two weeks. You won't always feel this raw.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We'll see.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you tell me more about the funeral? I don't wanna talk about your patients now when you've just been through this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you not think it's important for me to talk about my patients? How am I going to help my patients if my own life is in a mess? Would you use a plumber if you found out all the drains in his house were blocked?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's not the same thing. You're a trained psychotherapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But not a trained husband, father or son.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, you're not. As a man, you're like an animal in the wild. You're living day to day, you're trying to protect your territory and provide for your family. As a therapist, you're observing certain members of the herd through binoculars. These are two very different ways of experiencing life. But you can't observe yourself through your own binoculars.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But that's why I'm here.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right. Can you tell me more about the funeral?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not this week, please. I feel like...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I learned a lot about my father at the funeral.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I feel pretty wiped out. We don't have to talk about it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I'm interested. You said you were glad that your children were there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I was glad that the boys were there. Maybe they won't be as stupid as I was about it all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Stupid?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I learned more about my father at his funeral than I ever did when he was alive. Doesn't that sound stupid to you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you learn about him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, for one thing, I found out that he did a lot of free surgery in Bolivia. You didn't know that about him? No, of course didn't. And he made me executor of his estate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does that surprise you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And he gave me his half of a little brewery in Minnesota.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He owned a brewery in Minnesota?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: With one of his doctor friends. I guess he loaned some guy some start-up money 40 years ago. So if the lawsuit ends up costing me my license, I guess I can always go make beer. You see what I'm talking about? Who was this man? All I knew was this old story that I've told you. That he left us for a patient, my mother killed herself and I grew up alone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All these things are still true?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How the fuck would I know?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said my father hurt me, leaving mysteries behind with his death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If my father was this great guy, why didn't I know it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you beginning to think he was a great guy?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Even if he wasn't great, at least he was interesting. But what was I? Was I blind?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: People often can be very successful in the outside world and remain a complete mystery to their families. Mystery is putting it mildly, Gina. I don't think he was a complete mystery to you, Paul. I think as a boy, even though you didn't have all the facts, you knew he was an interesting man. That's why you were mad that he was never home. Maybe you wanted to live with him instead of your mother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, who wouldn't?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It wasn't your choice. Paul, he was the only one with a choice in your family. He chose his work, his investments, his women. That hurt you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wasn't hurt. I just hated the son of a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think the hatred grew so you could protect yourself from his rejection. I don't think you always hated him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I loved him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm saying it wasn't stupid of you not to know about these things. I mean, maybe he didn't want to call attention to his charity work.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said my father chose battles he could win over his family.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Or maybe he thought his singing was silly or the brewery was frivolous. Or maybe he wasn't home enough to have any conversation about anything or maybe by the time he got ready to talk, I didn't give a shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All these things are possible. Death leaves a lot of unanswered questions. You know, not everybody has what it takes to be a good parent. And sometimes, as in your father's case, the choices can be very difficult. Do you give yourself over to your sick wife and angry children and fight a losing battle? Or do you give yourself to your talent and hope that someday they'll understand?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you're saying his home life was a losing battle for him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm saying that he looked at his options and he fought the battle he thought he could win.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A less charitable view would be that he won the battle he chose to fight.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's true.

situation: I talked about my interactions with my father before his passing.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So it wasn't stupid of me to not know who my father was when I was a boy. It was stupid that I got to be this old and still didn't know who he was. Even sitting there at the bedside in the nursing home... He had maybe five minutes to live. And for the first time it was just me and him together. Sickness until death, and all that. The only person I learned anything about was me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm glad you saw him before he died.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was the strangest thing, you know? Everybody left and... I went downstairs and said goodbye to them... Got a coffee and I came back and he was... He was asleep. Well, he had a pulse anyway. And I sat down and I started talking to him and... And he didn't have a pulse anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were talking to him when he died?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was talking at him, Gina. I said... I'm sorry and... I said I was sorry that I hadn't seen more of him. I asked him if I could get him anything and... Then I just started complaining about my life... Like I always do. I looked up and he was... He was gone.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did it feel to you like he'd been waiting for you to come back to see him before he died?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. That's what the nurses say, but...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said my father could sense his children's presence and had passed away peacefully.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. That's what the nurses say, but... They say it happens a lot, but I don't believe it. I think it's crazy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, not really. On some unconscious level he might have known it was you. Or sensed it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, he didn't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Didn't you ever become suddenly aware of your children without them having said anything?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: With Max, I remember when he used to wake up in the middle of the night, he would come into my room and I would just wake up. And there he would be standing at the end of the bed, just... staring silently at me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So even though Max hadn't said a thing, you woke up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, great. So my father becomes aware of me on some level and he really doesn't want to listen to me complain so he just dies.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or he becomes aware of you on some level, and he's finally able to let go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd like to believe your version. Do you believe it? Or are you just saying it to make me feel better?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do I believe that there's some non-scientific connection between a parent and child? Absolutely. Does that mean that a parent knows what a child needs? No, it just means there's a connection.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, we're more than connected.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I wanted to talk about responsibility and obligation, while the therapist wanted to discuss me and my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's obligations between parents and children. There are things that they owe us and there are things that we owe them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, but, you know, I think obligation is maybe a subject for another day.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I want to talk about obligation today. My father owed me things... And he didn't come through for me. And I owed him things and I didn't come through for him. If I'm not gonna do any better by my kids and they're not gonna come and see me till I'm about to die, then we are all hopelessly screwed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that your father's watch?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't want to talk about this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. I don't want to talk about anything in general. I don't want to talk about obligations or family duty. I want to talk about you and your father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is his watch. I'm gonna wear it for a bit. I don't usually wear watches. But I'll wear this for a while. Because it's a pathetic excuse for... For grieving. There it is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you mean when you said the only person you learned anything about that day was you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I felt like I was in a movie I was watching.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said time was precious, and I wanted my father to fulfill his duties.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I felt like I was in a movie I was watching. Self-centered guy goes to the hospital to see his dying father, sits down, can't think of anything to say to his dad. Then he starts whining about his own little problems.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A divorce, the fear of losing touch with his children, a move to a new city, the threat to the man's work from a lawsuit.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They don't sound so little when you actually say them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These are big problems to somebody in the middle of their life. But to someone confronting death, like the father, it might seem that the son could work these problems out. The dying father doesn't have the time, but the son does.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No marriage, no children, no practice, just time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Without the time, you don't have any of the other things.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it's not a guess. It's true. Time's the precious thing. You already know that. That's why you're wearing his watch. Maybe you were telling him your problems because you were hoping he'd say something meaningful to you. Or finally be a father to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know.

situation: The therapist complimented me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. But after he was gone I wished the whining guy in the movie could have been some kind of comfort to his father. I wished I had... done or said something more than just take the man's watch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is there anything you wished you had asked him before he was gone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I wanted to ask him if... If he was proud of me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you know he was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do I?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're a good doctor to your patients. You're a good father to your children. And you love singing.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a terrible singer, Gina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't say you were a good singer. I said you liked singing.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I was afraid to know my father still loved me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I should have gone earlier. I know that. Guess I was afraid. Once I was there I thought, What the hell was I afraid of? My father is dying. What can he possibly do to me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you know what you were afraid of?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was afraid that after a lifetime of hating him... He was gonna love me anyway. And I think I waited till he couldn't talk anymore because... I just didn't want to hear him say it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would that have been so bad?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because if he could love me and not give me one minute of his time... Then love doesn't mean a thing and I don't want it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You can't intellectualize it. It's something we feel, sometimes with good reason, sometimes not.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said my father loved me, and I loved but also hated my father.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I was a pallbearer and... so was Ian. And as we came out of the church and carried the coffin to the churchyard, I looked over at him and I thought, One day he's gonna carry me... If I'm lucky enough not to mess it up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You won't mess it up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How can you be so sure?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because you already know that love is the only thing that has a chance against death. It causes us a lot of pain, but without it, we feel isolated, untethered, lost in space.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So... My father... loved me. And he did what he could.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. Your father loved you and he did what he did. And you loved him and you hated him because he ignored you.

situation: Alex's father wanted me to write a letter taking full responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not pretty. Is it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wish you could have had the father you deserved. But maybe you can be a father to yourself now and do for yourself what you do for your boys.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you have the father that you needed?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm a therapist! What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I gotta go. I've got to meet Alex's father. Maybe there's some way I can help. Thank you, Gina.

situation: I came to the clinic, very tired.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Hello, Mia. Would you like to come in?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's over. I'm not pregnant. I'm not feeling well. I really should've stayed home. I called in sick at work. That's a first.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did your doctor say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll live.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did he say anything else?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm so tired. I want to go back to bed. I'm not up for a whole session.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, why don't we just start and then we'll see how it... how it goes?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd rather stay here for now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can I get you a glass of water? Maybe some tea?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's very nice, but I'm fine. That's what you kept saying last week... I'm fine.

situation: I talked about my experience of miscarriage.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How have you been?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Fine. Would you like to tell me what happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's not much to tell. I went to work on friday... Started bleeding. I went home... And it didn't stop. End of story.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, emotionally, how are you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm kind of numb. It feels better that way.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought that I was gonna be a parent and now I know I'm not.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm really sorry, Mia.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just felt transformed for a couple of weeks. Like I had a real... purpose. And I was a different... a different me. You know, a woman has a baby and people stop asking questions: what's wrong with her? Or... she's so ambitious. Or pathetic or strange. It's easy then... she's a mother. It answers all the questions.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It seems to me that you had a lot of questions yourself last week.

situation: The therapist said there are other ways for me to become a mother, which I rejected.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe I melted down a little, but I still wanted to have the baby. The stupid thing is I can smoke now - and I don't even want to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So maybe you have changed a little.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nice try.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, There's other ways to be a parent if that's what you really want.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean compete with some young suburban couple for some pregnant teen's baby? I can't imagine picking ivy league sperm out of a catalogue to defrost and squirt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't want to adopt, you don't want a donor and yet you're sure that you wanted a baby. It isn't just about being a mother, like you said last week. You also wanted to have the perfect picture.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I kept waiting to meet the right guy but it... he didn't show up. Or more likely I pushed him away. And now no man and no kid.

situation: The therapist said I could come to him if something happened, and I said I had talked to my mother about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't want to talk about this. Let's switch to the weather. It was a really cold weekend, wasn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, it was surprisingly warm. Did you stay inside? Did you call anybody? You could've called me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're still in mourning and you were away over the weekend anyway, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mia, something like this... you call me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Actually, I did talk to someone. Believe it or not, I spoke to my mother. I'd certainly like to hear about that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think we could talk about it inside?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What is it with therapists? You hear the word mother and these bells go off?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Pretty much. It's... it's part of the training. So would you like to tell me about the conversation you had with your mother?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cara, one of my nieces, gave a piano recital on saturday,

situation: I talked about how music was the only thing that made me happy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Cara, one of my nieces, gave a piano recital on saturday, and when my mother saw that I wasn't there she called to see if I was okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your mother and not your father?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right. I haven't heard from him in a while. Anyway, my mother is the queen of protocol and I had missed a family event. This... it was Cara playing Chopin, and I have been paying for her lessons. I told my sisters that if any of the girls wanted music lessons that I would treat. I mean, what is the money for? I defend some pretty questionable doctors present company excluded... and how many pairs of high heels do I need?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that because you want to make sure that music isn't taken away from them in the way that it was for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Playing piano was... the one thing that always made me feel happy. Anyway, I didn't answer the phone, so she left a message. And then later that afternoon she showed up at my apartment with a platter of pierogis.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe she was concerned for you.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recounted my mother finding out about my miscarriage.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, there's always a first time, right? So how did it go? I was still in my pyjamas. She took one look at me, the heating pad, the tylenol, the tissues in front of me and she said, do you have the flu? And I shook my head no. I started to cry and she got it. And she said maybe that's nature's way. I don't know when I last cried in front of her or when she's last hugged me. And then she heated up the food, set the table nicely, poured us some nalewka.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a cherry-infused vodka. It's a traditional drink. Anyway, she tried to make a consolation toast. She said to better days... And then she told me that she was proud of me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, maybe she was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said that I should be grateful for what I have. My independence, my career, this interesting life I'm leading.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It sounds like some of the things that she might have wanted for herself.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My mother admitted her suffering was not caused by me, blaming me was just a cover, and having children ruined her sanity.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I snapped at her. I said, that's kind of a strange toast considering you've always blamed me for ruing your modeling career.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you tell her that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, you won't believe what she said. She said that she didn't really have much of a career. She wasn't that pretty and that she never would have risen above her job as an underwear model, which is not what I grew up hearing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right, her mantra.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Her false mantra. The same lie over and over until everyone accepts that it's true, especially me, the one that she loves to blame.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you ask her why she did that?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother said that it was... Kind of her cover story... That having me didn't ruin her looks. It destroyed her mind. She said that after I was born, she lost it. She couldn't get out of bed, she didn't want to eat. She said she stayed in her room because she was afraid that if she left it, she would kill herself, and that there was some small, sane part of her that didn't want to do that to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know there are some mothers who get so depressed that they lose sight of even that. So where was your father during all of this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said he just moved into the living room.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: My father took me away and drove a wedge between mother and daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He didn't try to get her professional help? Are you kidding? He was first generation. He would've been mortified to ask someone for help, to admit that his wife was crazy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So he took care of you during this time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He did everything. He had too. She didn't even want to breastfeed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, really, you weren't mothered for over a year.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When she came out of it somehow she did, she said she had this rush of feeling and that she wanted to be close to me, but by then my dad and I were just inseparable... I think the word she used was impenetrable that my father had never forgiven her and that he used our closeness to show her how she'd failed. She said that she was so guilt-ridden that she thought she didn't deserve me, and so she just kept away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's quite an admission. That must've given you a lot to take in about both your parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think her depression might also explain why she didn't get pregnant again for 10 years?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. She talked about that too. The twins the cherished twins they were an accident.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recounted my mother saying it was my father who wanted to send me away and denied not visiting me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said that she was terrified when she found out that she was pregnant again and that she asked my father to hire a sitter so someone would take care of us if she couldn't. And according to her, he said no. That he couldn't afford it. And she insisted that it was his idea to send me out to his sister's out in new jersey.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you don't believe her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course not. My father adored me. She also said that I was wrong about him coming out to visit me every sunday, that I must've made that up, because they came together once a month. That's not possible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, mia, it is... Because it's entirely possible you airbrushed her out of your memories of that time. Sometimes the need to protect one parent is so strong a child puts all the blame on the other.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you're getting this wrong. She, she is the one who blamed me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Until saturday, when she came to you with what sounds like an unburdening. I'm wondering what that must've been like for you to hear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It made me furious and if I hadn't been sick, I would have thrown her out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you know what it was that made you so angry?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She spent my whole life telling me that I ruined her life, and now she changes her mind

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about my feelings after hearing my mother's heart.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She spent my whole life telling me that I ruined her life, and now she changes her mind when I'm vulnerable, when I've cried in her arms.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, maybe feeling you cry in her arms is what made her open up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What kind of timing is that? What does she expect?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's a good question. What do you think she expected?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are we examining her motives? I'm fucking here because of her fucked-up motives. She wanted me to let her off the hook. Bless me, my daughter, for I have sinned. I'm supposed to listen until she's finished and grant absolution? What's the matter? You look horrified. What, I'm back to monster Mia here?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No no no no no, I understand your anger. She didn't take care of you, she lied, she was never there for you, then suddenly she wants to be close.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why... Did she give up? Okay, she was sick for a year, but after that... Why didn't she fight harder to be my mother? How, how come nobody sticks by me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But she did say that she tried but that there was something impenetrable about your father's bond with you.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist persuaded me that my mother might want to help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are you taking her side?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not trying to take her side. All I'm suggesting is that it may not be as black and white as you rember it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's black and black. She manipulated me one way for my entire life and now she wants to manipulate me the other way to get rid of her guilt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That might be true, but it's also possible, perhaps in her own clumsy way, that your mother was trying to reach out. She saw that you were in cris, in some way like her own crisis... there you were in pajamas, you were depressed, it was related to a pregnancy and she recognized it right away. She was trying to help.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So once again, I had a chance at intimacy and I screwed it up. I pushed her away. Is that your point? God damn it. Just stop all the therapy and tell me what you think.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your mother tells you all these things and you get angry. What about your father?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I felt bad for him.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said it was necessary to reassess the parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: His wife gives birth, he wants to celebrate and she's ready to jump out the window? Plus he has a crying, hungry infant to take care of. He has to be both the mother and the father, so good for him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Has it ever occurred to you he might have colluded in the lie that she told? You just said it: she told the lie.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But he never corrected it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think that is, Mia?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was helping her save face.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For 43 years?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can't you accept that he was a good father? Nobody in therapy has a good dad?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A good dad who shipped a 10-year-old girl off to New Jersey rather than pay for a babysitter? There had to be a way to keep you at home. I mean, families find a way of working things out.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, she's probably lying about all that too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She could be, but let's just take her at her word for a moment. What that means is that you have to reevaluate who your parents are and what they did. Maybe your father wasn't the ideal man that you thought. And maybe your mother was actually trying to connect with you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What's going on here? She decides to rewrite history and you just go along with it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, sometimes we find it easier to hold on to the fiction.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not fiction, Paul. I'm telling you my mother was never there for me and my father always was.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's your mantra, Mia, and maybe it's as false as your mother's. Look at the way you defend it, how angry you get if I challenge it. I ask you to see your parents in a different light... I just ask you to do that... and you go on the attack. You accuse me of taking sides.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist talked about his regrets towards his father, urging me to find out the truth.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe I just don't like it when you blame him for everything. I need a break. Shit. Sorry.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's okay. It's not about blame, Mia. What I'm asking you to do is more complex than that. I want you to question the way that you have thought about your parents for most of your life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, is that all?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know it isn't easy, but I can tell you from personal experience... It's better to do it when your parents are still alive. My whole life I had this... Distorted image of who my parents were. And I didn't want to let that go. I fought against it, and then finally I did, and it was too late. My father was... he was gone. And that was... a huge loss.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've had enough loss this week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know, but, Mia, if you don't go through this, you're gonna stay where you are, you're gonna keep punishing the men in your life for not being what you need... men like Bennett.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Bennett was an asshole.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or like me. You blamed me for the abortion, but wasn't it your father who arranged it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was just supporting me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or maybe he was, once again, trying to hold on too tight, to keep you as his little girl.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist sought clues to persuade me that my father was not good.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, the abortion was my idea. I told you that last week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said you haven't heard from him lately, even though he must've known you were sick.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He was... he was always there when I was a girl.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was he? How about your piano? You said it was the one thing that always made you happy. Did you mother talk about what happened to it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She said that he sold it. He said with two babies in the house there was enough noise.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Let me ask you something: what would happen if you believed her? If you actually let yourself feel the hurt and the anger that you might have buried for this perfect dad?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't do this, Paul. Okay? Not today, not this week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, maybe this is the perfect time. This is a week that's been filled with loss. You mother comes and she gives you... A new family history. The picture you've had of them is just torn up and thrown away. And earlier in the week you lost your own child, the baby that you wanted for so long. That new family also just taken away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's not quite true.

situation: I said I was not pregnant and might never be.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: On saturday my mother insisted on calling her doctor, and he had us meet him at his office in greenpoint on a saturday night. He's the same doctor who delivered the twins.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Hadn't you already seen your doctor?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I called on friday. My park avenue obgyn said, you know, wait it out and to call him if the pain got much worse. My mom drove us to brooklyn and there was old dr. Solomon, sitting behind his desk. He did some tests and he told me that... that I hadn't lost the baby because I wasn't ever pregnant. I told him about my f. s. h. level and he said that I probably never would be pregnant. And then he went on. He said that... He sees this kind of thing once a week: women like me... successful, no children, my age and older... who come in just convinced that they're pregnant. And he has to tell them that they're... they're not.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... So you hadn't done a test before that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No. why not? I don't know. I thought I would wait. I had an appointment for this week to see my doctor and I was just so sure. But I had it wrong and you have it wrong. I don't have to grieve for a child that I never had.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mia, last week you... you talked about the... the new life that... that you felt inside you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It wasn't there. But in a way it was. The strength of that desire to... to create new life. It's almost 7:45. Is it too early to get drunk? Who knows? I could get lucky and... meet another married man at the bar. I'm gonna go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Will you please call me during the week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Call you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I want to know how you are.

situation: The therapist asked me if I was angry with him, and I responded that I had left the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So, how was your week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine. How was yours?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How are you feeling about your dad? What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd rather talk about you.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Surprise sur-fucking-prise.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just worried that what happened last weekend may have changed our relationship.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We have no relationship. I've dumped people for less than what you did to me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you thinking of dumping me ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know what I'm doing here ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe you wanted to convey your anger toward me in person.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe I just wanted to get out of the hospital for a few hours.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does anybody know that you left ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I just hopped a fence or something ?

situation: The therapist told my mother that I had cancer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Call the doctors if you like ; you're all such good friends now. I'm doing fine, so they let me out for a few hours... I have to check back in tonight.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I had to tell her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's your mother and you were delirious.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You could've waited until I came out of it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what if you never came out of it ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then someone would've called her eventually.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You put me down as your emergency contact number.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you empowered me to make a decision on your behalf. If anything happened to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had a bad fever. It wasn't like I was in heart failure.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You had 105. They were packing ice onto you when I arrived.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I talked to the doctors Paul. I know what happened.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Really? I understand that you're angry with me. But I didn't make this decision lightly. And if I had to to it again, I would do exactly the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Has my insurance covered everything? You don't have to worry about that. Well, I'm leaving and I'm not coming back, so if I owe you anything, speak now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, please don't go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: the one thing - that I asked you not to do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't think it was right to let you lie there alone, on the brink of death.

situation: The therapist talked about meeting with my mother.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You really don't understand do you ? You don't understand what you were to me. What did she say ? When you called ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: At first she... she just, she just didn't understand. She didn't even know you were seeing a therapist. I asked her to meet me at a coffee shop, so we could discuss it in person. But she... she refused.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's paranoid.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I offered to go to her house, she hung up, and I called her back. I asked her if she'd meet me at the hospital in an hour.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She showed up ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you surprised ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you meet her in my room ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No. In the lobby.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How did you recognize each other ?
