dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She looks just like you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you just... walked up to her and said : Hi, I'm Paul Weston, your daughter is stage three non-Hodgkins lymphoma and she's dying on the fourth floor.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I explained to her that you'd come to see me several weeks ago with a diagnosis of lymphoma, and that you'd begun chemotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What did she say when you said cancer ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She seemed... stunned.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did she cry ? Was she angry at me ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Definitely not.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She hates being the last person to find something out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She did have a hard time believing you would keep something like this from her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What did you say to that ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I told her she'd have to speak to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How long was this conversation ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Couple of minutes. It wasn't me she wanted to see. She wanted to see you.

situation: I talked about waking up with my mother by my side, thinking I had returned to my childhood.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I woke up and she was sitting there. I thought... I thought for a moment that... I was at home, and that it all been in a bad dream. I was still a child and... I was sick and... my mom was taking care of me. And I'd never grown up... and I'd never gone to school... and I'd never gotten cancer. And I closed my eyes, and... I guess fell asleep. When I woke up she was still sitting there. Glaring at me, i'd gotten sick deliberately. You broke my heart, worst than Kyle.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry. That was never my intention.

situation: I disliked Kyle and changed my view of the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Kyle took me out for coffee last week. He's been harrassing me. So I finally went just to shut it up, like I'm still alive, I'm in chemo. Just leave me alone. And, he just seemed so young to me. Like a baby. I was thinking : I don't want a boy like you, I want someone like Paul. A man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was it like to see him again ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't wanna talk about Kyle. I brought him up because... Fuck it. Never mind. I thought you were a man.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So today, I'm... your betrayer ? But last week, you were equally certain that I was generous and good. Can you see how dramatically your opinion of me has changed ? Can you make sense of that for me ?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess I never really knew you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Or maybe you're still angry at me you're having a hard time seeing this situation from my perspective.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't lecture me on empathy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I am not talking about empathy. I'm talking about perspective. You feel deeply for people whom you believe are on your team, because they are, in your mind, basically extensions of yourself. You feel their pain as if its your own pain. But you do have a hard time understanding someone whose approaching from a different perspective.

situation: The therapist said he did not betray me; it was a choice he had to make.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You were using your perspective to fuck me over.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I thought you were in serious trouble, and your mother deserved to know.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why ? You have no allegiance to her. You never met her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: As a father myself...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll tell you what happened : you got scared. You didn't want to be my emergency contact. You didn't want that responsability. If I had a patient who asked me not to call her mother, I never would've called her mother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't have children ! It's so easy to betray you. It so easy to let you down. I make one mistake, not even a mistake, one decision that you don't agree with. And that's it for you. I'm worthless because I'm weak. That's a quality you can't accept in others because... you can't accept it in yourself. But you know that nobody can live up to your standards, because you can't even live up to them. This is life, April. There are days that are just... classless and cruel. But it is the only life that you've got.

situation: I said Leah was my friend, though unreliable.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Leah lets me down... all the time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Little things. And she's a flake. She'll show up an hour late or... she'll forget we've made a plan at all.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But that doesn't bother you ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what's special about your relationship with Leah ?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know she loves me. She's known me since I was six. Before I had done anything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So she loved you when you were a child. She led inside before you closed the gates.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's so depressing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is it ? To have one person who really knows who you are ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I used to be really different.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In what way ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was a total mess.

situation: I talked about my past self.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was a total mess. This really emotional kid. I would cry at the drop of a hat. I used to write my parents hate mail. Leave it on their pillows at night. Dear mom and dad, these are all the things you did today that upset me. Please respond.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did they respond ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother would tell me that I... I had to get tough. I couldn't let my emotions show on my face.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, when I was in... when I was in grad school, I had a professor... he said something I still remember. He used to say that, for better or for worse, that maturity in modern american society had become synonymus with a lack of emotions, to not feel anything too deeply.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's true.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But some people naturally have more heightened emotional responses than others. I think you are one of those people. So you've been working hard to change your nature... Which is probably a futile enterprise. But a continual effort to do that could make you very angry or insecure.

situation: The therapist thought I lacked a sense of security.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I'm insecure ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's no good way for me to answer that question. If I say no, I'm a narcissist. If I say yes, I'm a loser.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well the way I see it, if you say no, you're perfect. If you say yes,

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: it means you're human.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist speculated why my mother didn't let me show my happiness openly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you think your mother told you to... keep your feelings to yourself ?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She wanted to keep me from getting hurt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is it possible it had something to do with Daniel ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Daniel couldn't control his emotions and he became violent when he was upset. So maybe a heightened emotional response from you, even though it was an appropriate reaction to a given circumstance, maybe it reminded your mother of Daniel, and in some way its scared her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The world is a messed up place. She was just trying to teach me to protect myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But maybe she didn't give you time to get to know yourself first, to know who it is you are protecting.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I don't know myself ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think that you've been operating for a long time in reaction to your mother.

situation: I talked about my parents' different reactions during my chemotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: At the hospital, she was so mad she wouldn't even look at me. She just kept coming in and out of the room. Bossing the doctors around... I just wanted her to leave.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe she wasn't actually angry. Maybe she was scared.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It doesn't matter. It doesn't ? No, Paul. Not when I'm hooked up to three IVs. The only thing that matters, in that moment, is that my mother is there, and I can't deal with her. My dad came by later... and he was perfect. I was freezing, so... he went out and bought me a damn blanket. Now whenever he comes he brings me... something special. There's this dark chocolate that I love. It weighs a ton and I never get it for myself. He brought me some. And he sat by my bed and held my hand, and just said : April, you're a strong girl. You'll beat this. That's all I need. She's my mother, why doesn't she know that ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: He sounds very calm, your dad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He can be, under certain circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like hospitals ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you saying ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, that's what he does for a living. It might be easier for your father to give you what you need at the moment because he's had some practice. But your mother... was out of her element.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't understand : are you for this woman or against her ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: April, everything doesn't have to be black and white.

situation: I said the therapist had betrayed me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're so over me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sorry ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're so tired of this. You just want this to be done. You want to figure me out, fix my head, so you can check me off your ledger.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What about my behavior gave you that idea ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You turned on me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: By calling my mother.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Were back to that again. So what I did still doesn't make sense to you ?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you talking about ? For five sessions all I've talked about is why I can't call my mother. I was walking down Flatbush Avenue burning with fever, with a non-existent immune system, trying to hail a cab to take me to the emergency room, and I still didn't call her.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talked about how my mother would draw hooks on my hand, which I hated.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You pulled rank on me, Paul. You were like : I've humored this chick for too long, I'm the adult, I'm gonna call the other adult. so we can figure out how to... how to fuck up the world together.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You don't think of yourself as an adult ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess I am.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to be ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe that's because you barely had time to be a child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Your work here is done.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Our work here is only beginning.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: well, you're wrong... You can check me off now. Now I'm in chemo, my mother knows, whatever.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You keep using the term check me off. Does that mean anything to you ?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother... used to write a check on the back of my hand whenever I did a good deed, or aced a test, or something. She said I loved it, when I was little.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But something changed as you got older ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I felt like she was... you know, checking me off, like... April's fine. She's got a check. Don't need to worry about April. Got so tired of those goddamned checks, I stopped telling her things.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Like what ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist said I wanted to be a hero to my mother, and he was part of that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know... I'd raised money for autism research, by running a 10K.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you wouldn't tell her ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She'd find out later, from a teacher... or the school newspaper.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you give me another example ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When Leah's mom was dying, Leah couldn't handle it. Neither could her dad, so... I was over at their house, three times a week, helping out, just... buying groceries, making dinner.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But again your mother didn't know anything about this ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She found out at the funeral. Leah's dad came up to her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It seems like you wanted your mother to know these things, but you didn't want to tell her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what would happen if she found out ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was her little hero... her saving grace.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Her perfect child. April, is it possible that I've become part of that pattern ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You got cancer. You decided to fight it alone, just as you've always done. you didn't tell your mother, but you came to see me. You told me. Because, maybe you knew on some level, that I would eventually tell your mother. And you would become our hero. Again.

situation: The therapist said I was saving myself in a way, and I talked about not believing in anything anymore.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That is so fucked up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think it is, April. I think you saved yourself the only way you know how.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought that cancer would clean me out of all this bullshit. I thought I would finally stop obsessing over how to be the best at everything, and... all the reasons I should hate myself and everyone else. I thought I would... finally start to think about the big picture, but... it's just gotten darker inside my head. I don't believe in anything anymore. I don't believe in love. Or... my mother, not my body, or you. Because of all this stupid therapy, I don't even believe in myself anymore. I literally have no idea why I should get out of bed in the morning.

situation: The therapist said my dream represented rebirth.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because of all this stupid therapy, I don't even believe in myself anymore. I literally have no idea why I should get out of bed in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not a bad place to begin, April. Do you remember the dream that we talked about last week ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The one where I was dying ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Except that I think that dream could actually have been about... rebirth. About saying goodbye to the old self to make room for the new.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I could just be dying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When will you get the results of the blood tests ?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told you, end of the week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Then you will know for sure if the chemo is working. Will you let me know the results as soon as you get them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sure. Are we done here ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If you want to keep on talking...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really. Can you help me up ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

situation: I said I felt like a prisoner, trapped and uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I never thought I'd be happy to be back here. But it feels good to get out of that place, even if it's only for an hour.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you haven't been out at all this week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, a couple of times. Connie and... Natalie took me to lunch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how was that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was a cute little Irish place, actually, right across the street. You probably would have liked it. I had stew, soda bread. Connie cried. I sat there wondering if everyone in the restaurant made me for a guy being on lunch-leave from the rubber room.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I doubt they were thinking that, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's humiliating. My own daughter has to sign me out, sit in your waiting room, sign me back in like I'm a danger to society.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think the fear is that you might be a danger to yourself.

situation: I complained about the doctors at the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can I ask you something, Paul?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You said that this was one of the best facilities in the city?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It is very highly regarded.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then what are the rest of them like? I'm not complaining. You've been there yourself a few times now. It's clean, well lit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why don't you just tell me what it is that bothers you about the place?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's the staff: the therapists, social workers. Maybe I've been spoiled by you, but these people, they just... They're just not very bright.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, you're either bright or you're not. You can't fake it. When I talk to you I don't have to explain myself. You listen, you understand what I'm saying, you respond right away. If I mention a name even once, you remember it the next time. These people... They're just not up to speed. I have to backtrack all the time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I think that you and I have a relationship, Walter. And I can imagine how frustrating it must be to cover the same ground that we have in our sessions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but it's not only that. They talk to me like I'm a four-year-old... or maybe an 80-year-old who has to have everything explained to him loudly and slowly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you feel patronized.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, exactly. See, that's it. That's what I mean... you understand me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, to be honest, Walter, that wasn't a difficult one.

situation: I tried to ingratiate myself with the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've never felt patronized by you. You respected me, I respected you. We're equals.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I haven't really gotten that sense from you before, to be honest.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You haven't?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually I've always felt that I've kind of annoyed you, that our talking together was a waste of your time. For example, when I draw connections between your past and your present, you've belittled them. And me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you felt that way, I'm sorry. The truth is that right from that first blink test I could see you were top notch.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And yet, I think I remember that you questioned my academic credentials. And didn't you run a background check on me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There's that memory of yours... it won't let go of any details.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You can see why I might be a little surprised to hear that you're now singing my praises.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Boy, you have a hard time taking a compliment, don't you? Maybe you should talk to somebody about that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, since... since you have so much respect for my understanding of you... can I be blunt?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Absolutely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why are you sucking up to me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Excuse me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you're right, Walter. I have tried to empathize with you and I know that I've made some mistakes, but I think I have a pretty fair idea of your opinion of me. So I'll ask you again: why are you sucking up to me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let me show you something.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a potholder.

situation: I complained about group psychotherapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I made it myself... in occupational therapy. Tomorrow we're gonna glue little bits of tile together and make coasters.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't imagine you're the best candidate for occupational therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm used to being the glue, Paul, not playing with it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sure that's not all you're doing in there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, of course not. Then there's group therapy... which isn't only a waste of time, it's disturbing. I just sit there and I listen to strangers talking about how this one was abandoned or that one was molested, and how angry they are at their parents.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how do you feel about being on the same floor as these people?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I guess I'm supposed to relate to them or sympathize or you tell me. But come on, Paul. Two months ago I was a fully-engaged C.E.O., solving real-world problems. And now I'm sitting between one person who likes to wear diapers and another one who likes to cut herself with a razor.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's no denying that you have it rough. And you must be angry at me for saying that you need to be there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you were just doing your job.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can imagine you also might be angry that I wasn't able to save you from the depression you fell into. Or from the attempt that you made on your own life.

situation: I wanted to be discharged, so I tried to ingratiate myself with the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, one of the shrinks there said something like that. He said you were reckless. Said that you'd opened up Pandora's box at the worst possible time. I'm sorry... should I not have told you that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I'm sure that must have been unsettling for you to hear. What do you think he meant by that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I didn't trust it. I didn't trust him. I told him that if it hadn't have been for you, that I'd gone off the deep end a lot sooner. I also told him that his staff wasn't in your league.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're doing it again, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Bullshitting me. Now what is it that you want from me?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Out. I want out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you're hoping that if you flatter me enough that I'll sign off on your release, is that it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm climbing the walls, Paul. And it's another week before I can go before a judge.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look, I understand that a week may seem like a very long time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: God, another day is an eternity. Whatever you need me to say or sign, I'll do it. But please, call Dr. Wells.

situation: I described my experience last week as boring.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He'll listen to you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Before I do that, we need to talk more.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you want to know?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do I want to know? Isn't that what you said to me last week in the hospital? And then you proceeded to tell me that you had food poisoning. Drop the facade, Walter. It's a waste of your time and mine. You're just saying what you think I want to hear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was ashamed. And I didn't want Natalie to know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why don't you tell me what it's really been like this last week.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hell. I have nothing to do. There's one TV and the group votes on what crap they want to watch. There's a piano that no one can play. They give us chores, but it's make-work. I'm not doing anything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how do you pass the time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Walk the halls. It's 9:00 a.m. I pace, stare out the window. Hours go by. I think to myself, it must be getting close to lunchtime. I look at the clock. It's 9:15.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you stare out the windows, what do you think about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think about how much I could've already gotten done if I still had my job.

situation: The therapist said I needed to reflect on myself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think about how much I could've already gotten done if I still had my job. You're used to being busy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I can imagine it's... It's a pretty difficult adjustment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't adjust. I'm not comfortable just wasting time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's something that we might work on while you're there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You want me to work on wasting time?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, what I mean is sometimes when people are hospitalized the lack of day-to-day pressure can cause a relief. It finally gives them a chance to... To contemplate.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't follow you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, to reflect. To reflect on what's come before, what lies ahead. I think you've been running so hard for so long that you haven't had the chance to check in with yourself.

situation: I talked about what I thought about when I was bored.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Natalie said something like that. She said I should listen to my inner voice. I told her the last thing you want to do if you're in a nuthouse is start hearing voices.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you walk the halls, what do you find yourself thinking about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm just anxious. I think about money. I think about my net-worth numbers. They've gone down quite a bit. But... I think about is Connie keeping up with the bills, is the car battery dead in the garage... what happened to those... those poor kids... who drank the formula? I think about their families... How they're coping with it. what's going on...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think about them often?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that you had some sessions with the staff... shrink. What did he talk about?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They want to rehash the crisis, the firing.

situation: The therapist asked how the doctors in the asylum evaluated me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They want to rehash the crisis, the firing. I keep saying, could you just read my file?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And as you were retelling the story, can you... remember what emotions came up for you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Have you ever given a deposition? You say as little as possible and wait for it to end.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mentioned that Pandora's box had been opened. You've talked about some of those issues?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know. Your family history, your history with the Donaldsons, your anxiety about separation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not really. They didn't ask, I didn't tell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did they ask you about the night you tried to kill yourself?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course they asked about that. They had to, didn't they? Yes, they did. I've been where they are. We'd acquire a company. I'd go out there for the visit. The local... manager would walk me through it: how dedicated everyone was, how nothing need to change. And the whole time he's making his pitch, I'm running numbers. They were emotionally involved. I was there to evaluate.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So these doctors, you feel they're just... making clinical evaluations?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're just thinking about how much to medicate me, or... how much coverage I have.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think they might be assessing anything else?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Whether I'll try it again. That's what everybody's going to worry about for the rest of my life.

situation: I asked what the therapist would do in my place, and the therapist empathized.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's what everybody's going to worry about for the rest of my life. Isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to talk about that?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Pretty street you live on. I never noticed that before. It's always been dark when you've arrived.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's... nice to see the spring come.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now I have a chance to plant my garden. Smell the roses. Can I ask you something?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What would you have done if you were me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I've thought about that. I can really understand... what that pain was like, how it must have seemed unbearable... without end. And how, in that moment, you thought you'd found a solution... A way out of a hopeless situation. But, you know... I think that... the worst night of your life has passed, Walter. You've survived it. You've been given a second chance. And the void that you felt, maybe the void that you still feel can be filled... and that there's a possibility of renewal.

situation: I said there were two of me, and the one not working felt lost.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, I tried to fight it. I kept telling myself, Snap out of it, Walter. Snap out of it. I kept thinking that... I'd come up with some way to stop feeling.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Stop feeling what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To stop feeling. Period. I've always been able to will myself out of bed. Even if I was dead tired or sick... I was always able to work. Ring the bell, I answered.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But not this time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's like... there's the Walter Barnett that I knew, who could... stand up to any pressure. And then... there's this other Walter who I never knew existed... who crumbled... who couldn't handle the pain.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: These two Walters, one strong, the other weak... are there... any other differences between them?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Like I said, I don't know this other one.

situation: The therapist said my potential breakdown was due to no longer being busy with work, and I said I had let everyone down.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Like I said, I don't know this other one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The other one, you mean... The one without a job? You said anytime the bell rang, you answered. Maybe part of the reason you couldn't snap out of it this time was because for the first time in your life... you weren't on call. You weren't on duty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You pride yourself not just on your ability to work, but on your ability to work yourself beyond the brink of exhaustion. The first day you didn't even think that your panic attacks were worth mentioning. In the time that I've known you, I've never heard you mention a hobby, a day off, a night out.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You met me in the middle of a crisis.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And my guess is, before this crisis there was another crisis and before that there was another one. And it stretches right back... to childhood, to Vietnam, to the Donaldsons, to Connie's rehab. Connie's rehab?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? I never said anything about that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't, but when I spoke to Natalie at the hospital... She had no right to embarrass Connie like that! She wasn't trying to embarrass Connie. She assumed you'd told me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why would I have done that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's what people do in therapy. They talk about their... lives. If your wife has a problem with substance abuse...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Substance abuse? It was chardonnays. And a few pills. She's not a... Connie is a great wife. She made a fine home. She took care of the kids. She watched the home front like a hawk. The problem started... It's my fault.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What was your fault?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was away so much. I was always traveling. The doctors never understood what it was. It was... maybe a hypoglycemia, or lyme disease, something chemical. She gets in a mood and... she slides downhill.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you were there to catch her.

situation: The therapist said it was always about taking responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd be halfway around the world. I'd get a call from the boys or her mother. I'd be on the next flight back. I've always been her rock. Until now. Now I've let her down. I've let everyone down.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're a human being.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not supposed to malfunction, Paul, that's for other people.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But not Walter Barnett. He's a superman. Isn't that what your wife used to call you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's just a figure of speech.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But it's a pretty telling one. You've been everyone's rock... your entire life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You make it sound like that's something bad to be responsible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm just wondering about the toll that it's taken... the pressure or maybe even the need to always be the hero.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Need? Do you think I look for this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not what I meant.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I'm like a fireman who goes setting fires so I can put them out?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's not the point.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then what is your damn point? Come on, you know everything. Just tell me what you fucking think.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't think you want the crisis. But I do worry you have no idea what to do when you're not in one. You're angry at yourself... for crumbling under this pressure. But I'm amazed you've held everything together for as long as you did.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Thanks a lot.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The Walter you know... has been on the front line since his brother died... on call, taking care of everything, everybody, sleeping with one eye open. But without a mountain of responsibility, that Walter is completely lost. He doesn't know how not to be in charge. He's forgotten how to play. He can't just sit and be. Maybe that's why you're climbing the walls at the hospital.

situation: The therapist said it was a good time to find the other me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then get me out of there!

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And if I did... what would happen to the other Walter?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The Walter you said you didn't know existed, the little boy who had his childhood taken away from him when he was six years old. He's been sitting there... all this time in the dark... scared half to death... hoping that somebody would notice him... maybe comfort him. And maybe... Maybe this is his chance. Your chance... to find out who that boy is... To reconnect with a part of yourself that you've had to deny your entire life. Am I making any sense to you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You want me to connect to that part of myself that... that fell apart, that... crumbled under pressure? Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because, Walter, I don't think that's the part of you that crumbled. I think that's the part of you that wants to live.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry...

situation: I complain about the bank, dealing with my father's estate is troublesome.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry about the phone business. I'm trying to get my father's estate settled and I can't even get anybody to talk to me. All I get is Can you hold? Please, hold. Let me put you on hold. That's so irritating. If I believed the operators were actually helping somebody, I would wait. Sometimes I think the whole country is on hold.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Nobody is being helped.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They don't even call it help any more. They call it customer support. That's 'cause all they really do is say, I'm sorry you have a problem. That's too bad. Well, you know what? I don't want support. I want your help. So I hang up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is there something I can help you with?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Unless you want to proofread a letter I wrote.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure. What kind of letter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Remember last week I left here and I went to meet with Alex's father?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, how did that go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Disorienting.

situation: I talk about Alex's father demanding an apology letter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Disorienting. He offered to accept settlement money from the insurance company and drop his lawsuit against me...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, that's great.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ... in exchange for a letter from me admitting my guilt in Alex's death.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wrote the letter? What would he do with this letter?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He gave me his word he wouldn't do anything with it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know. You're right. Once he has it, technically, he can do anything he wants with it. Send it to the ethics board or post it online.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That would be the end of your career. What did your lawyer say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He says the letter will put an end to the lawsuit and that my insurance will cover the whole settlement. I won't end up owing a thing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happens if you don't send it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They have a preliminary hearing next week. The judge... He could just throw the whole case out. But if he doesn't, it might go to trial with a jury, in which case I will lose big time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you know that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The lawyer says that's what juries do.

situation: I mention that the lawyer is not optimistic about the case of a psychologist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The lawyer says that's what juries do. He says everybody hates therapists.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: They do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: According to this guy, therapy is bullshit. He says people go into treatment hoping that the therapist is gonna fix them. But that therapists either don't solve people's problems or they make them worse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And this man is representing you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He fights cases like this every week. He knows how they go. And he's worried that the jury is gonna see me as a stand-in for all the bad therapists in the world, and award Alex's father the entire $20 million.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If this lawyer knew what he was doing, he'd get the jury to see what a good therapist you are.

situation: I feel I haven't helped anyone and plan to resign.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Excuse me for a second, I'm just curious. What would you say if you were on trial and the lawyer asked you, What percentage of your patients do you think you've really helped? What are you asking? Would you say, on average, that the people you've treated have gotten a little better, a lot better, or they've stayed about the same?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're someone I treat. Are you asking me if I'll help you get better?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine, don't answer the question. This isn't about you anyway. This is about me. The way I feel about it is I'm not helping anybody. I'm going to mail this letter and I'm gonna quit being a therapist and find something better to do, something useful.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know you help people.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what I do? Most days, I sit there and I listen for 45 minutes. Then my patients go out the door and do whatever they were gonna do anyway.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul, you don't just listen. You make observations. You ask questions. You make interpretations. You encourage people to look at the patterns of their behavior.

situation: The therapist encourages me, but I can't give what my patients need.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That may be what I do, but it's not what people want.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what do they want?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They want to be loved, even by me. They want a child, or they want to be my child. They want a parent who loves them. They want attention, they want affection. They want hope, they want pills, and they want sex. It's a good list. But I don't give them those things. My patient Mia, the lawyer, do you know what she wants? She wants me to hold her, to comfort her. But what she really needs is a good husband and a family. And I know that I cannot give her those things. All I can do is show her she pushes away the very people who could help her and that she pulls on the people who won't. But that only leaves her feeling more lonely and unloved.
