dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Here's where you tell me how relieved I'll be when you walk out the door. And then you're going to say that you're like a knife in my neck, that it'll feel good when you're gone. That how it goes, isn't it? See, this is your specialty, Mia. And if you want to keep repeating that pattern, that's fine. Go ahead. But if you want to make a change in your life, I suggest that you stay in therapy. And it doesn't even need to be with me.

situation: I want to sleep with the therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can we talk about your patterns?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My patterns? Like what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How you like to have a woman on the couch who thinks she's in love with you, how you get off on that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Get off on it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've seen how you look at me. You hold up that neutral face pretty well, but I see when it slips and you're looking at my neck or my legs or my breasts and you're wondering what it would be like. Come on, paul, you said you'd be honest. How about you drop the act? You know you'd rather have me as a patient ten some hedge fund guy whose bonus has been reduced. Don't tell me you haven't had fantasies about us. Crazy chicks are hot in bed, right? What's the matter? Am I making you uncomfortable? Why don't we just go in the bedroom right now and fuck? Or how about on the kitchen counter? I bet you never did that with laura.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So there's nothing to be learned from therapy, so let's just go fuck? Is that it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: At least we'd get some relief from our miserable lives.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So that's your version of closure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It would make us feel better, instead of pretending that this talking nonsense actually helps.

situation: The therapist refuses, saying it's medical misconduct.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It would make us feel better, instead of pretending that this talking nonsense actually helps. What would it be like if you broke all the rules for me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean if I said yes?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So you want to?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What if I do? What would happen?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Would you finally feel special enough? Would it fix everything, to win like that? Or would you just blame me for crossing the line? You're a lawyer, for chrissake. You know what it would mean. Then I would be truly guilty of malpractice. You've probably represented doctors like that. Hell of a way to get out of therapy, I have to say turn me into one of your clients. That's not what I'm doing. Isn't it? Then I would need you. You would be in control. And that would be much more comfortable for you, to have me back in your office. Maybe maybe that's why you really do it.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist and I discuss my responsibility, he thinks I am defending my father to everyone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your job.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're changing the topic. Are you getting scared?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm trying to help you. That's my job. What's yours, mia? What do you do at work every day?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know as well as anyone what I do. How is your case going? I wasn't in last week. Don't you have a hearing coming up?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So they tell me. But you're right, you weren't in last week. If you had gone in, what cases would you have been working on?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No trials. I was supposed to meet a new client a pediatrician who misdiagnosed some nine-year-old kid, almost killed him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No wonder you stayed in bed.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't judge my clients, paul. I protect them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how many of your clients are powerful men who fail to protect the vulnerable and the innocent?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They're being sued, paul, just like you. That doesn't mean they're guilty.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how long have you been doing that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 17 years.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How often do you call in sick?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Since I got there? Five days, four.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In 17 years? And vacations?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't lose the weeks if you don't take them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I see. But last week, after confronting your father, you didn't go in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: According to you, I was depressed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you were. But I don't think it's a coincidence that suddenly you didn't want to defend somebody whose negligence had harmed a child. Look, I'm not saying they're all guilty, but every time you stand in that courtroom to defend a client, I think you're actually defending your father to everybody, especially yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Shit. How long have you known that one?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does it make sense to you?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I never made the connexion... and now I'm stuck with it.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says I need to take off the "blindfold."

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I never made the connexion... and now I'm stuck with it. I felt like I had nothing before. Now I have less than nothing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know it feels scary but maybe that's a good thing.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a good thing that I have nothing? Thank you. Thank you. You've helped me to realize that I've made poor choice after poor choice my whole life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you also have to realize, Mia, that you're at a critical juncture in your life, that now you do have the self-knowledge to make different, better choices.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't give me any of this Pollyanna shit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And sometimes when you're on the verge of real change, that's when you fight the hardest. When you first came back I tried to ask you about your connection to your father and you shut me down. You didn't want to know anything about it. This past week you confronted him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, look how well that worked out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not saying it was easy. But maybe it's worth it. To finally take off the blinders, even if you don't like what you see. Because what is the alternative? Put them back on again and wander around in the darkness?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you have to take them off? I didn't do it. You did.

situation: I worry about the rest of my life, the therapist says married people may also feel empty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you have to take them off? I didn't do it. You did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What are you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing. What am I going to do with the rest of my life? I want... the same things I wanted when I came here two months ago... a man, a home, a family. I'm no closer to getting them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you really think that getting married is going to make it all better? Do you have any idea of how many married people, how many parents feel as empty as you do? Let me ask you... when was the last time you felt real happiness?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A couple weeks ago when I thought that I was pregnant.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: The therapist says I want to connect with people.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A couple weeks ago when I thought that I was pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what about that made you feel good?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That it wasn't just me, that my life had meaning, that there would be this other person, always.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you ever considered that maybe it's not about a child, Mia, or a husband? Maybe that's just a picture in your head from your family, from your friends, from the culture. Not everyone needs that to live a full and contented life. Maybe what you really want, Mia, is to feel connected, authentically connected to somebody or something else.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And we both know that I can't have that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: An authentic connection? Me? I've never had that. I'm incapable.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure? What about in here?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you kidding me? I'm a mess in here.

problem_type: Life is confused or find yourself
situation: The therapist says I genuinely want to change.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a mess in here. I attack you. I've dumped on you. I've tried to seduce you. I've been a train wreck.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay, at times you have acted out. But if you hadn't, how could we examine it? It's been your way of communicating to both of us what you need. You've also been honest, caring. You've made yourself vulnerable. You've shown me who you really are. And you haven't walked away.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yet.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We both know that you really want to change. That's the real reason you keep coming back. Yes, of course you want intimacy in your life. And I know... I know that you're capable of that. Because we've had it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When? Name one time.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Now. Right now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Our time is up, right? Thank you, Paul. It was a good session.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Goodbye, Mia.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So... I guess I'll see you next week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'll be here.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about my imminent discharge.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sorry about earlier.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It happens.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't realize how many fellow patients there were. You're busy all the time, aren't you? So they... finally released me Monday afternoon. Thank you for your help. Connie and Natalie picked me up. We headed straight out for the bay. I have a few shacks there... that Connie likes to call a compound... on Shelter Island. We drove up... a warm day, first southerly wind of the new year.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was a beautiful day on Monday. It's amazing when the cold finally breaks.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about going on a trip with my wife and daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Everything was so muddy, though. They're a few weeks behind the city Weatherwise. The snow had just melted and the ground was just soaked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I imagine it felt good to be... outside, especially after the last few weeks. You could say that. But... it didn't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, no, the air felt great. It's just that... Connie and Natalie... They were just so... tentative with me. There's a separate studio near the main house that I've used as an office sometimes, or sometimes just to... for a little peace and quiet when the kids were younger. I wanted to go there but they kept asking me why.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was there anything you needed to do in your office?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, take care of some bills.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about needing peace, Natalie monitoring me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, take care of some bills. But mostly I just wanted to be by myself. I just wanted to have a little peace.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's unusual for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, Connie's a talker... She's always been a talker... and I guess over the years I've learned how to tune it out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But this time you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Something about her pitch... It just bothered me. So I went to the office, and a few minutes later I looked up and there's Natalie spying on me from her bedroom window.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: She's still... She's still on duty.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, like I was a little boy that someone had to babysit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You told me once that when you were a little boy yourself, you were the one on duty with your parents.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I didn't do that much, just kept an eye on things. Really it's nothing even worth talking about.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So what did you do when you saw Natalie keeping an eye on you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I glared. Then about minutes later she brought me some tea which I hadn't asked for. And she asked if she could just sit with me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how was that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Brief.

situation: The therapist compares seeing a psychologist to pruning branches.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's my daughter. I don't go to her with my problems.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You have a good relationship with her, though. You wrote to her almost every day when she was in Rwanda. I imagine she'd worry less if you talked to her a little bit more about what's been going on with you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I just didn't feel like talking. So I went to the shed and got this immense pair of clippers and, I started hacking away at the brush down by the water, limbing the trees and paring down the bushes. God, tore my hands up something terrible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All that brush-clearing... it's kind of like what we've been doing in here.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You lost me on that one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In the sense that we've been working on clearing paths, opening up your view of how you got to where you are. So when you mentioned this week's thaw, it made me think of the way our last session ended.

situation: The therapist and I recall the last counseling session.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, between the pills and the therapists I saw at the hospital, I'm not sure I even remember that one.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You really don't remember? I find that striking, given how emotional a moment that was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I know we talked about getting me out of the cuckoo's nest. And I showed you my pot holder. Then I got angry about you bringing up Connie's rehab.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I meant after that, when we talked about the two Walters... the one who you knew and the one you didn't know.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You seemed quite moved when we talked about reconnecting to the lost Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I might have teared up a bit, but I was tired and there's been a lot of stress.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand that, but my memory is that you didn't just tear up. You were actually sobbing. What is it, Walter? Where did you go?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just remembered a dream I had this week.

situation: I dream about returning to work but can't answer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I just remembered a dream I had this week. Mr. Donaldson called me in for a meeting. Only it wasn't in an office. It was... It was in an old garage. I went in, we shook hands and he told me they'd traced the source of the contamination and that it wasn't anything we'd done wrong. Some nut job deliberately tampering with the product and then putting it back on shelf. Go on. I felt vindicated. And then, the old man did something he never did... he apologized. He said that letting go of me was the biggest mistake he'd ever made, that he wanted me to take my old job back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You'd be Walter Barnett, C.E.O. again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I tried to answer, but I couldn't speak. I opened my mouth, but I couldn't get any words out. I woke up in a sweat. I kept trying to dive back into the dream, but I couldn't get there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wanted to finish the conversation? What did you make of that dream?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I guess I still want to think the whole mess never happened.

situation: The therapist says I am under pressure, but I'm good at hiding my feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I guess I still want to think the whole mess never happened. I want my old life back.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you? Because you said you couldn't get any words out. Is it possible that you weren't sure if you wanted to go back?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Probably just bargaining.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Could be. Or perhaps now with a little distance you have a greater sense of the enormous strain you've been under for so long.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It never used to feel like a strain.
dialogue.fine_label: 否认-最小化(B4)  来访者认为咨询

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's right. I think you genuinely didn't feel it. You've become exceptionally adept at overriding your feelings. That's what we were beginning to talk about last week. Do you remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right, how the weak Walter couldn't handle the stress.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you think about that Walter this week?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The lost boy? No, not really.

situation: I say the therapist reminds me of my father, talk about how my father felt after Tommy's death.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You did make me think about my father.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your father? How did I do that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just before, when I came early and I walked in on you, you just had a look on your face that reminded me of him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: In what way?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After Tommy... after the accident, he couldn't sleep nights anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Insomnia?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, and he started to work the graveyard shift. And when he'd come home from the factory, he didn't want to wake up my mother, so he'd go to sleep on the couch. And I'd come downstairs and I'd want to talk to him, you know, about... I don't know... the day before, what happened at school. And there was that look.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you describe it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How the hell do I get rid of you without making you feel bad? Come on, listen, it's okay. Really, you were busy. If it had been my session and somebody walked in, I would have been pissed off.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Still, you felt rejected, even abandoned.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was early.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Right, the same way you were too early for your dad.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Work comes first. That's life.

situation: I talk about my parents being too sad, so I had to put away boyishness.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My mother didn't see much of him either. She got used to it. She'd come home from the hospital... she was a nurse... and I'd fix her an old-fashioned. We'd eat. I'd fix her another. I had to get the cherry and the orange wedge just right. Then she'd go in her bedroom. I was always nervous that she'd fall asleep while she was smoking in bed, so I'd check in on her and make sure all the ashtrays were out.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's a lot of responsibility for a young boy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Listen, they were... you can't blame her... either of them. Their lives were ruined.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's any need to blame them in order to understand your loneliness.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They were too grief-stricken to take care of me. I had to put away my childish things.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actually, I think the verse is, When I became a man, I put away childish things. You were still a boy.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I talk about wanting to be close to my father, but my father wouldn't allow it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A lot of kids had it worse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you remember any good times? Did the three of you spend time together?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not so much. On weekends he was always tinkering with his car. That thing was a real money pit.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you have a garage?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. I used to peek in on him.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And he didn't let you in?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After a while I figured out how to stand on a garbage can and look through the window. It turned out... most of the time he wasn't working on the car. He was... staring at a picture of Tommy on the wall. One time he saw me. It was terrible.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You wanted to connect with him, but you felt he didn't want you there. Is that it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The boys used to spy on me the same way... when I worked on weekends. They'd want to play or... go swimming, and... I always had work to do. I probably gave them the same look. Maybe that's why we don't have anything to talk about now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, it's not too late for you to get to know them and for them to get to know you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think they'd be interested.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe they feel, I don't know, intimidated by you. Repairing those relationships is something that we can work on in here.

situation: I talk about moving away but often going back to find Tommy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I said I don't think they're interested.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were interested in talking to your father... about what you saw in that garage. In fact, you're still dreaming about it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We never discussed it. A few years later we moved... to the next coal town over. My mother didn't want to go, but... my father thought it would be better to start over again in a new place without... Tommy's presence hovering over everything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And how did you feel about it?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They didn't ask me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It must be hard, as a child, to know what your feelings are when you're not asked about them.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For awhile there after we moved... I'd run away... back to the old home. I'd get on my bike and... I'd just go there, I don't know... to check if Tommy was waiting for us. Go figure out a child.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would you do when you visited?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing.

situation: The therapist guesses I am searching for what I lost.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd just sit there for hours, waiting. He never came back, of course.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wonder if maybe... Maybe you didn't go back... just to look for Tommy. Maybe there was someone else you were looking for.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Who?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The boy that you were before Tommy was killed. Maybe the old house was... the only place you could let yourself feel your losses and... find intimacy with something that was gone, with your... with your dead brother and... your memories. There was nothing there for you, Walter. And there was nothing in the new home except... duty, loneliness.

situation: I remember my father wouldn't let me cry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Don't worry. I'm not gonna cry. I know how uncomfortable that made you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that how you thought I reacted, Walter, to last week?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Come on. You don't need to pretend. I know I've been a basket case in here. I know how that disgusted you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would I feel like that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a grown man. I'm not a six-year-old.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And... men don't cry.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe they do now. But... when I became a man, they didn't.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was that what your father taught you? He didn't have to.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Where I grew up, a boy wouldn't be caught dead crying.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How about when Tommy died? Did you cry then?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was upset. I knew it was my fault.

situation: The therapist thinks I alienated myself early on, taking on responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew it was my fault. Maybe I started to tremble. Maybe I started to cry. Because the old man, I remember, picked me up and... shook me... hard. Don't you dare, he said, in front of your mother. Don't... you... ever.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think that's when you started to maybe... shut down a little?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You mean... that other Walter of yours?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Maybe it's not really fair to call him the other Walter. The truth is, he's a part of you. A part of you that was split off and neglected... for a very long time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was doing fine without him all this time, wasn't I?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You did more than fine. You accomplished great things in your life, Walter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So, why is this split a bad thing?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It can be hard to live your life, to be genuinely fulfilled, when a part of your... your true self is locked away. I think that what happened was that the other part of you the part that took responsibility, that shouldered all these burdens... that's the part that got rewarded... early and often. The more you took on, the more praise you got. Your dad must have been relieved not to have to worry about his wife. And your mom, I can imagine... how important you felt just knowing that you were her lifeline.

situation: The therapist says I shine in James's realm, I'm taking responsibility, otherwise, I feel worthless.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She was tricky. We were always walking on eggshells. My father and I didn't even tell her I was going to Vietnam until... two or three days before I left.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you were... a hero in Vietnam as well.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: James Donaldson was the hero. I just did my part.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I'm sure you were a natural leader. And... in the chaos of the war people must have looked to you. And they were right to do so. You'd been trained from an early age to step up.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It helped me survive.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's always helped you survive. Even thrive. It's how you rose to the top of your field. Except that... it wasn't really your field, was it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It was James's. Have you ever wondered why you spent your working life building the Donaldsons' family business? Was it just another rescue that you took on, like... the way you nursed your mother... or... or your wife? See, that's the paradox... You've been rewarded for so long for your... grace under fire that... you just don't think you're of any value to anybody unless you're in that role. Now that you've launched them, your boys... don't want to get to know you. Natalie was done with you. I don't want to see you at the door. The only way to feel not rejected... is to carry the weight... and to keep carrying it, even though your mind and your body are screaming at you to stop.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've stopped now, haven't I?

situation: I say I missed out on life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I've stopped now, haven't I? Walter Barnett, the C.E.O... he's gone. He came to you with a sleeping problem... and within weeks his life was in shambles.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think we both understand that by the time you came to see me there was no way to prevent the crash.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You knew I was headed for this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The Walter you knew... the hero... he staved it off as long as humanly possible. If he could have held it together this time... he would have.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, it doesn't matter either way, does it? We both know what you're telling me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What is that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I missed it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did you miss?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My life. Isn't that what you're saying?

situation: The therapist suggests I seek a new life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm 68 years old... and I haven't lived one moment of my life for myself. What the hell am I supposed to do with that? Are you going to say anything?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Just that I think that now is the time to stop taking care of everybody else, Walter, and start reconnecting... to yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Was this your plan all along? To break me down so that I'd become dependent on you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This would not have been my conscious choice for you any more than it was yours. But the defenses that held you together your whole life... They just finally wore out. You have two choices now. We can try to wrap you back up. Work on simple behavioral changes. And you and I can both talk to your psychopharmacologist... get you back to managing things the way you always have. It's a valid approach.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Or?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: There's a more challenging route. If we can keep going, doing the work that we do, even at this stage of your life... I know that you can achieve a new way of being... with Connie, with Natalie and the boys, but most importantly... with yourself. And we can keep exploring those parts of yourself that we've just begun to discover.

situation: The therapist says I am worth his time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm an old dog, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: 70 isn't old. It will take work... genuine... introspection. And you'll have to come more often.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You really want to spend a couple more hours a week with... an old man?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wouldn't offer it if I didn't think it was worth your time... and mine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why is it worth your time?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Because you've rescued so many others... I want to be there when you go back and... rescue yourself.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine. Fine. When do we start?

situation: I talk about the hearing experience.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you going out? You look great.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd ask you where you were going but I know that you have your boundaries as a therapist. Look, I hate to do this, I hate it when my patients do it, but I've asked my lawyer to call me about the hearing. And... I'd rather be here if it's bad news, okay?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was so relieved that you didn't ask for the letter. I decided not to send it. Yeah, I was having lunch with the kids last Sunday and Rosie actually asked me about the case. And I told her about the settlement offer and she said, Dad, you can't do this. You can't confess to something you didn't do. You're the good guy. She'd been so rude to me all night about other stuff. I guess she's still angry about the divorce. And then suddenly in one sentence, she made me feel better than I'd felt all week. I'm glad. So then I called my lawyer and I said I wasn't interested in the settlement, which meant they went through with the hearing this morning.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how did that go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know yet. I wasn't there. The lawyer said technically, I didn't have to be.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You didn't go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I overslept.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And why do you think you chose this morning to oversleep?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, the subconscious thing. Probably because I didn't want to go. And I just didn't feel like begging some judge to let me keep my job.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You felt showing up would be begging?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know.

situation: I have been in purgatory for a year, under a lot of stress.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So why are you dressed up? I want to hear about your life.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You want to hear about my life? You don't wanna talk about your own life?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd rather talk about how your lawyer felt the hearing went. Did he say anything?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, he said not to quote him... 'cause these guys hate to be quoted but he said that he thought that it went well.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did he say when you'd find out?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anytime between today and God-knows-when.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you're in limbo.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Caught between heaven and hell, waiting for my fate to be decided, yeah. That must be what this whole year has felt like to you. You've been under enormous pressure.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I recall the therapist and David appearing together, everyone was fascinated by Gina.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is that why you dressed up? That blue looks really really good on you. It's the same color as the dress you had on that night I saw you and David coming out of that club on the eastern shore. It was the 4th of July.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I remember.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had this crummy summer job. And I was parking cars, and... I brought out the wrong car and he asked me to go back and get his convertible. And I looked at him and I thought, Of course. Why wouldn't she be with him?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, we had a wonderful dinner and we danced. And then we came outside and there was my most dedicated graduate student.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We were all so in love with you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Don't be silly.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How could we not be? You were brilliant, and we believed everything you said.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What are you talking about? You argued with everything that I said.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, but you made us do that. That was your technique. We were so fascinated by you.

situation: I receive good news from the lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We wanted to know everything about you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's happening with you today? What is it you don't wanna talk about? What happened here between us last week, or your case, or your patients, your children?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, none of the above. Can you tell me what it is? It's my lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you sure you want me to stay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Please. Hello, Ellis. I just spoke with your judge. I've got news. What sort of news? First off, he was livid. At me? No, at Mr. Prince, for wasting everybody's time. The judge hasn't written the ruling yet, and he said not to quote him, but there are no triable issues of fact. What? He said it's a tragic story, but he's going to dismiss the action. He's throwing the case out! Are you saying it's over, Ellis? I'm glad for you. I know this thing was a weight. Thank you so much, you know. I really appreciate everything that you've done. And... I know I haven't been the easiest person in the world to deal with, but I just wanted to say thank you. Nobody's nice when they're being sued. The important thing is justice was served. Come see me next week. We'll go over it. But tonight, you go out and celebrate. You hear me? Yeah. Thanks, Ellis. Good bye.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm so happy for you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My God, it's amazing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm so glad this judge could see what the truth was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How long do you think it's gonna be before I really...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: before I really feel it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Before you wake up some morning not thinking about it? Or not go to bed some night without thinking about it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's so great. Now you know you can keep your practice. What are you gonna do? You were in limbo about that last week as well. How did you do with your patients this week? Was it hard to see them?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did what you said.

situation: I talk about how I moved patients using Gina's method.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I acted as if I believed I really was helping.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did that help?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To be honest, I was kind of skeptical at first. I felt a bit like a hypocrite, and that they'd see that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course you'd feel that way.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But then weirdly enough, something started to happen. I was talking to Oliver's dad about the responsibility of what it means to be a father and keeping in touch with your kid. Really, I was talking for both of us. But I think I reached him. I mean, I was still doubting myself, but I just kept at it, you know? I just couldn't believe that something so simple could actually... could actually work. And it kept working, you know? You're a good therapist.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And I'm sure you did a lot of good work this week, despite how uncertain you felt.

situation: I talk about Apil no longer counseling, I understand.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: April left.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Therapy? Why? In part because I took her to chemo.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't regret it, but it did alter our relationship.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But also, I think she just needed to stop thinking about herself. She wanted some... space. She wanted to breathe, to live.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you try to convince her to stay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Of course I did. I'm worried that she doesn't have the tools to survive another crisis. But part of me, I have to say, is really proud of her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For rejecting you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For rejecting therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I meant, for acting out against you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's not what she was doing, though. She wasn't punishing me or her parents. She's fighting cancer. She needs all of her energy for that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you were able to accept that?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was surprised by my reaction. I know I have this need to rescue, but I really understood her reasoning completely.

situation: I understand practicing medicine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, Walter and April, they both think that the world is supposed to be on their shoulders, and they're both incapable of receiving support. One's stopping therapy, the other wants more sessions.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you're going to continue.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know what I realized this week? Practicing this way, I may never know whether I help people or not. It's not like I'm trying to get them to pass their driving test or do better on their SATs or something. The only measure I have of whether I'm helping somebody or not is how my patients feel about it and how their lives go on from there. And they won't know that until long after we've stopped therapy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I guess what I'm trying to say is that these people come to me, they want me to fix their problems, and the truth is, I think all I can do is just walk with them for a while, keep them company during a rough patch. I don't think anybody's life can be figured out, but it is in our nature to keep trying to make sense of it. And sometimes we can use help. That's when, if we're lucky, there's somebody in the room who can listen. It doesn't have to be somebody perfect, somebody... sufficiently screwed up to actually get what we might be going through.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Someone like you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: On occasion.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And not someone like me.

situation: My conversation with the therapist returns to our differences.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, Gina. Not for me. Not anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When did you come to this conclusion?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Please don't take this personally.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not... No, I'm not taking it personally. You know, I'm just... I'm just disappointed that we're here again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know. I know. But it is different this time. I'm not doing this in anger. And I appreciate everything that you've done for me. I want you to know that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Let's not drag it out, you know.

situation: The therapist says I see myself as a representative of those who struggle with work.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: After last week, really, what is there to say?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand. I just want to be sure you're aware of why you're doing what you're doing.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What is it you think I'm not aware of?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Obviously, last week took a toll, a big toll you know, on both of us, I know that I crossed a line, but you also lost two patients this week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, has it occurred to you that you're angry at them for abandoning you, and that may be why you've decided to abandon me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's a little reductive, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, but this is: you began the week questioning your value as a therapist, and you're ending it questioning mine.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not questioning you. I'm questioning the way we interact, you and I. I don't think it's healthy for either of us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're always questioning me, blaming me. I think I've come to represent everything you struggle with in your work... Emotional restraint, delayed gratification, not indulging your love or your desire for a patient. You've made me your boundary cop... The mentor who's prevented you from having anything you ever wanted.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I beat you up for that.

situation: I want to leave the therapist, I will go my own way.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It must have been exhausting to have to play my mother all these years. If I came running to you, it was because I needed my mother. If was angry at you, it was because I was angry at my mother. Honestly, I don't know how you put up with it. But you did, and you got me through it. All I'm saying is, you don't have to do it anymore.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're releasing me now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I am.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, Paul, if you need to go, you go.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But I'm concerned that you may be punishing me because I failed to protect you. But you didn't fail me, Gina. This has been my sanctuary. All the parts of myself that I don't like, that I'm ashamed of... I could bring them here, and it was always okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think there's a connection between the lawsuit ending and your stopping therapy?
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's just time. The things I needed for so long have changed. I can't keep coming to you for the mothering I didn't get, and you shouldn't have to provide it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you're not running away from home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd rather think of it as moving out.

situation: I want to change professions, the therapist suggests I become a supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm going to make my way in the world.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Where will you go?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not going anywhere. I'm still going to keep being a therapist... Maybe not all private sessions. Some days I just sit there in the room with a patient and I feel like... I don't know... I feel like we're two mice with our... legs caught in a glue trap.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh, god.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's a horrible feeling. Maybe it's the chair. I hate that fucking chair.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You could get a new one.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did. It felt good in the store. But here's the thing about a chair... You never really really know until you've sat in it for 40 hours a week for a month... Month in, month out. By then it's too late.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to practice standing up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe. Maybe I need to be in a group practice, so at least when a patient leaves I could go into the lounge and run into some other people and talk about politics or books or anything, for Christ's sake.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you thought about supervising?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't think I'm at a role-model place in my life right now, Gina.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think you'd be a good supervisor. I mean, you'd have compassion for your students. And the more a supervisor has seen, the more valuable he can be. I'm fairly certain at this point that no case would shock or surprise you. That would make a young therapist feel very safe.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Maybe you're right.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I want to live well, the therapist worries about me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The one thing I have figured out... I just need to be with more people. I don't need a break from being a therapist. I need a break from... Just from this. You know? I need to stop analyzing my life. I need to start living it. I need you to let me go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, part of me would love to. I just worry about the timing. You're still in mourning. You're alone. You're isolated. You don't have a life outside of your practice.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you talking about me or you, Gina?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm talking about you. Did something else happen this week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you meet someone?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why do you think that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: Wendy and I talk about redemption.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did have a conversation this week while I was... I was waiting for a coffee. I was on my way to the subway and she was on her way to the gym.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did you talk about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I told her she looked like a runner. She said that was the best part about running. And I said... Do you know this book, The Memory of Running?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Neither did she, but... it was just great to stand there and just talk to her about a book, you know? I got so excited, I ruined it for her. I told her the whole story.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's the book about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's about redemption, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you make a plan to see this woman again?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Her name is Wendy. We live on the same block. I'm sure we'll run into each other again.

situation: I thank the therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We live on the same block. I'm sure we'll run into each other again. And you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Me what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you have a date tonight? Is that why you're wearing that dress?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I knew it. So who's the lucky guy? Right. Boundaries until the bitter end. You're an excellent therapist, Gina. I never would have survived without you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Paul, this is the point where, you know, I'm supposed to say My door is always open, but I'm not going to say that. I understand.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So... our time is up. Good luck. for her.

situation: I talk about seeing my sister's psychologist with my sister's consent.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You shouldn't have. I'm sorry. I startled you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh no, not at all. You're just early.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, annoying habit. I apologize for that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's fine. Let me just put these... Please come in.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So do I look familiar?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I... I mean, I don't go to the movies that often.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, no no, I meant do I look like my sister?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, it's been what, 18 years now Since Patricia's been my patient?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, of course. Why would you remember, right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But yes, I do. I see the family resemblance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, Tricia looks more like our father And I look like mother, or so people say. Look, I didn't even know if you'd agree to see me. I don't know the rules.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, if enough time has passed, it's...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, as you said, 18 years.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And there's no chance that Patricia will be my patient again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: That's not... that's not a problem.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Then as long as she is comfortable with it...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's fine. Not that I need to get her permission. 'cause I'm the big sister.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you may not need to ask her permission, But... but I do.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, of course, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you... did you tell her That you'd made an appointment with me?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She speaks very highly of you. Oh, she does? Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you called you said that you'd been having Some trouble with remembering your lines, Some memory problems.

situation: I talked about returning to the stage but forgetting the words when reciting them.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wait, I called? Yeah, I'm back onstage. It's been years. night of the iguana. do you know it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, I've seen the ads all over town.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Stars And, well, former stars, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that how you perceive yourself... As a former star?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, is that how you see me? I'm sorry. I haven't been here five minutes And already I'm a parody of myself.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How so?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, you know, the archetypal actress... enough about me. What do you think about me? This is therapy. It's supposed to be about you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So have you been in therapy before?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I did est back in the day, And later lifespring. You remember all that? Hey, it blew my mind at the time. It kind of seems silly now, I guess. Let's see. What else? Oh, later I 12-stepped it for a while But that was mostly because my friends were doing it. I never got past the first step. I had trouble with that whole higher-power thing.

situation: I mention that traditional medical methods don't work for me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What else? Oh, I was on a film once in Ecuador And I had this session with a real-life shaman. I mean, that was a trip. It's unbelievable really, after all that Alternative counterculture crap, That I would wind up on a couch Like a 19th-century neurotic.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you surprised that you, As you say, wound up here? Well, back when my mother was dying,

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, when Patricia was seeing you in Baltimore, You really helped her. And I think my sister felt Like I should be seeing someone too. But you didn't? Oh, I was so overwhelmed with work. I was racing from one job to the next. And plus, you know, I've just never been attracted To traditional therapy. It just seemed very... Naked to me... Sitting across from someone, talking, Being scrutinized... A nightmare.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does this feel like a nightmare... Having to sit here with me now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, I wouldn't say that. More like a vague anxiety dream. Patricia's right. You're easy to talk to.

situation: I talk about not being able to remember my lines.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Patricia's right. You're easy to talk to. Besides, what can I do? I need help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: With your lines.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have them down verbatim the night before. And then I go into rehearsal and wham... they just disappear, I mean, sometimes in the middle of a sentence. I'm talking to another character and I just lose my place. I don't know where I am in the play. I don't know what's supposed to happen next. I can't even improvise my way out of it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So during rehearsal How often would you lose your lines?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, once, twice, maybe more.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm. Anything about the part That makes you feel uncomfortable?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you tend to trip over the same spots... Certain passages, Certain scenes that give you trouble?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, one day it's one place, And another... the next. No. Ava Gardner played the part in the movie. Did you see it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think so, years ago. Are you worried about Being compared to Ava Gardner?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh no, I have my own take on it.

situation: I hear rumors that someone in the director's team doesn't want me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'll be fine... Different, very different. I'm not afraid. As long as I can learn my fucking lines.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how long have you got?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, two more weeks of rehearsal, Two weeks of preview and then opening.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And that's the big night.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The producers are in a panic, Always hovering, Whispering in the director's ear.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think they're whispering about you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I heard a rumor that one of them didn't want me, Didn't think I was right for the part. In other words, too old. The little prick.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're angry with him.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I'm angry with myself. I mean, it's just not like me. I'm always prepared, No matter how much blathering on I have to do.

situation: I talk about my husband's infidelity and divorce.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did happy days in London. Do you know it? That's right. I mean, it's really a 90-minute monologue... that play. Winnie never stops talking. And I was a quick study. I mean, I nailed it every time. Back then I had some help.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: From whom?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, my husband Russell. He's a European history Professor at Columbia, Kind of a bigwig. Yeah, he used to get a kick out of running lines with me. I don't know. Maybe he just liked correcting me. He used to lie in bed And I'd pace back and forth around the room. He was like some kind of academic drill sergeant, You know, with his glasses down on his nose, Doing these ridiculous voices. What a ham. Well, now he's a pig.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So he's not helping you anymore?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, we divorced two years ago. Yeah. He was boffing one of his graduate students. She dumped him six months later. But it was enough to finish us off.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So how long were you married?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 16 years. That's quite a long run for someone in my business.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you and Russell have children?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Izzy... short for Isabel.

dialogue.text: Izzy... short for Isabel. She just turned 15.

dialogue.text: And how is she coping with the divorce?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Fine, I thought. I tried to change the custody arrangement When I got the play. I mean, usually We alternate weekends and split up the week. I just thought she could stay with me Full-time while I was in rehearsal Because I'd be home at night. And then she could go to her father's When I was in tech and preview.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And she wasn't happy with that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Somebody wasn't happy with that. Russell said Izzy felt manipulated by the change. I said let her speak for herself, right? Now she's staying with him full-time, Won't answer my calls.

dialogue.text: You sound frustrated.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah well, you have teenage kids. You know. Oh, Patricia told me That you were having babies when she saw you. So I figure they must be teenagers by now, right? Okay, so I mean, you get it.

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: I took a pass. Look, I'm sure you know this from Patricia, But when our mother was dying I was doing three or four films a year. I was under a lot of pressure... Both personal and professional. I mean, I would sometimes fly from the set to the hospital And I would have to be back in makeup by crack of dawn. I never missed a day... Not one. dialogue.text: You must have found work then To be a useful distraction.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Kept me sane. Only now it's making me crazy.

dialogue.text: But obviously that was a long time ago. Back then you probably could Handle the stress, the schedule, the jet lag. But you were much younger then. Yes, I know, but...

dialogue.text: What am I getting at?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: That is true, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not menopause.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Good.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, it's not for everyone?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, it is for most people, yeah.

dialogue.text: Sounds like you and Patricia talked about me quite a lot.

dialogue.text: Yeah, she found someone... Yvan. They met on some fellowship in France. They used to finish each other's sentences, Sometimes in several languages. Really nice to see her so happy. But he died, though.

dialogue.text: What's her prognosis?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: To say that kind of thing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Does she have somebody to talk to? I mean, is she seeing a therapist? Yes. I'm just concerned. She should be... she should be talking to somebody.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not sure. Well, death runs in the family. It's a family disease. If your mother dies of it, watch out. You're five times more likely to get it yourself.

situation: I mention my sister urging me to get genetic testing after her own treatment failed.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you all right?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes yes, I'm fine. You said it was a family disease.

dialogue.text: Yes, I know.

She still wants me to take the test. She harangues me every time she sees me. Of course I haven't seen her for close to a month. I've been so swamped.

dialogue.text: Does she still live in Baltimore?

dialogue.speaker: therapist

dialogue.text: I needed a job. I wanted to take a job. I hadn't worked in two years. I hadn't had a decent job in longer than that. So I grabbed it. Does that make me a cold-hearted egomaniac?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look, you've just come through A difficult divorce; Your daughter isn't relating to you; Your sister is sick; There's a genetic test that you're anxious about...

dialogue.text: No, I'm not anxious about the fucking test, okay? Patricia's the one who's anxious.

dialogue.text: Well, I would imagine that the play Provided a kind of an escape...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Escape? No, it's the problem, not the solution.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's the problem?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm failing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is it possible that some part of you Might be inclined towards failure? I mean, people sabotage themselves all the time For what they think are very good reasons.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, that's not me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, earlier you were talking about Izzy And how angry she is and how she resents you working. Did you notice during that that you lost your train of thought?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you did. And it was at a moment When you were judging yourself for being selfish. I'm just wondering if you're having a similar judgment About yourself in rehearsal... You know, about being selfish by being in the play.

dialogue.text: My God, did you aggravate Patricia like this? She said you were supremely supportive.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, maybe I've just become more aggravating In my middle years, yeah.

dialogue.text: Or maybe she was a nicer patient. I don't know. Was she a nicer patient?

dialogue.text: What if she was a nicer patient... A better patient, whatever that might mean? You know, I think it's interesting That you chose to see me... Your sister's former therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, as I said, you came highly recommended.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I'm sure that you had recommendations From a lot of people. Did you ask around?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, not really.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think there might be Something particular in coming to see me... Some special understanding that you might hope To gain about Patricia, Some insight into her maybe, Into her relationship with you bef...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What? Just say it. It's true. She's dying... Tricia. That's the first time I've said it out loud. Is it time? Because it must be time. Oh God. I tell you, rehearsal's gonna be.

dialogue.text: So are you on your way to work?
