Steve brings him into the architecture studio, teaches him... I don't even know the terms... line drawing, drafting, whatever it's called, how to use a mechanical pencil.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you spoken to Max about this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I haven't spoken with Max about much of anything. I was gonna sit him down as soon as he came back from Maryland and talk to him about what he found on my computer that night... you know, my Parkinson's research. But since my conversation with Rosie, I haven't been able to bring myself to do it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What are you afraid to hear Max say?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you... are you really gonna make me answer that?

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I think the therapist understands what happened last week and I think my son is trying to protect me. The therapist thought it was difficult for me to think about my son living with his stepfather.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, you... you saw perfectly what was happening last week more clearly than I saw it myself. I'm sure you know the answer without me having to say it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You think I know what you're going to say before you say it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was getting my son to worry about me. He won't tell me about Steve because he's trying to protect me. I... I can't stop myself from wondering if, you know... if he'd actually be better off in Maryland.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: With his mother and Steve. It's hard for you to consider that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They share this passion for drawing, for art.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I'm afraid that my son will be unhappy with me and deprive him of his happiness. The therapist will ask me how I take care of myself. I really wish my daughter didn't tell me this.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And Steve feeds it. I mean, how can I deny my son that? If I did, I'd be doing exactly what was done to me. I'd be... I'd be dragging him away from his vibrant teenage years and taking him to a dreary, lifeless apartment with a sick parent.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that how you see your existence... as dreary and lifeless?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sure that's how Max sees it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wasn't asking about Max.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I really wish Rosie had never told me about the fucking twin drafting tables. I really could have done without that detail.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that what gets to you most?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It all gets to me... the whole picture. And it's not just them either.

situation: I had lost my enthusiasm, and the therapist asked me how I had discovered it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Just about everybody I know has some kind of passion. Something or somebody drives them.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But not you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sometimes I... I try to pretend I do, yeah. I try to pretend I do, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you do that? What does that mean, you pretend?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Wendy... uh, my girlfriend... she stopped by the apartment at lunchtime today.

situation: I engage in an intimate encounter with my girlfriend but am distracted and unable to fully engage. The therapist explores my lack of passion and my fixation on a model sailboat.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And she knows I have an hour and a half without any patients. And... We... we haven't had sex for a while. And... Since she can't stay over and I can't stay at her place because of Max...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Max was away this weekend.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Right. That's true. I hadn't told her that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But you saw her today.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She has this thing, you know... she... for some reason she's been wanting to have sex on the couch in my office. So we did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This was your attempt at being passionate about something.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I suppose you're right.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was... I was distracted. I was...

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I got distracted while making out with my girlfriend, and my therapist asked me why. I tell about the office ship model.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was... I was thinking about other things.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What were you thinking about?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. Not her. I have this... I have this boat in my office. And I just found myself staring... you know, staring at it after Wendy and I were finished. It's a... a model, a sailboat. It's about that big.

problem_type: The relationship with friends and family
situation: I told about the ship model in the office that my son Max loved when he was a child, and the therapist asked why he only has one now.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I used to have about 26 of them, different sizes, you know, schooners, sloops.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you like to sail?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Never been. Anyway, these... these boats are... actually, the boats are the closest I've ever come to a hobby. And when Max was little, he really loved it. We used to go searching at these antique stores. Sometimes we'd build them from kits, you know. And we'd give them each a name and we'd make up these stories about the places it had been and the places that it would go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How come there's only one boat left?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He lost interest. Then when I moved up to Brooklyn, I just left the rest of them behind. They... I don't know, they just started to feel a bit pathetic... 22 reminders of all the places I'd never been and I would never get to.

situation: I described how each of my patients was enthusiastic about life, and so was the therapist, who asked for details.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The one that I saved... I keep it in my office. I see it over my patients' shoulders. So I sit and I listen to them talk, and every single one of them, they... no matter how sick or screwed up they are... they... they all have a real passion.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You find all your patients have something you don't, something you're missing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I do feel that way a lot, yeah. Jesse... he loves photography. He's got this fierce attachment to his camera. And frances has her acting. Although it's hard for her to admit, with all the guilt she has around it, there's no question of what it means to her. Other people... Kate devoted to her clinic, now to Max's new father. I mean, even Gina... suddenly a novelist. As much as I fucking hate her for what she's written, she has found her... you know, her calling. And there's... there's you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Me? Why do you include me? What do you consider my passion to be?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, isn't it this... your work, your patients? I mean, not that there aren't other things that you might feel strongly about, but from where I sit, you seem to be pretty engaged even in your cool detachment.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Am I engaged or detached?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'd... I'd say both.

situation: I discovered that the therapist valued her work and her situation, and the therapist asked me what I thought of her publications.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But... but it is clear that your work is very important to you. Am I wrong about that?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My work is important to me. I'm just wondering why you say that, how you arrive at this impression.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I went online, you know, the other night. It's become kind of a bad habit really. And I found myself back at my desk, typing in this thing on Parkinson's/ olfactory symptoms. And I... I just stopped. I made myself stop. And I... I just happened to type in your name instead.

situation: I told me that I had stopped writing articles recently, and the therapist asked me why. I told me that I had seen her information on the Internet, and asked about the reason for her name.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you know there's another Adele Brouse, also a therapist, in Portland, Oregon?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I wasn't aware of that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, an m.S.W., not a psychiatrist, not nearly as prolific as you. I mean, all this... a list of stuff comes up, all the articles that you've published over, you know... the amount of conferences that you've attended in Chicago, Prague, Paris.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did seeing that mean to you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, the last article that I wrote was in 1998.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why have you stopped?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Adele Saskia Brouse. Is that Dutch? Wasn't Rembrandt's wife called Saskia?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: My mother's father was from Holland.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't believe it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You just... you answered my question.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You still haven't answered mine. Why have you stopped?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, let's say that I... that I no longer share your professional drive.

situation: I think work is meaningful, but I have doubts about whether I am passionate about my work. The therapist asked me why, and I told about the patient Sunil on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My work does feel meaningful at times. When I'm in the room with my patients, I'm still interested mostly, but am I passionate?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean in the way you think I am. Were you ever?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: When I was your age, I published. I still thought I could save people.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you ever think that now?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Monday, for 40 minutes, I had a flash of that feeling.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What happened monday?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You remember Sunil. I told you about him.

situation: I told about the progress of my patient Sunil's treatment on Monday. He was able to express his emotions and open up to me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He took... he took a huge step. I'd been trying to get him to express his anger. And he'd been inching toward it. So we were sitting in my office over tea and we were talk...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: you were talking over tea?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It makes him feel like we're having more of a conversation than therapy. You know, he's a guy who spends all his time feeling like an outsider in what he perceives to be this strange, aggressive country. So he locks himself away in his room. So sharing tea with me makes him... you know, draws him out of his shell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you talking about him or you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm talking about him. Last week you told me that you didn't want to be my supervisor. Now you kind of sit there silently supervising. It's kind of obvious what you think.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What do I think?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He opened up to me.

situation: I am deeply affected by Sunil's session and reflect on my own experiences of passion. I realize a pattern of relying on others to feel emotions for me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He... he told me about this deeply passionate affair that he had at university... something he's never spoken of before to anybody and that's haunted him for years. You should have seen how transformed he was when he spoke about this love affair. It's like he... he came alive. I mean, this man isn't... he's not old. He felt passion at one point in his life. And I thought, why couldn't he have that again? Why couldn't he... ?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why couldn't he...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. It was... it was fleeting, what I saw in him, but a glimpse of somebody different, you know? Maybe I'm making too much of it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This recent session with Sunil had a powerful effect on you. You seem especially focused on his early love affair.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, it's a pretty powerful story, don't you think?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Have you ever felt that passion romantic passion?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My lunchtime session with Wendy doesn't qualify?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not according to you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: With Kate,

situation: I told me that I would look for people who are passionate about life, and let people around me help me feel the passion. The therapist asked me if I could express my passion, and used my reaction to sunil to analyze the phenomenon of me restraining myself, and said that two weeks ago I discovered it in my dream.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I suppose, when I fell in love with her all those years ago. Even with Wendy last year, at the very beginning. But now I... I'm beginning to realize I've got this pattern: I seek out people who have... who have... who have themselves a passion for life and I feed off them instead. I allow them to... to feel for both of us.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You allowed both Wendy and Kate to do your feeling for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, at least... at least in part.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Whatever emotion you do feel, do you openly express yourself at the time?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Not entirely.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You hold yourself back?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is... is that what you think?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Earlier, when you were talking about Sunil, you became engaged, excited, as you came alive yourself. You spoke with energy. You sat forward in your seat. And then you stopped yourself. It was striking. Does that description seem accurate to you? Do you find you have passionate or excited impulses, but stop yourself from expressing them? I made a similar observation a couple of weeks ago about you holding yourself back, and you had a strong reaction. Do you remember?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What... what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You told me about the beginning of your dream... running toward open gates along a wrought-iron fence, and then being dragged down, paralyzed. I asked if you were stopping yourself and you got very angry at me. You insisted it was your father who was stopping you.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was my school.

situation: I related the dream to my experience as a child in boarding school and being forced to leave when my father found a job in Baltimore. I was content and committed to boarding school and felt my father had deprived me of the possibility of thriving there.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was my school.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was my school. The fence... the iron fence ran around the outside of the boarding school I went to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When was this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I... I was 12.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were Max's age.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. Lancaster royal grammar school in the north of england. I wasn't there for very long, just a term and a half, but... well, my parents had already started to fight with each other. And yeah, it was our last year in dublin. And they sent me away to school.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was that hard for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, not at all. Most people talk about how miserable they are at boarding school, but I was really happy there. But I was there for less than six months when my father got his position at union memorial in Baltimore. Two weeks later we landed in... in America.

situation: My dream was about living in a boarding school as a child, but it was ruined by my father, who asked me why I liked boarding school.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I'm... I'm sure that's part of the dream that I'm, you know, reliving... being torn away from school by my father, from that feeling that I had... that great feeling of contentment that I'd found there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can you tell me what was so nice about the boarding school?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The place was... was just filled with activity.

situation: I was able to participate in various activities in school as a child, but my father ruined this. The therapist asked me what activities I participated in and helped me analyze the impact of things on me as a child.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: There were scores of clubs and things that you could do, teams you could sign up for... to play rugby, cross-country running, the school newspaper. It's just all these things my father tore me away from.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Cross-country running... did you run at school?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I was going to join the team.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did you play rugby, join the paper?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I was planning to. I'm not sure what you're getting at. The point I'm making is that I was happy there.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Actively engaged, content. It's interesting to hear you speak of the school in this way, because in your dream you're running outside the gates. When you told me the dream, you described a feeling of anticipation, of excitement, not of contentment. To me that difference seems significant. You say you planned to join the newspaper?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I hadn't been there that long.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A semester and a half? Surely that's enough time to join the paper if you'd wanted to.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I'm just saying that if I had stayed, I would have thrived. It was my father moving here that just took away that possibility.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did you find here instead?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The move to Baltimore marked the end of my childhood.

situation: I talk about the difficult times I went through when I moved to Baltimore as a child and the responsibilities my father took on. I described my feelings of alienation in a new country and expressed my determination to integrate into the then-new surroundings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My father walked out; My mother got sicker; And I was... I was forced to... to take care of her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The beginning of a very difficult period. And your father bears a great deal of the responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, who else? My mother... she was... she was ill.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand. You mentioned more than once how strongly you identify with Sunil's alienation in this country, that you continue to feel it at times. And I imagine you felt it when you first arrived.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I... I went from Lancaster royal grammar to p.S. 233, from beautiful gothic stone buildings and open green fields to brick and asphalt.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's tough for rugby.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The kids played stickball.

situation: I told the story of when I was young and determined to integrate into the new campus. I didn’t like it at all at the time, but I tried my best to integrate. The therapist thought it had something to do with the fact that my father had been away from the United States for a year and a half.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I remember watching them with such determination from the edge of the schoolyard.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Determination? What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was... I was determined to decode them, you know, to figure them out... how to play their game, how to fit in. Because everything about them was alien... the music that they listened to, the clothes that they wore, even their curse words. And the girls... the girls... forget it. They wouldn't even look in my direction.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You stayed on the edge of that schoolyard as well, outside the gates.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was trying to join in. I was trying to find my way. And I just... I just didn't get a chance to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were pulled away again.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How long was your family in America before your father walked out?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: 18 months.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A year and a half.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh okay, I get the point you're trying to make...

situation: When my mother was sick during that time when I was a child, I stayed with her and the treatment room asked me if I felt sorry or relieved.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: that I had time, like at boarding school, to join in. But see, the thing is, my father was... he was working really long hours. And my mother was already unwell.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You were expected to stay home with her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, I was. And I did. Yeah. It was a terrible blow.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Was it a terrible blow or was it also a relief?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was trying to be a good son.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I understand it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is that so awful?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Of course it's not awful. What I'm saying is that it may have been easier than the alternative.

situation: The therapist believes that taking care of my mother is one of the ways to save myself, so that I don’t have to take risks for life, don’t have to go out, and can self-paralyze myself and lose my enthusiasm for life. He also suggested that I look directly at my heart and take risks.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think I wanted to spend my teenage years with my chronically ill mother?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I mean... The first day I met you, you insisted that you and Gina had it all figured out, that your need to save people started with your mother's illness.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And does that seem far-fetched to you?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It doesn't. But I think caring for your mother was also a way of saving yourself. It was miserable, yes, but it was also safe and familiar. And it kept you from having to find any real connections elsewhere, from risking yourself in the outside world. And it also had the convenience of allowing you to blame it all on your father. And it's really not so different from what you do to this day, is it? You cloister yourself in your apartment or your burrow like office. You convince yourself you're sick. You accept a growing paralysis rather than taking a risk of finding where or towards whom your real passion lies. Is it any wonder you haven't found what drives you yet? You're 57 years old. At a certain point you have to move past the stories that you've assigned to your life, these steadfast explanations you've settled on years ago. You have to look at yourself again for real answers. You have to take that risk.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well...

situation: I thought the therapist could see things very clearly, but the therapist thought she could see better and thought I was good at hiding myself.I told how I was distracted while making out with Wendy because I thought about my therapist and thought she understood me.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You're so young and yet you're so confident.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: About what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You just seem so certain that you're right. You see everything clearly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think I see you clearly? Because I'd like to see you more clearly, but I find you're fairly expert at obscuring the view. That's not the first time you've heard that, is it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: In so many words. I... I told you earlier that I was distracted when I was with Wendy. And you asked me what I was thinking about. And I said I didn't know. You asked me if I hold myself back, and I didn't answer. Well, I do hold myself back. Do you know why? I was thinking about you.

situation: I express feelings of loneliness and acknowledge it as a form of transference. The therapist encourages me to explore these feelings and expresses gladness that I answered honestly. The therapist points out my tendency to dismiss my own feelings and suggests reflecting on why I do that. The session ends with the therapist scheduling the next session to continue the discussion.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I hear your voice a lot. I admire your clarity, your... you see me. I noticed that you don't wear a wedding ring. And I've imagined that you might understand something of my life, my loneliness. I know, I know... textbook transference. I know it's ridiculous, a fantasy. And it's my comeuppance for being on the receiving end of these sorts of feelings. But you did ask.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm glad you answered.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You look... you look kind of shocked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why do you say that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Nothing.
dialogue.fine_label: 答案: 回避-最小的回应(C1)

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you recognize what you're doing? You're holding yourself back again. As soon as you express your feelings, you dismiss them immediately, call it ridiculous, offer an excuse.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What... what exactly are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm saying that between now and next session you may want to think about why you do that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Are you telling me...? Are you trying to say...?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We have to stop. Let's pick this up next week. This will be an excellent place to start.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We'll talk more next week. Have a good weekend.

situation: I share worsening distress due to floods in India, feeling disconnected and helpless.I describe a haunting news image affecting my sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You know, I have to admit I was a little bit worried the last time at the end of our session.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Things are no better, Paul. In fact they are worse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why? Has something... has something happened?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Monsoons have flooded the region where my parents were raised... Entire village underwater.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, I... I had no idea. I'm so sorry to hear that.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How would you have any idea? Because floods have scarcely made the news here. Everything is about the New York Knicks. Who is this player... Amare Stoudemire? I'm searching to hear of the disaster in India and all they want to talk about is this basketball player, as if he's a superhero and he's going to save the world now. Now I'm all the time searching for news on the b.B.C. Channel or on this radio with this terrible reception. And... These pictures... they stay in my mind. And... and I'm having difficulty to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So when you do manage to sleep, are you having any more of these disturbing dreams?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I keep seeing the same image... You know, a boy, perhaps three or four.

situation: I describe a haunting news image affecting my sleep.I feel like an outsider, distant from life.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, a boy, perhaps three or four. He's clinging to an automobile tire, and his head barely above water and his eyes, you know... they are pleading.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This is in the dream?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No no, this is real. It was on the news... B.B.C. News. I wanted to pass through the television and rescue that poor child. People are traveling from other areas to help. And I'm trapped in Brooklyn, useless, locked away like a prisoner.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So is that what you feel like... like a prisoner in your son's home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: My son is gone. He's been gone for three days, attending a medical conference in St. Louis. Before he left we watched the early reports together. He pointed to the television and said, oh baba, I'm glad that you are not there.

situation: The therapist question the feasibility of moving from my son's home due to financial concerns.The therapist encourages me to discuss feelings with my son, but I respond defensively.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Hmm. I feel like I'm outside of my life. I feel like a... like a stranger.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: A prisoner, a stranger.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I cannot stop myself from watching. I cannot change how I feel.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I just wonder if there aren't other things that you might be able to change.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Other things, meaning what?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Look, Sunil, things can't go on as they are. What about the possibility of your moving from your son's home? I know you can't go back to Calcutta... you told me that... but finding someplace else to live.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And where... Where, please tell me, would that be?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your own apartment?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Okay. And... and who would pay... pay for this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You could get a job.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like selling printer cartridges at best buy or standing behind a kebab wagon? I cannot do that, Paul. I will not.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not suggesting that you...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you're just wasting your time, Paul. See, I'm as helpless to change my surroundings as those people in my country who are unable to save their houses from floodwaters. I know you are a hopeful man, my friend. You like to think that you can... You can fix everything.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think that you have to talk with your son. No, just... just hear me out on this. You're not happy where you are. And it's pretty obvious that having you in their home hasn't been easy for them either. Yet you've never spoken to your son about this. You've never expressed to him directly what you feel or what it is exactly that you want.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ( Speaks bengali )

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I didn't understand that.

situation: The therapist encourages me to discuss feelings with my son, but I respond defensively.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ( Speaks bengali ) ( Sighs ) I said that you are wasting my time too.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know, I know it can be difficult to talk to family, your children, in a completely honest way because you risk a painful conversation.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This is just a strategy, yes... to tell me you know how I feel?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No no, it's not a strategy. Look, Sunil, I have kids myself. I know what this is like... to sometimes want to put off difficult discussions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you don't know my son, Paul. You have no idea. I'm telling you with certainty there's nothing to be gained... absolutely nothing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're so convinced that he's not gonna help you. How can you know that for sure?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I've already spoken to him the night before he left.

situation: I recount my son's refusal, his wife's behavior, and stability concerns, feeling judged and misunderstood regarding my conflicting emotions toward his wife's safety.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was thinking of you, Paul... How you encourage me to express myself. So I told him the truth. I told him that seeing the images made me certain and I need to return. Here I'm useless. I'm only in the way here, to let me go.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did he say to that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He told me that he would never let me go back to Calcutta, he had made a promise, and he could never betray his mother. He also told me that... why do you want to make a fool of yourself? What will you do back in India, in all that water, jobless? Then he said, Julia will send a check to the red cross in your name, and that they would buy me a queen-sized mattress from Macy's departmental store. Later that night I overheard them talking in the kitchen. Julia was saying, oh, if he wants to go, let him go. And she said she was not comfortable staying with me alone in the house.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what did Arun say to that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He told Julia that she was being dramatic and ridiculous and that he felt better having a man there to protect her and the children while he was away.

situation: I describe witnessing my son's wife's intimate gesture with Ethan, feeling betrayed, and seek validation from the therapist.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then Julia called me unstable, this word unstable... like an old fruit wagon with loose wheels. To be called this word... I held a position of mathematics professor for 28 years. I was married to Kamala for 30 years. Is this a profile of someone who is unstable? If anything, she is unstable... Julia. She has been behaving like a madperson... madperson since Arun went away.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you mean, she's behaving like a madperson? What is she doing?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She's continuing her adventures with Mr. Ethan Barr... the pale fox. On Saturday night they went out, leaving Naya with an upset stomach.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you were watching the children?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No no, I'm not allowed. She would not allow that. Liza the nanny... She stayed late.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Uh-huh.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He actually came up to the door to pick her up.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you met him?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, he is not quite as handsome as he appears on the jacket cover.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you speak to him? Did he...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We shook hands. He's young, more modest than I thought. I congratulated him on his success. Then he said something which surprised me. He said that... I have heard quite a lot about you. When they walked down the stairs they looked back at me and they laughed.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You thought they were laughing at you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Please, Paul, you must trust me.

situation: I express distress over my son's wife's behavior and desire for her disappearance, leading the therapist to probe for clarity on extreme feelings.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you had seen for yourself, you could not doubt me this time... not this time. My son said he wanted me there to protect her, but I felt quite the opposite. I wished to smother her laughing.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: To... Let me get this straight... To smother the sound of her laughter or to smother her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They were laughing at me, Paul.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yeah, I understand...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, you don't understand. They were humiliating me. See, now look at your face. I have alarmed you now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes actually, because the words that you're using are...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm trying to share with you how their laughter disturbed me. I'm trying to express myself, as you say. You understand this, yes?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I think so, yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Good. Because it only grew worse. At 1:00 I heard talking in front of the building. My window faces the street. I saw Julia and Ethan barr. He escorted her up the steps and then... and then kissed her goodnight. What do you make of this?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, it depends what kind of a kiss it was.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: A kiss is a kiss. Don't you think I know what a kiss looks like?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, was it on the lips?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No no, it was on the cheek.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, that's not really an uncommon thing for people in America to do when they're saying goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know, I know. You will think what you want to think.

situation: I recount vivid, disturbing dreams involving protective urges turning violent, prompting the therapist to seek understanding of their significance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway, after he kissed her, Julia carefully lifted her hand to a spot below his eye and then gently drew the back of her curled fingers down his cheek. Julia never touches my son's face in this manner. How much proof do you need, Paul? Last week I brought you solid evidence... Her birth control pills... and you still want more. Is this not enough?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Not necessarily.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not acceptable, Paul. She is disgracing my family. After I witnessed the kiss, I could not move from the window. I could hear her down on the second floor, preparing her bed. And I thought I heard her lock her bedroom door. She did not even come upstairs to check on Naya. And then I wanted to go to sleep, but I could not stop myself thinking of Julia lying on her bed, who she was thinking of. I think it all would be better if she ran off with Mr. pale fox or she simply disappears.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Disappears? What do you... What do you mean by that... disappears? I have to say that some of the words that you've used today, Sunil... I really want to understand what it is that you are trying to say to me. If your feelings are as extreme as I'm hearing them today...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You asked me whether I had more disturbing dreams.

situation: I describe a dream where I felt the need to protect my grandchildren, which the therapist connects to past discussions about subconscious fears.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You asked me whether I had more disturbing dreams. I have had one again.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The same one?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, a different one. It was quite troubling.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you want to tell me about it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah. Perhaps it will help you to make sense of my feelings.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I hope so.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I saw my son Arun lying on the street in front of the house. And he was unconscious. The children were inside, looking out the window. They were afraid. Beyond the street there was a forest of thick black trees. And a woman with long dark hair came walking out of the forest. She wore a long white gown, bright as the moon. And I was standing over my son. And as the woman started walking towards the house, I was trying to hold my son's arm. And I pulled it and it broke cleanly off like a piece of old plaster. So I was thinking that I should use this arm to protect the children.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: To protect the children from this woman?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Now the arm was quite heavy, dense. I could hurt this woman very much. And... I woke up as I was about to strike her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So you were going to strike this woman to protect your grandchildren?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm quite confused by this woman. Who do you think she could be?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, sometimes it's not so much the physical similarity as the feeling.

situation: I deny any intention to harm and become defensive when discussing the dream, but the therapist emphasizes the importance of understanding its emotional impact.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Do you think it could be Julia? No, she had dark hair. It was dark, black as onyx. And Julia's hair is yellow. Perhaps it was Julia in disguise.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Is that how you see Julia... in disguise? Do you see her as a threat?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She has a secret life. The woman was most definitely not Kamala.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What makes you so sure of that?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I would never think of harming my wife.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you feel that you could harm Julia?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The thing I found strange was that I could not make out the details of the woman's face even when she drew very close. You know, I started to grip my son's arm with great force. I could feel the blood pulsing into my hands. And she was so close that I could almost smell the flower she wore in her hair, but I could not see her face.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The flower in her hair like in the El Greco painting?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Sorry?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: That's the painting you mentioned when you first spoke of Malini.

situation: I deny any intention to harm and become defensive when discussing the dream, but the therapist emphasizes the importance of understanding its emotional impact.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, you've just spoken about her death after 32 years of silence. It's not surprising that some form of her... even the slightest gesture or detail... might show up in your dream.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Like a rabbit in a hat? Bong! Oh, there she is.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You said that you felt you had this need to protect your grandchildren. You said you felt the blood rushing into your hands and that you were prepared to harm this woman.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: See, Paul, I no longer wish to discuss this dream.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I ask you why?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I cannot see the point of this exercise.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I'm confused.A moment ago you asked me to help you understand these nightmares that you're having, to help you make sense of the feelings that you're having. So that's what I'd like to do. For instance, this woman coming from the forest... It's clear that she has a big effect on you. Do you... you disagree with that? See, the image of you removing your son's arm... Well, sometimes there's something primal or animalistic <i>that dreams allow us to express that our conscious mind is...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ( shouting in bengali ) A man can only be pushed so far.

situation: The therapist addresses my concerns about family, homeland, and emotional intensity, recommending more frequent sessions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I have decided it was not Malini in my dream. And it upsets me very much for you to suggest this. I... I... I would never ever think of harming Malini.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why would you think I would assume you'd hurt Malini? Okay, we don't have to talk about that now.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: ( Speaks bengali )

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You have no idea what my life has been.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But I want to understand. I want to know. Can I ask you what you did when you woke up from the dream?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I checked on the children. They were fine, sleeping. I then went down to Julia's room. I could not resist. I wanted to check to see if her door was in fact locked.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What would you have done if her door wasn't locked?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Her door would not open, and this is all that matters.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, but I'm asking you, what would you have done if the door had been open?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I thought of calling you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Why didn't you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was the middle of the night. And things felt out of balance. Then I went upstairs to my room and I wrote to Kamala.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Can I ask you what you wrote?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I really did consider calling you.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: The next time I want you to do that. Okay?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah, perhaps.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sunil, there's so much going on in your life at the moment: You've lost your wife. You've started to talk about a love affair that ended in tragedy. You're worried about your son. You're worried about your grandchildren. You have these conflicted ideas about your daughter-in-law. You're anxious about the floods in your homeland... in India. I'm concerned about you, Sunil... that with all of these intense feelings coming to the surface I understand how difficult it could be for you to stay in control. And I... I want to suggest that you consider coming here a little more often, maybe twice a week.

situation: I worry about going crazy and am hesitant to burden my family, so the therapist offers to pray for my homeland.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You think I'm going crazy?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No no no no, you're not... you're not crazy, I assure you. I have patients who come to see me two-three times a week, but it doesn't mean they're crazy. It's just that they can benefit from working more on themselves, going deeper with therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Julia and Arun... they have done enough for me. And I would prefer not to ask anything more than this.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, would you like me to talk to them for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No no, please. I would not prefer that. Do you pray, Paul?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do I... do I pray?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Sometimes, yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Then please pray.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: For what?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For the rains to stop in India.

situation: I discuss difficulty starting sessions, silence dynamics, and reluctance to address test results. I reflect on strained communication with daughter Izzy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Is this normal?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: For it to be so hard to get started, you know, to sit here for so long and not say anything?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: It's actually only been a minute or two, but yeah, it's quite common.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If I didn't say anything for the whole hour, would you say something eventually or would you just sit there? 45 minutes later... It's time. We'll pick up here next week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Eventually I would say something, yeah, but the silences are instructive.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: How long before you intervene? What's the record? What's the longest silence by a patient?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: 20-25 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yeah? Who blinked first?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I did. Finally I said, what are you thinking about? And she said, I've just been sitting here wondering when you were gonna say something. So what are you thinking about? So last week as you were leaving you said that you'd gotten the results of your test, but you hadn't looked at them yet.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not ready to talk about that yet.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How come? Did you look at the results?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Izzy...

situation: I recount a tense encounter with Izzy, feeling ignored for Trish. Emotions surface regarding lack of meaningful interaction with my daughter.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm sitting here thinking about Izzy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You've heard from her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Only when she wants something. Last week I got an email, a text, three messages on my voicemail. It's more communication than I've had from her in months. She wanted to download some music and needed my password.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, maybe that was her way of breaking the ice.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, by whining and begging, issuing demands?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You sound like you're kind of angry with her. Maybe it's time you to see her.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I did.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: This week. I had her scarf, remember?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Oh yes, the one that you took from Tricia's.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And some other things. I had a t-shirt that she loved and some paperbacks. I stuffed them all in a backpack and I went down to her school and ambushed her.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Ambushed her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, if I'd told her I was coming, she never would have stayed put.

situation: I express concern for sick friend Trish, highlighting family neglect. Therapist probes my emotions about Trish's appearance, leading to a discussion on family dynamics and personal reactions.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Anyway, she was out front, chatting with some friends on the steps. She looked very grown-up, chic, full of life. I just stood there and watched her for a few minutes.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And what was that like?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was sort of surreal. It was like looking into the future. Who is this young woman? I mean, where'd she come from? I don't know. She... She looked sort of confused when she saw me, surprised. Her friends were gawking. And then this confident young woman just evaporated in front of my eyes and she went back to being this sullen, obnoxious little...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, they're grown-ups around their friends. But they're... they're still children with us. Did you speak to her?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She always licks her lips when she gets nervous, you know? It's compulsive. She did it all the time when she was a child. She used to have this red ring of irritation around her mouth. She started doing that when she was talking to me. I said, honey, don't do that, and I offered her some chapstick. You would have thought that I tried to scald her with a hot poker. I mean, she just fled.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did that hurt you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh no. I'm used to stuff like that. That didn't hurt me. What she did after hurt me.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What did she do?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: She texted me. Thanks for bringing the scarf.

situation: I divulge intimate encounter with a younger man, reflecting on maternal instincts and sensuality. Therapist explores my surprise and self-perception during the encounter, addressing potential shock and judgment.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You should call Trish. She's really sick now. She looks like a skeleton. It's always about Trish. You know, I haven't seen my daughter for months... I mean, not really, not in any meaningful way. She's been spending every waking minute with my sister. I finally reach out to her. I see her once, and what does she do? She texts me about Trish.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How did you feel when you heard that Patricia looked like a skeleton?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, how do you think I felt?
dialogue.fine_label: 答案: A1 争辩-挑战(A1)

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I don't know. I'm finding it kind of hard to read your reaction, but I imagine that it must have been hard to hear.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It was very hard. I couldn't even take it in. I just texted Izzy back and said, you know, great seeing you, darling. And I'll call Trish after the show.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And did you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why? You agree with Izzy? You think I should call my sister?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, I do. I think that you should call your sister.
dialogue.strategy: Guiding the Pace and Depth of the Conversation

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I went out and got laid instead. I know, I know you're judging me, but I don't care. I haven't been with anyone since Russell. 25 and very handsome. No body fat... none. Actually I was a little worried. I thought, I wonder if he gets cold in the winter.

situation: I challenge therapist's perceived squeamishness, linking past behaviors to current actions. Therapist connects my sexual encounter to sister's illness, questioning motivations and emotional shields regarding potential medical results.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Part of me wanted to fuck him, part of me wanted to take him home and wrap him in a blanket and give him a great big meal. It was that maternal-erotic thing you were talking about.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: So this man that you...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, he's in the cast... Eddie, Eduardo. Well, you know the script, right? He is one of Maxine's houseboys. After the preview I went out for a quick drink with the cast. And I was gonna call Tricia afterwards, when I got home. I knew she'd be up. She sleeps during the day and then she's up at night... you know, the morphine.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You haven't done that before, have you... gone out with the cast?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, they've been bugging me. I've just been avoiding it. ( Sighs ) He kept buying me martinis. I'm a lightweight. I only need one drink. But halfway through the third I asked him to show me where he lived, just like that. Wasn't that bold of me?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Do you think it was the alcohol that made you bold?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Didn't hurt. Two years. I kept telling myself, don't worry, Frances, it's like riding a bicycle.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And was it?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He took off my shirt and touched me, and I thought I was gonna lose it. I mean, he loved my breasts.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You sound surprised.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm not 25 or synthetic, if you know what I mean. And he just kept kissing them and touching them. Well, I forgot how sensitive they are. Are you shocked?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh please.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Are you trying to shock me?

situation: Therapist explores my fear of losing breasts' sensuality. I reflect on intimacy with Eddie, facing reality, and feeling relieved at home alone.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: No, I just know how squeamish you are.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What about my behavior would make you think I'm squeamish?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, your whole life seems squeamish to me. I mean, no wonder Trish loved you so much. She always had a thing for repressed men.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm... I'm struck by the fact that you went out and that you had sex for the first time in two years when you were confronted by the very real image of your sister being sick... very sick. What's the connection between the two events?

dialogue.speaker: client

dialogue.text: You know, I guess I felt that he'd been up here a month and I just wanted to get him home for his sake and also to...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Get it over with. He asked me inside for coffee.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You mean...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Steve. Kate wasn't there. You know, he seemed... he seemed, you know, okay... all-American, you know, a big smile, a strong handshake. He looked, you know, like dad.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Unlike you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Did you go in? I... I couldn't. I just had to get out of there. It made it easier in some ways, you know... his glaring decency, his ease with Max.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And yet in other ways I can imagine that was very difficult to see.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think maybe it was the hardest thing I've ever had to do, you know... walk away from that house leaving Max behind with him.

situation: I reflect on facing the truth and handling my client Jesse's emotional crisis.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But after our session last week I saw that... I saw that you were right, that I didn't have a choice, that I had to face the truth.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Will you tell me about your talk, how you got yourself to face the truth?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We were making pancakes late. And I was just beginning to get into it, you know, trying to find the right words. And the doorbell rings. And it's Jesse.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What time was this?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't know. About 10:30 maybe.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: And you let him in?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I had to.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He'd been to visit his birth parents and they fucking rejected him. The kid was devastated.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Did it feel easier for you to deal with Jesse's problems in your office than the ones with Max at home?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: If you'd seen what Jesse looked like, you would have let him in too.

situation: I emphasize the intensity of my partner's anger and seek the therapist's guidance on potential violence. but the therapist said the time is off

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So I said to Max, okay look, we'll talk about this later. This is an emergency. I have to deal with it. We'll make the pancakes for breakfast. Then I went in. I spoke to Jesse. 15 minutes later the smoke alarm goes off.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm sorry?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: He'd tried to make the pancakes himself and the pan went on fire. So I put the flames out and I realized that I had to talk to my son. I... I... I... I couldn't wait any longer.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You just told me you were determined to do it anyway.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: The point is that I did it.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Once Max set the stove on fire, once you left Jesse.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Oh, for fuck's sake.

situation: I confront the therapist about avoiding discussing my feelings from the previous week. The therapist seems unaware of my emotional turmoil, leading to a strained interaction about unaddressed issues.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm telling you about this traumatic event where I finally faced up to something that is extremely painful with my son, maybe the lowest moment of my life, which you have encouraged me to tackle, which took all the strength that I had, and all you can do is focus on a mistake that you think I made... that I, God forbid, tried to help a troubled patient?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I do see how wrenching this was for you. I do. And at the same time, since you've walked in, I've been fully aware of your clear need for me to grasp and acknowledge your pain.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, you are my therapist.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I do happen to be in pain.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I know that. I see that. You even brought in a prop to demonstrate in case I missed it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I do also have a fucking headache.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I believe you. But the more clearly I see the pain you're in, the greater the chance I'll see what you've done as courageous and heroic and less of a chance that I'd question or criticize any part of it.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, go ahead and criticize, if that's what you feel the need to do.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I do find I have some questions regarding your decision about Max. What made it so urgent for you to finally bring him...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Can I say something?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You say that I seem to be looking for a certain response from you, that I'm invested in your reaction.

situation: I confront the therapist about avoiding discussing my feelings from the previous week. The therapist seems unaware of my emotional turmoil, leading to a strained interaction about unaddressed issues.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: But you're avoiding any acknowledgment of why that might be.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm not sure I'm following.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I think you're dancing around the obvious reason you might think that. I would have thought you'd see the value in addressing it directly.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What's the obvious reason?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You really need me to say it?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'd like to hear what you think.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: We both know as therapists that that's the meat of all this anyway... not my day-to-day struggles, no matter how torturous, but what's actually happening right here, what's going on in the room. I just... I don't know. I find it strange that... I find it strange that you haven't mentioned what happened last week.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: From your point of view, what happened at the end of last week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You don't remember?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I remember our session quite well.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: So why the delicate evasion, the muted suggestion?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're talking about your pronouncement of your feelings for me? Have you been hurt by the fact that I haven't brought up what we discussed last week?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I was just surprised that you hadn't mentioned it. The truth is that this hasn't been foremost on my mind.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because for most of the week I've been concentrated on my son.

situation: I express a deep emotional connection to the therapist, questioning if our bond goes beyond transference. The therapist explores the impossibility and safety of such feelings within therapy.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean you weren't even on my radar. And... I thought those thoughts had disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: But they hadn't?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: They came back somewhere in Delaware. I was sitting in my car, just thinking about my life, my kids, plus everything that awaited me when I got back here... Wendy, my work, the next neurologist.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: What?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And I just realized that the only person I wanted to see when I got back to New York was... was you. I'm supposed to meet Wendy at my place for dinner. And all I could think was, I can't do it. Telling her what I went through today, telling her what it was like to say goodbye to my son... I just... I couldn't imagine it. But I knew that you would understand.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Last week you spoke about these feelings as ridiculous, a kind of comeuppance.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's true that I've seen this kind of thing before.

situation: I struggle with the idea of a personal relationship with the therapist, envisioning shared moments of support and understanding. The therapist probes further into my thoughts.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm familiar with the dynamic of transference. And... and yet I can't help but think that maybe this is something more. I don't know. I just can't shake the thought that somehow, someplace else we might... we might be able to help each other, that we might... that we might make each other happy.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: We might make each other happy. How do you imagine...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, I know it's impossible, of course that you and I could never be together.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Impossible that we could never?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Impossible that we could ever... there's no way it could happen. I should have kept my mouth shut.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This impossibility... your certainty that a relationship between us could never happen... I'm wondering if in part that's what allows you to contemplate it. I mean, does it feel safer within the confines of a therapist's office... of yours or mine... to allow yourself to engage in, to imagine a personal relationship?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Safer? I don't know about you, but I'm not feeling particularly safe right now.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: When you think about us making each other happy, what comes to mind? What do you imagine?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I... I don't know. I... I...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: tell me what you're thinking.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I suppose I just sense that you and I...

situation: I share concerns about a patient's intense emotions and dreams. The therapist acknowledges the limited time, prompting a brief discussion on the patient's behavior and statements.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: well, I... I imagine us having dinner at the end of a day of work, you know, having a glass of wine, talking about our minor triumphs with patients, helping each other to sort through difficult cases.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Anything else? Are there other things you imagine, other romantic situations you might...?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's not so crazy, is it really, to imagine sharing ideas, advice, encouragement with somebody who's engaged in the same kind of work as a profession, seen the same challenges?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: No, it's not crazy. No.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: You know, for instance, I've been wanting to talk to you about Sunil.

situation: I emphasize the intensity of my partner's anger and seek the therapist's guidance on potential violence. Scheduling conflicts arise, and I feel urgency.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm a little bit, I don't know, kind of... I've been thinking about my last session with him. And I'm not quite sure what to make of it, you know?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: This is the kind of conversation you might imagine we would have if we were involved in some sort of relationship?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Look, I've told you about Sunil's anger, his... the deep rage that he has toward his daughter-in-law.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Yes, you did tell me, but because we're just about out of time...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: and this week he told me this extremely vivid dream that he had where he imagined that he was defending his grandchildren against this woman who was walking towards them, and he was trying to strike her. And when I pressed him about this, he suddenly started to scream in bengali. And obviously I didn't know what he was saying, but then afterwards he said, a man can only be pushed so far. It was just... I mean, do you think that I should be worried about...?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I really couldn't answer that.

situation: I emphasize the intensity of my partner's anger and seek the therapist's guidance on potential violence. Scheduling conflicts arise, and I feel urgency.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I sit across from him and my gut instinct, you know, as a professional is that he is... he is... he is a gentle man. But then he uses this kind of alarming language like smother and strike. What do you think? Am I wrong to consider that he could become violent?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I honestly don't know. I've never met Sunil and I haven't heard the dream in any real detail.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Well, I can fill you in on the...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: I'm afraid you can't, actually. But we could schedule another appointment, continue this next week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I don't need another appointment.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well, there's a lot that came up today and there's not much time.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: It's the end of the day. It's Friday.

situation: The therapist highlights my paralysis in addressing personal and professional challenges and urge self-reflection.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I know that I'm your last patient. If we could just...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How do you know you're my last patient?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Because I stood outside last week and I looked at the building. Nobody came in or out, including you, for an hour.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Well... We can talk about what you were thinking while you were standing outside my building next week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: All I need is a minute or two to address this issue of Sunil which... his outburst was pretty ex...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: If we had two more minutes, this is what you'd like to discuss... your patient's outburst, not the fact that you stood

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Yes, the depth of his anger, his intensity... I need to know for my sake if you...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: if you're concerned about that, you know very well what you're supposed to do. You have...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm asking you to help me figure out whether I should be...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: you have a duty to notify the authorities or warn the potential victim. You know that already. Now it's 5:53. We really need to stop.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: How would 10:00 A.M. Monday morning work for you?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I can't do it. I have a patient.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right, how about Wednesday at 1:00?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm seeing a neurologist. And then I've got a 3:00, a 4:00, a 5:00. I actually have a practice where I routinely go five or 10 minutes over if necessary.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You're seeing another neurologist? About the Parkinson's?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I... why...? I don't understand why you can't be just a little bit more flexible.

situation: The therapist highlights my paralysis in addressing personal and professional challenges and urge self-reflection.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I mean, think about it: I've just lived through one of the worst moments of my life; I've got a patient who potentially could hurt somebody and...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: again if you believe that...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: And we've only had a half-an-hour session...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: we've only had half a session because...

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: because I left my kid in Baltimore; the traffic was insane and...

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Paul.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: Why are you so fucking rigid?

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: You've got an enormous amount going on right now and I would really like to help you see your way through, but whenever I dare ask you to look at yourself or your patterns of behavior, you get angry, you raise your voice, you get impatient and I think deeply afraid. You do anything you can to push our relationship past its prescribed time and purpose. You ask me to be your colleague, your supervisor, your life partner... anything except for what you came to me for... to be your therapist, to get me to challenge you to look at yourself. I don't think you realize just how paralyzed you've become. It took you weeks to speak to your son, and only after a real crisis forced you to do it. You have an inability to act decisively with one of your patients despite the fact that you say you're genuinely concerned for him. You have doubts about your current relationship which you've done nothing about. And you've convinced yourself you have a debilitating disease despite medical opinions to the contrary. Now I would really like to help you see your way through, but I cannot do it alone and I will not do it past 5:50. Now I really urge you to come see me twice next week.

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm... I'm unable to do that.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: All right then. For now we need to stop. Are you so paralyzed you're unable to stand up?

dialogue.speaker: client
dialogue.text: I'm standing. And I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: therapist
dialogue.text: Your pills.
